### On Music.

The Tritone is surpassed by the Semidiapente by the <term>Super 23-part-of-2025: A very small mathematical ratio (2048:2025) used to define the difference between certain musical intervals.</term>, which consists of approximately half a Comma.

**STR.** Are the Semidiapente and the Tritone of the ancients of the same measure and proportion as those of our modern musicians?

**BAR.** No, sir; because the interval that was considered a Tritone among the ancients fell under these numbers 729 to 512, which exceeds ours by a <term>Comma: A tiny interval, the difference between two sounds that are nearly identical but mathematically distinct in different tuning systems.</term>; and their Semidiapente fell under these others, 1024 to 729, which conversely is smaller than the <term>Super 19-part-of-45: A ratio (64:45) defining the modern diminished fifth.</term>, called by the moderns the Semidiapente, by such an interval; as can be clearly seen by subtracting one from the other.

<margin>Correct names of the intervals, No. 116.</margin>
**STR.** So, in such a way, are the majority of the names of musical intervals today (not to say all of them) corrupted and ruined?

**BAR.** Do not doubt it for a moment.

**STR.** Would it not be good to provide correct names for them before the matter grows old and spreads further into the minds of men?

<margin>Glareanus, in chapter 12 of book 3, calls the Sesquialtera, Sesquipla.</margin>
**BAR.** Truly yes, but this is a task for a man of authority and great value; however, regarding the names of intervals, we will proceed by following common usage (even if it is bad), if for no other reason than to be understood. But let us now come to the examination of the <term>Diapente: The ancient Greek term for the interval of a Perfect Fifth.</term>; which they say is contained in its true proportion of the <term>Sesquialtera: A ratio of 3:2, where the larger string length or frequency is one and a half times the smaller.</term>, also called Sesquipla, between these numbers in their lowest terms, 3 to 2. It contains primarily two major tones, one minor tone, and one major semitone. It can be considered in many ways, but its proper and principal way is as a composite of the major and minor Third, as the product we obtain from the numbers containing it will show (according to the example that follows); and it will be in its true harmonic essence whenever the major Third holds the lower (grave) position, and the minor holds the higher (acute) position.

<margin>Proximate and remote parts of intervals, what they are.</margin>
I have said the Fifth is composed of such intervals before any others because those are its most <term>proximate parts: The primary components that sum directly to the ratio of a larger interval.</term>. And so that you may well understand the reason for this too, I say: according to the opinion of theorists, the most proximate parts of intervals are those which, when the numbers containing them are multiplied together, give a product that is not only the same proportion as the whole, but very close to—and sometimes (as you have seen with the Tritone and the Semidiapente) in—its very lowest terms. Conversely, those are the "remote" parts which, compared to the lowest terms of their whole, give a more distant product. This is brought to us by their more imperfect and unequal parts, and the former by the more perfect and equal parts. And coming to consider the other parts of the Fifth and composing it from them, I say: it will still be a Fifth if it consists of a Fourth and a major Tone; because when the numbers of their proportions are multiplied together, the product they give (though a little further from its lowest terms) will yield its shown form.

<margin>Zarlino, at proposition 30 of the second discussion of his *Dimostrationi*.</margin>
<margin>The Diapente is not found between these strings.</margin>
Since the Fifth arises from those two shown intervals as was said, one can argue along with <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), the most famous music theorist of the Renaissance and Galilei’s teacher, whom Galilei often challenges in this work.</note> Zarlino that the intervals in the following example are not truly Fifths at all, but of a different proportion and genus. This goes against the opinion of the practical musician, and even more so when it is proved to him that they are dissonant. Their being of a different proportion from the first ones arises because they contain a Fourth and a minor Tone; these two intervals added together cannot give us a Fifth of the same proportion as the first two shown, but another that will be a Comma smaller, and therefore dissonant. To show how much it is diminished, here is the example that will confirm it.

# Dialogo del Galilei

4. 3. Form of the Fourth.
10. 9. Form of the Minor Tone.
40. 27. Form of the <term>Super 13-part-of-27: The ratio 40:27, which represents a musical interval slightly smaller than a perfect fifth.</term>

The interval obtained by adding together the Fourth and the Minor Tone is the Super 13-part-of-27; this consists of a Fifth diminished by a <term>Comma: A tiny musical interval, specifically the difference between a major and minor tone.</term>. One could be further assured of this truth by adding it to itself; for from both one would obtain the <term>Sesquialtera: The ratio 3:2, which is the mathematical form of the perfect Fifth (Diapente).</term> from both. One might doubt, based on what we have said, whether the following interval—considered as a Fourth in the high part and a Tone in the low part—was a Fifth of the first or the second species; to which I respond by saying that it is of the first and not of the second species in any way.

<image-desc>A musical notation example on two five-line staves. The upper staff shows the notes C and F followed by a G. The lower staff shows G and C followed by a D. Brackets and text labels indicate the Fourth and the Tone intervals mentioned in the text.</image-desc>

And if it were argued against me that the Tone it has in the lower part is a minor one—which (according to the way I have shown it to be composed of such intervals) ought to be a major tone—I would respond that this is very true, and that for this reason it becomes consonant in that place. This is because the Fourth it has in the high part is "superfluous" <note>original: "soperflua," meaning augmented or having an excess</note> by exactly as much as is missing from the minor Tone in the low part to make it equal to a major tone. In such a way, from that superfluous interval and from this diminished one—since the superfluity of the one is equal to what is lacking in the other—one obtains from them the Fifth in its true form and proportion; as anyone can sensibly see by adding together their lowest terms. It will also be found in its true form from the Tritone and the major Semitone; but certainly not from the <term>Semidiapente: A diminished fifth.</term> and the minor Semitone, as the following example makes manifest.

64. 45. Form of the Semidiapente.

From such a sum, we have obtained the Super 13-part-of-27, which (as has been said) consists of a Fifth diminished by a Comma; so that from the Semidiapente and the minor Semitone, one does not get (as the practical musician believes) the same product as from the major semitone and the Tritone. We must not leave behind the knowledge of how much the Fifth exceeds the Tone, and how much it exceeds the Semidiapente; the knowledge of which the two following examples will give us entirely.

### On Music.

**STROZZI.** This will be exceptionally helpful to me, as well as new and welcome.

**BARDI.** I am coming to treat every smallest detail that one could desire regarding the form of the **Minor Sixth**, also understood by modern practitioners as the **Minor Hexachord** <note>A scale or interval of six notes.</note>. They say this interval is that imperfect consonance contained by the <term>Supertripartientequinta: A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number plus three-fifths of it (8:5).</term> in its radical terms. It consists of two major tones, one minor tone, and two major semitones. It can be considered primarily as being composed of a **Fourth** and a **Minor Third**, as we shall see from the product yielded by adding together the smallest numbers of their proportions.

In this regard, there are some who criticize **Franchino** <note>Franchinus Gaffurius (1451–1522), a highly influential Italian music theorist.</note> for having said that the Minor Sixth is composed of the <term>Diatessaron: The Greek term for a perfect Fourth.</term> and the "greater chromatic interval." By this, he meant the **Trihemitone**, using it in place of the minor third, or more accurately, the **Semiditone**. These intervals, when added together, cannot in any way produce the minor sixth in the form shown in the following example; nor can they do so according to the **Diatonic Ditonic** <note>The Pythagorean tuning system, which uses only major tones (9:8).</note> system in which Franchino considers it. This perhaps happened because he did not hold this interval in such high esteem—being an imperfect consonance—as many others do.

<margin>Warning.</margin>
Regarding this imperfect consonance, another consideration must not be kept silent: the common people held for certain that every musical interval has one fewer "species" <note>A specific arrangement of tones and semitones within an interval.</note> than the number of its strings <note>Notes.</note>. However, this is not true, because the species of the Minor and Major Sixth are no more than three; furthermore, this rule does not hold true for several other intervals which we will omit for brevity. 

Returning to the Minor Sixth, I say it is also that which consists of the **Semidiapente** <note>A diminished fifth.</note> and the **Major Tone**. By adding together the numbers by which they are contained, their product will give its true form, as shown in the example that follows.

This truth being established, it follows (contrary to the opinion of the practical musician) that some of these intervals—or any other similar ones—are not Minor Sixths of the same proportion as the first ones shown. This arises because, between the notes shown, the Tone and the Semidiapente together cannot yield the Minor Sixth as they did above. This is because in these cases the Tone is **minor**; whereas, conversely, in the previous ones it was **major**. Thus, these necessarily become smaller than the others by a **Comma**. We shall now see which interval is produced from them by the product we get from adding their lowest terms together.

The interval obtained from these is the **Super 47-part-of-81**, which contains the true **Ancient Minor Hexachord** of the Diatonic Diatonic system in its lowest terms. This is one Comma smaller than the *Supertripartientequinta* (8:5) known today as the form of the Minor Sixth. This interval is also called the Minor Hexachord by some and is consonant, unlike that ancient one which is dissonant because it is (as has been said) a Comma smaller. Anyone who takes the care to subtract its form from the other will be certain of this. One can also obtain this imperfect consonance from the Fifth and the Major Semitone, as we shall see from their product by adding together...

Where one can also judge, not only by how much the minor Sixth is exceeded by the major, but also that these are major **Hexachords** <term>Hexachord: A scale or interval of six notes.</term>, and not major sixths as the practitioner <note>The "practitioner" refers to musicians who play by ear or tradition rather than mathematical theory.</note> believes. By having added together two **Sesquiteritians** <term>Sesquiteritian: The ratio 4:3, which defines the musical interval of a Fourth.</term>, the minor **Heptachord** <term>Heptachord: An interval of a seventh.</term> in its lowest terms has been obtained; despite this, I proved above that the minor Seventh was contained between those same strings. I said further that by adding together the parts of any interval divided in any way, they must necessarily—once reunited—render the whole of the same form and measure as it was at first. Where in this last example the simple practitioner <note>The "practitioner" refers to performing musicians who rely on their ears rather than the mathematical laws of tuning.</note> perceives an effect contrary to what my words first sounded like; nor does he see the cause of it. The cause is that he considers, among the shown strings, two **Fourths** of the same proportion and measure, whereas they are of different ones; and so with his poor rule, he comes to err in the principles, and marvels then that the account does not return to him according to the good rule—which it would do if it returned correctly. For the Fourth that holds the high position falls under this proportion, 27:20, as has been proved in its place: which, added together with that which the Theorist institutes for it, will give us the minor Seventh of the measure that I said at the beginning of our reasoning was assigned to it by him.

*STR.* I seem to begin to glimpse the harbor; and as soon as you make it clear to me through the senses, and not by the authority of anyone, that the **Ditone** <term>Ditone: A major third composed of two whole tones (81:64), characteristic of Pythagorean tuning.</term>, the **Semiditone** <term>Semiditone: A minor third (32:27).</term>, the major and minor **Hexachord** <term>Hexachord: An interval of a sixth.</term> are dissonant—in addition to the **Fifths** and **Fourths** <note>original: "Diapente & Diatessaton"</note> that you have named as such above—I will absolutely believe that what is sung (in the manner that is customary today) is in no way the **Syntonic Diatonic of Ptolemy** <note>A tuning system proposed by the ancient astronomer Ptolemy that uses "pure" thirds and sixths, which Bardi is arguing is not what modern singers actually use.</note>: since such intervals are in tune in the instruments and voices of men of our times; which I do not hold to be of a different property and nature from those of the ancients.

*BAR.* Let us continue to go forward now that the wind is favorable and the waves are calm; because, pleasing the Giver of all goods <note>A reference to God.</note>, I want you to see the truth of every smallest detail in the face, sensibly (having set aside every authority). Nor is there time to waste, for we are still many miles away from the harbor. I come to uncover another abuse of the practitioner; who holds for certain that the same space is occupied by the **Fifth** and the minor **Third** <note>original: "Quinta & la Terza minore"</note> in the example that follows, as is made by the **Semidiapente** <term>Semidiapente: A diminished fifth.</term> and the major **Third** added together; and consequently, that the numbers which contain their forms, once added together, give the same product for these as for those: a thing which (as we shall now see) is very far from the truth.

64. 45. Form of the Semidiapente.

} 320. 180. Form of the minor Heptachord outside of its radical terms.

From having added together the two shown intervals, the minor Heptachord has been obtained; and above, from coupling together the Fifth and the minor Third, the minor **Sixth** was obtained. It is not true, therefore, that such intervals added together occupy the same space; at which the practitioner greatly marvels. Nor does this arise from anything else, as I have said, than from wanting (not having knowledge of the intervals) all things from a single thing. Therefore, to satisfy him, I say that when he has newly examined and understood the size of the minor Third which has the minor Heptachord in the high part that I last showed you, he will be quieted. By common opinion, all the wise say that nature has made nothing in vain: with which proposition I want to prove to you that the shown Heptachord is no less the proper form of the minor Seventh of the **Syntonic** <note>Ptolemy's tuning system.</note> than is the **Superquadripartient-fifth** <term>Superquadripartient-fifth: The ratio 9:5, which defines the minor seventh in certain tuning systems.</term>; and the method will be this. Anyone of sound judgment can know from what I have proved and said so far, that neither the major nor minor **Tone**, nor likewise the major **Semitone**, has ever changed to a form different from that which was assigned to it at the beginning of our reasoning according to the mind of the Theorist; but indeed all the other intervals from the **Octave** and the major **Seventh** onwards [have changed]; which was born from not having yet examined them. Which, when they are considered by us with diligence, will not exceed the others in excellence (in this matter). Let us find, therefore, two different sorts of minor Sixths from which, by means of two different Tones, the Octave can be composed in its true being;

# ->Of Music.<-
### 23

First, one can compose an **Octave** from the minor **Heptachord** <term>Heptachord: An interval of a seventh.</term> and the **Sesquioctave** <term>Sesquioctave: The 9:8 ratio, which defines a whole tone.</term> or **Tone**; and likewise from the minor **Seventh** and the **Sesquinonal** <term>Sesquinonal: The 10:9 ratio, defining a "minor" whole tone.</term> ratio. This will be clearly recognized by summing their lowest terms together and seeing the product they yield. Just as the many lines drawn from the center to the circumference of a circle all return to its center, in the same way, every musical interval looks toward the **Octave** as if into a mirror—just as the stars do toward the Sun—receiving its being and perfection from it (each according to its capacity). Among the minor **Thirds**, we have two (to avoid searching too minutely for others) contained under different proportions; the "filling" of these to weave the **Octave** was found later. These were the two major **Sixths** contained under different forms; among the former, we numbered the **Semiditone** <term>Semiditone: A minor third, literally "half of two tones."</term>, and among the latter, the major **Hexachord** <term>Hexachord: An interval of a sixth.</term>; these intervals are common to the **Syntonic** and the **Diatonic** <note>These refer to specific ancient and Renaissance tuning systems or "genera" of scales.</note> as are many others. We also found the major **Third** and the **Ditone** <term>Ditone: A major third composed of two whole tones.</term>, and shortly thereafter, we obtained the minor **Sixth** and the minor **Hexachord**, from which one can compose an **Octave** far from any imperfect extreme. We found the **Diatessaron** <term>Diatessaron: The interval of a fourth.</term> contained in various ways, and afterward, the **Diapente** <term>Diapente: The interval of a fifth.</term> was seen contained under various numbers; this was for no other purpose (as we shall see in its proper place) than to be able to compose from them together an **Octave** of a single form. All this happens because kind Nature wishes to show her immense wisdom and liberality in every one of her operations; she does not tolerate a vacuum, nor does she do anything—or can she do anything—that is idle or harmful. It remains in this matter to show you by how much the minor **Seventh** exceeds the major and minor **Sixth**, which you can easily see by subtracting them from it. Let us now come to the consideration of the major **Seventh**, and having dispatched that, we shall pass on to conclude the proposed matter with the **Octave**. The masters of this modern practice of **Counterpoint** say, then, that the major **Seventh** is that dissonant interval contained in its radical terms by the **Super-7-partient-8** <term>Super-7-partient-8: A complex ratio name for 15:8, because 15 is one whole 8 plus 7 parts of 8.</term> proportion between these numbers, 15 and 8. They say it consists of three major **Tones**, two minor **Tones**, and one major **Semitone**. Because of the respect for the method mentioned many times, we will consider it primarily composed of a **Fifth** and a major **Third**, as appears in the example that follows.

<image-desc>Three musical staves showing intervals and ratios.</image-desc>

3 to 2. Form of the **Fifth**.
5 to 4. Form of the major **Third**.
15 to 8. Form of the major **Seventh**.

---

One can also obtain such an interval from the numbers that contain the form of the **Tritone** <term>Tritone: An interval of three whole tones, often called the "devil in music" for its harsh dissonance.</term> summed together with those of the **Fourth**; but it will not give it to us in that same measure (even if it goes against the opinion of the practitioner) if one adds together the minor **Tone** and the major **Sixth**, in the manner seen in the following example.

<image-desc>Three musical staves showing intervals and ratios.</image-desc>

5 to 3. Form of the major **Sixth**.
10 to 9. Form of the minor **Tone**.
50 to 27. Form of the **Super-23-partient-27** <term>Super-23-partient-27: The ratio 50:27, where 50 is one whole 27 plus 23 parts of 27.</term>.

---

From the product of the two said intervals, we have obtained the **Super-23-partient-27**, which is smaller than a major **Seventh** by a **Comma** <term>Comma: A very small interval, usually the difference between two types of whole tones.</term>, as you will sensibly see by subtracting it from the seventh. One can also obtain the major **Seventh** from the product of the major **Sixth** and the major **Tone**. We shall now see, by subtracting the minor from its form, by how much the major exceeds the minor.

15 to 8. Form of the major **Seventh**.
**X**
9 to 5. Form of the minor **Seventh**.

75 to 72. Form of the minor **Semitone**, outside of its lowest numbers.
25 to 24. In its lowest numbers <note>original: "Ne ſuoi minor numeri." This is the simplified ratio for the minor semitone.</note>.

According to this example, the minor **Seventh** remains exceeded by the major by one **Semitone**; from which one can understand that the major **Seventh** can also be composed of the minor Seventh and the minor **Semitone**.

<meta>This page continues the technical dialogue between Bardi and Strozzi. ### Ancient & Modern [Music]

...major and minor to one and the other D. After the flat <note>original: "b molle," the symbol for B-flat</note> was put into use, the natural <note>original: "h duro," the 'hard h' which became the natural and sharp signs</note> came to be considered by modern and skilled practitioners of practical music as a cipher; for no other purpose than to be able to transform one system into the other, and vice versa, as it pleased them or was convenient. However, this natural sign was never meant to be marked on any string other than its own; for other strings where such a need occurred, the sharp <note>original: "diesis X," referring to the # symbol</note> of the form recently shown was found. This practice is seen very well observed in their works. And if anyone should reply to me that the flat is commonly marked by everyone on the string **A-la-mi-re** <note>The pitch A</note> and on **E-la-mi** <note>The pitch E</note>, which are foreign to it; I would answer him that this arises from the small quantity of characters we have today compared to the ancients. They had a proper and particular character for every string, to demonstrate whatever desirable and convenient sound was wanted.

But the scarcity of symbols in our times for demonstrating the diversity of strings is not such that it causes any lack or imperfection regarding the goal for which today's music is used. If that were the case, others would have been found before now to supply such a defect. This has not happened because our current symbols are sufficient to give any string, in both the low and high registers, the form of every consonant interval that man has been able to imagine until now—particularly in the first two Genera of harmony, which are the Diatonic and the Chromatic. In the Enharmonic <note>The Enharmonic genus used microtones, specifically "diesis" smaller than a semitone</note>, they have uselessly added the present sign **x** to be able to divide the major semitone into two parts, called by the ancients "Enharmonic Diesis"; although moderns understand by this the present cipher **#** as you know, and claim it is worth two of those, which is not true at all. For the ancients divided the ratio 16:15 <note>original: "Sesquiquindecima"</note>, which they called the Diatonic semitone, while the moderns say they divide the ratio 16:15, which they call the major semitone; and we have already demonstrated the difference between them. It can also be gathered from what we have said that the distance between **B-natural** <note>original: "h mi"</note> and **B-flat** <note>original: "b fa"</note> is the same whether using the square-B or the round-B; and likewise the same distance is found between **C-sol-fa-ut** <note>The pitch C</note> and **B-natural** by the one as by the other. And lastly, I say that the note **D-la-sol-re** <note>The pitch D</note> is sharper when using the natural system <note>original: "h quadro"</note> than when using the flat system <note>original: "b rotondo"</note>.

STR. Explain this last point to me better, please.
BAR. I say that **D-la-sol-re** is sharper through the "hard-B" [natural] than through the "soft-B" [flat], for this reason: If we start from **A-la-mi-re**, a fixed string common to both systems, and we wish to ascend by conjoined Diatonic steps to **D-la-sol-re**; we will find that in the "disjunct" system (the natural system), there are two major tones and one major semitone. But in the "conjoined" system (the flat system), there is one major tone, one minor tone, and one major semitone. Consequently, in the flat system, **D-la-sol-re** necessarily ends up being one **comma** lower than in the natural system, as shown in the example below.

<image-desc>Two musical staves showing five notes each in the C-clef. The top staff illustrates a sequence of notes (A to D) with intervals labeled "Major Tone," "Major Semitone," and "Major Tone." The bottom staff illustrates a sequence (A to D) labeled "Major Semitone," "Major Tone," and "Minor Tone."</image-desc>

STR. I have understood perfectly, and it is truly so.

<margin>
That D-la-sol-re is sharper through the natural sign [h] than through the flat sign [b].
</margin>

BAR. The fact that there is the same distance from **C-sol-fa-ut** to **B-natural** in both the flat and natural systems arises because the major semitone of one and the other tone is always of the same quantity and proportion in both. For the same reason, the interval from **B-natural** to **B-flat** is the same in both systems.

STR. Do not be reluctant to tell me the reason why this ratio **16:15** <note>The ratio of a major semitone</note>, rather than another, is what contains the major semitone? Why **25:24** for the minor? Why **64:45** for the diminished fifth <note>original: "Semidiapente"</note>, and lastly **45:32** for the Tritone? And why can they not be contained by other numbers according to the "Syntonic" system of Ptolemy?

BAR. I thought I had satisfied you with what I said above, but I see that is not so. Therefore I am still your debtor; and I want you yourself to be the judge of whether they can be otherwise. This is on the condition, however, that you grant me that the true "form" of the minor sixth, the major and minor third, the fourth, and the major tone <note>original: "Tuono Sesquiottauo," the 9:8 ratio</note> are truly those assigned to them by the Theorist at the beginning of our discussion. I offer then, at the proper time and place if needed, to let you sensibly see and hear everything else you might desire by means of the **Monochord**. <term>Monochord: A scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge, used to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of musical intervals through sound.</term>

STR. Everything is granted to you for now.
BAR. I ask you first: by how much does the major third exceed the minor?
STR. By one minor semitone.
BAR. So, by subtracting the minor third from the major third, those numbers that remain will necessarily contain the minor semitone in its true form; is that not so?
STR. It is truly so.
BAR. Now let us come again to the proof of the fact with this example.

# Ancient & Modern

<margin>Various ways of tempering wine with water, according to the custom of ancient musicians.</margin>
...intent on some task, such as judges, disputants, or others of the sort; and for this reason, the proverb of the merry ones did not wish (says the writer) for the number four to meddle with their business in any way. This number is one of the foundations of the <term>Sesquiterza</term> <note>The ratio 4:3, which forms the interval of a fourth</note>; it was the last and most distant consonance for wine, just as the <term>Sesquiterza</term> and the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>Another name for the interval of a fourth</note> were for their drinking. However, it was not as delightful to the taste as was required for "good cheer," which aims for joy and the recreation of the spirits without the danger of drunkenness. Over a long duration at the table, drunkenness might perhaps be brought on by the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The ratio 2:1, or an octave</note>. Therefore, the disputant highly celebrated the <term>Diapente</term> <note>The ratio 3:2, or a perfect fifth</note>, considering the terms of its form summed together, as with the <term>Diapason</term>, but for the <term>Diatessaron</term> he considered only the greater term.

I believe the passage must be interpreted this way if we wish to follow the writer's intent, rather than considering how one compared to three makes a <term>Sesquiterza</term>, as that clearly cannot be. Thus, in that passage, Plutarch's intention is to consider only the greater term of each proportion of the three simple consonances. From this term, he subtracts a single unit for the wine, and the remaining parts are to be water. Now, because the greater term of the <term>Sesquiterza</term> is four, and if one unit is subtracted for wine (as was said), that which remains for water is three (as you know). Thus the author arrives at the <term>Sesquiterza</term> by comparing one to three. One can also say, as you have heard: of the four parts, three are water. In this way, mention is made of the proper terms of the <term>Sesquiterza</term> itself. This method of comparison, when used for the other consonances, works out very well.

When tempering wine according to the <term>Sesquiterza</term> (4:3), there must be, as said, three parts water and one part wine out of four; this potion makes the one who drinks it like its nature, which is languid and subdued. According to the <term>Sesquialtera</term> <note>The ratio 3:2, or a perfect fifth</note>, there should be two parts water and one part wine out of three; such a drink, taken often, makes one become cheerful, for such is the nature of the <term>Diapente</term>. Finally, according to the <term>Dupla</term> <note>The ratio 2:1, or an octave</note>, there should be one part water and one part wine out of two; this potion, when drunk, makes a man take on the nature of the <term>Diapason</term>, which is most joyful. However, one must consider the place, the time, the people, and the quality of the wine being drunk where these effects were produced, if one wishes to perfectly "tune the strings of this lyre." The ancient speculators of musical proportions had various other ways to temper wine with water, but let enough be said of that. Returning to where I left off, I say that you yourself (having understood what I have discussed) will be able to find the origin of the proportion of any musical interval you wish—and not only this, but any other doubt that might arise regarding the difference in size between one and another in any <term>Genre</term> or species of harmony. This is all I need to say and prove to you regarding the main point of the doubt you proposed; so, speak freely on what you feel about it.

**STROZZI:** I remain more confused than ever by your discourse (just when I least expected it), specifically regarding the understanding of which species it is that we sing today, which is the main head of the discussion we have had together.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
**BARDI:** Reveal this new difficulty of yours to me.

<margin>Regarding chapter 43 of the second book of his *Harmonic Institutions*.</margin>
<margin>In chapter 13 of the third book of the same *Institutions*.</margin>
**STROZZI:** Listen. If every modern practical <term>Contrapuntist</term> <note>A composer or theorist of counterpoint</note> uses, in any of his songs, the Tone and Semitone of whatever proportion, on whatever strings, by chance and without being capable of any of the considerations shown—I cannot imagine how it is that so many discrepancies do not manifest to a refined ear. You have realistically proven to me with effective reasons that these discrepancies ought to occur constantly. And if they do not occur, a greater inconvenience follows: that many of the things proposed to us as maxims by the theorists will be totally useless, impertinent, and not at all true. Among these would be the two things already mentioned concerning the position, difference in location, and value of the Major, Minor, and Mean Tone. In these two points (from what I have understood), everything you have discussed with me so far is principally founded—unless we want to say that the quantity of the <term>Comma</term> <note>A tiny musical interval, roughly 1/9th of a whole tone</note>, being so minimal when taken from or added to any interval, does not have the power to remove it from the nature of its first being. I do not believe this in any way, especially since Messer Gioseffo Zarlino <note>The most influential music theorist of the 16th century</note> holds that even half [a comma] added to or taken from a consonant interval has the power to make it dissonant. He later adds (in jest, I believe) that one should set aside consideration of the difference between Major and Minor Tones. Yet removing that also takes away the various species of Semitones. Thus, the <term>Diatonic</term> <note>The standard scale of seven notes</note> that is sung today—if it were Ptolemy’s <term>Syntono</term> <note>The "Syntonic Diatonic," a tuning system that uses both major (9:8) and minor (10:9) whole tones to achieve pure thirds</note>—becomes something else entirely if this single consideration is removed.

<margin>Solution to the doubt.</margin>
**BARDI:** You reason very well, and you have great cause to doubt this. But here is the solution to the doubt. If the <term>Genre</term> in which we have considered every interval with such exactness is Ptolemy's <term>Syntono</term>, I say that the system in which we compose, sing, and play today is not that at all; nor can it even be the ancient <term>Ditone Diatonic</term> <note>The Pythagorean tuning system, which used only 9:8 whole tones, resulting in "sharp" or dissonant thirds</note>.

**STROZZI:** Have both sects then been deceived (so to speak) in this matter of such great importance? Tell me, please.

# Dialogue on Music

BAR. They have certainly been mistaken; but listen, as I explain the matter to you with new authoritative examples, I will at the same time (not without benefit to you and quite relevantly) reveal which <term>species</term> <note>A specific arrangement of tones and semitones within a scale.</note> is truly used by keyboard instruments, which by the Lute, and which of them comes closest to perfection, and why.

STR. These will be some of the most welcome things you could clarify for me on this topic.

<margin>
Observations of the Author.

Which species of harmony stringed instruments play.
</margin>
BAR. I find through long observation that natural voices and man-made instruments do not actually play or sing any of the nine ancient Diatonic species in their simple form in our modern musical practice. Instead, practitioners today inadvertently use three species mixed together in different ways; they are these: the <term>Intense of Aristoxenus</term> <note>Aristoxenus was a Greek theorist who advocated for judging intervals by ear rather than strict math, leading toward equal temperament.</note>, the very ancient <term>Ditonic Diatonic</term> <note>Also known as Pythagorean tuning, based on pure fifths.</note>, and the <term>Syntonon of Ptolemy</term> <note>Ptolemy’s "Intense" diatonic, which uses ratios that produce "pure" major and minor thirds.</note>. Among stringed instruments, I maintain that the bowed viola, the Lute, and the keyed Lyre play the Intense Diatonic of Aristoxenus. What moves me to believe this is seeing and hearing in them an equality of Tones, each divided into two equal Semitones; and it was in this manner, as you will understand in the proper place, that the aforementioned "Intense" was distributed by Aristoxenus.

<margin>
Which species the Organ and other keyboard instruments play.
</margin>
The Organ, then, the <term>Harpsichord</term> <note>original: "Graui-cimbalo"</note>, and the modern Harp—modern in terms of the new addition of strings, not the instrument itself, which I consider very ancient—differ somewhat from the others. For example, in the division of the Tones, they have them separated into unequal Semitones <note>Referring to "meantone temperament," where sharps and flats (like G-sharp and A-flat) are not the same pitch.</note>.

<margin>
Which species other wind instruments play.
</margin>
Wind instruments, such as recorders, transverse flutes, cornetts, and others like them, have the ability—through the placement of their holes and the skill of a discerning and expert player—to approach one system or the other according to their need and will. The same applies to voices, provided they do not wish to bend against their nature and yield to the instruments.

<margin>
Which species is composed and sung today.
</margin>
Regarding the composition and singing of today, I am persuaded by what I have told you, and what I am about to tell you, that we mix the <term>Diatonic Ditonic</term> with the <term>Syntonon of Ptolemy</term>; and these are the reasons that move me to believe so.

<margin>
Inconveniences that would arise from singing Ptolemy's Syntonon.
</margin>
It is certain that if one sang the simple Syntonon, the Tones and the minor Semitones would be unequal and of different sizes, as I have proven their nature to be in that species. Through this inequality, one would sing—as you have seen according to the different proportions—two kinds of Fifths, two kinds of Fourths, three and perhaps four kinds of minor Thirds, and as many major Sixths; at least two species of the smaller of these and two of the larger. The same would happen with the dissonances, and finally with the Octaves. Furthermore, the <term>Paranete diezeugmenon</term> <note>A specific high note in the Ancient Greek "Greater Perfect System."</note> would exceed the pitch of the <term>Nete synemmenon</term> <note>A note in the "disjunct" tetrachord of the Greek system.</note> by as much as you know, and the Semitone found between B-flat and B-natural would be of a different measure. All other semitones derived from the major Tone as minor ones would not be the <term>Sesquiquindecima</term> <note>The ratio 16:15.</note> or the <term>Sesquiuntiquattresima</term> <note>The ratio 25:24.</note>. Regarding these things, as we have said before, not only have none (that I know of) been noticed by the masters of this art, but there is no one who has ever heard such a confused diversity of intervals in the singing of several parts together—which has been practiced for a hundred and fifty years now. In truth, such diversity never occurred, nor does it occur today. This seems to me a powerful argument to persuade us of this truth. And to further show you the variability of the intervals in this distribution, ask those who want it to be the system sung today: let them divide for you, in any way they like, the Major Thirteenth contained (according to the Syntonon) by these numbers **10** and **3** into three <term>Sesquialteras</term> <note>The ratio 3:2, a perfect fifth. Bardi is pointing out that three perfect fifths do not perfectly equal a major thirteenth.</note>, as they claim it contains. Ask them also, according to the following example, to divide the <term>Dupla Superbipartientequinta</term> <note>The ratio 12:5, a minor tenth.</note>, the form of the minor Tenth, into three <term>Sesquiterzas</term> <note>The ratio 4:3, a perfect fourth.</note>. Then ask them by how much this interval is exceeded by the other?

--- Page 41 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical dialogue between Count Giovanni de' Bardi and Piero Strozzi. Bardi is explaining why the tuning system used in modern 16th-century music is neither the ancient Pythagorean system (Ditonic) nor purely Ptolemy's "Syntonon" system, but a practical hybrid.</meta>

# Ancient & Modern

<margin>Disadvantages that would arise from singing the ancient Diatonic.</margin>
**THAT** it is not actually the Ditonic—or the very ancient Diatonic, as we might call it—which is the Diatonic <term>genus</term> <note>One of the three categories of Greek scales: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic.</note> sung today (as many have believed and some still believe today) will not be very difficult to prove. First, its **Ditone** <note>The Pythagorean major third, created by two "major" whole tones (9:8 ratio).</note> contains, as I have told you, two **Sesquioctave Tones** <note>A whole tone with a ratio of 9:8.</note>; this interval, whether heard alone or in harmony, is dissonant. Its **Semiditone** <note>A minor third.</note> is of the same nature, and the same applies to the major and minor **Hexachords** <note>Intervals of a sixth.</note>. Furthermore, the first and lowest interval of each <term>Tetrachord</term> <note>A four-note scale segment.</note> of that species is a minor Semitone, also called a **Leimma**; and between the *Trite synemmenon* and the *Paramese* <note>Names of specific notes in the Ancient Greek scale system.</note> is the major semitone called an **Apotome**. In contrast, in the scale sung today, the first and lowest interval of the Tetrachord is larger than the one found between the *Paramese* and the *Trite synemmenon*. We also find in that ancient Diatonic that the **Tritone** <note>An augmented fourth.</note> is larger than the **Semidiapente** <note>A diminished fifth.</note>, while in the scale sung today, the Semidiapente exceeds the Tritone. Now, because none of these specific characteristics are found in our Diatonic—and indeed, are in some ways the opposite—it necessarily follows that our system cannot be that ancient one.

The Diatonic of today does agree in some aspects with the **Syntonon of Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, a 2nd-century theorist who proposed a "just" tuning using simpler mathematical ratios like 5:4.</note>, which I will now explain. First, regarding the imperfect consonances <note>Thirds and sixths.</note> (leaving aside the dissonances for now), I believe I am not wrong in saying that they fall almost exactly into Ptolemy's ratios. However, I do not believe they are joined together from similar parts. For example: I hold that the **Major Third** is contained by an irrational ratio very close to the **Sesquiquarta** <note>The "pure" major third ratio of 5:4.</note>, but its sides (so to speak) are not one Sesquioctave Tone and one **Sesquinona** <note>A "minor" whole tone with a ratio of 10:9.</note>. Rather, it consists of two equal parts of said Third, divided in the manner of the Tetrachords of **Aristoxenus** <note>A theorist who argued for dividing intervals by ear rather than mathematical ratios, leading toward what we now call temperament.</note>, though not exactly. As for the **Minor Third**, I believe it is composed of a Tone of the same measurement as those in the major third, and another interval somewhat larger than a **Sesquiquindecima** <note>A ratio of 16:15, which is a "pure" semitone.</note>. In this way, and from these parts joined together, all the other intervals are formed. From the **Octave** upward, I maintain that no other interval is strictly contained by the ratios assigned to them, specifically in the way they are commonly sung today. We shall demonstrate this sensibly a little further on.

<margin>That no other interval besides the Octave is sung today in its true proportion.</margin>
Here is another point of agreement: the Tones whose extremes are most frequently marked by modern practical contrapuntists with accidental signs like the **Sharp (#)** and the **Flat (b)** are, among the "Syntonon" strings, the minor ones. This seems to warn us, and not without reason, that using such signs on the major Tones would result in some Semitones having different ratios, as they would be drawn from a larger whole. Our Diatonic also has some conformity with the **Ditonic** <note>The Pythagorean system.</note>, because each interval is found to be of the same measure and ratio one time after another, even though they have different forms. Furthermore, in each species of the **Diapason** <note>An octave.</note>, the **Diatessaron** <note>A perfect fourth.</note> is found four or five times, and the **Diapente** <note>A perfect fifth.</note> at least three or four times. I do not know if this occurs in any other species or genus except those of Aristoxenus (where they are even more plentiful), because they do not necessarily require the Tritone or the Semidiapente, as all other distributions of strings do. Thus, the perfect consonances as they are sung today approach the Ditonic Diatonic, and the imperfect ones approach the Syntonon of Ptolemy—or rather, of **Didymus** <note>A theorist who preceded Ptolemy and calculated the "comma" or small difference between different types of whole tones.</note>, as you will understand—but always with the same measurement and equality of Tones. To this one might add that our system matches neither the one nor the other exactly, because in the Ditonic one never actually finds the **Apotome**, nor the **Super 7-partient 128** <note>A complex ratio (135:128) representing a type of semitone.</note>, nor the **Sesquiquinquatrefima** <note>An extremely small mathematical interval or ratio.</note>, nor the Syntonon. Rather, the first two appear only by relationship when comparing the *Trite synemmenon* of the "conjunct" system to the *Paramese* of the "disjunct" system. Moreover, any interval beyond the Octave does not fall (as I said) under the ratio and measure of either species when sung in the manner customary today.

**STR.** Too many things at once and of too much importance, Signor Giovanni! My mind is so sluggish that it cannot follow your high concepts with the speed and readiness with which you explain them. We must slow the pace if we are to travel together. Although I clearly recognize—thanks to your extremely subtle, ingenious, vivid, and true reasons—that the Genere sung today in the Diatonic species is not simply the Diatonic nor the Syntonon, but a third thing mixed and composed of both; nevertheless (due to my little experience in these matters), new difficulties of no small importance constantly arise for me in fully grasping what you so broadly mean. Therefore, do not find it burdensome to answer me regarding what I need to ask for a greater understanding of this important business.

**BAR.** Speak freely then.

**STR.** First, I do not know how Aristoxenus distributed the strings of his Tetrachords; nor do I know the difference between the division of the **Lute** and that of the keyboard instrument; and consequently, which of them comes closer to perfection. # Dialogue on Music

...a manner so different from that one regarding the quantity and size of the intervals; and lastly, how among the intervals sung today, there are none from the <term>Octave</term> <note>The interval of an eighth.</note> upward that are contained within the proportions assigned to them by the Theorist.

**BARDI.** To remove each of the said difficulties, we shall do this: let us approach the <term>keyboard instrument</term> <note>Likely a harpsichord or spinet.</note> and first tune its <term>Fifths</term> <note>An interval of five scale steps.</note> with the greatest excellence you know; but according to the order that I shall tell you.

**STROZZI.** Can the sense of hearing not be easily deceived?

<margin>Method of knowing what a refined ear is.</margin>
**BARDI.** Most easily, as much as any other sense, and especially one that is not accustomed to such contemplations. Nevertheless, the refined ear of one who is well-practiced, accompanied by natural judgment and some good rules, is not so lightly deceived. Indeed, there are ears so perfect, accompanied by other circumstances, that they immediately grasp every difference, however minute. But let us come to our task without multiplying words. First tune the <term>Octave</term> between **A re** and **alamire** <note>These are names for specific notes in the medieval/Renaissance system: A2 and A3.</note>; above this, tune its higher Octave, which is **A alamire** <note>A4.</note>. Now loosen the string of **D solre** <note>D3.</note> which is below **alamire**, in such a way that it responds to it as a **Fifth** in that greatest desirable excellence. In that same perfection, tune the note above the same **alamire**, which will be **elami** <note>E4.</note>; and likewise **D lasolre** <note>D4.</note> below **A alamire**. Further, stretch to that same perfection the note that makes **Elami** <note>E3.</note> above **A re**. Shall we see now if the sense was deceived? Here is the way: among the <term>consonances</term> <note>Intervals that sound stable and pleasant together.</note>, there is none better understood by the ear, nor where one can be less deceived, than in the <term>Octave</term>. Let us see, then, if the strings **D solre** and **Elami** respond as a <term>Diapason</term> <note>The Greek term for an Octave.</note> with their replicates; if they are perfectly united in this way, it will be an evident sign that the ear was not at all deceived in the tuning and perfection of the **Fifths**.

**STROZZI.** They accord excellently.

**BARDI.** Continue to tune the others, according to the matches of these.

**STROZZI.** It is done.

**BARDI.** Now play.

**STROZZI.** Yes, sir.

**BARDI.** Consider then, in this particular distribution, how small that which was once major has become; and conversely, how large that which was minor has become.

**STROZZI.** You are quite right. Has this happened perhaps because the **Tones** have acquired that quantity which was taken away in each **Octave** from two major **Semitones**?

As if in those times they had no knowledge of that number of strings required to do so, or as if (when well-disposed) they did not produce a sweeter sound within the Octave than they do outside it. of those times did not use them in their songs, and because of their inconstancy. Pythagoras rejected and banished from the world all things mixed, impure, and varied, knowing that in them inconstancy and rashness held sway. <meta>The previous page established that the ancient Pythagorean tuning (the "Diatonic") results in harsh, dissonant thirds and sixths that modern ears find unpleasant. Bardi is now explaining how to "temper" or adjust these intervals on a keyboard to make them usable for modern music.</meta>

# Ancient & Modern

...would it be possible to remedy such inconveniences, and ensure that every interval, whether consonant or dissonant, fell under its true form and proportion?

**BARDI.** To clearly explain your new doubts, it was very appropriate to have tuned the instrument according to the <term>Diatonic</term> <note>Specifically the Pythagorean Diatonic, which uses pure mathematical ratios that result in dissonant-sounding thirds.</note>; in which distribution, as you have heard, those intervals that modern practitioners call <term>imperfect consonances</term> <note>Major and minor thirds and sixths.</note> become dissonant. This is not due to the "perfection" of the <term>Fifths</term>, as infinitely many dare to say, but because of the excessive size of the <term>Whole Tones</term> and the smallness of the <term>Semitones</term>. Now, wishing to temper the strings in such an instrument

->[A small musical staff showing a series of notes from C to c with corresponding letters below the staff (C, D, E, F, G, a, b, c).]<-

of the present <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "Diapason"</note> in such a way that each of its <term>Major Thirds</term> <note>original: "Ditono"</note> and <term>Minor Thirds</term> <note>original: "Semiditono"</note>, along with the Major and Minor <term>Sixths</term> <note>original: "Essacordo"</note>, become consonant, it is necessary to restore them to how they were before. This distribution approaches the order and proportion of the <term>Syntonic</term> <note>Ptolemy’s Syntonic Diatonic, which uses "just" ratios for sweeter-sounding thirds.</note>—not that it is exactly the same, as some believe and write, nor that its authors ever intended such a thing. Rather, it was achieved by them by chance in seeking to tune the intervals closer to the perfection that the nature of the instrument—or rather, the quantity and quality of the strings, the mechanics, and the skill of those craftsmen—allowed. They were always fleeing (as has been said elsewhere) the inequality of the Whole Tones, along with every inconvenience that could proceed from them in this modern practice. To do this now, we will primarily take—following the method of <term>Aristoxenus</term> <note>A Greek theorist who argued for dividing intervals by ear and geometry rather than strict math.</note>, since it is impossible to divide any <term>superparticular</term> <note>A ratio where the numerator is one greater than the denominator (e.g., 3:2, 4:3, 5:4).</note> interval into equal parts in any other way—four-sevenths of a <term>Comma</term> <note>A tiny musical interval resulting from the difference between two other intervals.</note> of our times,

<margin>By how much the intervals are altered in the temperament of the ordinary keyboard instrument.</margin>
to the interval that is between the string **F** <note>original: "F faut"</note> and **G** <note>original: "G solreut"</note>, by moving the latter closer to the former by that amount. And so that between **G** and **A** <note>original: "alamire"</note> there remains (after having lowered the former as much as was said) the same distance found between **F** and **G**, we will loosen the said **A** by an entire Comma, and additionally a seventh part of it. We will then make the string **B-natural** <note>original: "h mi"</note> lower than it currently is by one Comma and five-sevenths of its parts; thus, it will contain between itself and **A** the same space found between the two lower adjacent Whole Tones. Now, to leave between the string **B-natural** and **C** <note>original: "c solfaut"</note> all the remainder that was taken by ratio from three Whole Tones that contribute to the composition of the <term>Tritone</term> is not appropriate in any way. This is because not only is the <term>Minor Third</term> found between **A** and **C** dissonant to the ear (respecting the gain made), but also the <term>Half-step</term> <note>original: "Lemma"</note> that was previously between **B-natural** and **C**, in wanting to increase it to the limit of a ratio of 16:15 <note>original: "Sesquiquindecima"</note> or a bit more as I said, has become superfluous by half a Comma. But because the <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapente"</note> found between **F** and **C** should not remain diminished by so much, and so that the aforementioned Minor Third becomes (by moving a little closer to the less imperfect one) less languid and more pleasing to the ear, we will lower **C** two-sevenths of a Comma; and by that much, every Fifth will necessarily be diminished. This done, it will be necessary—if we want the same distance between **C** and **D** <note>original: "d lasolre"</note> that is found between **F** and **G** and the other diminished Whole Tones—to lower it six-sevenths of a Comma. And so that **E** <note>original: "elami"</note> does not exceed those, we will lower it a whole Comma and three-sevenths of its parts more. This remainder we will leave entirely to the interval between **E** and **F**; thus, both the <term>Minor Semitone</term> and the <term>Half-step</term> <note>original: "Lemma"</note> will have been increased by one Comma and three-sevenths of its parts. Although the Major Semitone of this new distribution slightly exceeds the 16:15 ratio, it is not an inconvenience, as it is drawn from a whole larger than the 9:8 ratio <note>original: "Sesquinono"</note>. By this order, one will proceed to distribute all the other strings that the Octave has below, above, inside, and outside its limits. You can now clearly understand from what has been said, not only that the Fifth is primarily lowered from its proportional state and the <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> tightened, but by what portion; and furthermore, that for anyone who wished to do the opposite—making the Fourth diminished and the Fifth superfluous—it is impossible. The matter cannot stand otherwise than in this manner, because the primary cause of this consists in the

<margin>From what the said imperfection arises.</margin>
quantity of Whole Tones that those consonances contain, and in that portion by which those Whole Tones are diminished, and the Semitones contained in such intervals are increased. You have also been able to see how much that portion is, between which strings, why, and how it is distributed. But it should be noted in this temperament that the strings which previously contained the <term>Pythagorean Third</term> <note>original: "Ditono"</note> now contain the <term>Major Third</term>, and those that contained the <term>Pythagorean Minor Third</term> <note>original: "Semiditono"</note> now contain the <term>Minor Third</term>. And between those strings where the <term>Major Sixth</term> <note>original: "Essacordo maggiore"</note> was found in the Diatonic, the <term>Major Sixth</term> <note>original: "maggior Sesta"</note> is found at present, and the <term>Minor Sixth</term> comes to be contained between those that enclosed the <term>Minor Sixth</term> <note>original: "minore Essacordo"</note>. It is found, therefore, in the temperament shown, that each Whole Tone has been diminished by four-sevenths of a Comma, the Major Third by an entire Comma and more than one-seventh part, the Fifth by two-sevenths, and the Major Sixth by six-sevenths; whereas, on the contrary, the Minor Sixth has been increased by a whole Comma and additionally one-seventh part, the Fourth by two-sevenths, and the Minor Third by six-sevenths. From this, one can argue how much those people are deceived who say the Comma is not perceptible; yet they have, despite all this, confessed that in keyboard instruments—of whose sound they claim to have great understanding—one finds diminished Fifths and superfluous Fourths. I will easily believe they have said this rather out of politeness than...

**STROZZI.** I want to take this opportunity to tell you what happened to me a few days ago while talking with one of these players. He insisted at all costs that by simply playing those two registers a <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Quinta"</note> apart—which are found in order in every church organ above the <term>Fifteenth</term> <note>original: "Quintadecima", an organ stop sounding two octaves and a fifth above the fundamental.</note>—they would produce a very fine sound, even without having the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "Ottaua"</note> and the <term>Principal</term> <note>The basic, fundamental stop of an organ.</note> beneath them. He did not realize that when the pipes are arranged in such a manner, a <term>Ninth</term> <note>original: "Nona"</note> always accompanies the Fifth, and a <term>Seventh</term> <note>original: "Settima"</note> accompanies the <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: "Quarta"</note>. Despite all my reasoning, it was impossible to make him understand. Thus, I was almost forced by him to go up to an organ. Once the two mentioned stops were opened and he began to play, he insisted in every way that the Fifths, Fourths, Major Thirds, and Minor Thirds with a Fifth in the high or low range sounded excellent (without having the usual base of the Octave and the Principal). This defect is hidden from the ears of the common people by the great noise made by the quantity and quality of the pipes playing at the same time. If a good fellow <note>original: "homicciatto"</note> who was pumping the bellows <note>original: "daua il vento alle Canne", literally "gave wind to the pipes".</note> had not intervened, the player’s persistence would have led me to lose my temper. The fellow said: "I believe you have come up here to mock me; either you play as you ought, or I shall stop raising the bellows." Another one of these "know-it-alls" once tried to persuade me that the two mentioned stops were a <term>Perfect Fifth</term> apart, and that each one separately among its particular pipes had Fifths that were narrower than those on other keyboard instruments. To him I replied: "Is the <term>G</term> <note>original: "G solreut"</note> of the lower register in unison with the <term>c</term> <note>original: "c solfaut"</note> of the higher one?" "You know well it is," he answered. Whereupon I replied that between two things equal in length, it was impossible for one to be shorter than the other, and conversely, if one is larger than the other, they cannot naturally be equal. At this, he came to his senses and fell silent.

**BARDI.** It is truly a great thing that the majority of men speak so freely and willingly about those things they understand the least. But let us leave them aside and return to our distribution of the strings. If we wish to apply this to the <term>Syntonic Diatonic</term> <note>Ptolemy's tuning system which used "just" or pure ratios for thirds, but was difficult to implement on fixed-pitch instruments like the organ.</note>, one must take away four-sevenths of a <term>Comma</term> <note>A tiny musical interval, the difference between two slightly different versions of the same note in different tuning systems.</note> from each Major Tone. Three of these parts will then be used to increase the interval of the <term>Sesquitone</term> <note>The minor tone (ratio 10:9).</note>, also called the Minor Tone; in this way, they are made equal. Furthermore, each <term>Sesquiquarta</term> <note>The ratio 5:4, which forms the Major Third.</note> is diminished by one-seventh of a comma, and the <term>Sesquiquinta</term> <note>The ratio 6:5, which forms the Minor Third.</note> is diminished by the same amount, since the <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapente"</note> remains short by two-sevenths of the said comma. Consequently, the <term>Sesquiquindecima</term> <note>The ratio 16:15, known today as the Major Semitone.</note> is increased by three-sevenths of the same interval. The <term>Sesquiquintatreesima</term> <note>The ratio 25:24, known as the Minor Semitone.</note> remains in its original form—exactly the opposite of what occurs with voices. If what I have said is true, the <term>Major Sixth</term> <note>original: "Superbipartiente terza", the ratio 5:3.</note> will have increased by the same amount that the Minor Third was diminished; and the <term>Minor Sixth</term> <note>original: "Supertripartientequinta", the ratio 8:5.</note> is likewise increased by the amount the Major Third was diminished. The Fourth is increased by the two-sevenths of a comma by which the Fifth was diminished. The <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "Ottaua", also referred to here as the "Dupla" or 2:1 ratio.</note>, always kept far from any defective extreme (for the reason to be stated below), remains in its usual perfect form. There have been others who, departing from this view in distributing the strings in the same species, wanted to take away a quarter part of the comma instead of two-sevenths from the Fifth and add it to the <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>. They did this to make both intervals, according to them, less imperfect by one-twenty-eighth of a comma. But then the Minor Sixth and Major Third remained the same size as they are in the Syntonic, because they took half a comma from the Major Tone and gave it to the Minor Tone to make them equal. I would consider this worthy of consideration if it were actually so; but since it is in fact the same as the first method, we shall set it aside with their other irrelevancies.

**STROZZI.** Why is it, Signor Giovanni, that when the strings of this instrument were distributed according to the <term>Ditonic</term> <note>The Pythagorean tuning system used in the Middle Ages.</note> order—where the so-called perfect consonances were tuned in their true proportions, but none of the Thirds or Sixths were in tune—that in this new system, where the Fourths are "superfluous" <note>Slightly larger than the pure mathematical ratio.</note> rather than in their true state, one does not hear those bad effects in the low or high range that were heard in the old system?

**BARDI.** Such a thing cannot happen, neither internally nor at the extremes of the Fourth. By diminishing the Tones and increasing the Minor Semitones, the cause of the dissonance in the Thirds and Sixths has been removed. It was these issues, and not the perfection of the Fifths and Fourths, that prevented those intervals from being in tune (as has been said). Furthermore, one can very well find the Fifths and Fourths in their true proportions on keyboard instruments without at all hindering the tuning of the imperfect ones, as anyone can clearly see and hear in the temperament we have newly discovered. In practice, this succeeds with the greatest excellence and perfection one could desire.

**STROZZI.** I am entirely satisfied; but let us look at the distributions of Didymus and Aristoxenus.

# 35 Ancient and Modern Music

**BARDI.** Didymus, a most noble Pythagorean musician, lived some years before Ptolemy. He created a new distribution of strings in each of the three <term>genera of harmony</term> <note>The three ways of dividing a tetrachord: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic.</note>; and among others, he created the <margin>The Syntonic as distributed by Didymus.</margin> **Syntonic** <note>A tuning system that uses "pure" thirds, often called Just Intonation today.</note> in the **Diatonic** genus. It proceeded in each of its <term>tetrachords</term> <note>A scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth.</note> in the manner you see in this one, which is the lowest part of the system called the **Hypaton**.

### The Hypaton Tetrachord of Didymus

E lami: 72 <note>E</note>
{72 to 81} <term>Sesquioctave</term> <note>A 9:8 ratio, making a Major Whole Tone.</note> and a Whole Tone. {9} difference.
D solre: 81 <note>D</note>
{81 to 90} <term>Sesquinonal</term> <note>A 10:9 ratio, making a Minor Whole Tone.</note>. {9} difference.
C faut: 90 <note>C</note>
{90 to 96} <term>Sesquiquindecimal</term> <note>A 16:15 ratio, making a Major Semitone.</note>. {6} difference.
B mi: 96 <note>B natural</note>

Ptolemy came later and changed the order of the two lower intervals of each tetrachord. He placed the middle one in the position of the lowest, and the lowest in the position of the middle one. He claimed that it was not appropriate for the larger interval to be placed there, but rather for the one smaller than it (yet still larger than the lowest) to occupy that spot. From this, you can understand what role Ptolemy played in the Syntonic system, and to whom the honor and the prize for it should truly be given.

**STROZZI.** For what reason should we believe that those who have tried to persuade us that what we sing today is entirely the Syntonic Diatonic, have said it belongs to Ptolemy rather than Didymus? As far as I can see, when applied to our way of composing and singing, neither distribution offers any greater advantage or disadvantage than the other.

**BARDI.** That which would not have bothered you or many others perhaps prejudiced the designs of the authors of these theories.

**STROZZI.** For instance?

**BARDI.** The interval found in Didymus's distribution between G-sol-re-ut <note>G</note> and B-mi <note>B natural</note> is a **Ditone** <note>A major third made of two major tones (81:64), which sounds sharper than a modern major third.</note>, and not a <term>Major Third</term> <note>original: "Terza maggiore"</note> of the kind that most people believe is sung today. Furthermore, the interval found between B-mi and that same G-sol-re-ut is a **Lesser Hexachord** <note>A ratio of 128:81.</note>, and not a <term>Minor Sixth</term> <note>original: "minor Sesta"</note>. Since these authors had previously stated in their writings that such intervals were dissonant—as you have heard they truly are—they would have been exposed too suddenly, providing an opportunity to block their plans. To see that these intervals appear as such, here is the first species of the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> distributed according to Didymus’s intention. If you examine it diligently, you will find what I have said to be true. Even though the same thing occurred in Ptolemy's version, as you have seen, it was not so obvious to the senses and judgment of the common people. <margin>Why the Syntonic is attributed to Ptolemy.</margin> Thus, it has been easier to deceive the general public about this matter until now. This was the reason we have said the Diatonic species sung today belongs more to Ptolemy than to Didymus—unless we wish to suggest (which I do not believe at all) that they were ignorant of the difference between them. From this it also followed that they gave the name **Comma** to the amount by which the Major Tone exceeds the Minor Tone; they did not follow the ancients, who used the term for the amount by which their Major Semitone exceeded the Minor, as they had sharper versions of these, as you have seen.

<margin>Aristoxenus in the first and second books of the *Elements*. Euclid in the *Introduction*. Vitruvius in the fourth chapter of the fifth book.</margin>
**STROZZI.** What do we believe was the reason for persuading so many of that first school—including many learned and reputed writers like Fabro, Gafurio, Glarean, Valgulio (a most lettered man of elevated genius), and infinite others—that what had been sung (from Guido d'Arezzo onwards, or even before, I suspect) was the "Ancient Diatonic"? Especially since so many great men had explicitly told them that intervals smaller than the **Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>, and those found between the **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note> and the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, were all dissonant. Among these, I do not know how Aristoxenus, Euclid, and Vitruvius could have said it more clearly in their writings; besides, the thing is so easy in itself to demonstrate to the sense of hearing.

He notes that classical authorities like Euclid and Vitruvius recognized these intervals as dissonant, despite modern claims to the contrary.</summary>

# 36 Dialogue on Music

<margin>Guido d'Arezzo <note>original: Guido Aretino</note> did not have knowledge of **imperfect consonances**. He was a monk of Saint Benedict.</margin>
**BARDI.** To Guido d'Arezzo, such a concept could hardly have come into consideration; because he was a monk, and his goal was to teach his monks to easily sing **plainsong** <note>original: "canto fermo"</note>. Since this was for a single voice, and no sort of consonance <note>meaning harmony between multiple voices</note> arose from it, he could not have doubted this in any way. As for the reason why, in his *Introductory* <note>referring to Guido's theoretical writings</note>, he marked the strings with the same numbers that Plato puts in his *Timaeus*, which were first assigned by Pythagoras and followed later by Boethius; he was led by no other motive (as far as I can estimate) than to give the matter **reputation**. He was adopting not only the most ancient and famous **Distribution of strings** ever known, but the very one given by nature to mortals. For the same reason, he did not want to mark the string **B-flat** <note>original: "B fa"</note> within the **B-natural** <note>original: "h mi"</note>, since neither the Greeks nor the Latins used it in their **Systems** <note>the *Greater Perfect System* of ancient music theory</note>. His opinion was first put into use by others, and afterwards greatly approved by infinite others.

**STROZZI.** So, do you believe that in the time of Guido d'Arezzo, the lowest interval of the **Tetrachords** was sung as a **limma** <note>original: "Lemma," a small Pythagorean semitone</note>, and not as a **major semitone** as it is today? And that they did not sing in consonance?

<margin>In what manner they sang in his times.</margin>
**BARDI.** That they did not sing in consonance, I hold for certain; for there is no memory of **imperfect consonances** <note>intervals like thirds and sixths, which are the basis of modern harmony but were considered dissonant in older systems</note> to be found in his *Introductory*. However, I do believe that they played them on instruments. As for whether the lowest interval of the Tetrachords was a minor or a major semitone, I would more easily believe the former was sung in that place; and this is the reason that moves me to believe it. In the time of Guido d'Arezzo, any light of virtue—and particularly of **regulated Music**—was still (so to speak) extinguished in Italy. Yet, it was not because of this that men had not maintained that way of singing which they naturally acquired at the beginning of the world; it is the same as that which rustic farmers use in cultivating the fields, and shepherds use through the woods and mountains behind their flocks, to drive away the boredom brought to their hearts by continuous and heavy labors. This sort of song has always been used among men from their creation until our times; nor will it end except with them, or with the

<margin>Singing: from whom it was learned.</margin>
world itself. Although **Athenaeus** <note>an ancient Greek rhetorician</note>, with the testimony of **Chamaeleon of Pontus**, says that men learned this faculty by trying to imitate the song of birds. Men had therefore, up until a short time before then, wept for many continuous centuries over their miseries; where afterwards, little by little, they began to give work to literature, to Music, and to the other beautiful arts. Hence the aforementioned Guido d'Arezzo, in those times most knowledgeable in the art of Music—as much as the fortune of the age allowed in that climate—began to reorder the way of singing. He gave not only new names to the strings, as had come into use shortly before him, denoting them with the same

<margin>Guido d'Arezzo adds six strings to the System. Demetrius of Phalerum.</margin>
characters of the Latin alphabet so that one could learn to carry the voices comfortably with greater ease and distinction; but he also named, beyond those of the **Greater System** (both conjunct and disjunct), five in the high part and one in the low. He then distributed them into seven **Hexachords** <note>six-note scales</note>, for there were as many letters as those he used, as appears in his *Introductory*. This was perhaps in imitation of what **Demetrius of Phalerum** says regarding the use of vowels, following the example of the **Priests of Egypt**, who likewise pronounced the notes of their sacred chants upon the sound of those seven vowels. The practical musicians who lived shortly before the time of Guido d'Arezzo used the same characters that the ancient Greeks once used to signify the strings of their songs, and also those of the Latins, marking them above seven lines in this manner—perhaps in imitation of the seven strings of the ancient **Lyre** <note>original: "Cithara"</note>.

### Ancient & Modern

<margin>Guido is the first who marks the notes in the space.</margin>
Wherefore Guido d’Arezzo <note>original: "Guido Aretino"</note> then removed the labor of many lines and clefs, upon which they used to place Points <note>the precursor to modern noteheads</note> instead of the notes of our times—which were later discovered in Paris by the great Doctor Jean de Muris <note>A 14th-century philosopher and music theorist</note>. This Guido placed these points even within the spaces found between one line and another, just as composers still do today. From this practice, they acquired the name of **Contrapuntists** <note>literally "point-against-point," referring to the method of layering one melody against another</note>, which was a very fitting name.

<margin>Each letter and string was a "key" <note>original: "chiaue"</note>.</margin>
<margin>Notes discovered by Jean de Muris.</margin>
<margin>Where the name "Contrapuntist" derives from.</margin>
For they composed their songs <note>original: "Cantilene"</note> using points, which have no existence in Nature other than in the human imagination, almost by chance—not differently than how superstitious **Geomancers** <note>Practitioners of divination who interpret patterns of dots or markings on the ground</note> today compose their figures to judge the questions put to them. They judge these based on what chance itself has caused (following, however, a few of their own principles and terms), without otherwise knowing beforehand the effects that could arise more from one manner of operation than another. And just as ten or more Geomancers—or even just one—will have as many different opinions on the same doubt, forming ten or more figures upon it; so too, if you give ten or more Contrapuntists the task of expressing one specific and particular affection of the soul <note>an emotional state or "affect"</note> with their music according to the usage of this century, they will express it in as many or more different ways and varied Tones. The same will happen with a single composer if he tries to express it ten or more times. This occurs for no other reason than having taken chance as their guide to art and knowledge; or, we might say, that their principles are woven of fog, filled with air and wind, in the manner of the garments (as Seneca tells us) of the most lascivious Roman noblewomen of that time.

<margin>Seneca, *On Benefits*, and also Petronius Arbiter.</margin>
**STROZZI.** Before Guido, then, did musicians only use lines when writing their music?

They also had various Greek ciphers that denoted their keys and notes, as you were able to understand in those examples.
