**BAR.** I do not hold that Guido d'Arezzo added any strings to the System; rather, he gave particular names to each one. As for those strings seen in his introduction beyond the fifteen of the ancient Greeks, I firmly believe he took them either from the **Tones of Boethius** <note>Boethius (c. 480–524 AD) was a philosopher whose musical treatises were foundational in the Middle Ages</note> (which are eight, the extremes of which require the same quantity of voices in the same order), or perhaps he took them from wind instruments like the **Organ**, or from the stringed instruments in use at that time—similar to, or perhaps the same as, the **Simicon** and **Epigonion** used by the Greeks. From these, he took for the **Diatonic** scale <note>original: "spezie Diatonica"</note>—which he intended to be sung in his time—the quantity that comfortably suited the diversity of human voices that sang various melodies upon them, though not at the same time. He assigned eight to the low part, eight to the middle, and the remainder to the high part. In this way, because the lowest of the middle eight is the same as the least low of the low ones, and the highest of those middle ones is the least high of the high ones, they sum to twenty-two notes and strings across three octaves, divided as I said. Others have said that he ordered these into seven **Hexachords** <term>Essacordi: a six-note scale</term> because he wished to show us, through the numbers six and seven, the excellence and perfection found in that distribution. This is because the number **six** is the first of the perfect numbers <note>A perfect number equals the sum of its divisors, e.g., 1+2+3=6</note>, just as the second is **twenty-eight**, which is produced by the **Seven** <note>original: "Settenario"</note> and its parts. Others have said they were ordered as major hexachords to contain, in each one arranged in such a manner, any of the three types of the **fourth** <term>Diatessaron: the musical interval of a perfect fourth</term>. Returning to the two stringed instruments just mentioned, I say that one of them had thirty-five strings and the other forty. From this quantity, one can argue that their players played in harmony; no longer striking them with the **Plectrum** <term>A pick; its use had been entirely forgotten by then</term>, but with the fingers, in the manner of the **Harp** <note>original: "Harpa"</note>. We have already declared which type of harmony is most suited of the three for consonances. From this manner of playing, this modern way of composing and singing many melodies together at the same time likely had its origin (as we shall show in its proper place). According to this distribution of strings, and not otherwise, did the singers of those times carry the musical intervals, and it has been conducted and preserved until today. They gave the name of "imperfect consonances" to major and minor **Thirds** and **Sixths**. This name must have caused common people to believe and say, without further thought, that they were the same as the **Ditone** and **Semiditone** <term>Pythagorean major and minor thirds</term> and the major and minor **Hexachord**, according to the form contained by the **Pythagorean numbers** in the introduction of Guido d'Arezzo. This is because that name of "imperfect consonances" was truly given to them with great judgment and discretion, not only for their indeterminate and variable nature, but because most of them (if not all) seem to be consonant rather than actually being so. Nevertheless, they have been accepted as such by modern practical **Contrapuntists** <term>Composers of polyphony</term> without further inquiry, due to the necessity they found themselves under. # Dialogue on Music

<margin>
Regarding the second book of the *Harmonic Elements* <note>original: "Harmonici Elementi," a treatise by Aristoxenus.</note>.
</margin>

I come now to the Distributions of Aristoxenus, and I say that *Aristoxenus*, a most noble musician and philosopher, created six different distributions of strings: namely, two Diatonic, three Chromatic, and one Enharmonic. But for the sake of brevity, we will treat only those which are necessary for our purpose, reserving the others for whenever they might be needed. This most learned musician made it a practice to assign to each interval of his tetrachords <note>A four-note scale segment.</note> that portion and quantity of sound of the *Octave* <note>original: "Diapason"</note> that suited their diverse genus and species. To do this, he first divided the *Fourth* <note>original: "Diateffaron"</note>—which consisted of two whole tones and an entire half of one, according to his designs—into sixty equal small parts. I speak here of the sound itself, and not the length of the line or string, even though such quantity was also considered therein. He then gave twelve of these parts to the lowest interval of each of his *Tetrachords*, twenty-four to the middle one, and the remainder to the highest. To this system, divided and ordered into such Tetrachords, he gave the name *Intense Diatonic* <note>original: "Diatonico incitato"</note>. He called the lowest interval of each Tetrachord a *Semitone*, and the other two higher ones *Tones*. Such were the Tones and Semitones he discussed in various parts of his Distributions. Of the three Chromatics he created, he gave one the name *Tonal Chromatic* <note>original: "Toniaco"</note>, which he ordered thus: he assigned twelve of the sixty aforementioned particles (into which he had divided the *Fourth*) to the lowest interval of each Tetrachord, gave just as many to the middle one, and the rest to the highest.

<margin>
Ptolemy in the first book of the *Harmonics*, chapter 12.
</margin>

->STR.<-

Would it not have been the same to divide the *Fourth* into five equal parts instead of sixty, and in the *Intense Diatonic* give one of those parts to the lowest interval of the Tetrachord, two to the middle, and the rest to the highest? And in the *Tonal Chromatic*, to have given one of them to the lowest interval, another to the middle, and the three remaining to the highest?

->BAR.<-

<margin>
Why Aristoxenus divides the Fourth into 60 particles.
</margin>

That would have worked for the two Distributions you mentioned; but since he wanted this division of the *Fourth* to serve for each of the other four differently distributed types, he could not divide it into a smaller quantity of parts without suffering the annoyance of fractions. For at times it was necessary to take half of a tone, and at other times a fourth part; and from the Semitone he needed not only these fractions, but a third part as well. Sometimes it was necessary to increase one or the other by such a portion to conveniently compose whatever other intervals were required for his various other Distributions. To achieve this, he chose the number sixty, as it is a number capable of being divided into two, three, four, five, and six parts.

->STR.<-

Was it for the same reason that the ancient musicians easily assigned those many tens of thousands to the strings of the *Ditone Diatonic* <note>original: "Diatonico Diatono," the Pythagorean tuning based on pure whole tones.</note>, so that the same numbers would conveniently serve for the *Chromatic* and the *Enharmonic*?

->BAR.<-

It was truly so; and this can be particularly observed in the ancient Enharmonic genus, between the string *Trite Synemmenon* <note>The third string of the "disjunct" tetrachord in the Greek system.</note> marked with the number 4491, and the *Paranete* of the same Tetrachord marked with the number 4374. I return, furthermore, to tell you concerning the Distributions of *Aristoxenus* that the *Intense Diatonic* and the *Tonal Chromatic*—the two species commonly used by the Lute and the bowed Viola—bring their consonances closer to perfection (understanding "perfection" here as the Fifth within the *Sesquialtera* <note>The 3:2 ratio.</note> and the Fourth within the *Sesquiterza* <note>The 4:3 ratio.</note>) than do those of the keyboard instrument. That keyboard tuning has been preached to us as a simple *Syntonon* <note>Ptolemy’s Syntonic Diatonic, later championed by Zarlino.</note> by those who have refuted the Distributions of *Aristoxenus* without saying why. By means of their particular Monochord, anyone who takes the care to examine them can sensibly see this truth.

->STR.<-

Could you not, with greater ease and exactness, show me how much the imperfect consonant intervals of the Lute and Viola are surplus or diminished from the true state in which the *Syntonon* contains them? And the perfect ones—to avoid bad and diverse relations, and confused, inconstant difficulties—how do they differ from those of the *Ditone Diatonic*?

->BAR.<-

It could be done with clarity and ease, but with no greater exactness than what the *Harmonic Rule* <note>A measuring tool or mathematical principle for intervals.</note> can show.

->STR.<-

Tell me, please.

->BAR.<-

<margin>
What the intervals of the Lute consist of.
</margin>

Firstly, the Octave on the Lute and the Viola (which proceed by the same degrees), being always far from any imperfection, consists, as you know, of six Tones, or we might say twelve Semitones. Or, to conform as much as possible to the usage of practitioners, we can also truly say that it consists of five Tones and two Semitones. Wherefore it should be known that each of their Tones is smaller than the *Sesquioctave* <note>The 9:8 ratio, a major whole tone.</note> and larger than the *Sesquinonary* <note>original: "Sesquinono," the 10:9 ratio, a minor whole tone.</note>. The Semitone is smaller than the *Sesquiquindecimal* <note>original: "Sesquiquindecima," the 16:15 ratio.</note> and larger than the *Sesquiseptadecimal* <note>original: "Sesquiquintattrefima," the 18:17 ratio, which Galilei famously proposed for lute fretting.</note>. The minor Third is surpassed by the *Sesquiquinta* <note>The 6:5 ratio.</note>; the major Third exceeds the *Sesquiquarta* <note>The 5:4 ratio.</note>. The Fourth <note>original: "Diateffaron"</note> exceeds the *Sesquiterza* <note>4:3 ratio</note>. The Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note> is smaller than the *Sesquialtera* <note>3:2 ratio</note>. The minor Sixth is surpassed by the *Supertripartient-fifth* <note>original: "Supertripartientequinta," the 8:5 ratio.</note>; the major Sixth exceeds the *Superbipartient-third* <note>original: "Superbipartienteterza," the 5:3 ratio.</note>. The Tritone and the Semidiapente <note>The diminished fifth.</note> are equal; therefore the latter is smaller and the former larger than those contained in the *Syntonon*.

->STR.<-

If I have well understood the method you previously told me for placing the frets on the Lute and Viola, it first seems to me that each of their Tones is a *Sesquioctave* <note>9:8 ratio</note>; and that the minor Third, besides many other intervals, is of the same form as that contained in the *Syntonon*, and not at all...

D

# Ancient and Modern.

...point by the irregular minor third <note>original: "Sesquiquinta"</note>.

**BAR.** How do you expect that to happen, since the Tones are equal—as I have told and proven to you—divided into two equal parts, and the Major Third is consonant?

**STR.** Please, pay attention. First, if the whole string is divided into eighteen equal parts, does not the Tone consist of two of those parts, specifically the space between the eighteenth part and the sixteenth? Is this not the same as saying the ratio is between nine and eight <note>The 9:8 ratio, known as the "Major Tone"</note>?

**BAR.** Go on; I see where you are trying to go with this.

**STR.** Does the minor third not contain three semitones? And are these not of the same value as three eighteenth-parts of the whole? And do the fifteen parts that remain, when compared to the eighteen, not have the same relationship as six to five <note>18:15 simplifies to 6:5</note>? This is the true form of the minor third according to the Syntonic system <note>The "Syntono" refers to Ptolemy’s tuning system, which used pure mathematical ratios</note>.

**BAR.** Now, take note. In this method of measurement, two eighteenth-parts are not actually equivalent to a ninth part of the whole. This is because these parts are considered as portions of the *sound* <note>meaning pitch increments</note>, and not as a physical quantity of the line or string. To prove this is true, here is the compass; by measuring it yourself, you will find that the first two semitones of the Lute do not occupy a ninth part of the string's length, just as three semitones do not equal an entire sixth part of it, but are rather somewhat less.

**STR.** I have understood all of that very well; however, please continue the argument you began.

**BAR.** Because the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note> has a greater correspondence and similarity to the Unison than any other musical interval, it is not only the simplest and most perfect interval, but also the one where the ear is least likely to be deceived. If you were to multiply its lower terms a thousand times and sum them together, the higher string is always contained by unity <note>meaning the ratio remains a clean power of 2</note>. This does not happen with any other interval, because they are not repeated in the same way as that consonant one. For this reason, and to avoid both difficulty and the danger of error, we will use the help of the Octave and its repetitions in this important business. 

First, one must know that each Tone on the Lute is smaller than the 9:8 ratio <note>original: "Sesquiottavo"</note> by one-sixth of an ancient Comma <note>A "Comma" is a tiny mathematical difference between two nearly identical intervals</note>. I prove this to you in this way: it is clear that six 9:8 ratios exceed an Octave by one of those Commas; therefore, if six Tones of the Lute fill an Octave exactly, without anything remaining or lacking, then each Tone must consequently be one-sixth of a Comma smaller than a 9:8 ratio. 

I say further that the 9:8 ratio is exceeded by each Tone of the Lute by three-quarters of the 81:80 ratio <note>original: "Sesquiottantesima," the Syntonic comma</note>, which, according to modern practitioners, is the Comma of our times. For each octave is capable (as can be clearly understood from what we have said above) of five 10:9 ratios <note>original: "Sesquinoni," or Minor Tones</note>, three Commas, and two major Semitones of the Syntonic system. These two major semitones give us one 10:9 ratio and about one and a half Commas more. In this way, we can consider each Octave as containing six 10:9 ratios and about four and a half Commas. When these four Commas are distributed proportionally among the six Tones, each receives two-thirds of a Comma, plus one-sixth of that remaining half-comma. Since two-thirds plus one-sixth of a half equals three-quarters of a whole, each Tone of the Lute necessarily exceeds the 10:9 ratio by that amount. 

Furthermore, each of the minor thirds on the Lute, when compared to the 6:5 ratios <note>original: "Sesquiquinte"</note>, is diminished by three-eighths of a Comma. I prove it to you thus: the Octave of the Lute consists exactly of four minor thirds. Let us see now, according to the example I will place here at the bottom, what remains when an Octave <note>original: "Dupla," or 2:1 ratio</note> is subtracted from four 6:5 ratios added together.

By subtracting one Octave from four 6:5 ratios added together, we are left with the ratio 648:625 <note>original: "Super 23 partiente 625"</note>. This clearly demonstrates that the minor thirds of the Lute, compared to the pure 6:5 ratios, are diminished, since four of them on the lute fill an Octave entirely. This 648:625 ratio consists of about one and a half Commas. When this interval is distributed among the four minor thirds, each will receive three-eighths of a Comma. As I have said, each minor third of the Lute is diminished by that amount compared to the pure 6:5 ratio. 

There is no doubt that since the Octave of this instrument is in its true proportion and far from any flawed extreme, and since each consists of a minor third and a major sixth, each of these sixths will be superfluous <note>larger than the pure ratio</note> by as much as each of the thirds is diminished. This ratio <note>128:125, known as the minor diesis</note> consists, as I proved to you at the beginning of our discourse, of about a Comma and a half; which Comma and a half, distributed proportionally among the said Major Thirds, will give each one a half; and by such an amount, each one will be successively superfluous, and any Minor Sixth will be diminished; which is proven in this other manner. There is no one who doubts, granting that the Minor Sixths on the Lute consist of eight semitones, that two Octaves (each containing twelve) are not worth the same as three Minor Sixths. <meta>This page continues the discussion on musical temperament. Having previously established the mathematical differences between intervals like the Fourth and Fifth, the author now addresses why the Lute's specific tuning system (which approximates equal temperament) works for fretted instruments but is traditionally avoided on keyboard instruments like the harpsichord or organ.</meta>

# Ancient & Modern.

<margin>Author's Considerations.</margin>
I proved to you above sufficiently that the <term>Diminished Fifth</term><note>An interval spanning five scale degrees that is smaller than a "pure" fifth; original: "Semidiapente."</note> exceeded the <term>Tritone</term><note>An augmented fourth, consisting of three whole tones.</note> by about half a <term>Comma</term>; so that when they are found to be equal on the Lute, the Tritone necessarily becomes superfluous <note>In this context, "superfluous" means slightly larger than its pure mathematical ratio.</note> and the Diminished Fifth is diminished by a quarter of a Comma, which is half of that excess by which the Diminished Fifth exceeds the Tritone. From this, one can understand how discreet, diligent, and considerate courteous Nature is in each of her operations: since those intervals that most closely approach perfection are so little distant from their true being. This same consideration was not necessary for those intervals further removed from perfection, and even less so for the imperfect and dissonant ones, as their deviations are not so manifest to the sense of hearing. One can also clearly know from what we have said so far how much further the <term>Keyboard instrument</term><note>Original: "Stromento di tasti," referring to instruments like the harpsichord or organ.</note> is from perfection than the Lute and the <term>Viola</term><note>Specifically the "viola da gamba," which, like the lute, uses frets.</note>; and furthermore, how difficult it is (due to poor relationships and false encounters between notes) for them to be played well together in the ensembles that occur daily, even if there were no other causes for the deformity of the <term>Semitones</term>. It should not be left without consideration that in the Lute's acquisition of perfection, as the Fifths are increased, the Fourths necessarily lose part of their imperfection by having their superfluous size diminished. The opposite, as has been shown, has happened to the Keyboard instrument; and with this, I believe I have satisfied each of your requests.

**STROZZI.** Truly so; but I desire next that you clarify another doubt for me, and then show me the method I must follow if I wish to construct any <term>Monochord</term><note>A single-stringed scientific instrument used to measure musical intervals.</note> of the kind we have discussed.

**BARDI.** I am ready to satisfy you; therefore, tell me what new doubt has arisen for you.

**STROZZI.** The doubt is this: since the tuning of the Lute is so much closer to perfection than that of the Keyboard instrument, I marvel greatly that the players of the latter, after having recognized this, have not reduced it to that same manner. For besides its excellence, the Lute has on every fret, in both the low and high registers, any desired interval of the <term>Excited Diatonic</term><note>Original: "Diatonico Incitato"; a specific tuning arrangement attributed by Renaissance theorists to the ancient Greeks.</note> and the <term>Tonic Chromatic of Aristoxenus</term><note>A Greek musical genus where the tetrachord is divided into a semitone, a semitone, and a minor third.</note>, as you told me above. Whereas, on the contrary, in the distribution of strings used by the Keyboard instrument, many are commonly missing. Because of this, even a practical and expert player cannot transpose every <term>Cantilena</term><note>A vocal melody or song.</note> up or down by a Tone or a Semitone (in those keys most commonly used) with the same ease and utility as one does on the Lute.

**BARDI.** This is one of those things I have often thought about myself; and I still search diligently to see if it could be used on the keys so that it would succeed as it does on the Lute. But I truly find that it does not succeed there at all; rather, many important defects are uncovered.

**STROZZI.** How can it be that the same thing is not of the same nature in every place and time? And that this specific distribution, which delights on the Lute, should be displeasing on the Keyboard instrument?

<margin>Why the distribution of the Lute does not produce a good effect on the Keyboard instrument.</margin>
**BARDI.** It can very well be so, as experience demonstrates to us. And although the cause of this is difficult to understand well, I do not wish to fail to tell you a few things that occur to me on this subject for your satisfaction. This perhaps arises from having accustomed the sense of hearing always to hear the intervals on the Lute in the manner I have already told you they are contained, and likewise we are used to hearing them differently from the Keyboard instrument. To wish now for the Keyboard to be tempered according to the usage of the Lute cannot pass without offending the sense of hearing in certain particular places where the difference between them is greatly manifest, because the ear has grown old in that established temperament. These particular places are mainly those where one hears the difference between the <term>Major and Minor Semitones</term><note>In non-equal temperaments, the distance between C and C-sharp is not the same as the distance between C-sharp and D.</note>. For as you know, the Lute has divided the Tone into equal parts, while the Keyboard instrument has separated it into unequal parts. The most apparent places are between the G-sharp <note>Original: "diesis X di G solreut."</note> and the A-flat <note>Original: "b molle d'alamire."</note>, and between the D-sharp <note>Original: "diesis X di d la solre"</note> and the E-flat <note>Original: "b molle d'elami."</note>. Because when on the Keyboard instrument we have tuned the D-sharp to be a <term>Major Tenth</term> with B <note>Original: "h mi."</note>, and we want that same D-sharp to perform the same office as the E-flat (as it does on the Lute), serving as a <term>Minor Tenth</term> with Middle C <note>Original: "C solfaut"</note>, it becomes so languid and weak that it is intolerable. And if, on the contrary, we sharpen it as much as is necessary to make it tune sweetly with Middle C as a Minor Tenth, when it must then serve as a Major Tenth with B, it is so tense and incited that it cannot be tolerated; and the same happens in other places where there is such a difference between them. Furthermore, these intervals can better reveal their quality and nature on the Keyboard instrument than they do on the Lute and the Viola, due to the conformity that the practice of singing has with its temperament, as well as the quality and quantity of the sound regarding the different nature of the "accidents" that concur in its generation: for the sound of the strings of the Keyboard instrument strikes the ear with greater violence than those of the Lute. It is clearly seen, then, that the sound of the strings of the instrument, tempered according to the disposition of the intervals

# Dialogue on Music

among which this is common: that Thirds, Tenths, and likewise Major Sixths, greatly offend the ear because of their high-pitched sharpness. The reason these intervals manifest their quality more harshly than others arises from nothing else than the material of the strings and the "agent" that strikes them <note>The "agent" refers to the plectrum or jack in a harpsichord, or the fingers on a lute.</note>, which have more force and efficacy in their activity to strike the hearing with greater vehemence. This does not happen with the strings of the Lute due to the different quality of both the subject and the object. This same difference and variety can be considered in glowing iron and wood: for the iron heats with more force and speed than the wood, and introduces its new form <note>In Aristotelian terms, "form" here refers to the state of being hot.</note> into whatever subject is fit to receive it. To prove that this is the cause, if one tunes the Harp according to the manner of the Lute—where the strings and the agent that strikes them are the same—the harmonies will undoubtedly become no less tolerable than on the Lute itself. Conversely, they would become intolerable on the Lute every time the agent and the material of the strings were changed, as we have experienced many times. The same can be considered when receiving a blow from an ivory ball, or one of hard, heavy, well-polished wood, after it has been struck against a hard, smooth stone; and receiving a blow from another ball made of cork, struck with the same force against a poorly-finished willow board; or we might compare the blow and the passage of an acute angle to that of an obtuse one.

<margin>A very ingenious and beautiful keyboard instrument.</margin>
Another example of a keyboard instrument comes to mind, which is more effective than any other for this purpose; it was once given by the Elector August, Duke of Saxony, to the late Albert of Bavaria. This instrument has strings like those of a Lute, but they are bowed <note>Original: "secate," literally "cut" or "sawed," referring to the friction of the bow.</note> in the manner of a Viola by a clever arrangement made of the same horsehair used for the bows of Violas. This mass of hair is easily rotated with a foot by the player, and by means of a wheel over which it passes, it continuously bows the amount of string required by the player’s fingers. When I was at that court two years ago, I tuned this instrument according to the usage of the Lute, and when well-played, it sounded like nothing other than a consort of Violas—a most sweet sound to hear.

<margin>Method of constructing the Diatonic Monochord.</margin>
<margin>Zarlino teaches another method in chapter 40 of his *Institutions*.</margin>
I come now to the construction of Monochords <note>A <term>Monochord</term> is a scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge used to measure musical intervals.</note>. I say that whenever it has been necessary for me to distribute the strings according to the Diatonic <term>Diatonon</term> <note>The standard "natural" scale of the Greeks.</note>, among the various ways I could have used, I followed this order. First, with a compass, I divided the whole line, length, or string (whatever we wish to call it) of the board or ruler upon which I wanted to fit it, into four equal parts. I called the lowest extreme point **A**, denoting with it the string <term>A-re</term> <note>The lowest note in the medieval "Gamut" or scale, corresponding to a low A.</note>, and I called the highest extreme point **B**, without further meaning. Then, at the point that divides the whole length into two equal parts, I marked <term>A-la-mi-re</term> <note>The note A, one octave above the starting point.</note>. In the spot that separates *A-re* from *A-la-mi-re*, I marked <term>D-sol-re</term> <note>The note D.</note>, as the fourth part of the whole is contained between it and *A-re*. To give this *D-sol-re* its Octave in the high register, I open the compass and make two parts of the interval between it and the extreme high point **B**; at the point separating the two, I mark <term>d-la-sol-re</term> <note>The note D, an octave higher.</note>. I divide the whole again into three parts, distinguishing them with four points as their boundaries. At the second point—following the <term>Boethian</term> <note>Referring to the naming system of Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), whose works were the foundation of medieval music theory.</note> method of always calling the one at the lowest extreme "first"—I mark <term>E-la-mi</term> <note>The note E.</note>, and at the third, <term>e-la-mi</term> <note>The note E, an octave higher.</note>. Placing one leg of the compass on this string, I place the other on the line toward the high end; where it ends, I mark <term>b-mi</term> <note>The note B-natural.</note>. Removing it from there while holding the other leg steady, I move it toward the low end; where it rests, I mark <term>B-mi</term> <note>The note B-natural, an octave lower.</note>. This done, I divide the entire line between *d-la-sol-re* and the extreme high point into two parts. Then, placing one leg of the compass on that *d-la-sol-re* and moving toward the low end with the other, I mark <term>G-sol-re-ut</term> <note>The note G.</note> where it ends. To find its Octave in the high register, I open the compass again and divide the interval between it and point **B** into two parts; in the center, I mark <term>g-sol-re-ut</term> <note>The note G, an octave higher.</note>. Without changing the width of the compass legs, I place one on *G-sol-re-ut* and move toward the low end with the other; where it rests, I mark <term>C-fa-ut</term> <note>The note C.</note>. I find its octave in the high register by dividing the space between it and the extreme point **B** into two parts, placing <term>C-sol-fa-ut</term> <note>The note C, an octave higher.</note> in the middle. If I again divide the whole remaining interval above it toward that side into two parts, and place one leg of the compass on it, moving toward the low end with the other, I find the position of <term>F-fa-ut</term> <note>The note F.</note> where it ends. Its higher octave is acquired by dividing the space from it to point **B** into two parts, dwelling in its center. The Diatonic Monochord lacks only the string <term>b-fa</term> <note>The note B-flat.</note>, which I find in this way: I divide the line between **B** and *f-fa-ut* into two portions; I then place one leg of the compass on that *F-fa-ut* and move toward the low end with the other; where it ends, I mark *b-fa*. Its octave toward that side I find by opening the compass so wide that its legs contain the entire void between *b-fa* and the high extreme point; removing the compass leg while keeping the other steady, I move it toward the low end; where it rests, I mark **B-fa**. With this, I have completed the Diatonic Ditonic Monochord, which the ancient Greek musicians

<margin>Method for constructing the ancient Chromatic Monochord.</margin>
<margin>Method for constructing the ancient Enharmonic Monochord.</margin>
The difference between one and the other consists of nothing else than arranging the third string of each Tetrachord <note>A Tetrachord is a series of four notes spanning a perfect fourth, the building block of ancient Greek scales.</note> so that it forms a "Trihemitone" <note>literally "three half-tones," roughly equivalent to a minor third</note> with the highest string. The proportion of this interval, as you have heard, falls within these numbers: 19 to 16. To achieve this, follow this order: divide the line found between B and *E-la-mi* <note>The highest string of the Principal Tetrachord, or *Hypaton*</note> into 16 equal parts. By adding three similar parts toward the bass end, we will mark at that furthest point the chromatic string *D-sol-re*, which will create the Trihemitone with *E-la-mi*. This same order is followed to mark the other Chromatic strings in the other Tetrachords. In this distribution, some criticize Franchino <note>Franchinus Gaffurius (1451–1522), a famous Italian music theorist</note> for varying the middle and high intervals of each Tetrachord from the ancients. He placed the middle interval within the ratio 18 to 17—which is the smaller part of a whole tone when it should be the larger—and labeled the Trihemitone with the numbers 153 to 128, which is more than it truly should be. Furthermore, if you wish to tune the same Diatonic Monochord according to the use of the ancient Enharmonic genus, it will suffice simply to divide the space between those two strings containing the minor Semitone or *Leimma* <note>A "Leimma" is the small Pythagorean semitone</note> into two equal parts with a compass. At the point that divides them equally, the second Enharmonic string will be placed in each Tetrachord; the third string will be the one that was the second in the Diatonic and Chromatic scales. Thus, we will have the minor Enharmonic Diesis <note>A very small interval, roughly a quarter-tone</note> in the lowest interval, the major one in the middle, and the Ditone <note>A major third</note> in the highest, according to the instructions of the original authors. It should also be noted that in the "conjunct" Monochord <note>original: *Synemmenon*, referring to a specific overlapping tetrachord in the Greek system</note> of the Chromatic genus, the three highest strings differ from the "disjunct" version, and the same applies to the Enharmonic; however, the outer strings always remain the same, regardless of the genus of harmony.

<margin>Method for constructing the Syntonic Monochord.</margin>
<margin>Why it is called Syntonic.</margin>
If we then wish to tune the Monochord of the most ancient Diatonic according to Ptolemy’s Syntonic Diatonic <note>Ptolemy’s "Intense" or "Tuned-up" scale, which uses ratios closer to pure major and minor thirds</note>, it is necessary (so to speak) to move the second, third, fifth, sixth, and eighth keys from their places. That is, they must be sharpened. Because of this effect, it perhaps acquired the name "Intense" from its author, Didymus. In each octave of the disjunct system, if you wish to do as described, it is necessary to sharpen *C-fa-ut*, *D-sol-re*, *F-fa-ut*, and *G-sol-re-ut*. In each octave of the conjunct system, sharpen *B-flat*, *C-fa-ut*, *D-sol-re*, *F-fa-ut*, and *G-sol-re-ut*. To do this, I follow this order: I divide the entire line into six parts, and moving toward the high end where the first part ends (starting from *A-re*), I mark *C-fa-ut*. I find its octave at the midpoint of the space between it and the highest point B, and I note it as *C-sol-fa-ut*. In the middle of these two strings, I place *F-fa-ut*; I find its higher octave at the point that divides the interval between it and B into two parts. Having done this, I divide the line between *C-fa-ut* and the highest point into nine parts; where the first part ends toward the high side, I mark *D-sol-re*. I find its octave in the high range by making two parts of the space between it and B; in the middle of that, I mark *d-la-sol-re*. I then find *G-sol-re-ut* by dividing the entire line between *C-fa-ut* and B into three equal parts; at the end of the first part toward the high side, I note *G-sol-re-ut*. I find its octave at the point that separates the space between it and B into two parts, marking it *g-sol-re-ut*. To find both versions of *B-flat*, I follow the same order as in the Diatonic and mark them in the same way; thus, I have finished the method for constructing Ptolemy’s Syntonic Monochord.

<margin>Method for constructing Aristoxenus’s Intense Monochord and the Tonic Chromatic.</margin>
<margin>The second square number is 9, and its double is 18.</margin>
<margin>The geometric instrument called the "Sixth" [Compass]. Zarlino claims in chapter 14 of the first part of his *Institutions* that its opening is exactly the 6th part of a circle, which is false. A warning.</margin>
I now come to show you the method you must follow in building what Aristoxenus calls the "Intense Diatonic," and afterward his "Tonic Chromatic." The distribution of frets on the Lute corresponds greatly with these; the frets of the Bowed Viola <note>Viola da gamba</note>—both modern instruments—have been distributed in imitation of these, where the whole tone is divided into two equal parts as said above. In this construction, the second square number (or its double, which is eighteen) is greatly necessary. We will use eighteen to more clearly and easily apply its power in the required distribution. I therefore divide the entire line A–B into eighteen parts, and moving toward the high end (starting from the bass), where that first part ends, I place the first fret. I divide the entire remainder again into the same number of parts, and on the same side, below the first, I place the second fret. With this same order, I continue distributing the space that remains below the frets until the twelfth fret; this leads me exactly to where the half-way point of the entire string ends. I find that I have divided the first and lowest octave into twelve equal Semitones and six Tones, as Aristoxenus called them. That no other number but eighteen is suitable for this is shown by this: seventeen is not suitable at all, because it would give us a smaller number of frets than we need; sixteen and fifteen would give even fewer. Likewise, nineteen is not suitable because it would give us a greater quantity, and even more so with twenty and twenty-one. Thus, eighteen is the most proper divisor. However, the same thing happens here that happens with a compass (the "Sixth") when trying to measure the circumference of a circle exactly six times with its own opening (which, as you know, is the distance from the center to the circumference). Therefore, I warn the industrious practitioner to use their discretion and diligence to overcome that small discrepancy between the measurer and the measured.

STR. I have understood everything quite well; but I pray you, remove another doubt of mine regarding this.

<margin>Which strings are stable, which are movable, and which are not entirely stable nor entirely movable.</margin>First, the outermost strings of any tetrachord in every genus and species of harmony are always the same, as you know; and for this reason, they are called **stable**. Whereas those that have the power to change the Diatonic into Chromatic, or into Enharmonic, and vice versa, are called **movable** due to their instability. Those that are common to two genera—such as the <term>Trite</term> and the <term>Parhypate</term> <note>The "third" and "next-to-lowest" strings.</note>, which remain the same in the Diatonic as in the Chromatic—are called **neither entirely stable nor entirely movable**. Those strings, therefore, which have the power to change the system from Diatonic to Chromatic are the third strings of each tetrachord. The occasion, then, that induced the ancient musicians to leave that specific space between the <term>Trite</term> and the <term>Paranete</term> in the Hyperbolaion tetrachord, rather than another, was taken from here: they added half of the difference found between the Diatonic <term>Paranete</term> and the <term>Nete</term> of the same tetrachord to the number denoting the <term>Paranete</term>. That difference is 144, the total being 288 (as you could see in the example). This half, added together as I have said to 2592, makes 2736; and with that number, they marked the Chromatic <term>Paranete</term> in that tetrachord, leaving the other strings with the same numbers and positions as in the Diatonic, as appears in the example; and they did the same in the other tetrachords.

<summary>Bardi explains Aristoxenus's theory of thirteen musical modes, which was based on dividing the octave into twelve equal semitones. This system prioritized human auditory perception of "affetto" (emotion) over rigid mathematical ratios, a stance that led to criticism from later theorists like Ptolemy.</summary>

# Ancient, & Modern [Music].
E 3
<meta>catchword: layer</meta>

The first point concerns the distribution of strings; the second involves the division of the whole tone into equal parts; and the third and final point concerns the number of modes <note>The "modes" refer to the ancient Greek musical scales.</note>. Thus, Ptolemy says the following: If a string, for example, is stretched over a flat surface and its half-length is divided with a compass into twelve equal parts, it will be clear that based on the sound produced by the whole string compared to its half—which constitutes an **octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note>—the eighth and ninth spaces will contain a larger portion of the sound than the first and second spaces. By using this method of measurement, if one were to continue too far, one of the final parts would contain four, five, or many more times the sound of the first and second parts. For no other reason do we see, as I have said, the frets on the neck of the **Lute** and the **Bowed Viol** becoming narrower and moving closer to one another as the sound of that same string becomes higher as it is shortened. Because a string stretched over a flat surface that was, for example, one **arm's length** <note>The "braccio" (arm) was a common Italian unit of measurement roughly equal to 23 inches.</note> long, would produce its higher octave from its half-point (which would be half an arm's length) every time it was struck together with the whole string or one similar to it. If it were two arms long, the higher octave would be one arm, and the lower would be four. Through this demonstration by Ptolemy, it appears that he has, as the proverb says, "arguments to spare"; however, the reality is not quite so.

<margin>Aristoxenus defended by the Author.</margin>
It happens that Aristoxenus never intended for frets to be distributed by first dividing the half-length of the string and line into twelve equal parts, as was said in the example of the Lute neck. Because Aristoxenus knew very well (as I have shown you) that he had to distribute the *quality* of the sound into equal parts, and not the *quantity* of the line, string, or space. In this, he was acting as a Musician concerning the **sonorous body** <note>The physical object producing the sound.</note>, and not as a simple Mathematician concerning **continuous quantity** <note>Physical measurement of length.</note>. Thus, he intended for the first fret to occupy the ninth part of the string's entire half—or we might say the eighteenth part of the whole string—and the second fret to occupy the ninth part of what remained of that first half after the first **semitone** <note>A half-step.</note> had been removed; and that the third fret should likewise occupy the ninth part of the space remaining in the half of the string after taking away the first and second semitones; or, let us say, the eighteenth part of the remaining whole, and so on for the others in order. This is always understood with the condition mentioned above: that the half of the string must be taken not at the point where it was first divided into two equal parts, but where it ended after subtracting the necessary number of semitones.

<margin>Method for placing frets correctly on the Lute and Viol.</margin>
And such, as I have said elsewhere, is the rule to be observed when one wishes to distribute frets accurately on instruments that require them, such as the Lute, the Bowed Viol, and others. Furthermore, Ptolemy rebukes him, claiming that a **whole tone** <note>A whole step.</note> cannot be divided into two equal parts; he wishes to prove this demonstratively in the following manner, saying: the whole tone is contained within the ratios of 18 and 16 units <note>This refers to the 9:8 ratio (18:16) of a whole tone.</note>, between which no other number falls except 17. This number 17, when considered as a divisor of the **nine-to-eight ratio** <note>original: "Sesquiottauo"</note>, divides it into unequal parts; for the part contained by the **sixteen-to-fifteen ratio** <note>original: "Sesquidecimasefta" [sic]</note> is larger than that contained by the **seventeen-to-sixteen ratio** <note>original: "Sesquidecimasettima"</note>, such an interval being 289 to 288. From this, it necessarily follows that the tone cannot be divided into two equal parts. Regarding this matter, no man is so slow-witted that he would doubt it according to the rules of arithmetic; but Aristoxenus did not speak or intend it so. Rather, he meant it in the manner I specifically demonstrated to you regarding the placement of frets on the Lute, in which one can truly divide any musical interval into as many equal parts as one wishes, not otherwise than by means of the **monochord** <note>A single-stringed instrument used for measuring musical intervals.</note>. For in 그act, the sound is considered by the Musician as **qualitative** and not as **quantitative**, even if

<margin>Regarding chapter four of the fifth [book].</margin>
Daniel Barbaro, in his commentary on Vitruvius, understands it to the contrary; and Ptolemy's demonstration is the same:

<margin>Comparisons.</margin>
one might say that between the lower terms of the octave, no other interval can be accommodated by means of numbers; nevertheless, between the **lowest note** <note>original: "Hypate"</note> and the **highest note** <note>original: "Nete"</note>, there are also, besides other strings, the **forefinger-note** <note>original: "Licanos"</note> and the **note-next-to-middle** <note>original: "Paramese"</note>, which give the third and the fifth to the low part, and the fourth and the sixth to the high part. Similarly, between the **low F** <note>original: "F faut"</note> and the **high f** <note>original: "f faut"</note> of the Lute, there is also (besides the tone divided into two equal parts) the **B-natural** <note>original: "h mi"</note> which separates it into two equal portions as has been said. Furthermore, if you have two strings, each two arms long, tuned in unison, every time you take one and a half arms from one and three-quarters of an arm from the other, these portions played together will undoubtedly produce an octave. Regarding the number of tones, what we have discussed above through the persona of Aristoxenus is so clear in itself that it faces no contradiction.

**STR.** This is all well and good, but who is there to persuade us to believe that in the time of Aristoxenus those modes were in use, separated from one another by a **minor semitone** as you have said?

**BAR.** Aristotle, regarding Philoxenus—who, as you will hear later, was the author of the **Hypodorian Mode**, the last to be discovered—and Ptolemy, in the tenth chapter of the second book, shows the intervals they maintained between them according to the constitution of their inventors.

**STR.** I marvel then at Ptolemy, that he would write so boldly against Aristoxenus, knowing how many volumes he had written on the faculty of Arithmetic and how valuable they were; having been, moreover, not only a student of Aristotle and a contemporary of Theophrastus, but having learned all the doctrine of Pythagoras from Xenophanes, the noble Pythagorean, in addition to what has been shown.

It argues that while math suggests intervals cannot be perfectly halved, the musician's "qualitative" approach allows for equal temperament and practical tuning.</summary>

# Dialogue on Music
A
<meta>catchword: than</meta>

<margin>Demonstration of the thirteen modes, according to the mind of Aristoxenus.</margin>

...you have shown me to be greatly in the wrong.

<margin>Plato, rebuked by Aristotle.</margin>
BAR. It is not at all surprising, as the same has happened among many others. What greater example can be cited than that which Aristotle first wrote regarding matters of philosophy against his divine teacher Plato, while the latter was still alive? It is true that Aristotle, as a friend of truth, wished (as was fitting for a philosopher) to have more respect for the truth than for his master, or for Socrates after him. Ptolemy also wrote against the opinion held by the Pythagoreans concerning the <term>Octave-plus-Fourth<note>original: "Diapason diatessaron," an interval consisting of eleven semitones.</note></term>; the opinion of this Ptolemy is refuted with lively arguments by Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>original: "Iacopo Fabro Stapulense," a French Renaissance humanist and theologian who wrote on music theory.</note>.

<margin>In chapter 24 of the third [book] of the Musical Elements.</margin>
STR. That is truly so; but let us look, please, at another matter concerning the distribution of the modes of Aristoxenus, which causes me great doubt.

BAR. Tell me what it is.

STR. You said above that Aristoxenus divided the <term>tetrachord<note>A scale of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth.</note></term> into sixty equal particles. In his <term>Intense Diatonic<note>original: "Diatonico Incitato," a specific tuning used in ancient Greek music theory where the intervals are adjusted for a sharper, more driven sound.</note></term>, he gave twelve of these parts to the first and lowest interval, twenty-four to the middle one, and the remainder to the highest. In this way, the <term>semitone<note>original: "Semituono"</note></term> did not occupy the full half of the <term>major second<note>original: "Sesquioctave and Tone" (ratio 9:8).</note></term>, but something less.

BAR. That is indeed the case.

STR. Now, for the sake of example, in the species of <term>octave<note>original: "Diapason"</note></term> found between E and E <note>original: "E lami," the note E in the medieval hexachord system.</note>, there are two tetrachords separated by the <term>whole tone of disjunction<note>The tone that separates two tetrachords to complete an octave.</note></term>. Each of these tetrachords would contain six of those parts that made up the number twelve. Thus, the one that divided that "tone of disjunction" into two equal parts—which would be the <term>Ionian mode<note>original: "Ionico"</note></term>—would necessarily mean that each of its adjacent extremes would be further from it than any other connected parts.

BAR. I like your doubt, for I see it is very close to true knowledge. But you must note that Aristoxenus did not divide one member and then the other in that way, but rather, as I have said, the entire body of the octave together. For this reason, if you remember the precise words I used above regarding his distributions, they were always qualified; that is, I said the <term>fourth<note>original: "Diatessaron"</note></term> was shaped according to his designs.

<margin>Fifths and Fourths altered in the distributions of Aristoxenus.</margin>
STR. Therefore, in his systems, are the <term>fifths diminished and the fourths augmented<note>original: "quinte diminuite, & superflue le quarte"</note></term>, just as they are on the Lute? And similarly between one and the other in relation?

BAR. Yes, sir—compared, however, to those that are not contained by the <term>ratio of 3:2<note>original: "Sesquialtera"</note></term> and the <term>ratio of 4:3<note>original: "Sesquiterza"</note></term>, assigned to us by Pythagoras as their true forms.

STR. Oh, this seems to me an impropriety quite unworthy of Aristoxenus; that he distributed the strings of his systems in such a way that one would continually have fifths and fourths outside of their true proportions.

<margin>Modern singing is little different from the distributions of Aristoxenus.</margin>
BAR. Do not be so quick to rebuke Aristoxenus, because I am here to defend him if necessary against all those who would speak against him; for he was truly one of the most judicious and learned musicians the world has ever had. But listen, please. How do you believe consonant intervals are sung today? I mean by the most excellent singers and those of refined hearing?

STR. I believe they are sung within their true proportions, even though artificial instruments—as you have clearly shown me—play them some further and some closer to those proportions.

<margin>Zarlino in chapter 45 of the second part of the [Harmonic] Institutions.</margin>
BAR. Which has consonant intervals closer to perfection: the Lute, or the keyboard instrument? Understanding "perfection" here to mean the forms previously mentioned.

STR. The Lute.

BAR. If I show you plainly that singing today is no less "imperfect" regarding the precision of intervals than instrument playing is, what will you say?

STR. This would be one of the newest things I could ever imagine; I cannot believe it in any way.

BAR. Now, take note. Will you grant me that in the diatonic genre used today, every musical interval is always sung with the same measure? And that the major third is consonant for the reasons said above, while the <term>ditone<note>A major third formed by two major whole tones (ratio 81:64), which sounds slightly dissonant compared to the "pure" major third (5:4).</note></term> is dissonant? And that the space contained by the whole tone is about half of one of our <term>commas<note>A very small musical interval, the difference between two slightly different tunings of the same note.</note></term> smaller than the 9:8 ratio?

STR. The reasons you have brought forward on this matter convince me to believe and say yes.

BAR. Since this is true, it is necessary that any Fourth, when sung according to modern practice, always becomes augmented, and every Fifth becomes diminished. I will prove this to you in this manner: Suppose we ascend in singing from <term>C<note>original: "C faut"</note></term> to <term>F<note>original: "F faut"</note></term>. I say that interval is then an augmented fourth. Because if one then ascends from there to <term>G<note>original: "G solreut"</note></term> with a space smaller than the 9:8 ratio (as has been said), it would follow that from C to G there would be a Fifth so diminished that it would be dissonant; because the 3:2 ratio exceeds the 4:3 ratio by exactly one 9:8 whole tone, as you know.

STR. I do not deny that the 3:2 ratio exceeds the 4:3 ratio by a whole tone; but...

# Ancient & Modern [Music]

...so that the note <term>C-faut<note>A specific pitch in the medieval hexachord system, corresponding to C.</note></term> is found in such a manner when singing, at the distance of an <term>imperfect Fifth<note>A fifth that has been narrowed or "tempered" from its pure mathematical ratio.</note></term> from <term>G-solreut<note>The note G.</note></term>. For by as much as the <term>Fourth<note>The interval of a fourth (Diatessaron).</note></term> that was sung was <term>superfluous<note>Augmented; larger than the perfect interval.</note></term> (as you said) from C-faut to <term>F-faut<note>The note F.</note></term>, by just as much can the <term>Tone<note>The interval of a whole step.</note></term> between F-faut and G-solreut be diminished; just as you said a moment ago when considering the Fifth in its true form, composed of a superfluous Fourth and a diminished Tone; and thus, between C-faut and G-solreut, it comes to contain a perfect Fifth within the <term>Sesquialtera<note>original: "Sesquialtera," the 3:2 ratio that defines a mathematically pure perfect fifth.</note></term> proportion.

BARDI: It is true that I said what you say; but in that instance, the excess of the Fourth was equal to the deficiency of the Tone, which does not happen here. Furthermore, if what you say were true—which it is in no way—it would follow that by then ascending from G-solreut to <term>c-solfaut<note>The note C, one octave higher than C-faut.</note></term> with a Fourth of the same measure as the first, one would not find a perfect and consonant <term>Octave<note>original: "Diapason."</note></term> between it and C-faut. This is impossible in the manner in which we sing today. Or truly, if it were so, it would be necessary to concede that the <term>Fourth<note>original: "Diatessaron."</note></term> sung from G-solreut to c-solfaut is of a different proportion and measure than the one previously between C-faut and F-faut; which is not appropriate to say in any way. It follows then, necessarily and contrary to common opinion, that <term>Fifths<note>original: "Quinte."</note></term> are sung diminished today, and <term>Fourths<note>original: "Quarte."</note></term> are sung superfluous from their true being. Because of this (as I said), from the Octave onwards, we come to sing almost every other interval outside of its true proportion; and consequently, they are unlike those contained by the <term>Senario<note>The "number of six," a concept from Gioseffo Zarlino where the first six integers define all primary musical consonants.</note></term> and by the <term>Syntono<note>The "Syntonic Diatonic" scale of Ptolemy, which was the theoretical basis for Renaissance vocal music.</note></term>. Although the public approves of them as perfect and is entirely satisfied by them—having never heard the true ones—they have lost any hope of being able to improve them. It could also be said that the intervals sung today are, by means of the inequality of the <term>semitones<note>Half-steps.</note></term>, more conforming and similar to those found in the <term>temperament<note>A system of tuning where intervals are slightly adjusted to allow for playing in different keys.</note></term> of keyboard instruments than to those of the <term>Lute<note>A fretted string instrument.</note></term>. I tell you further, that the Fifth is universally understood with more pleasure according to the measure given to it by <term>Aristoxenus<note>A Greek theorist who favored the judgment of the ear over mathematical ratios.</note></term> than within its primary form, the Sesquialtera. Nor do I truly believe this happens for any other reason than that bad habit has corrupted our senses. For the Fifth within the Sesquialtera ratio not only seems to be at the extreme height of where it can go, but rather seems to have a bit of hardness, if not to say (along with others of delicate hearing) harshness. Whereas in the manner of Aristoxenus, it seems that that little bit of deficiency gives it grace, and makes it become more according to the modern taste: soft and languid. I believe this happens, as I have said, for no other reason than being accustomed to hearing them continuously in such a form or similar. From this, one draws an important and effective argument to persuade us of what you will hear shortly in its proper place: that is, that we have learned to sing in this way from stringed instruments, and particularly from those that do not have frets, unlike the Lute and the <term>Viola<note>Specifically the viola da gamba, which uses gut frets.</note></term>.

STROZZI: This has been as dear and new a thing to me as anything I have ever heard in this genre; please, continue.

<margin>Warning.</margin>
BARDI: Now consider, from this abuse alone, the imperfection of the music of our times; and how much the general public is deceived, and how with such difficulty the truth of things can be known, and how little knowledge they have of true music. Until this day, they have not even known the size, let alone the quality and nature, of the singable and audible intervals, which are its simple elements and principles. These things, together with all the others belonging to the profession of Music (which are many), were understood by Aristoxenus and the majority of the ancient Musicians in supreme excellence. Besides, the perfection or imperfection of the intervals did not matter at all to the way of singing in those times, because they did not use them (as you will hear) in the manner that we do today.

<margin>Zarlino, in chapter 3 of the fourth part of his *Institutions*, says that Aristoxenus made 15 modes; and in chapter 16 of the 2nd part, he despises his distributions without any reason.</margin>
The quality of these intervals can still be considered, as I said, by the relationship of highness and lowness between one or another constitution of the thirteen modes that he made (and not fifteen, as others have said) when comparing this string to that one. For example, the <term>lowest note<note>original: "Proslambanomene," the lowest note of the Greek Greater Perfect System.</note></term> of the system of the <term>Phrygian mode<note>One of the ancient Greek musical scales or "tonoi."</note></term>, I say, is higher by a deficient <term>Fifth<note>original: "Diapente."</note></term> than that of the <term>Hypodorian<note>Another Greek mode, usually lower in pitch.</note></term>; or we might say that the <term>middle note<note>original: "Mese."</note></term> of the system of the <term>Hypolydian<note>A specific Greek mode.</note></term> is higher by a superfluous <term>Fourth<note>original: "Diatessaron."</note></term> than that of the Phrygian.

STROZZI: I have understood very well, and I remain completely satisfied. But tell me, for what reason is the deficient Fifth and the diminished Fourth tolerated, and not the contrary: the sharp Fifth and the flat Fourth? And furthermore, why does the Octave not suffer alteration, in this or that direction?

BARDI: I have already told you that the Fifth, with respect to bad habit, when it is in its true form, presents itself to our hearing as rather high (not to say, as others do, annoying) than otherwise. Now think how much more it would become so by stretching it further than what its Sesquialtera proportion contains. Furthermore, in the playing and singing of today, for the reason I have demonstrated to you, they cannot come about in any other way than that which you have seen above. As for why the Octave does not behave as either diminished or superfluous, this happens not only from its perfection, but from the fact that by taking it multiple times, it composes a consonance of the same quality. If one were to alter two of them in the high or low range and then join them together, the extremes would become intolerable. This does not happen with other consonances, because they do not compose anything other than dissonant intervals; and being as they are, the ear does not so easily perceive that small difference found between them.

<summary>Bardi argues that modern singing relies on tempered intervals borrowed from instruments rather than pure mathematical ratios, noting that listeners actually prefer these "imperfect" sounds over the "harsh" purity of the ancients. He critiques contemporary theorists like Zarlino for misunderstanding the Greek modes and explains why the Octave must remain pure while other intervals can be adjusted.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical dialogue between Bardi and Strozzi. Having previously discussed the mathematical ratios of intervals, they now shift to the historical classification of the Greek "Tones" (Modes) according to different schools of thought, specifically the Aristoxenians, Ptolemy, and Boethius.</meta>

# Dialogue on Music

<margin>In the ninth and last book where he treats of music.</margin>
STROZZI: You have satisfied me greatly; therefore, continue the begun reasoning regarding the <term>Tones<note>In this context, "Tones" refers to the ancient Greek musical modes or keys, rather than just a single interval.</note></term>, according to the opinion of the <term>Aristoxenians<note>Followers of Aristoxenus, an ancient theorist who argued that musical intervals should be judged by the ear rather than by strict mathematical ratios.</note></term>.

BARDI: By the followers of the said Aristoxenus, two others were added toward the <term>acute<note>Higher in pitch.</note></term> to his thirteen modes; the extreme notes of the <term>Diapason<note>The interval of an Octave.</note></term> of these modes fell outside the ordinary <term>System<note>The "Greater Perfect System," the standard range of notes in ancient Greek music theory.</note></term> in that direction; for which reason they were later refuted by many, of which Martianus Capella makes particular mention. For they considered that the human voice was divided into three parts: namely <term>grave<note>Low-pitched.</note></term>, acute, and middle; and that the number of thirteen could not well be distributed into three equal portions, and therefore they increased them to the number of fifteen. They gave the name of "Principal" to the five in the middle,
<margin>In Book 2, chapter ten of Glareanus, with the testimony of Apuleius in the first of the *Florida*.</margin>
which are the warlike **Dorian**, the varied **Hyastian**, the religious **Phrygian**, the simple **Aeolian**, and the plaintive **Lydian**. They gave the name of "<term>Plagal<note>Derived from the Greek "plagios" meaning side or oblique; these are the lower versions of the modes.</note></term>" to the five modes lower than these, denoting them with such names: **Hypodorian**, **Hypoastian**, **Hypophrygian**, **Hypoeolian**, and **Hypolydian**. The five modes higher than the principals they called "<term>Authentic<note>The "primary" or higher versions of the modes.</note></term>," distinguishing them thus: **Hyperdorian**, **Hyperiastian**, **Hyperphrygian**, **Hypereolian**, and **Hyperlydian**. By this order, the Principals were higher than the Plagals by a <term>Diatessaron<note>The interval of a Fourth.</note></term>, and by such an interval, they were found below the Authentics, so that from the Hypodorian to the Hyperdorian, the distance was a <term>minor Seventh<note>In this period, theorists often calculated distances by counting the tones and semitones between modes.</note></term>—or we might say five Tones or ten Semitones, which amounts to the same thing according to the usage of Aristoxenus. Their intention was greatly favored by having found that the extremes of the thirteen modes he made corresponded by an octave, and not by a seventh like those of Ptolemy. The highest of these, called the **Hypermixolydian**, was nothing other than the repetition of the **Hypodorian**. They did the same, then, to the Hypoastian and the Hypophrygian, by raising them an Octave to form the acute Hypereolian and the extremely high Hyperlydian; these were ordered and arranged in the manner seen here below in the Demonstration, distinguished by their names. After these came <term>Ptolemy<note>Claudius Ptolemy, the famous astronomer and music theorist who preferred a system of seven or eight modes.</note></term>, whose order and opinion—being very ingenious and difficult to understand well—we will reserve to demonstrate last. However, we will first speak of the opinion of <term>Boethius<note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose "De Institutione Musica" became the standard textbook for medieval music theory.</note></term>, as it is less difficult. He was of the opinion (even though such an opinion had been previously refuted by Ptolemy) that there were eight Tones. He further intended that the particular System of each should proceed from the grave to the acute by the same order and degrees, and with the same names of strings, as the natural and common system—which is that which serves the **Dorian** mode. He made the **Phrygian** one Tone higher than it, and the **Lydian** higher than the Phrygian by a similar interval. He further intended that their Plagals should correspond by a Fourth in the grave, that the **Mixolydian** should be a Semitone higher than the Lydian, and that the **Hypermixolydian**

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the exploration of Greek versus Latin (medieval) music theory, specifically transitioning from the Aristoxenian modes discussed on the previous page to the influential eight-mode system of Boethius and the species of consonances defined by Claudius Ptolemy.</meta>

# Ancient & Modern

<margin>In chapter 14 of the fourth [book of Boethius].</margin>
<margin>Zarlino in chapter 8 of the 4th [book] of the *Institutes*.</margin>
<margin>In the second [book] of the *Harmonics*, at the third [chapter].</margin>
<margin>Aristoxenus at the end of the third [book] of the *Elements*.</margin>

IN which demonstration, one sees clearly every minimal detail that Boethius considered regarding these Tones <note>original: "Tuoni"; refers here to the musical modes or scales</note>; as for example, it makes manifest what the particular species of the Octave <term>Diapason: the interval of an octave, composed of eight notes</term> of each mode is, and where it is located within its particular System <note>The Greater Perfect System, the standard framework of Greek music</note>, and between which strings. One also sees which modes are lower <note>original: "più gravi"</note> or higher <note>original: "più acuti"</note> than the others by a whole tone—which he calls a "Page" <note>original: "Pagina"; a term used in Boethius’s layout</note> in that place—or by a semitone—naming it then a "Verse" <note>original: "Verso"</note>. One likewise sees which of these Tones is the Right part and which is the Left; how the Lowest Note <term>Proslambanomene: the lowest string of the Greek musical system</term> marked in the Hypermixolydian with an ω <note>the Greek letter omega</note> is the Middle Note <term>Mese: the central tuning note of the system</term> of the Hypodorian marked with the same character; and that the Highest of the Extreme Notes <term>Netehyperboleon</term> of this [Hypodorian] noted with a Γ <note>the Greek letter gamma</note> is, conversely, the Middle Note of that [Hypermixolydian]. Furthermore, one sees that the system of the Dorian Tone is (according to what he says) distant from the Mixolydian by a Fourth <term>Diatessaron: the interval of a fourth</term> toward the low end, and by a Fifth <term>Diapente: the interval of a fifth</term> from the Hypermixolydian; besides many other important details omitted for brevity. 

Despite all this, there is no lack of doubt particularly concerning the characters <note>notational symbols</note> with which the ancient Greeks used to mark the strings of their songs, which will be cleared up shortly; moreover, the demonstration found in the text of Boethius does not agree in some parts regarding the pitch height and depth of the Tones with the words he uses to describe them. I strongly suspect this was a powerful reason why some less diligent—not to say less judicious—men have boldly claimed, perhaps for their own convenience, that the text in that place is corrupt; this is false. Rather, the demonstration is poorly guided and badly handled due to the lack of accuracy—not to mention the lack of understanding <note>original: "intelligenza"</note>, as would be more fitting—of those who in Venice in the year 1491 took care to print it. Boethius likely followed the advice of Alypius <note>A 4th-century Greek author who provided a detailed catalog of musical signs</note> regarding the number of Tones, even if he does not mention him; finding in him, as we will show in due place, the characters to distinctly mark the strings of each of these eight modes; in addition to seeing that with only seven modes, he would not have occupied (as he says) all fifteen strings of the System. Let this suffice for now regarding the understanding of the Tones according to the mind of Boethius.

To now properly understand the order and number of these according to the opinion of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, 2nd-century astronomer and music theorist</note>, retracing the argument a little, I say this: among the ancient Greek musicians, according to the authority of Ptolemy himself, the first of their seven species of the Octave was received as that contained between the strings B-natural <note>original: "h mi"</note> and B-natural; and for the first species of the four they had for the Fifth, they accepted that found between the string E <note>original: "Elami"</note> and B-natural; and for the first of the three species of the Fourth, they took that placed between B-natural and E. For the second species of the Octave, they accepted the interval contained by the strings C and C <note>original: "C faut" and "c solfaut"</note>; they said the third was between D and D; the fourth between E and E; the fifth between F and F; the sixth between G and G; and the seventh and last necessarily came to be contained between the string A <note>original: "alamire"</note> and the [higher] A. The three other species of the Fifth and the two of the Fourth were those which, ascending by conjunct steps toward the high end, followed the order of the first proposed ones, as seen noted in this example.

->Species of the Octave. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Of the Fifth. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Of the Fourth.<-

<margin>Order of the consonances <note>original: "consonãze"</note> according to the Greeks. Ptolemy in chapter five of the 2nd [book].</margin>

<image-desc>A musical diagram showing seven octave scales, four fifth-based scales, and three fourth-based scales, all ascending according to the Greek system described by Ptolemy.</image-desc>

The Latins after these received for the first species of the Octave that which is found between A and A; for the first of the Fifth, that which is between B-natural and E; and for the first of the Fourth, that which is between B-natural and E; the other species following by descending through conjunct steps; and such was the order of their intervals, if by them we wish to understand what Boethius wrote of them; and the example is this.
