# Dialogue on Music

<margin>
Zarlino is of the opposite opinion in the same place. <note>Refers to Gioseffo Zarlino, the most influential music theorist of the Renaissance and Galilei’s former teacher, with whom he often disagreed.</note>
</margin>
And although some have believed and said that these proceed in the opposite way to those of the Greeks—doubting perhaps that Boethius had understood how the lower species of the <term>Diapason: the interval of an octave</term> could serve the higher Tone, and the higher species the lower—we will show them that it is not so. It is indeed true that in the order of numbering the consonances, Boethius appears to some to have taken no account of naming the <term>Semidiapente: a diminished fifth or "false" fifth</term> which is found between F-fa-ut and B-mi <note>original: "F faut & h mi"; F and B-natural, forming a tritone or diminished fifth</note>, as the fourth species of the <term>Diapente: the interval of a fifth</term>. In this regard, it is likely and reasonable that Boethius intended for the <term>Hypate Hypaton: the lowest note of the Greek tetrachord system</term> to correspond by an octave with the <term>Trite synemmenon: a specific note in the "soft" or "conjunct" Greek tetrachord</term>. This is because each of his Tones, as you have been able to see in the Demonstration, encompasses both Systems <note>The "Greater Perfect System" and the "Lesser Perfect System" of Greek theory</note>. Furthermore, regarding the naming of these species applied by us to modern practice, proceeding from high to low in this order: *mi, mi; la, re; sol, ut;* and *fa, mi*—or rather *fa, fa*—he undoubtedly understood them in his great intellect. There have been other moderns who have called this species of the Fifth the second, even though Boethius called it the Fourth, and others something else, according to their various designs. They say the first species of the Octave is between A-re and A-la-mi-re <note>A to A</note>; the first of the Fifth between D-sol-re and A-la-mi-re <note>D to A</note>; and that of the <term>Diatessaron: the interval of a fourth</term> between said D-sol-re and G-sol-re-ut <note>D to G</note>, following the other species by joint degrees toward the high notes. Others have spoken differently as it suited them, without bringing any evidence of the truth other than their own opinions; and all say they have imitated Boethius. It must be that the text from the editions of Basel, Paris, and the one named above—despite all the diligence used to see it—has not come to our notice; though I have also seen it in manuscript in various famous libraries.

**STR.** <note>Bardi's interlocutor, Piero Strozzi</note> For what reason did the ancient Greeks not want to accept as the first species of their Octave, Fifth, and Fourth, that which begins on the very low <term>Proslambanomene: "the added note," the lowest string of the ancient Greek musical system</term>, which was accepted later (according to the opinion of some) by the Latins as you have said?

**BAR.** <note>The main speaker, Count Giovanni de' Bardi</note> I never said that the Latins accepted as the first species of any of their consonances the one that begins on the *Proslambanomene*. Others are of that opinion, which I do not know where it is founded; but I do say that if you observe the order of the species of consonances according to the opinion of the Greeks, you will find that they agree with those of the Latins.

**STR.** I do not know how this can be, given that you say their first species of the Octave is that which is found between B-mi and B-mi <note>original: "h mi & h mi"; the natural B</note>, and [others say] between A and A; furthermore, those of the Greeks, starting from the low notes, go by joint degrees proceeding toward the high, while those of the Latins, departing on the contrary from the high, go toward the low.

<margin>
The order of consonances according to the Greeks and Latins is the same.
</margin>
**BAR.** That is all quite right; now pay attention, please. In the Demonstration that you will see shortly of the Tones according to the mind of Ptolemy, the species of the Octave found between B-mi and B-mi—taken by the Greeks as the first and which serves the Mixolydian Tone—matches string for string with the one that was likewise known by the Latins by the same name in the Dorian mode, and so with the others in order. In this way they agree very well together; and that little difference between them regarding the size of the interval arises from nothing else but the diversity of their goals in applying this or that species of Octave to one or another System. One could also consider the two extreme strings of this Octave to serve the Hypodorian Mode, but among those of the Dorian System. The ancient Greek musicians always accustomed themselves to begin numbering the strings of the Systems from the high, coming toward the low. Therefore, they said the first species of the Octave was that which served the Mixolydian Tone, and the others in descending order; and they did likewise for the other species of their consonances. The reason they did not accept as the first species of the Octave and other consonances those beginning on the lowest string, the *Proslambanomene*, was so as not to interfere in any genus of harmony or different distribution of species, neither among the "fixed" strings nor the "movable" strings of their <term>tetrachords: groups of four notes that formed the building blocks of Greek scales</term>; besides it being the last in their numbering. And although, as has been said, it does not fall between the strings that enclose or are enclosed within the tetrachords, it is not for this reason unstable in each Greater and Perfect System, for the reason that will be stated below. To tell you further, not only was this string the last added to the Cithara, but it was added after they were ordered and distributed into tetrachords; and the reasons for its addition were two or three of not much importance. The first of these derived from nothing else than so that the <term>Mese: the "middle" note and primary tuning reference</term> would come in the middle of that System according to its name; without the help of that [lowest] part, this was impossible. The second reason was so that the extreme high string and the extreme low string would resonate as a <term>Disdiapason: a double octave</term> or <term>Fifteenth: the same as a double octave</term>; so that it would not lack any of the intervals they reputed to be consonant; and so that the *Mese* would correspond with the extremes as an Octave. I said reasons of "not much importance" because, even without it, every species of Octave appeared in the System in the same order and without any impediment; and consequently every mode and Tone, if not perfectly in practice regarding their entire constitutions, at least in potential regarding the species of the Octave. Respect for this must be the principal reason why the Lyre and Cithara—which were the same thing to them according to some of the best [authors]—having been received from Mercury (its author) in those early times with only four strings, increased in the process of time to the number of fifteen.

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the dialogue between Strozzi and Bardi, moving from a discussion of musical modes and the theories of Boethius and Zarlino to a specific investigation into the nature of ancient stringed instruments—specifically whether the Lyre and the Kithara were distinct or identical.</meta>

# Ancient & Modern Music

**STR.** Are you then of the opinion that the Lyre and the **Cithara** <note>Also spelled Kithara; a professional version of the lyre with a wooden sounding box</note> were the same instrument among the ancient Greek and Latin musicians?

<margin>In the fourth book.</margin>
**BAR.** I have almost no doubt of it, given the many points of agreement among authorities; even though Pausanias says that the Lyre was invented by Mercury and the **Cithara** by Apollo.

**STR.** I judge this opinion of yours to be quite contrary to the common view.

<margin>Zarlino in the *Institutions*, chapter 3 and 4 of the 2nd part, and in the first of the 4th.</margin>
**BAR.** I hold for certain that you will agree, as will anyone else who has the patience to listen to me.

**STR.** It will be most pleasing to me to understand this matter.

<margin>In how many ways the Lyre was named by the Greeks.</margin>
**BAR.** I will briefly bring forward the most famous authorities I have gathered in favor of one side and the other; leaving it then to you and anyone else of sound mind to judge what seems most appropriate. Listen then. Among the Greeks, one finds five names for musical instruments (among many others they have with different meanings) which, from what can be gathered from their writings, appear to mean the same thing: and these are **Lyre**, **Chelys**, **Cithara**, **Cethra**, and **Phorminx**. Primarily, there is no one who doubts that the **Lyre** and the <term>Chelys: originally meaning tortoise, referring to the shell used as a resonator</term> are the same instrument; and that both are likewise the same as what the Latins later called the <term>Testudo: the Latin word for tortoise or a vaulted shell</term>. Likewise, they maintain that the **Cithara** and the **Cethra** are the same thing; the Poet <note>Referring to Homer</note> calling it most often by the former name, and the Orator by the latter. <margin>Suidas.</margin> That the **Phorminx** is then the same instrument as the **Cithara** is clear; for <note>original: "Suida"</note> Suidas affirms this, writing: "*Phorminx*, that is, *Cithara*." <margin>Homer.</margin> Furthermore, Homer in the *Odyssey* relates that when the banquet servant gave the **Cithara** to Phemius, he added these words: "Certainly he **Phormizon**" <note>original: "Formison"; a Greek verb meaning to play the phorminx</note>. <margin>Didymus.</margin> Here Didymus the interpreter declares *Phormizon* to mean "playing with the **Cithara**." Therefore, if we now demonstrate that the **Lyre** is the same thing as the **Phorminx**, there will be no doubt that the **Lyre** is the same as the **Cithara**. <margin>Horace.</margin> Horace can sufficiently teach us this. <margin>Pindar.</margin> For having translated almost word for word from Pindar that song of his which begins:
> O Clio, what man, or what Hero will you begin to celebrate with your **Lyre**, or with the shrill <term>Tibia: an ancient reed instrument similar to an oboe</term>?
Where Pindar, instead of **Lyre**, says: <term>Anaxiphorminges: Greek for "lords of the lyre"</term>. From this, one clearly recognizes that Horace calls "**Lyre**" that which Pindar first called "**Phorminx**." But from the words of Pindar himself, this same conclusion can easily be gathered; for a little further down he writes:
> We shall take up the **Lyre**.
In which passage Pindar calls "**Lyre**" that same instrument which above he called "**Phorminx**."

**STR.** I grant you that the **Phorminx** was the same thing as the **Lyre**, but it does not necessarily follow that the **Lyre** was the same as the **Cithara**; the name could easily be ambiguous.

**BAR.** I will set aside the commentator on Pindar, who in several places uses "**Lyre**" and "**Cithara**" interchangeably; because I can prove this same point to you more clearly with the authority of more serious writers. First, with the authority of Xenophon, who in his book *On Household Management* says: "Those who first learn to play the **Cithara**, spoil the **Lyre**." <margin>In the first *Alcibiades*.</margin> Furthermore, Socrates in Plato says that Alcibiades learned to play the **Cithara**, and shortly thereafter, he calls what he had previously termed "**Cithara**" a "**Lyre**." <margin>Lyre and cithara being the same thing.</margin> But why do I go on gathering arguments in favor of this side, when with a single witness worthy of faith—and this is Suidas—I can make you see the truth face to face? He uses these words: "The **Cithara** is a musical instrument, which is otherwise called a **Lyre**." Can anything be said more plainly and openly than this? Now hear, on the contrary, what I have gathered in favor of the other side, which seems in a certain way to persuade us otherwise. Plato, in the third book of the *Republic*, says: "The **Lyre**, then, remains, and the **Cithara** is useful in the city, and the **Syrinx** <note>Panpipes</note> is convenient in the pastoral countryside." Athenaeus, at the end of the fourth book: "The **Magadis** is an instrument like the **Cithara**, the **Lyre**, and the **Barbitos**." And in the same place, citing a certain Anaxilas from a work titled *The Lyre-Maker*, he lists two among others in which, in the same order, one reads words that correspond to these: "But I had suspended **Barbitoi**, **Trichords**, **Pectides**, **Citharas**, **Lyres**, and **Scindapsoi**." Pollux, in the fourth book: "Of those [instruments] that are played, there will be the **Lyre**, the **Cithara**, and the **Barbitos**." <margin>In the dialogue *Laches*.</margin> Plato, in another place that troubles us more, always speaks of the **Cithara** nobly, and on the contrary treats the **Lyre** as an instrument for pastime and play. Thus it seems impossible to many that, since the **Cithara** is the same as the **Lyre** (as shown above), it could have been spoken of by so many in the manner you have heard. Nevertheless, by merely considering the diversity of names by which we call our modern keyboard instrument, every doubt that the words of these grave and famous writers might bring is easily removed. As everyone knows, it is called by us by the names of <term>Clavicordo: Clavichord</term>, <term>Harpicordo: Harpsichord</term>, <term>Clavicimbalo: Clavicymbal</term>, <term>Spinetta: Spinet</term>, <term>Buonaccordo: A small virginal</term>, <term>Archicimbalo: A complex microtonal keyboard</term>, and others; only because of the diversity in the quantity and quality of the strings and registers, and the size and shape of the instrument. Yet in its essence, one is the same thing as the other, and he who knows how to play one, likewise plays the other. Nor would any person of sound mind, comparing a mellow <term>Grauicimbalo: Harpsichord/early piano type</term> to a shrill Spinet, fail to judge the latter, in comparison to the former, a thing for pastime and play; and so too when comparing an organ...

It is seen, moreover, that the **Viola da gamba**, the **Harp**, and many of the wind instruments that we use every day in grave and important musical concerts, are also used for pastime in balls and dances; but among the craftsmen who play them in one way or the other, one can consider there to be the same difference that Plato places between the dignity of the **Cithara** and the play of the **Lyre**.

<margin>In the eighth book of the *Politics*.</margin>
It may very well be, too, that when Xenophon says that those who learn to play the **Cithara** spoil the **Lyre**, he means to imply that the children of his time, in wanting to learn to play the **Cithara**, first practiced on the **Lyre**; as it was of a more convenient shape and also of a sound suited to that tender age due to its high pitch or other factors. And so, through their inexperience in those beginnings, they came to spoil the strings with both the plectrum and their nails; not unlike what happens daily to our own children, who, in wanting to learn to play the **Organ**, or let us say the **Harpsichord**, most often practice on a **Spinet** or on a small **Buonaccordo** <note>A small, portable keyboard instrument similar to a virginal</note>, so as not to stretch the outer fingers of the short hands of children of that tender age to an octave on a large instrument. Thus, one could still truly say today, for the same reason, that those who learn to play the **Organ** or the **Harpsichord** spoil the **Spinet** and the **Buonaccordo**. In this sentiment, the opinion of Pausanias also concurs without being distorted, when he says that Apollo found the **Cithara** and Mercury the **Lyre**; because the latter found it in his childhood as an instrument suitable for such an age, and the former after having become a man. Or perhaps we want to say that the invention of the **Cithara** was attributed to Apollo and the **Lyre** to Mercury to distinguish the status of the persons. Aristotle also agrees with this opinion of ours in treating the diversity of harmonies, as you will hear below; and I will tell you in its proper place what the difference really was (if indeed there was any) between the **Cithara** and the **Lyre**.

**STR.** You have greatly satisfied me; therefore, if it pleases you, you may return to where you left off and follow the discourse begun concerning the Tones and modes of the ancient Greek musicians, according to the mind of Ptolemy; and afterwards, pray excuse me.

**BAR.** I was telling you above that the ancient musicians went about little by little increasing the strings of their **Cithara** and **Lyre** up to the number of fifteen; which they distributed in the manner seen ordinarily in the <term>Great Perfect Disjunct System: the standard 15-note scale of Greek music theory</term> of the Dorian mode. With this quantity, they remained content for many, many years, knowing them to be conveniently suited to effectively express any human affection.

<margin>Proslambanomenos, what it signifies.</margin>
I told you further that the meaning of the name of the lowest string, <term>Proslambanomene: Greek for "the added note," the lowest note in their scale</term>, the last added to the Perfect System, and also the last in numbering them according to Greek usage (though first for the Latins and in the modern way), meant the same in that language as it does in ours: "Added," or "taken besides," or "at an advantage." This meaning, as I said, seems to warn us that this was done not out of any necessity, but by choice. The reason why it is called "stable" in any Great Perfect System arises from the constant correspondence it has in each genus and species of harmony with the **Nete hyperboleon** <note>The highest note of the Greek scale</note>. Thus, since the **Nete** is stable—which is the nature of all the extreme strings of any <term>tetrachord: a scale of four notes</term>—the **Proslambanomene** is also necessarily stable, because it is continually found at the distance we have mentioned from that and the other stable strings. Furthermore, the Great Disjunct System, of which examples are given by infinite writers, has its strings tuned, as I said above, according to the Dorian Tone and mode.

<margin>Dorian Harmony, why it was more reputed than others.</margin>
Its harmony was more reputed, approved, and prized than any other by every ancient musician, poet, and philosopher. This, if I am not mistaken, arose primarily from nothing other than the fact that the strings in its system were tuned according to the Tone in which one commonly speaks without violence. Nor can the human voice more comfortably sing all the strings of an entire system than those tuned according to this Dorian mode. Its excellence has caused it to be continually brought forward as an example by every famous man who has written on the faculty of music, which has not happened with the others. Nor should we wonder at this, since the very high Tones and the too low ones were rejected by the Platonists, especially in their well-ordered Republic, for the former being plaintive and the latter mournful; and they received only those of the middle, just as occurs among them regarding numbers and rhythms.

<margin>The Platonists refute harmonies that are too high or too low.</margin>
<margin>Rhythm, that is, dance and body movement.</margin>
Their opinion was later refuted by Aristotle, who said that the relaxed harmonies are not to be despised with respect to men of age, who, because of their years, cannot sing the "tightened" <note>High-pitched</note> harmonies. The high ones, then, like the Lydian, he grants to children, to produce in them, he says, both ornament and discipline at the same time.

<margin>At the end of the *Politics*.</margin>
From this, an argument is made—even if there were no other meeting of authority on this—that the songs of the ancients were truly sung according to the sound of the strings in which they were written by their composer; and the opposite happens today with ours.

<margin>Ptolemy. Boethius. Guido of Arezzo. Franchino.</margin>
One has particularly the example of the Dorian Tone System, and not the others, in Ptolemy, in Boethius, in the *Introductory* of Guido of Arezzo, in the *Theory* and *Practice* of Franchino <note>Franchino Gaffurio</note>, in the *Music* of Glarean, in the *Harmonic Institutions* of Zarlino, and finally in the *Timaeus* of Plato there is a hint of it

<margin>Glareanus. Zarlino. Plato.</margin>
...born for the greater and better part in the **Ditonic Diatonic** species <note>The "Ditonic Diatonic" refers to the Pythagorean tuning system where the whole tone is a 9:8 ratio (sesquioctave) and the semitone is a limma</note>, as are all the others mentioned; besides many other passages from other authors: the species of the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The interval of an octave</note> of this mode is the fourth, which is placed, as I said, between the string of **E-la-mi** and **e-la-mi**; in which place
<margin>Why Boethius varies the species of the Octave from the Greeks.</margin>
**Boethius** placed that mode an interval of a <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>original: "Sesquiottauo"; the 9:8 ratio representing a whole tone</note> lower than this one, for no other reason than to give room for the **Hypermixolydian** tone. This was something he could not do except by assigning to the **Dorian** mode that which **Ptolemy** first assigned to the **Phrygian**. In these two tones, comic and tragic personages spoke continuously, as did those of **Satire**, reciting their poems to the sound of the <term>Tibia</term> <note>An ancient double-reed pipe, often called an aulos</note> on the theater stage. Above this tone, there were three higher ones, and it had three lower ones beneath it. The three higher ones were the **Phrygian**, the **Lydian**, and the very high **Mixolydian**; which were distributed under these conditions. By raising the pitch by a sesquioctave interval from the ordinary <term>disjunct system</term> <note>original: "Systema disgiunto"; the Greek Greater Perfect System</note>, in which as I said the **Dorian** mode was sung—discovered by the great **Thamyris of Thrace**—one had the **Phrygian**. The inventor of this was
<margin>Thamyris of Thrace finds the Dorian harmony.</margin>
**Marsyas**, or **Massyas** as we might call him, son of **Hyagnis the Phrygian**; and following the opinion of **Aristotle**, teacher of the great **Olympus**. This **Marsyas** was the first who played the <term>Piffero</term> <note>A generic term for a pipe or flute</note> with finger-holes, these not having been known before him; he even played two of them with a single breath, and he was
<margin>Marsyas finds the Phrygian.</margin>
likewise the first of all to mix the low sound with the high. To the sound of this instrument, **Elegies** were later sung in an orderly manner. The chorus of **Tragedy** made much use of the **Phrygian** harmony, and likewise of the **Lydian**; for the latter is proper to the angry man and to the
<margin>In the eighth book of the Politics.</margin>
<margin>Which harmonies the chorus of tragedy used.</margin>
suffering man who shrieks; and the former to him who exults with joy. These were repudiated by **Socrates** as being fit to introduce affects into a man that were not suitable for him. For this reason, he also repudiated the **Lydian** harmony and the low **Ionian** <note>original: "Hyastia graue"</note>, as being relaxed and proper to drunkards; not when they are infuriated, but when they are languid. He allowed the **Dorian** and the **Phrygian** as being useful for war. I say the species of the octave of the **Phrygian** mode is found between **D-sol-re** and **d-la-sol-re**, and that its <term>Media</term> <note>The "mese" or central pitch of the mode</note> must necessarily be **G-sol-re-ut**, whereas that of the **Dorian** is **a-la-mi-re**. By raising the system again by a whole tone more than that which serves the **Phrygian** mode, one will have that of the **Lydian** tone, of which **Amphion** was the inventor; although others say
<margin>Amphion, inventor of the Lydian harmony.</margin>
<margin>In the Paeans.</margin>
**Melanippides**, and others **Torebus**. **Pindar** maintains that **Antippus** was the one who first taught the **Lydian** harmony at the wedding of **Niobe**. It was customary in this mode to sing **Epithalamiums** <note>Wedding songs</note> in particular; and it is that which was called by **Plato** the "Intense Lydian," perhaps to distinguish it from its relaxed plagal form. The species of its octave is contained between **C-fa-ut** and **c-sol-fa-ut**, and its middle note is **f-fa-ut**. **Plutarch** recounts, according to the mind of **Aristoxenus**, that the first use of such a harmony was born from a certain mournful event; and that before all others, **Olympus**
<margin>Olympus, at the death of Python, sings the Lydian mode on the tibia.</margin>
at the death of **Python**, sang funeral verses on the <term>Tibia</term> according to the **Lydian** custom. Of this mode, **Plato** speaks thus in describing its nature, speaking ill of it: "the **Lydian** harmony is high, angry, and shrill; and is at the same time suited to lamentations." Now, this system, transposed higher by a minor semitone and a <term>limma</term> <note>original: "Lemma"; a Pythagorean small semitone</note>, will give the strings tuned according to the **Mixolydian** mode; which is full of much melodic affect, and is very suitable for tragedies. Its middle note is **e-la-mi**, and its octave species is that found between **b-mi** and **b-mi**. The names of the three
<margin>Plagal modes, why they are so called.</margin>
tones beneath the **Dorian** are these: **Hypolydian**, **Hypophrygian**, and **Hypodorian**. These were called <term>Plagal</term> <note>original: "Plagij"</note>, for being proper to those who fear and who pray supplicantly; and they are created and formed in this manner. By lowering the system of the **Lydian** tone by a <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>A perfect fourth</note>, or by a semitone from that of the **Dorian**, one will have the **Hypolydian** mode; discovered along with the <term>Orthian law</term> <note>A specific type of high-pitched nomos or musical rule</note> (from which derived the **Trochee**, the giver of the sign) by **Polymnastus of Colophon**.
<margin>Polymnastus, inventor of the Hypolydian harmony.</margin>
In his songs, he sought more strings than any other musician of his time. The species of its octave is between **F-fa-ut** and **f-fa-ut**, and its middle note is **b-mi**. If one again lowers the system of the **Phrygian** mode by a fourth, or let us say by a tone below that of the **Hypolydian** (which amounts to the same thing regarding the effect), one will have the **Hypophrygian** mode, called by **Plato**
<margin>The invention of the Hypophrygian harmony, unknown to the Author.</margin>
the "Relaxed Ionian" <note>original: "Hyastio rimesso"</note>; the author of which, despite the diligence used, I have not yet been able to find. Its octave is contained between the string of **G-sol-re-ut** and **g-sol-re-ut**, and its middle note is **c-sol-fa-ut**. Finally, if we transpose the system of the **Dorian** tone to the bass by a fourth, or by a tone below the **Hypophrygian**, we will have the **Hypodorian** mode, lower than any other; the invention of which is attributed to **Philoxenus**. This tone was the last to come into use.
<margin>Philoxenus, inventor of the Hypodorian harmony, recently discovered.</margin>
Its octave is contained between **a-la-mi-re** and **A-la-mi-re**, and its middle note is consequently **d-la-sol-re**. Such were really the number and measure of the tones and modes of the ancient Greek musicians according to the opinion of **Ptolemy**. Among them all, there were no more than seven, as there were no other new species of the octave to occupy. They required twenty-one notes; and repeating the same toward the low or toward the high—such as for example that of the **Hypermixolydian**
<margin>In chapter 10 and 11 of the second book.</margin>
refuted by **Ptolemy**—resulted in going outside the natural and common system. Furthermore, in the demonstration by **Boethius**, the same occurred even to the **Mixolydian** tone, because he differed from **Ptolemy** in considering the strings of the octave of these tones; which is a matter worthy of no small consideration.

# Ancient and Modern [Music]

<margin>
Zarlino <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), a famous music theorist and Galilei’s former teacher, with whom he often publicly disagreed.</note> claims that according to Ptolemy there were 8 Tones, which Ptolemy never said; in fact, he rejected the eighth mode in chapter 3 of the 4th book of his instructions.
</margin>
According to *Ptolemy*, they sought the extremes of their Systems <note>original: "Constitutioni"; refers to the formal structure of the scales.</note>, both conjunct and disjunct in each genre of harmony, using no more than twenty-one notes as I have said, and there were twenty-seven differences between them. Thus, the *Mixolydian*, being higher than any other, was sung a Semitone above the *Lydian*, and the Lydian a Whole Tone above the *Phrygian*. The *Dorian* was sung a Whole Tone below the Phrygian and a fourth <note>An interval of four scale degrees.</note> above the *Hypodorian*. A Semitone and a fourth below the Lydian was the *Hypolydian*; descending a Whole Tone below this and a fourth below the Phrygian was the *Hypophrygian*. Finally, the *System* of the *Hypodorian* was reached by lowering that of the Dorian by a fourth, or indeed the *Hypophrygian* by a Whole Tone. According to *Ptolemy*, the Prince of Mathematicians, these were the true and legitimate intervals by which the *Tones* of the ancient Greek musicians were lower or higher than one another, along with the strings upon which they were sung. The description is as follows; to make it understandable, I have reduced it to the easiest method I could imagine. It is primarily to be considered that just as the Middle Note <note>original: "Media"; the *Mese*, the central structural pitch of the Greek scale.</note> and the species of the Octave <note>original: "Diapason".</note> of each *System* is different, so too the entire order of the scale—regarding the steps of ascending and descending from start to finish by Tones and Semitones—is different. This leads to that common proverb they used, which said:

<margin>
In chapter 10 of the second [book]. Aristoxenus in the second.
</margin>
<margin>
Proverb of the ancient Greek musicians.
</margin>
"We shall pass from the Dorian harmony to the Phrygian"—meaning from serious matters to the ridiculous. This derived not only from the opposite nature of the harmonies and Tones but from the contrary way of ascending and descending through the steps of Tones and Semitones in each. For by those same steps that the Dorian descended, the Phrygian ascended, as can be clearly seen in their examples.

<margin>
Tones, called by various names and why.
</margin>
The arrangements of these were named by the ancient Greeks for various reasons with these three names, differing in sound and sense: Tones, Tropes, and Ethoi <note>original: "Iti"; from the Greek *ethos*, referring to the moral or emotional character of music.</note>.

<margin>
Why called Ethoi.
</margin>
They were called *Ethoi* because they demonstrated character; *Tropes*, because in passing from one to another the *System* was turned <note>original: "si rivolgeua"; "trope" comes from the Greek *tropos*, meaning a turn or shift.</note>; and *Tones*, in respect to their highness and lowness of pitch.

<margin>
Why called Tropes.
</margin>
They demonstrated character because some of them (especially through the example of those who performed them) induced grave and severe thoughts in the listeners, while others induced soft and effeminate ones, and the listeners became such upon hearing them. The *System* was "turned" every time one passed from one to another, as for example in moving from the Dorian to the Phrygian. For those same intervals that the latter used in proceeding from low to high, the former (as has been said) used when moving from high to low.

<margin>
Why called Tones.
</margin>
They also differed in highness and lowness, given that the Phrygian was a Whole Tone higher than the Dorian, and was found a similar interval below the Lydian. To this we add another consideration: they were called Tones and not Semitones because the three principal and most ancient ones—the Dorian, Phrygian, and Lydian just named—were distant from one another by a Whole Tone. They acquired this name before the other four came to be known. Yet it would not have been inappropriate to call them Tones even after all seven were in use; for among the intervals by which their Systems proceeded from low to high or vice versa, they contained a smaller Heptachord <note>original: "Epthacordo"; a seven-note scale fragment.</note> of the manner seen noted here, in which the Semitone is counted only twice and the Whole Tone four times. Furthermore, this arrangement is more natural and closer to the perfection of the consonant interval than the other.

<margin>
Order of the modes.
</margin>
<image-desc>A musical staff showing a series of notes with arcs above and below indicating melodic intervals. The left side contains letters representing musical pitches or modes. The text to the right identifies this as the "Order of the modes."</image-desc>

STR. I have always heard from scientific and learned men that understanding well how the Tones of the ancient musicians stood and were sung, and how many they were in number—not to mention the many other details they considered—is one of the most difficult things to know and understand in all of music. I now see by experience that this is so. Despite all your diligence, I am not yet entirely satisfied or capable of grasping what you have said and shown me with examples. Therefore, please do not find it burdensome to answer what I shall ask you, so that I may be fully satisfied; and please excuse my persistent and perhaps impertinent requests.

BAR. Speak freely, for I will not fail you except where my knowledge does not reach.

STR. I understand primarily that Ptolemy himself says that the specific Middle Note <note>The *Mese*.</note> of each Tone is what I am about to tell you, applying his words to modern practice: the Middle Note of the Mixolydian is d <note>d la-sol-re in the hexachord system.</note>, that of the Lydian is c <note>c sol-fa-ut.</note>, of the Phrygian is b-natural <note>h mi.</note>, of the Dorian is a <note>a la-mi-re.</note>, of the Hypolydian is G <note>G sol-re-ut.</note>, of the Hypophrygian is F <note>F fa-ut.</note>, and finally of the Hypodorian is E <note>E la-mi.</note>.

BAR. You speak very well, and you are entirely right; you will find these same notes in my description if you consider it more carefully.

STR. I cannot find them without your help.

<margin>
In chapter 11 of the 3rd [book].
</margin>
BAR. Here they are. When Ptolemy describes the order of the Middle Notes of the Tones in the manner you recited, he considers all seven within the natural and ordinary *System*. But in the order I explained to you, I consider each of them within their specific...

...constitution: which in my example you will find have no contradiction among themselves. **STR.** I understand it very well now; but Ptolemy further requires that the Systems be distant, following one after the other in the order you have shown me, by Ditones and Semiditones; and you instead have mentioned Whole Tones and Semitones; I do not know how such a difference can exist between you.

<margin>
Ditones and Semiditones, as considered within the Tones.
</margin>

**BAR.** I mentioned those smaller intervals <note>Whole tones and semitones.</note> as being more necessary for the understanding of those Tones I seek to give you; and if you had wished to exert your intellect a little, you would have quite clearly found in my demonstration the Ditones <note>An interval of two whole tones, a major third.</note> and the Semiditones <note>An interval of a tone and a half, a minor third.</note> as well, between this Tone and that one. This is found simply by having considered and compared each particular string of one System with that of another: as for example, the B-mi <note>original: "h mi"; the note B-natural.</note> of the Dorian with that of the Phrygian, or the latter with that of the Lydian. But the whole of one compared with the whole of another—or any part of them we might choose—leaving aside the particular names of the strings according to modern practice, is truly no more than a Whole Tone or a Semitone, as I said before, between those that are joined. This diversity seen in the example I gave you arises from nothing other than having the Lowest Note <note>original: "Proslambanomene"; the lowest note of the Greek scale.</note>, the Middle, and the extreme Highest Note <note>original: "Nete"; the highest note of the scale.</note>—and thus all the other strings of each—marked with different characters. This did not occur in the demonstration of *Boethius*, because the strings were marked with the same symbols, and they proceeded by the same order of degrees in one scale as in the other, so to speak.

Other observations of the Author regarding the Tones of Ptolemy.
</margin>

I do not wish to remain silent on this other observation regarding the Demonstration of the Tones distributed according to Ptolemy's order. It is this: those Tones higher than the Dorian appear to the eye to be distant from one another by the same degrees as the notes of its constitution <note>The scale structure.</note> as they move from the Highest Note <note>original: "Nete Hyperboleon."</note> to ascend to a third C-sol-f-ut; and those he made lower proceed by the same intervals found in moving from the Lowest Note <note>original: "Proslambanomene."</note> of the same system to descend to a third B-mi. This does not happen in the Demonstration made by Boethius, both because of the difference in steps and the quantity of those Tones. Thus, with wonderful order, those of Ptolemy—joining the beginning with the end—are seen to move like the celestial spheres in a perpetual circle, as the present Wheel clearly demonstrates:

The names of musical notes could be greatly improved.

However, take heed. You must keep in mind what I told you above regarding what "Trope" <note>A term for a musical mode or key.</note> signifies, and exert your fine intellect a little, and you will understand everything perfectly with the help of this other consideration. It must be noted, then, that the species of the Octave of the Dorian mode is that of E [Elami]; of the Phrygian, D [D solre]; of the Lydian, C [C faut]; and of the Mixolydian, B [h mi]; <note>These refer to the "Guidonian hand" solmization system where notes were identified by their position in overlapping hexachords.</note> which, by the intervals I mentioned, are naturally distant from one another. But to then apply them to the Modes they serve, they are transposed—from the Dorian onward—to the high pitch: some by a seventh, some by a fifth, and some by a Ditone <note>A major third, or an interval of two whole tones.</note>. Whereas, on the contrary, the species of the Octave of the Hypolydian, Hypophrygian, and Hypodorian are transposed by the same intervals into the low pitch; as could be seen in the example. The reason for this was none other than those species being below the low string of the Dorian Octave, and above these; considered however in the natural System; besides having wanted (and deservedly so) that the first species of the Octave serve as the first for the highest Mode, and the last for the lowest, as the last to be found among the order and the manner of numbering their strings. I want next to remind you that having to demonstrate a thing that is in itself very difficult, by means of its suitable and proper tools which are not only very different but entirely contrary, is most of the time not only uneasy to do well with all the necessary circumstances that would be appropriate, but difficult, not to say impossible. Therefore, it is not at all to be wondered at if the example of the modes formed by me for your understanding does not have in itself that exquisite clarity so that every minimal detail is understood with that greater ease that one might desire. The ancient Greek Musicians had, to denote each of their particular strings, a particular character that signified its proper sound; without any need for lines or spaces, or clefs like these of our times; all of which things are a supreme hindrance; and they could be removed and greatly improved with very great utility to students of modern practical music; the way to do which I will easily tell you before I bring our discussion to an end.

The greater Superparticular consonances are the fifth and the fourth. <note>original: "Superparticolari"; a ratio where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator (e.g., 3:2 for a fifth, 4:3 for a fourth).</note>
</margin>

<margin>
How Ptolemy formed the Modes by means of the two greater Superparticular intervals.
</margin>

BAR. Ptolemy derived from the Dorian mode, by means of the fourth [Diatessaron], the highest and the lowest Mode, which are, as you know, the Mixolydian and the Hypodorian, by ascending and descending by such an interval from that Dorian. Then, ascending above the lowest by a fifth, he created the Phrygian; and descending below that Phrygian by a fourth, he formed the Hypophrygian: above which, ascending by a fifth, he formed the Lydian, and descending below it by a fourth, he formed the Hypolydian; and thus all seven modes were formed by means of the two greater Superparticular intervals.

BAR. Neither Ptolemy nor I ever said—speaking, however, according to his principles and terms—that the Middle of the Phrygian and the Hypophrygian were tuned as a fourth; but I may well have said that they consonated by such an interval.

STR. Is consonating not the same as tuning?

BAR. No, sir, according to Ptolemy; because he says a consonant interval is that which, in reaching the ear, strikes it without offense; and such, according to him, are the Fourths [Diatessaron], called for this reason *Synfone* <note>original: "Synfone"; Greek for "sounding together."</note>. Then those which, in reaching the ear, strike it not only without offense, but with sweetness, he said "accorded" [tuned/harmonized]; and these are the Fifths [Diapente], called for this reason *Parafone* <note>original: "Parafone"; Greek for "sounding alongside."</note>. The others then were those that, in being heard, not only struck the sense without offense and with sweetness, but were such that one desired nothing further, and such are the Octaves [Diapason]; which, to signify this, they called *Homofone* [Homophonic] or if you like, *Antifone* [Antiphonic]: a distinction that Aristotle also makes.

# Ancient and Modern [Music]

<margin>
Dissonants are necessarily dissonant, as are the homophones <note>original: "homofone"; sounds in unison.</note> and Antiphones <note>original: "Antifone"; sounds an octave apart.</note> in many places in the *Problems of Harmony* <note>A reference to Aristotle’s *Problems*, specifically Section XIX which deals with music theory.</note>.
---
The Author's considerations regarding musical intervals.
</margin>
...major [second], and the minor Seventh resolved <note>A "resolution" is the movement of a dissonant note to a consonant one to create a sense of rest.</note> by that from the minor Third and from the major Sixth, which are not resolved like the others; and you will find the ear is struck with less harshness by the Tritone <note>An interval of three whole tones; an augmented fourth.</note> and the Semidiapente <note>original: "Semidiapente"; a diminished fifth.</note> resolved by the minor Sixth and the major Third, than it was by the first ones named. This is perhaps due to the pleasantness of the combined and contrary movement of the major Semitone that the parts make at the same time, whereas in those first ones, only one part did so while the other proceeded by a whole Tone. And when this happens to the high part while moving away, it always has greater grace than when it occurs in the low part; and the opposite happens when they approach each other. This is perhaps due to the motion, which in the latter becomes languid and in the former incited; or because, in moving away with contrary motion, small intervals are more natural for the high parts than for the low, and the opposite when approaching. But such an opinion can also arise in a person from having the ear so accustomed to it. 

It may also happen that, since in that place both Sevenths are resolved by the Sixth, and both Seconds by the Third, the major of these and the minor of those are less noisy, as they are closer to their "safety." For these same reasons, the major Sixth might seem harsher to us than the minor when moving from the former to the Octave and from the latter to the Fifth; this is caused in that place by the low part, creating a certain [indescribable effect]. Moving from the Tritone to the Diapente <note>original: "Diapente"; a perfect fifth.</note>, it would do less harm to make the low part descend while the high stays still, than if, on the contrary, the high part ascended while the low stayed still. This occurs for no other reason than that the Tritone has a certain suitability with the Fifth that the low part causes in that place; perhaps because of the languidness of the motion and the softness of the interval between those strings. For the Semitone always represents itself as larger to the ear when ascending than when descending. 

The occurrences narrated above, and for the same reason, cause the sense [of hearing] to be less offended by the Tritone than by the Semidiapente; perhaps also because it is found in the middle of the two minor consonances called today "perfect," or truly because the former can become a Diapente [fifth] and the latter a Diatessaron <note>original: "Diatessaron"; a perfect fourth.</note> without altering any string, as can be clearly seen and heard from the following example.

| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Minor Seventh** <br> dissonant. | **Major Seventh** <br> more dissonant. | **Major Second** <br> dissonant. | **Minor Second** <br> more dissonant. |
| **Tritone** <br> much less dissonant. | **Semidiapente** <br> less tolerable. | **Major Sixth** <br> harsh. | **Minor Sixth** <br> less harsh, indeed languid. |

<margin>
Why consonance pleases, and dissonance displeases the ear.
</margin>
Which diversity of harmony in the consonances arises from nothing else than from the little or much conformity that their extreme sounds have together; whereas dissonances, which on the contrary have them deformed and contrary, strike the ear harshly. Because each of the extreme sounds seeks to preserve itself in a certain way as a whole and does not want to yield to the other, they come to strike the sense harshly. But the ear is more unpleasantly offended by the Seventh than by the Semidiapente, and less by the Tritone; perhaps because the Tritone has the same quantity of steps as the Fourth, and the Semidiapente has the same as the Fifth, or because the one falls into the major Third and the other into the minor Sixth, where it is more imperfect. 

And just as the Fourth is less consonant than the Fifth, so likewise among the dissonances contained by the same quantity of strings in the Diatonic genus, that which corresponds with the Fifth is more dissonant than that which has a correspondence with the Fourth. Nor is this a marvel, since even well-proportioned humors <note>In Renaissance medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids that determined health and temperament.</note> are altered more by the slightest accident than those that are not so well-matched and united; and this is perceived, as I have shown you above, in the first two dissonances named; in addition to the inconstant distance found between them and their contiguous consonances, which are the Sixth and the Third commonly used for their resolution. And to tell you further, you will find the minor Third, which is between these strings and similar ones, 
C-fa-ut <note>A note name in the hexachord system, corresponding to C.</note>

<note>C fa ut and A re</note> have a mournful quality when descending; and you will find those located between them and their like—<note>E la mi and G sol re ut</note>—to be of the opposite nature. All these considerations, more in this part than in that, demonstrate their qualities and produce their effects with greater efficacy.

**STR.** From your discourse, I gather this among other most important lessons: that a sharp <note>original: "diesis"</note> placed in the high part makes the melody <note>original: "Cantilena"</note> cheerful, and a flat <note>original: "b molle"</note> in the low part makes it mournful. This is true especially when the parts move away from each other by contrary motion, or even when the low part approaches the high with separate and disjoined steps. The same must easily happen when passing by contrary motion from a minor Sixth to a major Third, or from the smaller of these to the larger of those; and they must have the opposite nature when arranged conversely. These occurrences must be less perceived by the senses as the number of voices increases, and the low part reveals them more clearly than the high or middle parts.

**STR.** On the contrary, considering them as you now say, there will be an even larger interval; because the Middle note of the Hypophrygian mode is <term>C fa ut</term> <note>The note C in the medieval solmization system.</note> and that of the Phrygian is <term>G sol re ut</term> <note>The note G.</note>, which is a Fifth higher.

That is, the Middle note of the Phrygian must be higher than that of the Hypophrygian by the same amount that <term>C fa ut</term> is lower than (and not higher than) <term>G sol re ut</term>, just as <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century mathematician and music theorist whose works were rediscovered in the Renaissance.</note> told you when finding the positions of the Modes by means of the two major <term>superparticular consonances</term> <note>Ratios like 3:2 (a fifth) or 4:3 (a fourth) where the numerator is one greater than the denominator.</note>. Nonetheless, we read of this fact: that <term>Sappho</term>, the Illustrious Poetess and inventor of the Mixolydian, being unable (according to many) as a woman to comfortably sing her poems and those of others in the Lydian mode, raised its system by a Semitone and thus created a new mode which she called "Mixolydian"—as if to say that because of its proximity to the Lydian, it was mixed with it. To their opinion, we shall add this other more solid and firm consideration: that Sappho was driven to such necessity not by being a woman, but by the greater conformity that the music of her poetry had with the property and nature of that particular harmony. For being a woman, as I have said, of small stature, not very beautiful of face, and moreover (as writers tell us) of a profession not very modest; she was often given occasion—as seen in fragments of her poems—to complain and lament of Love, while she burned for the beauty of the youth <term>Phaon</term> <note>A legendary boatman of Lesbos whom Sappho supposedly loved.</note>. Furthermore, that the people of Phrygia ordinarily sang their airs a tone higher than the Dorians and a tone lower than the Lydians is a clear and well-worn fact due to many supporting authorities. Nonetheless, for anyone who wanted to distribute the species of the octave in the way we lately mentioned, the example would show the opposite effect; because from the Dorian to the Phrygian mode, there would be no more than a Semitone by that order of proceeding. Yet the truth is, as you have heard, that the Phrygians sang a whole Tone and not a Semitone higher than the Dorians. Thus, wanting the modes distant from each other by these intervals and order, and between the particular strings and...

# Ancient & Modern Music

...the proper species of the Octave <term>Diapason: the interval of an octave</term>, in which they were truly sung by ancient Musicians, Ptolemy—or those who arranged them before him—could not have accommodated them in any better way than shown.

**STR.** I have understood very well; but tell me, who was the author of this difference between low and high Tones? And why were they assigned to these or those peoples? Was it their custom?

<margin>Tuscans speak with a voice less high than the Ligurians, and less low than the Lombards</margin>
<margin>Nature is the inventor of singing Diatonically.</margin>
**BAR.** Of the three principal ones—which are the Dorian, Phrygian, and Lydian—nature was the author. For in naturally uttering words, whether singing or speaking, or speaking-singing <note>The author refers to the natural melodic inflection of speech</note>, each nation had a difference in pitch regarding height and depth, as you have heard. But it was not exactly as art later established and instituted it. Anyone who considers what happens every day in many other provinces, and particularly in Italy, sees and hears this. For the Lombards generally speak and sing in a lower Tone than the Tuscans; and the people of Liguria speak with a higher voice than these, without even looking to the Sicilians or more remote nations, and keeping as close to the borders of our province as I can. Whether this happens because of food, water, air, or climate, we shall leave the natural philosophers to dispute; it is enough that the same thing that occurs today in Italy occurred and must occur daily in Asia among the peoples of Lydia, Phrygia, and Doris. The same occurred with Diatonic modulation, although each of its intervals was later regulated by Pythagoras, just as Jubal Cain <note>A biblical figure often credited with the invention of music</note> did before the Great Flood; to whom the invention of such a faculty was later attributed by the common people.

**STR.** What authority persuades us that the Phrygians sang one Tone higher or lower in interval than the Lydians, and by such a space above the Dorians?

**BAR.** Particularly the description that Aristoxenus makes of these Tones, placing the Ionian at the interval of a Semitone between the Dorian and Phrygian; and the Aeolian between the Phrygian and Lydian; and furthermore what Ptolemy and Boethius say about it, besides many other authoritative writers who wrote before and after them.

**STR.** Regarding the beginning and end of the melodies <term>Cantilene: songs or melodic lines</term> of the ancient Musicians, did they have a specific and particular string <note>meaning a specific starting or ending pitch</note>?

<margin>Zarlino in chapter 9 of the fourth part of his Institutions. Harmonic and Arithmetic division has no part in the Tones of the moderns.</margin>
**BAR.** No, sir; because the difference between one Tone and another, and their modes, consisted principally in the tension and slackness of the strings of the systems <term>constitutions: the structural arrangement of pitches</term>; and in the diversity, so to speak, of long and short keys, placed in different orders in each System; and not like that of modern practical Contrapuntalists, which they have placed entirely in the final note. Even though some, to show themselves more wise and learned than others, add the Arithmetic and Harmonic division of the Octave <term>Diapason</term>; which division—as far as making them different in harmony, affection, or Tone—has less to do with it than you have with the Kingdom of Peru. And according to their word, they have twelve different Tones and modes, even though they continually compose, play, and sing in one and the same unknown and foreign style; which, without noticing it at all, they use indiscriminately at weddings and funerals.

**STR.** From where do we believe the origin came for applying this consideration of Arithmetic and Harmonic division to the Tones of modern practical Contrapuntalists? And by what do we believe they were induced to believe that such a difference has the power to vary one from another regarding the diversity of the harmony <note>concento: the sounding together of voices</note>?

**BAR.** These truly are two of those things that I have many times thought about myself; and in truth, I have never been able to resolve them entirely.

**STR.** Despite this, I would be grateful to hear your opinion: to see if the cause of my doubting regarding this first point is in any way consistent with what you feel about it. For I suspect they have drawn such vanity from what Boethius says concerning the beginnings of the Tones and the arrangement of the notes of each mode and sound; who at the beginning of the fourteenth chapter of the fourth book of his *Music* says thus:
> From the species of consonances, therefore, those which are called modes are born. <note>original Latin: "Ex conſonantiarum igitur ſpeciebus, ii qui modi dicuntur, exiſtunt."</note>
Or perhaps such a thing had its origin in the method Ptolemy held in forming the Tones found between the extremes and the middle one, through the use of the Fifth <term>Diapente</term> and the Fourth <term>Diateſſaron</term>.

<margin>Description of the 8 Tones of the Church.</margin>
**BAR.** I do not dislike these considerations of yours; but to make you fully capable of understanding everything I believe about this matter, it is first necessary to remember well the order by which the eight Tones of the Church <term>Ecclesiastics</term> are arranged; who, among the strings of the different species of their Octave <term>Diapason</term>, have instituted them as follows.

# Dialogue on Music

**STR.** You have noted much in this description of the Dorian, Phrygian, and Lydian, and the other names of the ancient modes; do these perhaps have any conformity with the ones we use today?

<margin>Zarlino in chapter 8 of the 4th book of the *Institutions*.</margin>
**BAR.** Do not doubt it at all, and particularly with those of the Latins described by *Boethius* <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), whose "De institutione musica" was the standard music theory text for a millennium.</note>; rather, in my view, they were derived from him—even if this goes against the opinion of some—as you will hear.

**STR.** Tell me two other things. Who was the author of these Tones <term>Tones: here referring to the Ecclesiastical or Church Modes</term> as they are made? And what do we believe induced their composers to call this one "third" rather than "first"; or that melody <note>original: "aria"</note> rather of the "second" than of the "fourth" Tone? And for what reason did they not go beyond the Eighth Mode?

<margin>Who was the author of the Ecclesiastical Tones.</margin>
**BAR.** The oldest memory I have found of the Ecclesiastical Tones is in the *Introductory* of *Guido d'Arezzo* <note>Guido d'Arezzo (c. 991–1033), the inventor of modern staff notation.</note>; who flourished during the Papacy of John XX <note>Historically John XIX; a common error in medieval/Renaissance papal numbering</note> around the year 1020. And if I remember correctly, *Oddo* <note>Odo of Cluny</note> and others treated them shortly before him, as *Guido* himself shows in that place, and as I have seen in some very ancient books I have with me. This is as much as I can tell you regarding the origin of the Tones. As for asking why one is called first rather than second, or third rather than fourth... you will understand that this was done (as far as my small intellect can penetrate by way of conjecture) not without consideration and judgment; for regarding such things, there is no book in my possession that speaks of it.

**STR.** Who then was the author of considering and applying Harmonic and Arithmetic division to the Tones in figured song <term>figured song: polyphonic music, as opposed to monophonic plainchant</term>? And who was the first to mention and introduce twelve Modes, there being no more than eight in use before?

<margin>
Frachino <note>Franchinus Gaffurius</note> was the author of applying Harmonic and Arithmetic division to the tones, in the first [part], chapter seven of his *Prattica*.
Glareanus adds 4 Tones to the first 8. He reproaches Frachino, who is defended by the Author.
Glareanus does not understand the matter of the Tones of Aristoxenus. Chapter 15, book two.
Zarlino, in the eighth [chapter] of the 4th part of his *Institutions*.
Another error of Glareanus. Book two, chapter 9.
Glareanus in book 1, chapters 21 & 22. Book 2, chapter seven.
Zarlino in chapter 8, fourth part of the *Institutions*.
</margin>
**BAR.** I pray you, let us not bring so many disputes onto the field at once; let us decide them chapter by chapter. To avoid confusion, let the second not come until the first has been decided. Regarding the consideration of Harmonic and Arithmetic division <note>Mathematical ways of dividing an octave into a fifth and a fourth to define a mode's structure</note> in the Tones of both plainchant and figured song, the author was *Gaffurius*. And for the four Tones added to the first eight, it was *Glareanus*. In that work, [Gaffurius] is greatly and unfairly reproached and torn apart by [Glareanus] regarding two things of no small importance. I do not wish to remain silent about this in any way, and I will seek to remove such a stain from *Gaffurius* with the greatest brevity of words I can.

First, *Glareanus* wonders why *Gaffurius*, having knowledge of the Harmonic and Arithmetic division of the Octave <term>Diapason: the interval of an octave</term>, and having considered it in the first eight Tones, did not have the same realization that came later to him regarding the other four, so as to bring the number up to twelve; here he greatly reproaches him for ignorance. Secondly, he admonishes him for not having understood the order of the Tones of *Aristoxenus*. Both of these slanders are as unjust as any man could imagine.

That *Gaffurius* primarily understood the order of the Tones of *Aristoxenus* <note>Aristoxenus (4th century BC), a Greek theorist who emphasized human hearing over mathematical ratios</note> par excellence is clearly known from the demonstration he makes and from the words he uses to describe them. These are the same as those used by *Bryennius* and *Aristides Quintilianus*, as I said above when describing the Tones according to the mind of *Aristoxenus* drawn from their writings. That *Glareanus* (and others more modern than him), on the contrary, did not understand them—or perhaps, as will be said later, did not want to understand them for their own particular interest—can be clearly understood from here: *Glareanus* claims that the Lydian mode, according to *Aristoxenus*, is a Semitone below the Mixolydian; and likewise that the Hypophrygian is below the Hypolydian by such an interval. *Aristoxenus*, on the contrary, says there is a whole Tone there. He further says that the Lydian is a Third below the Aeolian, while *Aristoxenus* says the latter is a Semitone above the former. Furthermore, *Glareanus* wants the Dorian to be a Fourth below the Hypodorian, when *Aristoxenus* says it is a Third. But let us say this last: that *Glareanus*, from the Dorian and Phrygian and their Plagals <term>Plagal: a version of a mode with a lower range</term> onwards, distorted all the others from the mind of *Aristoxenus*. And he does all this because he wants to reconcile those [ancient modes] with these of today; a thing that is as possible as making an Ethiopian white.

*Glareanus* and some other more modern writers could never understand how the Lydian Tone could be higher than the Phrygian by the space of a whole Tone; for the species of the octave of the latter was (according to the Text of *Boethius*, which they cite as authority and have tried to imitate) *E-la-mi* <note>The pitch E</note>, and of the former *F-fa-ut* <note>The pitch F</note>, which are a Semitone apart. They had the same difficulty with their Plagals: for the species of the octave of the Hypophrygian was *B-mi* <note>The pitch B</note>, and of the Hypolydian *C-fa-ut* <note>The pitch C</note>. Being ignorant of the matter, it made them say (rather than admit they did not understand how the thing stood) that the texts of *Boethius*, *Franchino*, *Giorgio Valla*, and others were corrupt on this point. I cannot imagine how such a thought could enter their heads, since the aforementioned interpreters place the Aeolian between the Phrygian and the Lydian, and the Hypoaeolian between the Hypophrygian and the Hypolydian, separated by a Semitone. Thus, from the Phrygian to the Lydian, and their Plagals, there was necessarily a whole Tone, as has been said many times. Moreover, *Ptolemy* places the same intervals between them as *Aristoxenus* and *Boethius* do, even if he attributes various species of the Octave to them differently considered. Would it then be such a great thing in this modern practice, after having sung *Ancor che col partire* by *Cipriano* <note>Cipriano de Rore's famous madrigal "Even though at parting"</note> for four voices, to immediately sing a Tone higher *Donna ch'ornata siete* <note>"Lady, you who are adorned"</note>, of—

<summary>Bardi defends the theorist Gaffurius against the criticisms of Glareanus, arguing that the latter misunderstood the ancient Greek modal system of Aristoxenus. The discussion focuses on the mathematical and historical origins of the eight ecclesiastical tones versus the newer twelve-mode system.</summary>

# Ancient & Modern [Music]

...of the same? I well know that the Bass of this one begins and ends in F <note>original: "F faut"; refers to the note F in the medieval hexachord system</note>, and that other in E <note>original: "Elami"; the note E</note>, which is the distance of a semitone? Or rather, after having sung that same *Ancor che col partire* <note>A famous madrigal by Cipriano de Rore, often used as a technical example</note>, to then sing immediately after it, a semitone lower, the *Immortal Justice* <note>original: "la giustitia immortale"; another work by Rore</note> by the same author, also for four voices; even though it ends in D <note>original: "D solre"; the note D</note>, a whole tone away from E? Certainly not; but coming to the second point, I say: that for Franchino <note>Franchinus Gaffurius (1451–1522), an influential Italian music theorist</note>, even though he had considered the four Authentic modes of the first eight Tones divided harmonically, and the four Plagal modes divided arithmetically; and that such consideration was truly sufficient, without more, to bring him to knowledge of the other four that Glarean <note>Heinrich Glarean (1488–1563), who proposed a 12-mode system in his book *Dodecachordon*</note> later added;

<margin>The prudence of Franchino.</margin>

one must not, for the reasons that will be stated later, attribute it to ignorance (as those people believe) for not having introduced them; but rather to prudence and great knowledge. For he found that with the first seven Modes, each of the seven species of the Octave <term>Diapason: the interval of an octave, which can be built in seven different patterns of whole and half steps</term> was occupied. He considered, furthermore, that the highest string of the seventh mode, together with the lowest string of the second, embraced all fifteen strings of the Greatest System <note>The *Greater Perfect System* of ancient Greek music theory</note>; and that by adding others above or below, one would end up going outside the natural limits, merely repeating the same ones and not producing new ones. Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the ancient astronomer and music theorist</note> held the same respect; although Zarlino <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), the most famous theorist of the age and Galilei's former teacher</note> says the opposite in chapter seven of the fourth part of the *Harmonic Institutions*. Besides holding this view, he argued that this was the cause of the variation between the first Tone and the second—not because of the different division of the varying species of Octave, as Glarean later did; but because the second Tone seeks the low notes more than the first by the interval of a Fourth <term>Diatessaron: the interval of a perfect fourth</term>, and thus makes the harmony more languid and relaxed, and therefore of a different nature from that of the first.

->[Image: A large isosceles triangle diagram illustrating the mathematical proportions of musical intervals. Arcs on the left define the "Double octave with the fifth," "Octave" (Diapason), "Fifth" (Diapente), "Fourth" (Diatessaron), "Major Third," "Minor Third," and "Whole Tone." The center of the triangle is filled with ratios such as "Sesquioctave" (9:8) and "Sesquiterza" (4:3), which represent the physical string lengths required to produce these intervals.]<-

<margin>The reason that induces Franchino to consider the harmonic and arithmetic division in the tones.</margin>

STR. Do not find it troublesome to tell me what moved him to consider such division in the Tones, and why the harmonic division of the Octave and the Fifth <term>Diapente: the interval of a perfect fifth</term> delights the ear more than the arithmetic division?

<margin>Harmonic division.</margin>

<margin>Why the harmonic division delights the ear more than the arithmetic.</margin>

BAR. As for the harmonic and arithmetic division of the Octave, I have never been able to find any reason valid enough to persuade me why the former delights more than the latter—though many things of no consequence are said about it—and even less so why the Octave pleases us while the Seventh displeases us. I have, however, considered that the same thing that happens to the ear with sounds occurs similarly to the sight with visible objects; as, for example: in looking at a Pyramid, the sight delights us more when its sharp part looks to the sky and the obtuse part to the earth, than the opposite. This is perhaps because of the proportion and suitability that a solid body in that specific form and posture has with our sight when viewing it from the plane of its base:

He uses a geometric analogy—the stability of a pyramid—to explain why certain musical divisions (harmonic vs. arithmetic) are more pleasing to the human senses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion between Bardi and Strozzi regarding the mathematical division of musical intervals (octaves, fifths, and fourths) and how these divisions define the "character" or "affect" of the ecclesiastical Tones. It specifically addresses why the "Authentic" modes are divided harmonically and critiques recent changes made by theorists like Zarlino.</meta>

# Dialogue on Music

base: and the same can arise from musical intervals regarding the pleasure and displeasure they cause the ear; as you can easily understand from the following example, and afterwards why both the Major and Minor Third <note>original: "l'vna & l'vtra Terza"</note> represent themselves to our senses as more full of spirit, and likewise the Fifth when it is placed above the Octave rather than within it. It must also be considered that the power of this emotional affect does not consist simply in having the larger part of the interval situated in the bass <note>original: "parte graue"</note> and the smaller in the treble <note>original: "parte acuta"</note> as some believe, but in the fact that the part occupying that position is the one closest to perfection. Indeed, this arrangement undoubtedly plays a greater role than the other; as you will perceive through the senses by examining with your usual diligence the minor tenth divided by a middle string into a Fifth in the bass and a minor Sixth in the treble, and likewise by its contrary. Similarly, you will hear it in the major sixth separated by a middle string into a Fourth in the bass and a Major Third in the treble: although such a chord is today rather abhorred by certain delicate ears, yet it is greatly embraced by modern Cittern players <note>The Cittern was a wire-strung instrument popular in the Renaissance</note>. And to tell you further, those Tones according to modern practice which do not have the Fifth below the final note and the Fourth above—for example, the fifth and sixth Tones, or to speak according to the most modern usage (though further from the truth) the seventh and eighth—their endings always feel cut off and imperfect, and the ear is not entirely satisfied as it is with those others that have it. But coming to treat the order of the

<margin>Whether the manner of numbering the Tones is accidental or done in an orderly way.</margin>
Tones, I say this: it is a clear thing that to distinguish one from another, a diversity of names was necessary, as seen in those used by the Greeks, or numbers as used by the Churchmen. But as for why they chose to call one progression of notes "the first" rather than the third or another Tone, perhaps this was the reason: They said the first Mode was that melody which moved between the strings of the species of the Octave <term>Diapason: the Greek term for an octave</term> that formerly served the Dorian mode. They were moved by no other reason than that this Tone was the principal and most honorable among ancient musicians; nor for any other cause did they call that particular species of Octave "the first."

<margin>Why the First Tone is divided more harmonically than arithmetically, and likewise the other authentic modes.</margin>
**STR.** What then moved Franchino <note>Franchinus Gaffurius (1451–1522), a major theorist of the time</note> to consider that specific melody of the first Tone as being divided harmonically rather than arithmetically?

**BAR.** From this: The Middle <note>The "Mese" or central note</note> of the Greatest and Perfect System separates the species of the Octave in that same Dorian mode harmonically. While it was divided arithmetically according to the order of Ptolemy, the moderns followed this path by imitating Boethius, as I have said. I do not say this because I think Franchino, Boethius, or Ptolemy, or anyone more ancient than them, ever thought or sought to apply such a trifle to the Tones—for their different virtues consisted in something else, as has been shown and will be shown further. Franchino was therefore moved to the consideration you heard for the reason cited; and furthermore, since the quality of the harmony and the ensemble <note>original: "conceto"</note> had to be considered in such a way, it did not require being divided in any other manner. From this partitioning of the Octave, modern practitioners also took the opportunity to call its larger side, the Fifth <term>Diapente: the Greek term for the interval of a fifth</term>, the "first species," and the smaller side they called the first species of the Fourth <term>Diatessaron: the Greek term for the interval of a fourth</term>.

<margin>B-natural <note>h duro</note>, used before B-flat <note>b molle</note>.</margin>
In this matter, they came to imitate the Greeks rather than the Latins. From this, one clearly sees that the moderns sang using B-natural <note>original: "h duro"; the "hard" B or B-square</note> before they used B-flat <note>original: "b molle"; the "soft" B</note>. Because this species of the Octave is found so divided between D <note>D solre</note> and d <note>d lasolre</note>, and since the first species of the Fourth is said to be *re-sol* as mentioned, if there had been a B-flat in the scale of that Octave instead of B-natural, the Fourth in that place would have been *mi-la*. Furthermore, instead of the second species, one would have had a Tritone <note>An unstable interval of three whole tones, often avoided in early music</note>. Therefore, their Tones were composed and sung first using B-natural rather than B-flat. According to the use of modern practitioners, the first species of the Octave is found between D and d, that of the Fifth between D and A, and that of the Fourth between A and d; and the others proceed by conjunct steps toward the treble, assuming B-natural <note>original: "h quadro"</note>.

<margin>Zarlino in chapters 10 & 11 of the 4th part of his *Institutions*.</margin>
From this, one can argue how much those people have been deceived who lately changed, without any reason, the order of the Tones and the species of consonances—imagining that with such a change they would draw closer to the order of the Modes of the ancients. I do not know what this has brought or can bring other than the opposite effect, as much in position as in distance, as well as in the quality of the harmony.

**STR.** I did not understand before, nor do I understand now, why any division other than that one would not suit the quality of the harmony and the ensemble of the Dorian mode?

<margin>What correspondence the Tones of the Churchmen have with those of the Greeks.</margin>
**BAR.** Because the Churchmen, having established their first Tone within the same species of Octave that served the Dorian mode—and that mode being, as you will hear another time, stable and quiet in nature, without violence, and fit to induce grave and severe thoughts and the habits of strong men in the minds of listeners—it did not, I say, require being separated in any other way, because such is the nature of its ensemble among those strings. Its quality is revealed even more when it is applied to words suited to it; whereas, on the contrary, an arithmetic division would have made it conform in many ways to its Plagal <note>The "Plagal" modes are the lower-range versions of the "Authentic" modes</note> counterpart, which was not appropriate, as that mode is languid, tearful, and fearful; as can be perceived...

He critiques modern theorists like Zarlino for trying to reorder these Tones and argues that the use of B-natural predates B-flat in these systems.</summary>
