->Ancient, & Modern [Music]<-

<margin>
Arithmetic division of the second Tone.
</margin>
...[clearly] hear by striking together three strings arranged in such a way, which possess such a property not only when all three are struck at the same time: but the simple movement of each of the intervals separately as they depart from the **Middle** <note>original: "Media"; referring to the middle string or pitch that divides an octave</note> to find either of the **extremes** <note>The outer notes of an octave</note>; and likewise by adding another part in the treble, which proceeds with its own natural movement conforming to the bass, they manifest themselves to the senses as such when sung together.

<image-desc>Two musical tablatures for a six-stringed instrument, showing various chords and intervals.</image-desc>

And to see that this is true, consider first what nature the harmony of the interval possesses—as has been said—which is found starting from the middle of the **Dorian** <note>The Dorian mode, often associated with the pitch D</note> to go and find either of the extremes of its **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note>; as in descending from **A** <note>original: "alamire"</note> to **D** <note>original: "D solre"</note>, or ascending from that same **A** to **high d** <note>original: "d lasolre"</note> in this manner.

The movement of this part, because it is the bass and that which gives the "air" <note>The melodic character or tune</note> to the Song, accompanied by another in the treble that proceeds with movement conforming to its position—as for example here; or rather in this other way—you will hear what harmony they will make when sung together with the other, or each of them at the same time.

<image-desc>Three musical tablatures side-by-side, each showing a different chord or interval configuration.</image-desc>

**STR.** The harmony of each part in itself, and the sonority that comes from both, or from all three together arranged in this manner, is truly such as you have described; but let us, if you please, better consider each of these occurrences in the **arithmetic separation** <note>The mathematical division of an interval where the smaller interval (the Fourth) is placed below the larger one (the Fifth)</note>.

<margin>
The Author’s considerations regarding the Tones.
</margin>
**BAR.** We shall do so in its proper place; let us continue to see each of them regarding the matter of the **Modes** <note>The "Modi" or Tones are the scales used in ancient and church music</note>. The ancient Musicians divided their Tones into **Plagal** <note>original: "Plagij"</note> and **Authentic**; leaving between one and the other—as you have seen in each of the demonstrations according to their use—the space of a **Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>. Now, in the same way, the Churchmen desired that from the first Tone, called Authentic, to the second, called Plagal, there should be the distance of a Fourth; and thus the latter necessarily came to occupy the place of the Octave of the **Hypodorian Mode** <note>original: "Modo Hypodorio"</note>: understanding this always according to the mind of **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works transmitted Greek music theory to the Middle Ages</note>, and not any other ancient writer. The reason for their different **mediations** <note>The way the octave is divided by a middle note</note> did not originate from anywhere else but the desire that the harmony arising from them should conform as much as possible to the nature of the Tones of the ancients from whom they had drawn them. 

Furthermore, as some say, it was so that the final note of the first (called Authentic) and the second (called Plagal) would be common to both. This rule, being irrelevant, was not entirely approved by the authors of the Ecclesiastical chants; so much so that the first and second Tone came to be contained within the strings that embrace the same sides of the **first species of Octave**; but with this difference: that while the Authentic has its larger side <note>The Perfect Fifth</note> in the bass part and the smaller <note>The Perfect Fourth</note> in the treble; the Plagal, by contrast, transports the species of the Fourth of its Authentic by an octave to the side opposite the treble, joining it to the bass of that same **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note> without moving it from its place. 

And so the Plagal comes to seek a Fourth more in this part than its Authentic, and the Authentic, conversely, extends further than the Plagal into the treble by a similar interval. This cause varies the species of the Octave: for from the **First species** it was in the Authentic, it becomes the **Fifth species** in the Plagal; and regarding the mediation, we have been considered differently by modern practitioners. Wherefore, in that first simplicity of **plainchants** <note>original: "canti fermi"</note>, where these conditions were all observed, there arose among them a variety of harmony, and consequently of **affect** <note>Emotional response or mood</note>. This occurred primarily from the small quantity of strings they required, and from the diversity of those strings and their movements. 

To make this truth clear to you, consider every tiny part of this division; how different its nature is from that first one; not only in the sound and movement of a single part—such as that which suits the bass, wanting to depart from **D** <note>original: "D solre"</note>, its middle, to find either of the extremes of its Octave—but accompanied by another part placed in the treble that proceeds with movement conforming to the bass, as for example here, or rather in this other manner; and

<image-desc>Musical tablature on a six-line staff showing a chord.</image-desc>

also in hearing at the same time the extreme strings of the simple Octave together with its middle, or even the three parts together; which, as I told you, you will find to be **sad and subdued** <note>original: "mesto, & rimesso"</note>.

<image-desc>Three musical tablatures on six-line staves showing various chordal positions.</image-desc>

Which character is not far from that attributed to the Hypodorian mode. Nor is it at all surprising that the diversity of sound regarding highness and lowness, together with the difference of movement and interval, produces a variety of harmony and affect; for Nature does not ordinarily produce similar things from contraries, nor these with means of the same quality, but rather the opposite. When the suitability of **Rhythm** <note>original: "Rithmo"</note> and the conformity of concepts are added to the consideration of these things, what force and virtue do we believe that melody would then have? So much, certainly, that it would be capable—as it once was—of swaying the minds

STR. The Author’s consideration regarding the nature of intervals.

For starting in the Disjunct System <note>original: "Systema disgiunto"; a Greek-derived method of organizing the scale</note> of G-sol-re-ut <note>The pitch G</note> with the bass part, and descending by a Fifth, or ascending by a Fourth, you will find such movement to have something of the cheerful, the excited, and so to speak, of the virile and natural; and likewise sung together with other parts higher than the bass, which proceed with movement conforming to it, as for example thus. Nor for any other reason do I believe this happens in this way of proceeding, than because one finds between the parts the Third and the Tenth, naturally major and minor in that [composition]; and having to make them so by means of accidental signs <note>Sharps and flats</note>, they become—since Nature always operates its effects more vigorously than art—in the manner you have heard: and when the parts above the bass become higher, the harmony would become even more as we have described it; always understanding soundly and discreetly: and that the bass part is truly that which gives the "air" <note>The melodic character or mood</note> (when singing in harmony) to the Song; observe, in this last example, that joint movement of a Tone <note>A whole step</note>, which the Contralto part makes in ascending, has a great deal of the virile; and on the contrary, having sung in the previous one the same interval in the same way, and between the same strings, even if one or more parts were added in the high register that performed the same function as they do in this last one; it would nonetheless have something of the sad and submissive, like its first [version]: and the same would happen to such a part if it were transposed an Octave higher.

<image-desc>Three short musical fragments in mensural notation on five-line staves. The first fragment shows two voices. The second fragment shows a three-voice texture with vertical alignment. STR. It is undoubtedly as you say, and I marvel that these things have not been considered and put into practice by the practical Counterpoint-writer before now; but before you return to tell me how the distribution of the other Modes went, besides the two already mentioned, I pray you to tell me another detail.

BAR. Tell me what it is.

STR. Which has a greater role in giving the "air" to the Songs: slowness and speed, or the highness and lowness of the sound? And which of these two means is more effective in manifesting them as they are to the ear?

BAR. Each of them concurs in their appropriate operations, no differently than lines and colors do in revealing beauty and ugliness of the body to the sight: and just as in doing that, lines always have a greater part than colors, so likewise in this, the slow and fast have a greater part than the low and high sound. Outlines without colors can signify to the sight the proportion and disproportion of the body; just as the fast and slow motion of the sound in a single pitch can communicate the "air" of some Song to the ear; but there is such a close kinship between these two attributes <note>original: "accidenti"; properties of the sound</note> that one cannot entirely manifest the quality of the "air" without the other, just as lines can without colors among those other two. Returning to the invention and use of the Church Modes <note>original: "Modi Ecclesiastici"</note>, I tell you that the authors of them

-># Ancient and Modern [Music]<-

<margin>
Franchino in the first [book] of his *Practice*, in the seventh and eleventh chapters. <note>original: "Frāchino nel primo della sua prattica." Refers to Franchino Gaffurio (1451–1522), a major Italian Renaissance music theorist.</note>
</margin>
They furthermore wished to establish the Seventh among the strings that contain the species of the Octave <term>Diapason (Octave)</term> of the Mixolydian Mode; and to the Eighth and last, they assigned the same species that they assigned to the first. Because of this correspondence, it was called—in imitation of the other Plagal modes <note>Plagal modes are "lower" versions of the standard (Authentic) church modes</note>—by the name Hypomixolydio <note>Hypomixolydian; "Hypo" is Greek for "under" or "below"</note>, and not Hypermixolydio <note>Hypermixolydian; "Hyper" is Greek for "above"</note>, as some have dreamed; since *Hypo* means "below" and *Hyper* means "above," as you know. Glareanus <note>Heinrich Glarean (1488–1563), a Swiss theorist who expanded the system of musical modes</note> once used these words: "The Hypermixolydian was named by Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the ancient Greek astronomer and music theorist</note> because it was above the Mixolydian, and it is our Eighth." In this description of the eight Tones <note>Modes</note>, applied to modern practice without further consideration, one finds the same inconveniences regarding the distances of highness and lowness that I mentioned above. For it seems their authors made no account of the fact that (among other things) the interval found between the Lydian Mode and the Mixolydian of the ancients was the distance of a Semitone, and not a Tone, as is found between the Fifth and Seventh of the Ecclesiastics <note>Church modes</note>. Perhaps they lacked the skill to harmonize the species of the Octave with the intervals found between one Tone and another; thus, they came to set aside—despite its great importance—that which they least understood and which most needed to be understood.

**STR.** What difference will there be, then, between the eighth Mode of the Church and the first? Since both occupy the same species of the Octave and the same strings?

<margin>
That there cannot be more than seven modes.
</margin>
**BAR.** Here lies the whole importance of the matter: nothing other, certainly, than the final note <note>The 'finalis,' the note on which a melody ends</note> and the diversity of the division, considered harmonically in the one and arithmetically in the other. Now you see, in modern songs composed for many voices and sung in the manner customary today, what must be done regarding the diversity of the harmony between this and that Tone: the final note, and the variety of the division of the species of the Octave.

<margin>
Hermippus, Athenian Painter.
</margin>
**STR.** In truth, these Modes of theirs, being so fashioned, remind me of the paintings of the singular Hermippus of Athens. Whether because of a natural dislike for beards and clothing, or for some other personal interest, in painting males and females, he made them continually so similar that it was impossible to distinguish one from the other except by their sex—as if industrious Nature had not formed them differently in a thousand other perceptible ways. Likewise, with the Tones of the modern Counterpoint-writers; it is truly impossible, in hearing them sung, to distinguish the first from the second, or the third from the fourth, and so on, regarding their highness and lowness. One can only tell by the final note; even though, when seen in writing, some often appear higher or lower than others.

<margin>
<insert>abuse</insert>
Another doubt of modern practitioners.
</margin>
**BAR.** I want to tell you another thing that occurs to me on this subject. Where the ancient Musicians, in varying their Tones, changed not only the species of the Octave but the entire System <term>Systema (The Scale/Pitch range)</term> from low to high, or vice versa; those of our times claim to vary them while singing the same species of the Octave within the same tension and slowness of the System—and not just the adjacent modes, but the extremes, such as the first and the eighth. I say further: if each of their Tones has the particular power to move this or that different emotion in the listener, as they affirm (though contrary to all reason), how does it happen that when they set a Sonnet about mournful things, they sing its first four lines in the second Tone and the next three in the ninth, or otherwise? Furthermore, who is so lacking in judgment that they do not notice that in any of their songs composed for no more than four voices, while the Bass is singing (for example) among the strings of the Octave serving the first Tone, the Tenore will be singing among those of the second? And the Contralto will be singing the Hypermixolydian <note>The high-mixolydian</note> while the Bass sings the Hypodorian <note>The low-dorian</note> by virtue of singing an octave above it? And the Soprano will do the same with the Tenore? Such a confused and contrary mixture of notes cannot move any emotion in the listener. Even if each part had its own property to induce a specific affection (which it does not have in this modern practice of counterpoint), the parts confound each other and, being contrary, impede their natural operations. But let us come to our point regarding the addition of the four last Modes, and let these men remain in their opinions.

<margin>
On considering Glarean adding the four Tones to the first eight.
</margin>
In considering then the aforementioned Glareanus—a man truly most learned and of great literature—who made the eighth Tone of the Church different from the first only by the final note and the imagination of the different Harmonic and Arithmetic division applied to this new way of composing and singing so many melodies together; he was so driven by the thirst for inventing such useless novelty, which he considered most important and necessary. This is clearly shown by the title of his books on Music, which he calls *Dodecachordon* <note>original: "Dodecacordon." Greek for "Twelve-stringed [instrument or system]," reflecting his theory of 12 modes.</note>. On the first page of these, one reads of such unheard-of wonders, where he says at length that he has imitated Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and music theorist</note>; though we have already demonstrated the actual conformity they have. Such was, I say, what Glareanus went about discussing within himself: "Since the species of the Octave that serves the first Tone has the power to form the Eighth merely by considering that one is divided harmonically and this one arithmetically; for what reason should these same separations not create a variation of harmony in the other species containing the other Tones?" To which appearance...

They do not notice or consider that the Musicians of the ecclesiastical chants, and later the learned Franchino <note>Franchino Gaffurio (1451–1522)</note>, did not wish to speculate upon or introduce a greater number of Tones—not out of

Boethius in their number than because they truly recognized it as capable of introducing any new and necessary affect. These things were very well known by Franchino, who would have sooner refuted them than formed new ones without purpose. But finding the system already embraced by everyone, he accepted it as the lesser evil. Furthermore, for that sort of song for a single voice, sung according to the sound of the strings among which they are written (as was the custom when they were first introduced), without altering them at all, it was not unsuitable—whereas in today's songs for multiple voices, it is unsuitable. Truly, among the strings of their chants, there is a difference of harmony and melody, especially when

words conforming to them are applied. For any song put into action always 
<margin>Modern Tones are no more than one.</margin>
requires the same quantity and quality of strings regarding the high and low, proceeding in each of the parts with the same rhythm in terms of fast and slow movement. The counterpoint composer uses notes of whatever value and every interval at his pleasure, thoughtlessly, and without considering the concept of the words at all. It will be proven in its proper place that the diversity and virtue of harmonies and melodies consist principally in these accidents. In this way, the Tones and the songs of today necessarily become of the same quality, quantity, and form; and of the same color, so to speak, flavor, and smell as one another. Regarding this, it seems to me that the example of Philoxenus, a most noble Musician, would be a powerful argument to persuade us how different the Tones of the moderns are from those of the 
<margin>Aristotle in the 8th book of the *Politics*.</margin>
ancients, and to further confirm this truth. This Philoxenus, having once begun a <term>Dithyramb</term> in the Dorian Tone, was forced by the nature of the subject to give it an end in the Phrygian Tone, which was suited to it.

STR. From what did this arise, pray tell?
BAR. In our times, I believe, it can hardly be explained in a way that provides full understanding, because no memory of these things has remained. But if you are 
<margin>Dithyramb among the Greeks, what it was and who discovered it.</margin>
content to know what I estimate and believe of it, I am happy to tell you. The Dithyramb among the ancient Greek poets was a form of song in praise of Bacchus, of which Arion was the author. Its melody imitated the concepts and customs of the Bacchants—heated, intoxicated, cheerful, and such; and being sung by a choir representing such people, they were all accustomed to being composed (as far as I estimate) in an Incited Tone. But because great artists sometimes wish to experiment with their art, and thus set out to push the boundaries of their principles, Philoxenus, being one of those, wished to experiment with something new. When this did not succeed in capturing his concept, being overcome by the nature of the subject, he passed over to the natural...

# Ancient & Modern

<margin>
Philoxenus began the Dithyramb in the Dorian Tone so that he would be forced to end it in the Phrygian.
<note>Philoxenus of Cythera (c. 435–380 BC) was a famous Greek dithyrambic poet known for his innovations.</note>
</margin>
...and thus, having begun the <term>Dithyramb</term> <note>A wild, choral hymn sung in honor of Dionysus</note> in the Dorian Tone—the harmony of which is, as has been said, quiet and without any emotional violence—and abhorring the unseemly softness of such subject matter and the flatteries of that verse, he felt (skilled as he was) that as he proceeded, the harmony failed to support his imitation. He abandoned it without hesitation and passed, almost violently, to the Phrygian, which is higher than the Dorian and by nature more incited and suited to expressing the concepts he had at hand. Nor is it surprising that such a concept occurred to Philoxenus, for he was by nature and temperament a lover of grave and quiet harmonies, even the gravest; this is evidenced by his having discovered, after all others, the Hypodorian, which is slower and lower than any other. And this is as much as I can tell you on this matter. From the example of this Philoxenus, one can also understand how much the composing and singing of today is without rule, without mode, and without order—done at random and by mere practice. Modern "practical" composers know nothing else except that this is a consonant interval and that is a dissonant one. Whatever the concept may be (to the spite of Philoxenus), the modern <term>Contrapuntists</term> <note>Composers of polyphonic music where multiple independent melodies are played together</note> sing it in whichever of their Tones they please. They have entirely abandoned every observation and law, making themselves prey to the sheer will and power of their own technical devices, without any more considered limitation or rule that might be good.

<margin>
Another abuse of modern practical contrapuntists.
</margin>
*STR.* Did the ancient musicians, then, not use a mixture of one Tone with another?

<margin>
Sacadas of Argos, inventor of the mixing of Tones.
</margin>
*BAR.* Certainly not, until the arrival of Sacadas of Argos, a musician and poet most famous for three victories he achieved in those festivals the Spartans held in honor of Apollo on his birthday, called the <term>Carnea</term>. He was the author of the practice of moving within the same song from the first to the second, and from that to the third Tone, or otherwise.

<margin>
The Carnea festivals, and what they were. Plutarch in the 3rd book of the *Apophthegmata* among the orders and customs of the Lacedaemonians.
</margin>
*STR.* Is this the same Sacadas who was also the inventor of Elegies? And who, in Sparta itself, devised that kind of song and dance performed together called the <term>Gymnopediæ</term>? Pindar, among other writers, kept a particular record of his work.

*BAR.* That is the man.

*STR.* If it is not a burden, tell me what kind of mixture of Tones he used, and also what the *Gymnopediæ* were.

<margin>
Hypodorian Tone, the last discovery.
</margin>
*BAR.* I will tell you everything after I have proven to you that the Hypodorian Tone was not only discovered by Philoxenus, but was the last of them all; since this is an older debt, I must reasonably satisfy it first. Therefore, take note. You should know that this Tone was called by various names among the ancients, as you can partly understand from that introduction printed in both Greek and Latin under the name of Euclid. Among others, some call it <term>Locrian</term> and others Hypodorian. Now, Julius Pollux, in recounting the harmonies, although he does not name the Hypodorian, says that the Locrian was discovered by Philoxenus. Since these two are one and the same (as writers tell us), we already have proof that Philoxenus was its discoverer. As for it being the last to come into use, besides the fact that it is quite likely in itself—being the eighth Tone and the last in number—this is clearly drawn from Bryennius in the fourth chapter of the third book of his *Music*. There, having discussed the other higher Tones and explaining why the Hypophrygian was called a "low" Tone by the ancients even though the Hypodorian is lower, he shows that it was so named because before the Hypodorian came into use, the Hypophrygian was naturally the lowest of all. Thus, it was commonly called by that name, and the name stuck even after the Hypodorian—deeper by nature—appeared. From this discourse, it is clearly gathered that the Hypodorian was the last of all eight Tones to be discovered.

<margin>
In the 4th book of his *Onomasticon*. Locrian and Hypodorian are the same tone.
</margin>
The *Gymnopediæ* among the Spartans were choirs of boys who went about barefoot, dancing and singing the praises of the gods and in honor of those Spartans who had fallen in battle for their country on the fields of <term>Thyrea</term>. The mixtures of Tones that Sacadas used (according to what Plutarch tells us) were as follows. In his time, there was knowledge of only the three principal species of harmonies, which are, as you know, the Dorian, the Phrygian, and the Lydian. Although Athenaeus, citing Heraclides Ponticus, suggests that the Phrygian and Lydian harmonies—perhaps being "barbaric"—should be called Aeolian and Ionian to further honor the Greeks. This point does not pass without some disturbance from those who accurately examine the names and order of the Modes according to Socrates, Plato, and Aristoxenus. But be that as it may—since the pages are full of such controversies regarding the Tones—let us say how Sacadas used the mixture of them, which he used primarily in the chorus in this manner.

<margin>
Gymnopediæ, what they were.
</margin>
He would first place (whenever it suited the quality of the poem) the Dorian change; after this the Phrygian, and then the Lydian. This rule and law was called "Tripartite." But this variety of harmony was arranged by him throughout the song with such industry that his work and skill were held in the highest esteem. He matched the harmony to the subject of the words with the greatest judgment, expressing with marvelous art all the <term>affects</term> <note>The specific emotional states or "passions" that music was intended to provoke</note> that the poet had unfolded in the text. This most important and principal part of the musical art is held in no account by the "practical" musicians of today; and would to God that their errors ended here, but it is much worse; for all...

# Dialogue on Music

<margin>Other abuses of today's practitioners.</margin>
...all the rules and observations that they currently use are directly contrary to expressing the emotions and concepts of any poem whatsoever. I wish to commemorate some of these for you now. One is the inviolable law they have established—without citing any authority or reason—that it is not permitted in any way to use two perfect consonances of the same species one after another. Furthermore, they insist that when one moves from an imperfect consonance, one must proceed to the nearest available perfect one. To this, they have added a strict regard for the relationship of the <term>Tritone</term> <note>An interval of three whole tones, historically called the "devil in music" because of its dissonance</note> and the <term>Semidiapente</term> <note>A diminished fifth</note>. Now, the observation of these two precepts alone is enough to prevent one from ever expressing any emotion; this is in addition to other inconveniences that I reserve the right to show you at a more convenient time and place.

**STR.** It will certainly require more industry and effort than it did just now to make me see plainly that the Lyre and the Cithara of the ancient Greeks and Latins were the same thing, if you are to persuade the public of this new—indeed, most new—opinion of yours.

**BAR.** I offer to make this even more clear to you, or to anyone else of sound intellect, than anything else I have said to you thus far or might say in the future. But if it pleases you, let us save that for its proper place.

**STR.** Are there, then, other reasons that prevent the music and singing of today from producing in listeners those emotions that ancient music produced?

**BAR.** There are many others; indeed, as I told you, all their rules are contrary to these effects.

**STR.** Please do not be burdened by telling me some other particulars, so that I may escape this ignorance and learn how to respond to today’s practitioners. They insist that the music of the ancients, compared to theirs, was a joke to be laughed at; they claim that the wonder the ancients caused in the souls and minds of men arose from nothing other than the fact that those people were coarse and unrefined—a matter they have made much noise about in their books.

<margin>
The Author’s reasons for proving the excellence of ancient music and the impertinence of modern music.
</margin>
**BAR.** See how rash these men are, who laugh at the effects of a thing when they do not know what it was, nor understand its nature and properties, nor how it could work such wonders. What greater argument do you want to convince them than the "miracles," so to speak, that it performed? These are recounted to us by the most worthy and famous writers the world has ever known—men outside the profession of music. But let us set this aside and come to a clear, sensible example. It is a certain thing, from what I have been able to gather from various sources, that the practice of singing so many melodies together today has been in use for no more than one hundred and fifty years; indeed, if someone wanted an authoritative example of this modern practice that was that old, I do not know if they could even find it. From that time until today, all the best practitioners agree in believing and saying that music has reached the peak of perfection that man can imagine.

<margin>
Cipriano de Rore, a singular practical musician.
</margin>
Indeed, they say that since the death of Cipriano de Rore—a truly singular musician in this style of <term>Counterpoint</term> <note>Cipriano de Rore (1515–1565) was a Flemish composer famous for his expressive madrigals</note>—music has been in decline rather than in growth.

<margin>
Reasons why the lesser parts of the musical faculty have been retained.
</margin>
Now, if in a hundred years or a little more that music has been practiced in such a way—by people who are ordinarily of little or no value, of unknown birth, possessing few or no goods of fortune, and who barely even know how to read—it has come to that peak of excellence they claim, how much more stupendous and marvelous must it have been among the Greeks and Latins? There, it lasted for many, many centuries, continuously in the hands of the wisest, most learned, most judicious, most wealthy, and most valorous kings and great captains the world has ever had.

<margin>
Aemilius Probus, in his life of the same. In the fourth book.
<note>Reference to Cornelius Nepos, whose works were sometimes attributed to Aemilius Probus</note>
</margin>
It was a most shameful thing, a sign of ignorance, to be without the sort of music appropriate for a nobleman of any rank, as can be understood in part from the example of Themistocles and from what the historian Polybius says. Those who, by some accident, did not play the Lyre, were not ignorant of the <term>Tibia</term> <note>An ancient wind instrument, similar to an aulos or flute</note>.

<margin>
Proverb of the ancient Greeks.
</margin>
From this arose that proverb so common among the Greeks, which said: "If not a <term>Citharedo</term>, then at least an <term>Auledo</term>." <note>Original: "Se non Citharedo, almeno Auledo." Meaning: "If not a cithara player, at least a pipe player."</note>

<margin>
The Greeks loved music greatly, although Zarlino is of the contrary opinion in chapter 4 of the 2nd part of the *Institutions*.
<note>Gioseffo Zarlino was the most influential music theorist of the 16th century and Galilei's rival</note>
</margin>
That these people attended to and greatly loved music—even though some have said, without reason, that they were devoted more to labor than to festivals—can be known for the most part from this: while being besieged by the numerous army of Xerxes, they never neglected any of their public festivals in which all sorts of music were practiced. This gave Xerxes frequent cause for doubt; for he knew for certain (so to speak) that they were dying of hardship and hunger, yet he saw and heard them day and night dancing, singing, and playing.

<margin>
In the Eighth [book of the Politics].
</margin>
But why do I spend more words on this, when Aristotle himself, that supernatural philosopher, expressly commands in his books on the Republic that children must learn music with great study, so that they do not have to learn it once they are grown men? But he does not mean the music of the theater, made for the satisfaction of the common people (which is almost the same as ours), but that which befits those born noble—which is true music, not feigned.

<margin>
Precepts of music.
</margin>
This was for no other reason than to gradually introduce them to taking honest pleasure with dignity and reason. The fruit gathered from music is divided into three parts: one refers to erudition and discipline; another to the purgation of the soul by venting and mitigating it—a faculty that harmonies and melodies had when they conformed to those passions (and sometimes even the opposite ones); and the third was effective...

# Ancient and Modern

<margin>
Music today has no specific properties or character.
</margin>
...a means, he says, of passing life joyfully in rest and tranquility, while calling a truce with the overly heavy cares that keep souls besieged. At another time, along with others, he divided it into the moral, the active, and that which fills souls with divine frenzy. The moral was the *Dorian*, the active was the *Phrygian*, and that which filled souls with divine frenzy was the *Lydian*. These last two types of harmony, the Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle</note> maintains, should be avoided and not used, except perhaps by those fit to judge them. Today, not only do the heads of Republics and Senators not play or sing in such a manner, but even private gentlemen are ashamed of it. Regarding the importance and stimulus it provides to professors of music to be near nobles or under a Prince who loves and appreciates it, it would be the same vanity and impertinence to try to demonstrate this as it would be for one who took care to further persuade others that the ancient *Greeks* and *Latins* gave it more effort and study than is done today, or that they surpassed the men of our times in every art and science; for every book of any important faculty we possess was first composed and written by them. Despite all the height of excellence in the practical music of the moderns, one does not hear or see today even the slightest sign of the effects that ancient music produced; nor is it even read that it produced them fifty or a hundred years ago when it was not so common and familiar to men. Thus, neither its novelty nor its excellence has ever had the power among our practitioners to produce any of those virtuous effects that ancient music produced, from which infinite utility and comfort were drawn. From this, one necessarily concludes either that music or human nature has changed from its first being; but what the music of the ancients was, and what that of today is, and why this could and can happen, will be shown in its proper place.

**STR.** I hear these novelties with such pleasure—which you seek to persuade me of with so many sensible and vivid reasons—that if you are willing, and without spoiling the order you have proposed to yourself in your Idea regarding these matters, I would gladly hear all else you wish to tell me on this subject.

<margin>
In the preface of the Histories, for what purpose Music was introduced.
</margin>
<margin>
Diverse nature of sounds and motions.
</margin>
<margin>
Singing in consonance is an absurdity; *Zarlino* on the contrary says that without it, harmony is imperfect, in the *Institutions* <note>original: "instituit." referring to Gioseffo Zarlino's *Le Istitutioni harmoniche*</note> in chapter 1 of book 15, and in chapter 49 of book 2.
</margin>
<margin>
Diverse nature of consonances.
</margin>
<margin>
The <term>Diapason</term> <note>The interval of an octave</note> is the smallest multiple interval.
</margin>
**BAR.** If it pleases you so, it pleases me equally; especially since we have moved quite far forward, I will not have to repeat the same things to you many times. Let us, then, make a trial of how much truth can ever be seen by us in the proposed subject; not fearing (since the end of our desire is solely the public benefit) those imputations that may follow us for having had the daring to be the first to break this ice, so hard, deep, and wide. Note this: if the use of music—I speak at present of the true music that is useful to all men, as *Polybius* <note>A Greek historian who argued music was essential for civilizing harsh climates</note> says, and not of that which according to *Ephorus* <note>A Greek historian who viewed music as a mere deception</note> was found to mock and deceive them—if the use of music, I say, was introduced by men for the respect and purpose that all the wise say by common opinion (which arose primarily from nothing other than expressing the concepts of their souls with greater efficacy in celebrating the praises of the Gods, the Genii, and the heroes, as can be partly understood from the firm and plain Church chants, the origin of our music for many voices); and secondarily to imprint these with equal force in the minds of mortals for their utility and comfort; then it will be a clear thing that the rules of modern <term>Contrapuntists</term> <note>Composers who write multiple independent melodic lines (counterpoint)</note>, observed as inviolable laws—in addition to those they use so frequently by choice to show off their knowledge—will all be directly contrary to the perfection of the best and true harmonies and melodies. To prove, demonstrate, and persuade one of this will not be very difficult; provided, however, that those who remember all that has been said here regarding this will set aside their own interests, envy, bad habits, and ignorance. As the foundation of this subject, I will succinctly mention only two main and important heads, promising to declare them more fully a little further below. Therefore, I say that the nature of the low <note>original: "grave"</note> sound is one thing, that of the high <note>original: "acuto"</note> is another, and different from both of these, I say, is that of the middle sound. Likewise, I say that fast motion has one property, slow motion another, and far from both of these is moderate motion. Now, these two principles being true—as they are most true—it can easily be gathered from them (truth being one) that singing in <term>consonance</term> <note>Harmonious intervals like the third, fifth, or octave</note> in the manner modern practitioners use is an impertinence <note>In the sense of being irrelevant or illogical to the goal of expressing emotion</note>. This is because consonance is nothing other than a mixture of low and high sound, which (as you have heard above) strikes the hearing without offense, with delight, or most sweetly. Therefore, if such a contrariety of affection is found between the extreme sounds of simple consonances, how much more will such diverse natures be found in replicated and composite ones, by means of the greater distance between the extremes? And even more in those that are composed and replicated many times? These, being further from their origin, are less pure, less understood by the senses, and less grasped by the intellect. Nonetheless, they are sought with great industry by modern practitioners in instruments made by art and nature. And such being the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The Octave</note> and the <term>Diapente</term> <note>The Fifth</note>—whose extreme sounds unite so separately in each of them, and particularly those of the smallest multiple interval, that due to the agreement they have together they seem almost the same thing joined in a single term—how much more will the extremes of imperfect consonances be of diverse nature, and even more so the dissonances with which their songs <note>original: "Cantilene"</note> are filled? Now, if such diversity is found between only two parts...

# Dialogue on Music

<margin>Contrary motion, and to what end it serves.</margin>
If it is difficult for two voices to sing a single interval together, whether simple or compound, how much more difficult is it when four, six, or more sing together at the same time? In modern music, these voices are often composed of different natures and intervals, which the **Contrapuntalists** <note>Composers who write music with multiple independent melodies playing at once, known as counterpoint.</note> typically use in their songs to the great ruin of true music. To these obstacles caused by the diversity of sounds and variety of voices, let us add those arising from the inequality of the **Motion** <term>Moto: the rhythmic speed or melodic direction of a musical part</term> of the parts, which are no less important than the first. These obstacles occur because often the **Soprano** part barely moves due to the "laziness" of its slow notes, while by contrast, the **Bass** part flies along, and the **Tenor** and **Contralto** parts go walking with a slow pace. Or perhaps one part flies while another walks, and yet another remains almost motionless. 

The result is that while one part tries to pull the listener toward a specific emotion through its movement and sound—and even more so when accompanied by words suited to that sound and motion—the other parts, being contrary, push the listener away. It is no different than what would happen to a column: if it were placed evenly on its base, and someone, in order to topple it, attached two or more equal ropes to the capital, each pulled in opposite directions by equal forces from an equal distance. Despite all the effort used, the column would not move a bit from its place, unless it were already failing in some part due to its own defect. This is because the opposing force resists the violence placed against it. But if someone, using all those same tools and forces, were to pull it from one side only, I believe it would not be a marvelous thing at all if that combined effort had enough power to topple it.

<margin>A very famous rule of today's composers.</margin>
Let us further add to these obstacles that, in order to create their **Fugues** <term>Fughe: a technique where different voices enter one after another with the same melody, "chasing" each other</term>—whether they call them straight or reversed—composers are often deprived of that kind of harmony they prize so much. This harmony requires that the lower part never lack a **Third** nor a **Fifth**, or sometimes a **Sixth** or their octaves, especially when at least four parts are singing together.

<margin>Why rests were introduced into today's songs; thus, what Zarlino says on this subject in Chapter 53 of Part 3 is not true.</margin>
To observe these rules, they have introduced a variety of **Rests** <note>original: "Poſe ò pauſe"</note> without caring that, while one part is singing the beginning of the words (whether in prose or verse), another part is singing not only the middle or the end of the same phrase, but perhaps the beginning, middle, or end of an entirely different verse or concept. Often, contrary to all duty and besides repeating the same syllables four or six times, they place one syllable in heaven, another on earth, and if there are more, in the abyss <note>A critique of "word-painting," where the music mimics the literal meaning of words—high notes for "heaven," low notes for "abyss"—often resulting in fragmented text.</note>. 

They claim this is well done to imitate the concepts, the words, and the parts. They frequently drag one of these syllables under twenty or more different notes, sometimes imitating the chirping of birds and other times the howling of dogs. How much imperfection this causes, and how much power it takes away from the expression of the **Affection** <term>Affetto: the specific emotion or "state of soul" the music is meant to evoke</term>—which naturally moves a similar feeling in the listener—need not be discussed further. To ensure that no such emotion ever enters the minds of the listeners, modern practical Contrapuntalists have, among their many confused rules, accepted as a fatal law that it is not permitted to have two or more perfect consonances of the same proportion and species <note>Referencing the rule against "parallel fifths" or "parallel octaves."</note> one after another.

<margin>Different notes: why they were introduced into Counterpoint.</margin>
By following this rule, they have—without purpose and against the reason of the natural movement of the voice—invented more types of notes than were necessary for expressing concepts, just so they could more easily follow that precept. They made this rule for no other end than because perfect consonances do not have the power to distract a man into different emotions the way imperfect consonances and dissonances do (due to the disproportion of their extremes). They allow as many of these imperfect sounds as the Contrapuntalist pleases. In approving this specific rule, they fail to see how much they deserve to be considered crude and ignorant. I do not mean those who first instituted these laws—which, as you will hear, were made with great judgment for the specific goals of their authors—but rather those who have used and approved them until now for a different purpose, without ever caring to know where they came from or why they should be observed. They grant them unquestioning faith without even a hope of being able to improve them, going along with the crowd and, as the proverb says, "following the cries" without understanding the cause. 

What is worse, they have continually used all their strength and knowledge to seek out occasions where, when they speak through singing, no sense or structure can be gathered from their concepts. Indeed, not a single word can be understood, as if they were ashamed to be not men, but rational animals. They even marvel at, and laugh at (as you did earlier), the knowledge of the **Ancient Musicians** and the marvelous effects they produced in various subjects, wishing to measure the perfect and learned science of the ancients by their own confused ignorance.

<margin>Rules of the Contrapuntalists: where they derived from.</margin>
The modern way of composing and singing multiple melodies together in consonance derived, if I am not mistaken, from stringed instruments similar to the **Epigonion** and the **Simikon** <note>Ancient Greek instruments with many strings (the Epigonion had 40).</note>. Since these instruments had a great number of strings arranged in the manner shown above, the **Citharists** <term>Cithariſti: players of the kithara (a professional lyre)</term> of those times began—either to surpass the **Citharedes** <term>Citharedi: musicians who both sang and played the kithara</term> or to avoid the obligation of having a singer always nearby for the perfection of the melody, since the voice and the instru...

# Ancient & Modern [Music]

<margin>Playing in consonance, and why it was introduced.</margin>
...instrument of that which they were making; they began, I say, with what little light of Music they possessed, without any respect for the laws of Terpander <note>An ancient Greek poet and musician credited with establishing the first formal rules of music.</note> or any other approved legislator of authority; they went investigating a way in which they could, without their help, delight the sense of hearing in some manner with the simple sound of the instrument. To color this design, they judged the diversity of consonances and chords to be an effective means. In the past, these were never approved by anyone of sound intellect (for the purpose we have mentioned), but were greatly and with just cause abhorred; for they knew very well that consonance had the power to "un-tune" the well-composed minds of the listeners. Concerning this, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> reasons thus:

<margin>Consonance: what it is suited for.</margin>
<margin>In the eighth [book] of the Politics.</margin>
"But taking away the artificial education of musical instruments and such exercises, and positing that artificial music is that which serves the spectacles: for he who uses it in them does not strive within for any virtuous end, but to give pleasure to the hearer, and that this pleasure is furthermore basely made: therefore we affirm such exercises to belong not to free men, but to servile and mechanical craftsmen." Having said a little before that "affective harmonies" should be used for discipline, while "active and abstractive" harmonies should be heard by means of others who sing and play them to entertain themselves in leisure, to relax the soul, and to find quiet from business.

<margin>The noblest part of Music, and what it may be.</margin>
Nevertheless, the **Citharists** <note>Players of the cithara, an ancient Greek professional lyre.</note> went on investigating this, necessitated by the aforementioned obligation due to the poor quality of their voices. Through this defect, they found themselves deprived of the most noble, important, and principal part of music, which is the "concepts of the soul" expressed by means of words—and not the chords of the various parts, as modern practitioners say and believe. These moderns have made their reason a slave to their appetites. One does not find among the Greeks that the Poets and Musicians were servants to the practical composers and singers, just as it has never been the custom that precious jewels are adapted to serve the gold setting; rather, it is quite the opposite.

<margin>The singer, player, and Counterpoint-writer being servants and instruments of the true musician. An Example.</margin>
Wishing then to compensate for their defect, the Citharists introduced into artificial instruments the method of playing these multiple melodies together in consonance. Exercising themselves in this for a long time, always aiming at the prescribed goal, they began through long experience to recognize what was displeasing, what generated boredom, and what finally delighted the ear. To have a wider and more spacious field, they introduced for this purpose not only the use of "imperfect" consonances <note>Intervals like thirds and sixths, which were considered less stable than "perfect" octaves or fifths.</note>—which were discreetly called so because they *seem* rather than truly *are* consonant—but even dissonances:

<margin>Imperfect consonances and dissonances: why they were introduced into modern Counterpoint.</margin>
seeing that with only the five consonances that the ancient Musicians took into consideration (called today "perfect"), the matter proved difficult and tedious. From the use of these imperfect consonances derived the change of the **Diatonic Ditonic** <term>Diatonia Ditoniea: a traditional Greek tuning system based on pure whole tones</term> species which existed before, into something like the **Intense Diatonic** <term>Syntona incitata: Ptolemy's tuning system, which used smaller intervals and was closer to the tuning used in the Renaissance</term>. This change necessarily caused, for the reasons mentioned above regarding particularly its poorly tempered chords, a simultaneous change in the way of singing regarding the size and smallness of intervals, and consequently, the moral character (*costume*). For that highly reputed species, which was truly ordained by Nature and used in its simplicity, was grave, virile, and constant; whereas, by contrast, this modern one is, by its inconstancy, ridiculous, effeminate, and varied. It has reached the point that from the "severe matron" that Music was in ancient times, she has today become a lascivious (not to say shameless) harlot. For this defect, the Poets are no less to be blamed than the **Contrapuntists** <note>Composers of polyphony.</note>. From this it happens that the music of today is so reviled and despised by the intelligent, and on the contrary, prized by the foolish commoners; for the latter willingly practice things conforming to themselves, and converse with those men who, even if they wished to, are too ignorant to rebuke them.

<margin>How the ancient way of singing has changed into today's, and what caused it. Aristoxenus in the first [book] of the Harmonic Elements.</margin>
<margin>Today's Music is, according to Zarlino, a miraculous thing; and that of the ancients was a most unhappy thing, in chapters 1 and 4 of the 2nd part of the Institutes. Today's music, why it is despised by the intelligent and appreciated by the common folk. Plato's precept refuted by Zarlino in chapter 41 of the 2nd part.</margin>
On the contrary, they abhor all those things and the men associated with them who are able to improve them through their virtuous and well-mannered example. Ignorance is the only cause of this—which the commoners would be forced to confess (however unwillingly) every time they admitted needing the knowledge of the wise. These things being known by the Divine Plato, he expressly commanded in his laws that one should sing and play *Proschorda* and not *Simphone* <note>original: "Proschorda, & non Simphone" — meaning "in unison" rather than "in harmony" or "in consonance".</note>; that is, in Unison and not in consonance. He had previously said in the *Timaeus* that harmony, although it has movements joined and suitable to the discourses of our soul, is useful to the man who uses the Muses with his intellect, and not for "irrational pleasure" as it now seems to be. Thus it is clearly seen that even until the time of that Divine Philosopher, it was the custom for some to sing and play in consonance: but they never uttered the syllables of the same word one after the other, nor did they ruin and break the order and measure of the verses as is the custom today. Plutarch lamented the same thing, as did Carlo Valgulio shortly before **Gaffurio** <note>Franchino Gaffurio (1451–1522), a major Italian music theorist.</note>, saying:

<margin>Plutarch laments the music of his times, and likewise Carlo Valgulio.</margin>
> One sees flourishing today,
> Certain adulterated songs,
> That make music a bastard.

Not content with all the diversity of intervals contained within the boundaries of the fifteen strings of the **Great Pythagorean System**, our practitioners made even more be heard, passing—despite its nature—toward the deep and toward the high beyond the Quadruple <note>An interval of two octaves.</note>, into the nineteenths, the twenty-seconds, and "further beyond" even to the antipodes, truly against every nature of emotion. This is because...

# Dialogue on Music

<margin>Precept of Aristotle in the Politics, Book 8.</margin>
<margin>The goal of today’s music, what it is. The goal of sense and of reason, what they are.</margin>
<margin>What difference there is between the Musician, the singer, the player, and the Contrapuntist.</margin>
<margin>Nature of the sense.</margin>
...as everyone can commonly hear, one who laments never departs from the high notes <note>original: "corde," literally "strings," but referring to pitch levels</note>; and on the contrary, one who is mournful never distances himself from the low ones except by a slight distance. Such a distance never reaches the middle state—let alone surpasses it—because it would be neither suited nor fit for such a purpose. Yet, we hear this done in the songs of our modern Musicians, who, not only with the entire body of all these melodies mixed together, but very often with a single part—be it Soprano or Tenor—arrive by jumping now upwards and now downwards, either step-wise or by leaps, across the span of eleven or twelve notes <note>original: "corde & voci"</note>. They do this without taking any account of what Plato warns us, and likewise Aristotle, when he says that music which does not serve the character of the soul <note>original: "costume dell'animo," referring to the ethical effect or *ethos* of music</note> is truly to be despised. Among the ancient Musicians of merit, severity and humble diligence were always highly reputed; whereas, on the contrary, those of our times have—without any respect and in the manner of the Epicureans <note>Followers of Epicurus, here used to imply those who prioritize sensory pleasure over intellectual or moral purpose.</note>—placed novelty for the delight of the sense above all other things. They argue that the judgment of hearing is that which has the faculty to measure and taste musical intervals. To them, we shall respond for now that the sense of hearing truly perceives the entire beginning of this faculty; for if hearing did not exist, there would be no dispute over voices and sounds. The same would happen whenever motion (from which sound derives its being) ceased. But as for the distance by which musical intervals differ from one another, it is not the simple virtue of the ears to discern it. Their judgment in this affair is dull, if not to say deaf; they submit to reason and rules in such a way that the sense obeys like a servant, and reason is the guide and mistress. For who is of such sound intellect and such purified hearing that he could or would know how to extract the ninth or tenth part of an Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note> at his pleasure? Or, conversely, to increase it now by three-quarters and now by a third? No one, in my opinion, without the help of the harmonic rule. Thus, likewise, knowing the nature of musical intervals is not a simple virtue of the sense. But why do I go gathering authorities and examples if this alone can suffice to persuade you which is more noble and deserves more praise: the practitioner or the speculative [theorist]? In the labor of buildings brought to fruition by craftsmen, or of cities conquered and subjugated by means of soldiers and engines of war, no account is taken—nor is mention ever made—of the labor and service through which such enterprises are completed; but only of the Architect and the General of the armies. Now, the same difference is found between the speculative Musician <note>In this period, a "Musician" was a scholar of the science of music, distinct from a mere performer.</note> and the practical singer, player, and Contrapuntist <note>A composer of counterpoint.</note>, who must obey the Musician as instruments directed and governed by him. And although the senses recognize white and black, or bitter and sweet, they do not recognize them in a way that allows them to discern that one is to be desired and the other to be avoided.

---

<margin>Zarlino in chapter 2 of the 3rd [book] of his *Institutions* <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), the most influential music theorist of the Renaissance.</note>.</margin>
<margin>The presumption of certain modern keyboard players.</margin>
<margin>Comparison.</margin>
<margin>From the manner of playing in consonance derived the way of composing and singing these multiple melodies together.</margin>
The practical players of those times began, therefore, to form their rules and laws upon the instruments I mentioned above. The first of these is that it is not permitted, when playing no more than two strings at a time, to make two of those consonances called today "perfect" <note>Unisons, fifths, and octaves.</note> one after another of the same species and genus. This was for no other reason than to avoid delighting the hearing entirely through the simplicity of the extreme sounds between only two strings; for the hearing, like all other senses, willingly feeds on the diversity of its proper objects. On the contrary, they permitted two or three "imperfect" consonances <note>Thirds and sixths.</note> as being less simple and more variable. This was not because of the difference between the major or minor Tone found between them, as some dare to say, but because of the variety of their extremes, which do not unite as perfectly in that part as the perfect ones do. That such a law against making two or more perfect consonances in succession was instituted by those legislators only for when one plays two and no more strings at the same time is clearly signaled by the fact that when playing three, four, or more together on artificial instruments, they permitted them—as is still tolerated today—without the hearing being offended in any part. I know well that some arrogant men of our times (for lack of a more honest name to call them) dare to tell those simpler than themselves—who listen to them as if they were miracles—that two perfect consonances are avoided on the keyboard instrument <note>original: "Strumento di tasti"</note> they profess by the diversity of the fingers, as seen by the sight and not by the hearing of those who observe them closely. See, I pray you, what unheard-of foolishness this is: to want sight to be a competent judge of the diversity of sounds, which is the same as saying hearing has a part in discerning the differences between colors. From this manner of playing in consonance, I say, it came to the consideration of the practical Musicians who lived shortly before our ancestors that one could also compose and sing in such a manner. That ancient and learned manner had already been entirely lost many, many years before due to wars or other accidents. We shall make mention of it a little further below and give it—beyond what we have given so far—the greatest light possible for our weak strengths. This is for no other end than to excite great and virtuous minds to labor at such a noble science, and to see if it can be reduced to its first and happy state. I do not consider this impossible, knowing that for those who first invented it and led it to the height of perfection, it was not infused by the stars, but was rather acquired through their industrious toil and assiduous study. Ancient Music was lost, I say, together with all the fine arts and sciences, of which so little light remains that many repute its marvelous excellence to be a dream or a fable.

### Ancient & Modern [Music]

After the loss of that [ancient music], people began to derive rules and standards for composing and singing—as they played upon them—multiple melodies together from string and wind instruments, such as the Organ <note>The author notes that the organs of that time differed from the 16th-century instruments known to his readers.</note> which was in use in those days. They embraced as laws the same observations that the *Citharists* <term>Citharists: players of the kithara or cittern</term> and *Organists* had used before them. However, they made an exception regarding the use of two perfect consonances of the same kind <note>original: "due perfette consonanze d'un'istessa spezie," referring to the rule against parallel fifths or octaves</note>, even when four or more voices sang together. This was done perhaps to increase the difficulty of the task, or to appear to have a more refined and delicate sense of hearing than others, or truly believing that the same issues that arise between two parts also occur among four, six, or more parts singing together.

<margin>The common people are always ignorant of what is good in things.</margin>
This manner of composing and singing—because of the novelty it brought, along with the ease of quickly becoming a "Musician"—pleased the general public. This is what usually happens, thanks to the public's imperfection and little knowledge of what is truly good and true in things. This gave craftsmen the opportunity to go on fantasizing and introducing new observations beyond the first ones. These later composers did not want to follow or entirely approve of the footsteps and works of those before them, so as not to seem—by a sort of silent consent—to confess themselves inferior in industry and genius to the first inventors. They kept their aim always on leading music to the final ruin in which it now finds itself. From this, they added to that precept—that it was permissible to make two imperfect consonances—the rule that they must necessarily be of different kinds. Furthermore, they dictated that when moving from an imperfect to a perfect consonance, one should move to the nearest one; this was always intended for compositions of two voices. Now you see how, little by little, enticed by ambition, they went about—without noticing it at all—submitting reason to sense, form to matter, and truth to falsehood.

<margin>Other impertinences of the Contrapuntists.</margin>
Not content with this, those of our times added to the method of proceeding from an imperfect to a perfect consonance, and from one imperfect consonance to another, the requirement that one must respect and avoid the relation of the *Tritone* <term>Tritone: an unstable interval of three whole steps, often called "the devil in music" in this period</term> and the *Semidiapente* <term>Semidiapente: a diminished fifth</term> that could arise between this or that part. Therefore, they insisted that when a major *Sixth* was followed by a *Third*, the third should be minor, provided the parts changed position by contrary motion. And if one of those followed the major version of these, it should always be minor, and vice versa. They further insisted that when four or more parts sing together, the lowest part should never lack the *Third* nor the *Fifth*, or in place of the latter, the *Sixth* or one of their octaves. Because of the simple delight the ear takes in chords, there is no one who—considering their variety—would not judge these observations to be excellent and necessary; but for the expression of concepts, they are pestilential. For they are suited to nothing other than making the harmony varied and full, a thing which is not always—indeed, never—appropriate for the expression of any concept of the *Poet* or the *Orator*. And so I say again, that if the aforementioned

<margin>What the rules and observations of the Contrapuntists are fit for.</margin>
observations had been applied to the goal of their origin, those who have expanded them in modern times would deserve no less praise than the first lawmakers. But the whole error is that the goal today is different, even directly contrary to that of the first inventors of the craft; and what the truth of it is has already been understood. It was never their intention that such rules should serve for the use of harmonies intended to express the concept of the soul through words, and with that appropriate affection <note>original: "affetto," referring to the emotional state or "affect" of the music</note>. Rather, they were meant for the simple sound of artificial instruments, both wind and strings, as can be gathered from what we have said so far about the first authors of these rules. But the matter has always been understood backward by those who followed, and this belief has grown so old that I consider it a very difficult, if not impossible, thing to remove and dissuade from the minds of men—particularly those who are simple practitioners of this kind of counterpoint. These men are therefore esteemed and prized by the common people, salaried by various lords, and have up to now informed everyone else about the things pertaining to that

<margin>In the Eighth [book] of his Republic.</margin>
practice they call music. To persuade such people that they are ignorant of true music, one would need not the rhetoric and eloquence of *Cicero* or *Demosthenes*, but the sword of *Orlando Paladino* <note>Roland, the legendary knight; implying that only force, not logic, can change their minds.</note> or the authority of some great Prince who is a friend of truth. Such a Prince, leaving this [modern] music in the hands of the common people as something suited to them, could persuade the nobles by his example to apply themselves to the music appropriate for them; which is, as *Aristotle* says, the honest music used with dignity. For in a well-ordered Republic, as he says in the eighth book of his *Politics* <note>original: "nella sua all'ottauo," referring to Aristotle's Politics, though the margin notes "Republic."</note>, music that is corrupt and far from the true mode of music is granted to the common people, just as today's music is so admired and prized by them; for everyone naturally desires his own likeness. But enough has been said of this. Consider every rule of the modern Contrapuntists, either individually or all together: they tend toward nothing but the delight of the ear, if "delight" is the right word. As for the manner of expressing the concepts of the soul and impressing them with the greatest possible efficacy into the minds of the listeners for their benefit and use, there is no book among them that speaks of it, nor is it ever thought of—nor has it been since this invention [of counterpoint]. Instead, they think only of tearing it further apart, if there is still room to do so. It is true that today no one thinks at all of expressing the concepts of the words with the affection they require, except in that ridiculous manner that will be described shortly below. A manifest sign of this is that their observations and rules comprise nothing but the manner of moving around musical intervals, seeking to weave the song out of varied chords according to the precepts mentioned above, without any other...

Being devoid of sense, motion, intellect, speech, discourse, reason, and soul, they are capable of nothing more. But men, who have been endowed by nature with all these beautiful, noble, and excellent parts, should seek by means of them not only to delight, but as imitators of the good ancients, to be useful at the same time, since they are suited for this; because doing otherwise, they act against nature, which is the minister of God. # Ancient & Modern

<margin>
Another impertinence of the <term>Contrapuntists</term> <note>Composers who write polyphonic music where multiple independent melodies are played at once.</note>.
</margin>
...who today are called Musicians by the common people. Among their impertinences and novelties, we also find that of sometimes transposing a piece toward the bass or toward the treble—as expert <term>Organists</term> <note>Players of the pipe organ.</note> usually do for the convenience of the choir—by a whole Tone, a Third, or some other interval. Using <term>accidental signs</term> <note>Sharps, flats, or naturals that alter a note's pitch.</note>, they take songs originally composed for natural and common singable movements and move them into <term>foreign notes</term> <note>Playing in difficult or unusual keys that were not standard for the time.</note>, making them unsingable and extraordinary, and full of artifice. They do this for no other reason than to have a wider stage to preach about themselves and their works as miracles to those who understand less than they do. Furthermore, there has been no shortage among the most famous of those who first composed the notes according to their own whims, and then adapted whatever words they pleased to them; without placing any value on the fact that between the words and the notes there is as much or greater deformity as that which was said to exist between the <term>Dithyramb</term> <note>A wild, passionate ancient Greek hymn, often associated with Dionysus.</note> and <term>Dorian harmony</term> <note>The Dorian mode, considered by the Greeks to be stable, brave, and solemn.</note>. Some people of status are then surprised that most of today’s songs sound better when well-played on instruments than when well-sung. They do not realize that the purpose of these songs is to be communicated to the ear by means of artificial instruments, and not natural ones; because they are the product of artifice itself, and not at all natural. And to further remove such wonder from them, and the labor from me of so often reciting the words of others, let them read on this subject in section nineteen, the tenth problem of Aristotle, which will satisfy them. Modern <term>Counterpoint</term> <note>The technique of combining two or more melodic lines.</note> has nothing else ingenious or rare about it except the use of <term>dissonances</term> <note>Clashing sounds that create musical tension.</note>; provided, however, they are accommodated with the proper means and resolved with judgment. Furthermore, it possesses the charm and grace of <term>consonances</term> <note>Harmonious intervals that sound pleasing to the ear.</note>. But both of these, when it comes to expressing concepts to impress the <term>affections</term> <note>Emotional states or passions that music was intended to evoke.</note> upon the listener, are not only a great hindrance but the worst poison.

<margin>
Why the use of consonances and dissonances in singing is harmful.
</margin>
The reason is this: the continuous delicacy of the diversity of chords, mixed with that little bit of harshness and bitterness from the various dissonances—besides a thousand other excessive manners of artifice that the <term>Contrapuntists</term> of our times have sought with such industry to entice the ears (which I will skip telling to avoid being tedious)—are, as I said, a supreme obstacle to moving the soul to any affection. The soul, occupied and almost bound primarily by these snares of such pleasure, is given no time to understand, let alone consider, the poorly uttered words. All these things are contrary to what is necessary for an emotion by its nature; because emotion and character want to be something simple and natural, or at

<margin>
The goal of the ancient Musician.
</margin>
least appear to be so, and have as their only aim to move oneself in others.

**STR.** It seems from what you have said so far, among many other important things, that the music of today is not of much value for expressing the concepts of the soul by means of words; but it is certainly valuable for simple wind and string instruments. From these, the ear desires and experiences nothing else but to feed sweetly on the diversity of their chords, accompanied by suitable and proportionate movements, of which they are copious; these are then manifested to the ear by means of some practitioner who is practiced and skilled in them.

**BAR.** What you say would be the case if the harmonies of various artificial instruments were fit for nothing else than to amuse and excite the ears, as you said; and if the <term>Contrapuntists</term> of our times had been content with having mangled only that part of music which belongs to the expression of concepts. But they were not content with that; for even this part, which pertains to the simple chords of artificial instruments and the delight of the senses without passing further into the soul, they have treated no better than the first. In fact, they have reduced it to such a state that if it were to worsen even slightly, it would need to be buried rather than cured.

**STR.** How so, pray tell?

<margin>
That part of music belonging to artificial instruments is also corrupted.
</margin>
**BAR.** Do you not notice the particular persistence of the <term>Fugues</term> <note>A musical technique where a short melody is introduced by one part and successively taken up by others.</note>, both direct and reversed, which they use so frequently and obstinately? I mean in that genre of <term>Counterpoint</term> they call <term>Ricercars</term> <note>An elaborate instrumental composition, a precursor to the fugue.</note>, which are the proper and peculiar part of music for artificial instruments. They usually compose these for four voices without the obligation of words, for no other purpose than to have a wider field to better satisfy the ear with the diverse quality of the notes, the chords, and the movements, communicating them through an agent who is well-practiced. But the imitation in these <term>Fugues</term>, because of the excessive adherence most composers give them—driven by nothing other than ambition—often causes the bass part, when all four are singing together, to lack a Third, or at other times a Fifth or a Sixth, or any of the doubled intervals as has been said so many times; besides the disproportionate movements and rhythms.

<margin>
A comparison.
</margin>

What shall we say next of that other impertinence concerning the value of the

<margin>

Notes from which they often compose the aforementioned <term>Fugues</term>? Such as using <term>Semibreves</term> <note>Whole notes.</note> with a dot, and <term>Breves</term> <note>Double whole notes.</note>, to say nothing of those composed of notes of even greater value. It is simply this: if they were not played with better judgment on the <term>Lute</term> and the <term>Harpsichord</term>—both most noble instruments—than they were originally composed by their authors, they could not be heard in many places with any taste at all, due to the poverty of the chords. I will say only this for the height of their confusion: that because of the vain desire they have to be considered intelligent by those who know less than they do, they attribute it to great ignorance, on any important occasion, to mark the <term>sharp</term> <note>original: "dieſis X"</note> in F or in G, when departing from there they ascend to B-flat or to C. They say on firm ground that it is not reasonable to proceed by dissonant intervals such as the <term>diminished fourths</term> <note>original: "Semidiateſſaron"</note>. They would even be indignant with those who, when performing one of their compositions where this occurs as mentioned, did not do so; because truly, in that manner, it is most sweet to hear, particularly on the lute, which has <term>major thirds</term> in place of diminished fourths; nor can they arise there in any way, as I have proved to you above.

**STROZZI:** It is at least a good thing that they have enough discretion and judgment to be ashamed to do what they were not ashamed to say.
