**BARDI:** Quite the opposite; they are ashamed to say what they have not been ashamed to do. For the true "doing" in this sort of practice they call Music is the means of operating either with natural voices or by means of artificial instruments, and not by writing this or that cipher near the notes. I had intended to discourse with you about that other ambitious vanity of which our practical musicians make such a clamor—at least with those who understand their Music less—such as making one or more parts of their compositions wrap around the <term>device</term> <note>An "impresa" or heraldic symbol.</note> or coat of arms of the person to whom they wish to give it as a gift. Or perhaps writing it to be read in a mirror, or on the fingers of the hands; or one part will sing the beginning at the same time the other sings the end or the middle of the same part; and another time they will make the notes silent and the rests <note>original: "poſe"</note> sung. Not content with this, others want it to be sung sometimes without lines, with the names of the notes signified by vowels over the words, and their value indicated by certain extravagant and bizarre <term>Chaldean or Egyptian ciphers</term> <note>Referring to esoteric or "eye-music" notations that look like ancient or mystical codes.</note>. Or instead of these, they paint beautiful and diverse flowers and leaves across the papers, the singers of which represent to the sight of the listeners so many <term>Asclepiuses</term> <note>The Greek god of medicine; perhaps implying they look like wise healers or performers of miracles.</note>, besides a thousand other ridiculous vanities. All of these things, if used with the proper means at the appropriate time and place, would not be totally to be despised. But wanting to preach them to us out of season as supernatural things is not reasonable to endure. The true place and time for these concepts of theirs would be, in my opinion, at <term>Carnival vigils</term> as a joke and a prank; or perhaps sometimes after dinner instead of the <term>melon seeds</term> that are customarily eaten in their season for amusement, to have less occasion to think in that moment and to soothe the boredom of the heat. Such inventions are like those musical instruments in whose construction one sees the greatest labor, diligence, and industry of the craftsmen, but when played afterward—even by a learned and excellent hand—render their sounds and voices raw and disordered. The delight drawn from them is entirely for the sight, even though the intention of the craftsmen (even if the effect did not follow the primary intent) was principally for the satisfaction of the hearing. As I have said, one could show them a thousand other momentous inconveniences, which we will refer to another time.

# Ancient and Modern.

H 3

...there are some [voices] that say "flee," or "fly"; which they utter with such speed and so little grace as can be imagined. Regarding those words where they have said "vanish," "faint," "die," or "extinguished," they have made the parts fall silent in an instant with such violence that, instead of inducing any of those affects, they have moved the listeners to laughter, and at other times to indignation, feeling as if they were being mocked. Then, when they have said "alone," "two," or "together," they have made a single person, two, or everyone sing together with unusual "gallantry."

<margin>New abuses by the <term>Contrapuntists</term> <note>Composers of polyphonic music, where multiple independent melodies are sung at once.</note> regarding the imitation of words.</margin>
Others, in singing this particular verse from one of the <term>Sestinas</term> <note>A complex, six-stanza poetic form.</note> of Petrarch: *And with the lame ox he will go hunting Laura* <note>original: "Et col bue zoppo andrà cacciando Laura"</note>, have uttered it under notes that are jerky, wavering, and syncopated, no differently than if they had the hiccups. And when the concept they have in hand makes mention (as sometimes happens) of the noise of a drum, or the sound of trumpets, or another such instrument, they have tried to represent its sound to the ear with their singing, without any regard for having pronounced such words in any unusual manner. When they have found words denoting a diversity of colors, such as "dark" or "fair" hair and the like, they have placed black and white notes beneath them to express that very concept cleverly and with style (according to them); thereby subjecting the sense of hearing to the accidents of shapes and colors—objects which belong specifically to sight and touch in solid bodies. There have even been those who, being more corrupted, tried to depict "blue" or "purple" voices with the notes according to the sound of the words, no differently than how string-makers today color gut strings. At another time, when a verse says: *Into Hell he descended into the lap of Pluto* <note>original: "Nell'inferno discese in grembo à Pluto"</note>, they have made one of the parts of the song descend in such a way that the singer sounded more like someone trying to frighten children by moaning than someone who is speaking through song. Conversely, when saying: *He aspired to the stars* <note>original: "Questi aspirò alle stelle"</note>, they have ascended so high in uttering them that no one shrieking from any excessive internal or external pain ever reached such a height. Under a word that says, as occasionally occurs: "weeping," "laughing," "singing," "shouting," "shrieking," or truly "false deceits," "harsh chains," "hard bonds," "rugged mountain," "rigid cliff," "cruel woman," or other such things—leaving aside those sighs of theirs, the diffuse forms, and other tricks—they utter them to "color" their impertinent and vain designs in ways more unusual than any remote barbarian. Unfortunate men! They do not realize that if <term>Isocrates</term> or <term>Corax</term> <note>Famous ancient Greek teachers of rhetoric and oratory.</note>, or other more celebrated orators, had uttered even twice while speaking those words in such a fashion, they would have moved all their listeners to laughter and indignation at the same time; and they would have been mocked and despised by them as foolish, abject men of no value.

They then marvel that the music of their times does not produce any of those notable effects that ancient music did, whereas, on the contrary, this music is so far removed and different from that—indeed, its contrary and mortal enemy, as has been said and shown, and will be shown even more. They should instead be astonished if it *did* produce any effect, since it has no way of even thinking about it,

<margin>What the difference is between the goal of today's musicians and that of the ancients.</margin>
much less achieving it. For the goal of this modern music is nothing other than the delight of the ear, while the goal of ancient music was to lead another, through that means, into the very same emotion as oneself. No person of judgment understands expressing the concepts of the soul through words in that ridiculous manner; but in another way, far distant and different from it.

**STR.** <note>Strozzi, the student in this dialogue.</note> Tell me how, I pray you.

**BAR.** <note>Count Bardi, the mentor in this dialogue.</note> In the same way that those two famous orators mentioned a little above expressed them among many others in their orations; and as every ancient musician of worth did. And if they wish to understand the method, I am content to show them where and from whom they can learn it without much labor or boredom—indeed, with great pleasure—and it shall be this:

<margin>From whom modern practitioners can learn the imitation of words.</margin>
When they go for their amusement to the tragedies and comedies performed by the <term>Zanni</term> <note>The comic servant characters of the *Commedia dell'arte*, known for their expressive physical and vocal performances.</note>, they should occasionally set aside their immoderate laughter; and in its place, observe, please, in what manner one gentleman speaks with another: with what voice regarding pitch (high or low), with what volume of sound, with what sort of accents and gestures, and how they are uttered regarding the speed and slowness of motion. Let them attend a little to the difference that occurs among all those things when one of them speaks with his servant, or when one servant speaks with another. Let them consider what happens when a Prince is conversing with one of his subjects or vassals; when a petitioner is recommending himself; how the enraged or agitated man does it; how the married woman; how the young girl; how the simple child; how the clever courtesan; how the lover when speaking with his beloved while seeking to bend her to his will; how those who lament; how those who shout; how the fearful; and how those who exult with joy. From these various "accidents," if they are observed with attention and examined with diligence, they can take a standard for what is appropriate for the expression of any other concept that might come into their hands.

<margin>Voice: why it was given to animals.</margin>
Every animal has the natural faculty of being able to communicate to those of its own species, at least, the pleasure and pain of the body and soul through its voice; nor for any other reason was it given to them by nature. And among rational beings, there are some so stupid that, because they do not know how to put this into practice (thanks to their own ineptitude) and use it when the occasion arises, they believe themselves to be naturally deprived of it.

# Dialogue on Music
90

<margin>Observations of the ancient musicians.</margin> In singing any poem whatsoever, the ancient Musician first most diligently examined the quality of the person speaking: their age, sex, to whom they spoke, and what they sought to achieve through those means. These concepts, having first been clothed by the Poet in choice words appropriate for such a need, were then expressed by the Musician in that Tone, with those accents and gestures, with that quantity and quality of sound, and with that rhythm that was suitable for such a character in that action. Thus, regarding <margin>Timotheus provokes Alexander to battle.</margin> Timotheus, one reads (who, according to Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Greek encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note>, was a <term>Tibicine</term> <note>A player of the tibia or aulos, an ancient reed instrument similar to an oboe.</note> and not a <term>Citharedo</term> <note>A professional performer who sings while playing the kithara, a type of lyre.</note>) that when he provoked Alexander the Great to fight against enemy armies with the arduous mode of Minerva, the aforementioned circumstances were perceived not only in the rhythms, words, and concepts of the entire song, according to his desire; but his clothing, the expression of his face, and every particular gesture and limb must have, in my opinion, at least seemed in that business to burn with the desire to fight, and to overcome and conquer the enemy. Thus Alexander was forced to cry out for his arms and say that such ought to be the songs of Kings—and rightly so. For every <margin>The Virtue of the Musician: where it consists.</margin> time that the Musician (once impediments are removed) does not have the power to bend the souls of the listeners to his will, his science and knowledge are to be reputed as nothing and vain; since the musical faculty was instituted and numbered among the liberal arts for no other end.

STR. Did the simple sound of an artificial instrument have the power to work any effect on the listener?

<margin>Properties of the simple sound of an artificial instrument.</margin> BAR. Do not doubt it at all, even though Zarlino <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), the most famous music theorist of the time, whose focus on harmony Galilei often challenged.</note> is of the contrary opinion in chapter 7 of the second part of his *Institutions*. The sound of an instrument made by art, without the use of words, had—as I hinted to you above and as Aristotle maintains—a nature suited to imitating character and possessing it within itself, and a very great power to work in the souls of listeners a great part of the affects that pleased the skilled player. And to confirm that this is true, I give you the example of that <term>Tibicine</term> to whom Pythagoras said: *Muta modum* <note>original: "Change the mode."</note>. By changing (as he was commanded) the rhythm from the fast <term>dactyl</term> <note>A poetic meter consisting of one long syllable followed by two short ones.</note> it was before into the slow <term>spondee</term> <note>A meter of two long syllables, creating a much slower, more solemn tempo.</note>; and the Tone from high to low, and the volume from much to little sound, he so calmed the infuriated youth of Tauromenium that he did not burn down the house of the courtesan against whom he was greatly incensed. Furthermore, Sophocles, in one <margin>In the second Song of the Tragedy titled *The Trachiniae*.</margin> of his tragedies, was accustomed to calling the *Aulos* the "Tyrant of souls": for no other reason than the power it had to pull them, almost violently, to that side which pleased the well-practiced <term>Auledo</term> <note>An aulos player.</note>. And to tell you further, some maintain that Alexander the Great was provoked to take up arms by the simple sound of the <term>Tibia</term>; although Plutarch maintains that <margin>Author's warning. Antigenidas, a most famous Tibicine.</margin> Antigenidas, a most famous <term>Tibicine</term>, accompanied him with song, and not Timotheus at all, as the latter was a <term>Citharedo</term> as was said and shown above. The discordant opinions of these writers could be reconciled by saying that Alexander, as one desirous of glory, was incited to fight many times by various Musicians of his day. Nor is it because of this that the Kithara lacked the power to work many other effects; but for inciting souls and moving them to fury, the <term>Tibia</term> was more suitable than it. One reads also in Julius Pollux that Herodotus the <margin>Herodotus of Megara, a singular Trumpeter.</margin> Trumpeter, a compatriot of Euclid, greatly filled the soldiers with daring with the sound of his Trumpet—besides us proving it ourselves all day long when hearing this or that musical instrument play various melodies, to say nothing of the Drum: the confused noise of which can be called "noisy" with more reason than "sonorous" or "rational." And to tell you further in this <margin>The Pagrus fish, caught by the sound of the Photingios. Aelian, in his *History of Animals*, chapters 31 and 44 of book 12.</margin> matter, Aelian maintains that the Pagrus fish is caught by the sound of the <term>Photingios</term> <note>A small ancient flute, often associated with shepherds.</note>; which fish is such a friend to this harmony that it even comes out of the water onto the shore to hear it, and becomes the prey of others. He maintains, furthermore, that deer are caught by the sound of the <term>Tibia</term>, no differently than what we see done every hour to birds by the cautious fowler by means of a whistle. He further maintains that the Indians sweeten the indignant souls of elephants with singing to the sound of the <margin>Scindassos, a stringed instrument.</margin> <term>Scindassos</term> <note>An ancient four-stringed instrument.</note>; and that the Libyans, with the sound of the transverse <term>Tibiae</term>, make the fierce and untamed horses gentle; and let this suffice regarding that. I do not wish to remain silent about another meddling of our modern practical <term>Contrapuntists</term> <note>Composers who write polyphony (multiple independent melodies), whom Bardi/Galilei accuse of obscuring the text.</note>; who, in setting to music (as they say) any sort of verses, whether free or bound by rhyme, sing them under their notes in such a way that they are not distinguished from prose. By means of which thing, the verses are deprived of their natural virtue, and consequently lose the force to work those effects in the listener that they would work by their own nature if they were simply read and uttered as befits their quality and that of the Poem. And this is as much as I need to tell you regarding the observations and rules of the modern <term>Contrapuntists</term>. This rough explanation, if considered by them with a healthy eye—besides showing my well-disposed mind toward them for having sought with all my industry and knowledge to show them the truth—could be an effective means of opening the way for them to those more reserved and profound speculations which, in so noble <margin>Another observation of the ancient musicians, refuted by Zarlino in chapter 47 of the 3rd part of the *Institutions*.</margin> a science, can be more subtly considered (as I said) by an intellect entirely capable of it. And returning to discourse with you about the other things that contribute to the understanding of the observations of the ancient Greek Musicians, one particularly important one was this: they were accustomed in their songs to linger a great deal around the <term>Mese</term> <note>The "middle" note of the ancient Greek musical system, serving as a functional center or "tonic."</note> of the Tone they were singing, and thus they went about seeking as few strings as they could, which thing...

This is evident by the fact that many hundreds of years after him, his compositions and melodies were held in very high regard, being most excellent when compared to those of others.

They knew it principally by the <term>Systema</term> <note>The "Greater Perfect System," the total range of notes used in Greek music.</note> being more or less tense or relaxed; and by the different species of the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The Greek term for an octave, categorized by the arrangement of whole and half steps.</note> which, as has been said and shown with examples, ascended and descended through different steps in one Tone than in another; and furthermore by the variety of notation characters. Also found in that book are the different signs that the ancients used 

<margin>
In Chapter 3 of Book 4.

to denote the specific strings of the Instrument, as distinct from those that signified the sound of the voice, as Boethius also hints. Where he [Boethius] intends that the first of each pair of signs be that which denotes the voice, and the second that which signifies the string of the Instrument. They had so many different types of these characters, as many as there were differences in the strings of their Tones and modes, which in total amounted to the number of forty-eight, by means of descending (with conjoined movement) sometimes by a Tone and sometimes by a Semitone; and they were formed from the simple elements of the Alphabet and their parts. In imitation of this, one sees the strings of the <term>Maximal System</term> <note>The complete range of medieval music.</note> noted in the *Introductory* of Guido d'Arezzo using the Latin letters.

STR. Would it be possible to see an example of them?

BAR. Not only possible, but very easy. Here first, according to Alypius, are the characters of each of the eight Tones, in the order they are described by Boethius. These denote any particular string of each of the eight Systems, according to the Diatonic distribution. Here also are noted those that signify the strings of their Instruments, to distinguish them from the others that denote the voice. And the reason given why these were different from those, and not the same, was so as not to confuse the melody of the instrument with that of the voice. Because if the same words were sung with a different vocal melody than that of the instrument (as was the custom for some), and the characters were used to follow one another above each syllable as the composer had ordered—if the characters had been the same, confusion would easily have arisen. This would be especially true in those parts where sometimes one was silent and the other continued, or otherwise. Nevertheless, others are of the opinion that the same characters could have conveniently served for everything without causing any inconvenience. In the margin of these, for greater understanding and ease, I have wanted to mark the corresponding Latin characters according to the usage of modern practice; and they are these.

<summary>Bardi explains that ancient Greek musicians like Olympus used only 3 or 4 notes to maintain emotional focus, and discusses the complex Greek notation system (recorded by Alypius and Boethius) which used separate symbols for voice and instrument.</summary>

<margin>Notice.</margin>
Here follows a new description of the eight Modes <note>term: "Tuoni" (Tones/Modes). The author refers to the ancient Greek musical scales.</note> according to the mind of Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher who transmitted Greek music theory to the Middle Ages.</note>. To each <term>Systema</term> <note>The Greek term for a scale or range of notes.</note> of these, the characters described by Alypius <note>A 4th-century Greek writer who provided the most complete list of ancient musical notation.</note> have been applied to their proper strings. Regarding these Systems, we shall consider matters of greater importance. First, those characters found on the same string in terms of high or low pitch—even if in different Systems and denoted by different names—are nonetheless always the same; except for those that change the size of the step when descending. This occurs both for those denoting the voice <note>vocal notation</note> and those signifying the string <note>instrumental notation</note>. This rule is seen to fail only twice. The first is between the <term>Paramese</term> of the Hypolydian and the <term>Tritesynemmenon</term> of the Dorian; the second is between this and that of the Lydian and Mixolydian. This could easily <margin>The opinion of Zarlino, in chapter 3 of the 2nd part of his *Institutions*, refuted by the Author.</margin> have happened due to the corruption and antiquity of the text, by failing to distinguish between small characters and degrees. It should also be noted that strings with different names and positions in the <term>Disjunct System</term> <note>original: "Systema disgiunto"</note> from those in the <term>Conjunct System</term> <note>original: "Systema congiunto"</note> also have varying signs to distinguish one from the other. Furthermore, those before Guido of Arezzo <note>The 11th-century monk credited with inventing modern staff notation and the solfège system.</note> who marked the lowest string of the Disjunct System (as Guido himself shows in his *Introductory*) with a Greek <term>Gamma</term>, did not do so out of honor or memory of the Greeks as inventors of Music, but because that string was the octave of the <term>Lycanosmeson</term>, marked by those using the Latin alphabet with the character G; in addition to being marked as the same...

### Demonstration of the eight Modes <note>original: "Tuoni"; in this context, the term refers to the ancient Greek "tonoi" or keys of transposition.</note> according to the interpretation of Boethius, to whose notes <note>original: "corde," literally "strings" of the lyre</note> the symbols are applied according to the usage of the ancient Greeks.

->[DIAGRAM OF THE MODES]<-

<note>This diagram visualizes the "Great Perfect System"—the standard range of ancient Greek music—as it is transposed into eight different keys. Each row represents a mode, staggered horizontally to show how they shift in pitch relative to one another. The letters on the left indicate the modern pitch equivalents used in the Renaissance, while the Greek characters within the grid represent the specific notation for vocal and instrumental music.</note>

**The Eight Modes depicted are:**

*   **Hypermixolydian mode** <note>The highest mode in this system, often added to complete the octave relationship with the Hypodorian.</note>
*   **Mixolydian mode**
*   **Lydian mode**
*   **Phrygian mode**
*   **Dorian mode** <note>Considered the central and most "manly" or stable mode by ancient Greek standards.</note>
*   **Hypolydian mode**
*   **Hypophrygian mode**
*   **Hypodorian mode** <note>The lowest mode in the system.</note>

<note>Boethius (c. 480–524 AD) was the primary source through which ancient Greek music theory reached the Middle Ages and Renaissance. However, his interpretation of how these modes were named and ordered differed from earlier Greek sources like Aristoxenus or Ptolemy, a point of significant debate among Renaissance humanists like the author of this text.</note>

The author, Bardi, argues that this notation system was derived from instrumental practice rather than vocal music, challenging the common belief that these symbols were a later medieval invention.</meta>

# Dialogue on Music

...notated by the Greeks in the same Mode <note>original: "Tuono"; refers to a musical key or transposition scale.</note>. This confirms what I said above: that they derived the notes added to the Great System <note>The "Great Perfect System" was the standard two-octave scale of ancient Greek music theory.</note> from the instruments that were in use in those times; because the double Gamma <note>original: "doppio Gamma"; the Greek letter Γ used to denote the lowest pitch of the medieval scale.</note> in that place denotes the string of the instrument, and not the sound of the voice.

<margin>Zarlino's error.</margin>
STROZZI: It was not, then, the invention of Guido <note>Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–1033), the monk traditionally credited with inventing the modern musical staff and solfège.</note> (as Zarlino says in chapter 30 of the second part of his *Institutions*) to mark notes with the characters of the Latin alphabet.

BARDI: By no means; and to prove that this is true, here are two examples of plainchant <note>Gregorian chant.</note>, of which I have a book written some decades before he [Guido] was born. For better understanding, I wish to adapt them for you according to the usage of modern practice.

And returning to the demonstration that Boethius <note>A 6th-century Roman philosopher whose works were the primary source for Greek music theory in the Renaissance.</note> makes of the Modes, I say it should not be left without consideration that in the eight Systems, one find no more than three notes <note>original: "corde," literally "strings."</note> common to each of them: these are the highest note of the lowest mode, the Middle note <note>original: "Media," likely referring to the *mese*, the central pitch of the Greek system.</note> of the Dorian, and the lowest note of the highest mode; whereas in those of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), an influential astronomer and music theorist.</note> there are none. Furthermore, it is likely that Boethius was led to believe and state—by the characters of Alypius <note>A Greek writer whose "Introduction to Music" provided the tables of notation Galilei is analyzing.</note> shown above—that the Modes of the ancient musicians were not eight, but that each of them proceeded in its own particular System through the order of steps demonstrated in his Description. For in Ptolemy’s description, they cannot be adapted so as to fit well; besides the fact that he does not allow more than seven Modes. By excluding the Hypermixolydian, Ptolemy silently implies that it was no longer in use, or not to be used; and yet the characters for the Hypermixolydian found with the testimony of Alypius prove the contrary to us. 

Therefore, it may perhaps not be inconvenient to say that Ptolemy and Boethius recount the facts of the Modes regarding their quantity according to what they believed, or according to the way they would have ordered and arranged them, rather than according to the truth of the fact and their actual use—if, however, we are to believe that Alypius truly collected the characters with which the ancient Greeks noted the strings of their modes, which likely must have been seen by Ptolemy no less than by Boethius. 

Nevertheless, it must be considered that if the order of the species of the octave <term>Diapason: the Greek term for the interval of an octave.</term> recounted to us by Ptolemy is truly the one by which the ancient Greeks numbered them, then the Modes among them were no more than seven. For if they had approved the Hypermixolydian, or any other above the Mixolydian, they would consequently have taken as the first species of the octave (as the highest) the one that served it; which, according to Ptolemy’s order, would have been between <term>Aa lamire: a specific high pitch in the medieval hexachord system, roughly equivalent to A5.</term> and the same pitch an octave lower, and not between <term>h mi: the note B-natural in the medieval system.</term> and the same pitch an octave lower. For this reason and the others mentioned above, all those knowledgeable in this faculty today agree on the matter of the ancient Greek Modes with the opinion of Ptolemy and not the others, as he spoke with greater foundation than anyone who wrote before or after him. 

You can also understand from these same characters why I spoke earlier regarding that Song which begins "Let our voice ring out today" <note>original: "Clangat hodie vox nostra," a medieval sequence.</note>; namely, that it was in the Mixolydian Mode and intended to be played on an instrument. Here follow (as shown by their appearance, form, and style) four ancient Songs <note>These are the "Hymns of Mesomedes," which Galilei was the first to publish in modern times.</note> composed in the Lydian mode by one of the ancient Greek musicians. These were found in Rome by a Florentine gentleman of ours, in the library of Cardinal Sant'Angiolo, on some papers that followed a very ancient manuscript book of the *Music* of Aristides Quintilianus and Bryennius <note>Two important Greek music theorists whose manuscripts were rediscovered during the Renaissance.</note>. They were most faithfully transcribed by him and, through his kindness, sent to me in this same copy, which I freely give to you as a gift.

The Dorian Cithara and Phrygian Pipe; what they are.

In the sixth [book of the Aeneid].

BAR. This could first arise from the inventor of the thing, from the homeland, or from the excellence of the Citharist and the Pipe-player <note>original: *tibicine* or *auledo* (aulete)</note>, or however we wish to call him. This is made clear by Virgil when speaking of Orpheus when he goes to the underworld to recover his beautiful Eurydice. Orpheus, as you know, was Thracian and, according to Pliny, the inventor of the Lyre. In that passage by the Poet, we read: *Relying on the Thracian Cithara and the sounding strings* <note>original: "Threicia fretus cithara, fidesque canoris"</note>. To which, after having introduced him to the Elysian Fields, he adds: *The Thracian Priest in his long robe sings the seven different notes of the strings; now he strikes them with his fingers, now with an ivory plectrum* <note>original: "Nec non Threicius longa cum veste sacerdos / Obloquitur numeris septem discrimina vocum, / Iamque eadem digitis, iam pectine pulsat eburno." First, from the words of these two illustrious Poets, a new argument is gathered (besides those mentioned above) to persuade us that the ancient Lyre and Cithara were the same thing, not only among the Greeks but also among the Latins. Furthermore, we see that the strings were struck with a plectrum and not bowed <note>original: *segauano* (literally "sawed"). At the time this was written, there was a common misconception that the ancients used bows like modern violins.</note>, as has been almost universally believed until this day. We shall make use of these authorities when the occasion requires. That epithet of "Dorian Cithara" and "Phrygian Pipe" could also derive from such instruments being frequently used by people of those nations; or because in wind and string instruments, there were differences regarding high and low pitch <note>original: *acutezza, & grauità*</note>, and regarding the steps of the scale. The strings of the Lyre used by the Dorians were tuned differently, and the holes of the Pipe were arranged in a different order than the Lyre and Pipe used by the Phrygians. As was said above, the Phrygians sang a whole tone higher than the Dorians and moved through different steps

of the different species of the Octave <term>Diapason: the Greek term for an octave scale.</term> for the Dorians and the Phrygians in their particular System and Mode. Thus, in the specific instruments of this or that province, there likely arose the same variety and difference we described in singing. In the same order that you saw the voices arranged in the Perfect Systems, the strings were tuned and the holes of their particular instruments were arranged in the same manner and order. It would be a great absurdity to believe and claim that they sang in one way and played in another, as some in our own times have believed and claimed; this is false (as has been demonstrated above with effective reasoning). From the variety of these circumstances, it followed that those who simply knew how to play the Dorian Lyre and Pipe <note>original: *Piffero* (Fife or Pipe)</note> did not necessarily know how to play those of the Phrygians and Lydians unless they had first learned them separately. For this reason, in the demonstration of the Tones arranged according to the mind of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, a 2nd-century mathematician and music theorist.</note>, high species of the Octave are seen for the low Tones, and low species for the high ones; for it was in these species that the ancients first sang. That the temperaments of the instruments were truly different from one another can be gathered from, among other places, what Athenaeus says regarding Pythagoras of Zacynthus <note>A 5th-century BC musician and instrument builder.</note>, who flourished in the same years as or shortly after the Samian [Pythagoras]. This Zacynthian invented that beautiful and ingenious instrument called the Tripod, in imitation of the Delphic Tripod. The Tripod of the said Pythagoras had three sides, and on each was strung a specific quantity of strings. On the first side, they were arranged according to the Dorian Mode; on the second, the Phrygian; and on the third, the Lydian. Anyone who heard it without seeing it played would have judged it to be three different citharas. Its use was soon lost due to its industrious difficulty. From what we have said, one can also understand what the difference actually was between the Cithara and the Lyre; which was nothing other than a different temperament regarding the size of the intervals, the order, and the high and low pitch of the strings. The Cithara was, therefore, that which played low harmonies like the Dorian, while the Lyre, on the contrary, played the high ones like the Lydian and Phrygian. From this difference arose the proverb I mentioned above. Perhaps even the "out-of-tune lyre" of Polyphemus in the hand of Eumelus the Aeolian was considered a Cithara, and the "tuned Cithara" of Orpheus in the hand of Neanthus was considered a Lyre. I will also easily believe that when Philoxenus changed the Dorian Mode to the Phrygian—necessitated, as has been said, by the nature of the Dithyramb—he did not set aside the Cithara as a low-sounding instrument (assuming he accompanied the singing of the chorus with it) and take up the Lyre as high-pitched, but rather that he only changed the quality of the intervals of the strings. And where previously in the Dorian he struck the low notes of the fourth species of the Octave slowly, in the Phrygian he struck the high notes of the third species quickly; and thus they sought in their songs not many strings, although Philoxenus is counted among those who more than others...

He argues the Cithara and Lyre were identical instruments plucked with a plectrum, differing only in the grave or acute musical modes they were tuned to perform.</summary>

<margin>
How the ancients recognized the brevity and length of the notes.
</margin>

BAR. The value of the Notes and their ciphers was manifested by nothing other than the diversity of the long and short feet of the verse over which they were set; and those who say otherwise are greatly mistaken.

STR. So, the ancient musicians had only two sorts of notes and time—that is, long and short. But tell me further: at the beginning of their learning to sing, it is not to be believed that they started all at once saying the words of the *Cantilene* <note>Ancient songs or melodies.</note>, but rather the Notes, as is still the custom today. Now, in those beginnings, how is it to be believed, for example, that they managed to keep a choir of boys together who were learning to carry their voices (as happens all day in the schools of the masters of this practice), or in the singing of a single student with the master—that one should hold the notes for the same time as the other? Since they had such knowledge only from the measure and quality of the Poet’s verse, and in those beginnings, the notes being sufficient for the time, they must not have been without them. And with what names did they utter them? Certainly not with the names given to them by their first authors; because if any of those had to be uttered under a single note and syllable, they are exceedingly long.

<margin>
The Author’s considerations.
</margin>

BAR. I hold for certain that in learning to carry their voices, they went about vocalizing, so to speak, without expressing any proper and particular name. Firstly, because one does not find described by the ancient Greeks the strings with any names other than those you have heard before, the majority of which are, as you said, very long. And truly, to have to utter under a single extension one of those names of theirs—such as, for example, *Proslábanomenos* <note>The lowest note in the Greek Greater Perfect System.</note>, *Tritediezeugmenon* <note>A specific note in the Greek system, literally "the third [string] of the disjoined [tetrachord]."</note>, or any other similar one—the mere thought of it seems ridiculous to me. But it should be noted that they constantly used to sing to an instrument; and rarely, if never, was the instrument heard without the voice, or the voice without the instrument. I do not say by this that it always happened that the same person who sang also played the Lyre or the Cithara; for rare were those who knew how to do that well. These were highly regarded and held in high esteem, and to honor them they were called *Citharedi* <note>Kitharodes: performers who sang while accompanying themselves on the kithara.</note>, as distinct from those who simply played without singing, who were called *Citharisti* <note>Kitharists: those who only played the instrument.</note>. Among the first who practiced this well is numbered the Thracian *Tamira* <note>Thamyris, a legendary Thracian singer mentioned in Greek mythology.</note>.

<margin>
The difference between the Citharedo and the Citharista.
</margin>

STR. The *Citharedo* must have spent a great deal of time composing his songs and committing them to memory to recite them later before the Prince, or the Senate, or wherever he was required. For according to what I have heard and read, that song which the ancient musician recited—when he sought to effect some significant impact on the listener—was not always a Madrigal, or a Song, or a brief *Napoletana* <note>A light, popular vocal form from Naples.</note>, but most often an entire history, or fable, or some heroic deed, or something similar, in which he often spent one or two hours of time.

<margin>
Ancient songs; how they were composed by them.
</margin>

BAR. It is not credible, from what can be gathered particularly from the example of *Filosseno* <note>Philoxenus of Cythera, a famous Greek dithyrambic poet.</note>, that the ancient musicians and singers were in the habit of always first composing their songs and then, having learned them by heart, reciting them. Rather, they held the Poem in memory, which most of the time (if not always) was composed by the same persons. For at that time, the Musician was not separated from poetry, nor was the Poet separated from Music; and it would truly have been too great an obligation and a waste of their time to have first composed the melody, then committed it to memory along with the words, and furthermore, which strings they were to be played upon. Therefore, having first carefully considered the Poetry, History, Fable, or whatever it was, and in which Tone and mode and which melody was most suitable, they then sang it to the Cithara (so to speak) extemporaneously and from the imagination. This same thing is still practiced—according to modern usage, however—by learned and practical contrapuntists who are also players of the lute and keyboards. They use this when, for their own pleasure, they sing over these instruments alone, without having to coordinate with anyone else but the instrument they are playing. They would produce the same effects that the ancients did, whenever they expressed the concept of the words in the manner that has been said to be appropriate, and removed the impediments narrated above.

STR. That is very well; but those who sang to the *Tibia* <note>An ancient wind instrument, similar to the Greek aulos, often consisting of two pipes.</note> could not both play and sing at the same time, unless they had someone else who, having first filled the instrument with air, breathed little by little into the *Tibia* while they sang. Or perhaps some bellows fitted under the armpits, as I once saw used by a Neapolitan street performer; while he spoke with the spectators, he played his own adapted *Piua* <note>A type of bagpipe or pipe instrument.</note> of several *Auli* <note>Auloi: plural of aulos, the Greek double-pipe.</note> quite elegantly. He provided the wind with such skill that it was difficult for the spectators to understand how the *Piua* was being inflated by the same man who was playing and singing at the same time. Or truly they did it in the same way as the *Blind Man of Furli* <note>Francesco de' Gregori, a famous blind musician from Forlì.</note> does today; who, as you may have seen, has a boy who provides the wind to one of his straight Flutes, and in that time, singing various airs, he closes and opens these and those holes with his fingers, according to the needs of his...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Bardi and Strozzi. They have just been discussing how ancient musicians indicated rhythm and the physical act of playing. Here, Bardi moves into the practicalities of how the voice and instruments interacted in ancient performance, specifically focusing on the variety of instruments (like the pipes) and a curious Egyptian practice involving vowels.</meta>

->Dialogue on Music<-

its melody; quite the opposite of what you said a moment ago happened to Marsyas <note>A satyr in Greek mythology who challenged Apollo to a musical contest and was flayed alive after losing.</note>, who with his own breath and his very fingers played the pipes at the same time.

<margin>
The Egyptian priests used vowels instead of the Aulos and the Kithara.
</margin>

**BAR.** The music that occurred between those who simply played an instrument and those who knew nothing but how to sing—or when songs were performed in such a manner—were most often short and simple airs. For the most part, they were created for nothing other than the satisfaction of the common people. Over the sound of these melodies, the same tune was repeated for every two, three, or four verses, no differently than what we see every day when singing a *capitolo* <note>A poetic form, specifically *terza rima*, often sung to a standard melodic formula.</note> to the Lute, or in the songs and dances of the common and rustic folk. This manner of playing and singing was quite common, together with dancing, in the choruses of Satyr plays, Comedies, and Tragedies. The chorus, accompanied by the *tibia* <note>The Latin name for the *aulos*, an ancient double-reed pipe instrument.</note> or another instrument, sang whatever air was most suitable to express the concept at hand, just as was said above regarding the Dithyramb <note>An ancient Greek hymn sung and danced in honor of Dionysus.</note>.

**STR.** In this way of operating, who took the lead: the instrument or the voice?

**BAR.** The *tibicini* <note>Pipe players.</note> and the *citharists* <note>Lyre or kithara players.</note> were most often the ones who composed the airs, and the chorus followed them. However, the priests of Egypt, according to what Demetrius of Phalerum <note>A Greek orator and statesman (c. 350–280 BCE).</note> tells us, used their seven vowels in place of the *aulos* and the *kithara* when praising the gods, sounding them in order with sweetness of voice.

**STR.** I do not understand in what manner the Egyptian priests praised the gods with their seven vowels, and used them instead of the *aulos* and the *kithara*.

**BAR.** The text of Demetrius in that passage is truly obscure on this matter; nonetheless, we interpret it thus: the priest, in pronouncing the vowels with his voice—as one does today, for example, with musical Notes—the Chorus sang the praises of the gods to the sound of those vowels. Thus, as the priest uttered them distinctly with an articulated and measurable voice, he served as a guide for the Chorus, performing the office of the *kithara* and the *tibia* used by many other nations. We defer this opinion of ours, like all others, to whoever might understand it better than we do.

<margin>
Zarlino in the *Institutions*, chapter 4 of the second book.
</margin>

**STR.** I like your interpretation very much, as well as the decision of those priests to banish the *tibiae* from their choral songs. It seems a great thing to me, Lord Giovanni, that the simple sound of them could delight the ear, given they were made of nothing (as I have read in some authors) but the shinbones of cranes, eagles, and vultures—leaving aside for now those first ones made of barley and oat straws—with their shrill and very piercing sharpness being so annoying.

<margin>
What ancient *tibiae* were made of.
</margin>
<margin>
Papinius Statius.
</margin>
<margin>
Plutarch.
</margin>
<margin>
Castorean law.
</margin>
<margin>
Aristotle in *Problem* 49 of the section on Harmony, and Terence in the inscriptions of his comedies.
</margin>
<margin>
In the dance of Ajax.
</margin>
<margin>
Telestes, an extraordinary dancer. Athenaeus, in the first book, chapter 16.
</margin>

**BAR.** *Tibiae* made of the materials you mentioned were not used by everyone, but rather by specific nations. Those made of eagle and vulture shinbones were used in Scythia by the *Androphagi* <note>Literally "man-eaters" or cannibals described by ancient geographers.</note>, the *Arimaspi* <note>A legendary tribe of one-eyed people.</note>, and the *Malachei*. Those made of barley stalks were used by Osiris among the Egyptians. Later, they were made by other nations from various types of reeds, lotus wood, boxwood, horn, bronze, silver, the shinbones of donkeys or deer, laurel branches, elderberry wood, raw leather, and other things. Thus, through the diversity of size and material, some rendered a small and high-pitched sound, and others (as was needed) a large and deep one. That there were such instruments among them—not just in terms of material, which is a common fact, but in terms of size—is evidenced by what Papinius Statius says, with the testimony of Boethius: "The pipe with its hooked horn bellows a deep sound" <note>original Latin: *Tibia adunco cornu grave mugit*</note>. Furthermore, one reads in Plutarch that the Spartans used them in their armies. At their sound, having first arranged the battle lines, they moved the soldiers at the appropriate pace and encouraged them with the "Castorean law" <note>A Spartan battle-song or rhythmic tune associated with Castor and Pollux.</note> to use their hands bravely against the enemy. And although the Swiss and Germans move their armies with transverse flutes or fifes (as they call them), they do not use them alone, but together with drums, in the same way the people of Ireland use the bagpipe (or *piva*, as we wish to call it). Moreover, the ancient Greek and Latin actors recited their Comedies and Tragedies to the sound of the *tibia* and the *kithara*; therefore, it was necessary to use high-pitched, deep, and medium ones, according to the quality of the characters who appeared in them. To further prove this truth to you, Lucian, in his work *On the Dance*, speaks of a certain man who, in a dance, represented the enraged Ajax <note>A Greek hero of the Trojan War who went mad when Achilles' armor was awarded to Odysseus.</note> through the movement of his body alone without speaking. This Ajax, as you know, went mad with the grief he felt when, under the walls of Troy, the captains of Greece gave the judgment in favor of Ulysses in the dispute over who should have the armor of Achilles, who died in the siege. The imitator of this event (who was no less excellent in the art of dancing than Telestes was in representing the Theban war) took such pleasure in it that he seemed not one who was imitating the case of the unhappy Ajax, but the man himself in the height of his fury. In such a state, he violently snatched a *tibia* (or fife, as we might call it) from the hand of one of the musicians on stage and struck the one who sat among the others representing Ulysses so hard on the head that he laid him out at his feet for dead. If a padded hat had not resisted the force of the blow, it would have taken his life. Realizing this, the dancer immediately came to his senses and was so disgusted with himself that, as excellent as he was, he never again wanted to perform such games, even though he was many times urged and persuaded by dear friends. Consider now: if an instrument made of the shinbone of a crane or a vulture...

the eagle's [wing-bone] <note>original: "δ d'Aquila". I will not dispute at present—as my mind would be invited to do by this fine opportunity—whether the equal and unequal <term>pipes</term> <note>original: "Tibie", the Roman name for the Greek aulos, a double-reed instrument.</note> took their names from the difference in the size of the reed, the number of holes, or the number of them played at the same time. Nor will I treat whether the "right-handed" and "left-handed" pipes acquired such a difference in name from being held in one hand or the other while playing; or perhaps from the pipe-players standing sometimes on the right and sometimes on the left wing of the stage; or truly from the relationship they had with the spectators, since what was left to some was right to others, no differently than what happens between two people wrestling together. I will also leave aside whether the right-handed ones, yielding a high-pitched sound, were matched with the *Parthenie* <note>maiden-pipes</note>; and the left-handed ones, yielding a low sound, with the *Hypertelie* <note>perfected or "over-complete" pipes</note>, or truly the opposite. Or if, when both pipes were right-handed, they were "equal," and "unequal" when both were left-handed. Likewise, I will omit which were the *Gingrine* and which were the *Serrane*; and whether the latter, which took their name from the noise and high-pitched sound a saw makes when sawing, matched with the Phrygian pipes; and whether the former, named *Gingre* by the Phoenicians after the faint crying and squawking of geese (of which they were the originators), matched as the highest-pitched with the Lydian pipes, or truly the opposite. I will also pass over in silence whether the *Spina Catto* <note>likely a type of boxwood or thorny plant</note> that grew particularly in Sicily truly had the power to wound stags in such a rare and hidden way that pipes made from their leg bones would later be hoarse when played—at least according to what Antigonus tells us in his *Marvels*. And the same happened, according to Pliny, to those made of elderberry if they had heard the crowing of a rooster; besides other considerations. For in truth, after having fatigued myself greatly over this, and having discussed it many times with most knowledgeable men, I have never been able to extract anything but confusion from them, nor from the authors who treat these matters for various purposes. Indeed, what Pollux, Varro, Pliny, Donatus, Servius, and Terence feel about it in the inscriptions of his Comedies, has had the effect upon me that you have heard. I have well observed in several ancient bronzes and marbles—not to be disregarded—where one sees in low relief some pipe-players sounding two pipes at the same time; and having the high-pitched one on the right and the low-pitched one on the left, if we want to take the short and thin one for the high-pitched (as is likely) and the long and thicker one for the low-pitched. But let enough be said of this. I promise another time, with greater leisure, to speak at length on many important things regarding all wind instruments, and to expand further upon most of the matters which at present I am only mentioning in passing.

Returning to our main intent, I say that one would perhaps not be far from the truth in saying that when the ancients first learned to carry their voices, they applied their sounds to the words of the verse by striking the string of the instrument that was in unison with the voice, using the string as a guide for the voice. Such an opinion could be supported, besides many other passages by grave writers, by what Boethius says in the twentieth chapter of the first book of his *Music*; where he clearly manifests the diligence that ancient musicians placed in artificial instruments, from which it seems in a certain way they learned to sing; a thing for which they were many times rebuked for negligence by judicious men.

<margin>
Chorus: how it accorded together in singing.
</margin>

As for according together regarding the length and brevity of time in holding their notes when they first learned to sing, one could answer that they sang them continuously following the verse, as is still the custom today. From the verse, they could very well understand the brevity and length of the notes, which was very easy for them to know: both because they were composed in their mother tongue, and because they were not ignorant of such things, attending to that faculty in which they were employed in a different manner than is customary today. Furthermore, they had removed many difficulties and irrelevances from the way of singing that are in use at present: such as the diversity of rhythmic figures, the quantity of strings, the disproportionate mixture of Tones that are sung together at the same time, and the diverse mixing of genres, besides the other vanities mentioned above that have been introduced against all reason.

<margin>
The Beat [the pulse], not used by ancient musicians.
</margin>

Nor is it to be believed that it was necessary for the *Corago* <note>the Chorus leader</note> of those times to beat time in the manner that is customary today to keep the singers together; first because there is no memory of such authority that I know of, nor do I see why it would have been necessary for them. This is because they did not sing more than one melody at a time, and no matter how many singers there were—as we hear in Church from the Choir, especially of Friars and Monks, in the antiphons, responsories, introits, and the chanting of psalms—

# Dialogue on Music

...and in short, all the singing called Plainchant <note>original: "canto detto Piano"</note> did not require such diligence in maintaining the voices of everyone in the same range, united together under the same rhythm. It seems to some that a small trace and shadow of such a thing could be drawn from the words used by Plutarch at the end of the *Life of Demetrius*, regarding Xenophantus the Piper <term>Tibicine</term> <note>a player of the *aulos*, an ancient Greek double-reed wind instrument</note>, and the rowing of sailors; but because we consider this matter trivial and of no value, we will say no more of it.

STR. Was each Tone <term>Tuono</term> <note>In ancient Greek theory, a "Tone" or Mode was a specific scale or melodic pattern believed to possess a unique emotional character or "ethos."</note> suited to express any affect one might wish?

<margin>
Whether each tone was suited to express any affect.

Number, that is, the movement of the body when dancing.
</margin>

BAR. From the example of Philoxenus, one can argue that each Tone was not suited to express any concept, nor to introduce any affect into a person. For the middle ones, which are between the low and the high, were suited to induce quiet and a moderate disposition of affect in the listeners; and those subjects who were naturally, or by some accident, predisposed to such a state would find it increasing further. The high ones were suited to move and uplift them; and the low ones to induce in them abject, submissive, and mournful thoughts. This is no different than how a middle tempo <note>original: "numero"</note> between speed and slowness shows a settled, quiet mind without passions; the fast is agitated and lamenting; and the slow is lazy, sluggish, and fearful. All this variety arose principally from the different quality of the pitch <note>original: "sito"</note>, the sound, the quantity of it, and the diversity of the rhythm regarding the value of time. For some of these brought low sound to the ear, and some others high; one brought it loud and much, and another small and little; some others had their movements and rhythms <note>original: "numeri"</note> fast and short, and others had them slow and long; besides those that had each of these qualities in a moderate degree, or closer to one than the other. These various properties worked more or less according to how close they were to the middle or to one of the extremes, and depending on how they found the subject disposed. For just as it would be impossible for a painter, however excellent, to represent a delicate face to the sight upon a board, canvas, or wall that was rough, harsh, and coarse to the touch, using thick and hastily ground colors; so too the Musician was not able, with all his great knowledge, to produce any significant affect in a man if he had not first removed the impediments and prepared him to receive that form which he sought to introduce; and all this occurred through a defect of the subject, and not of the art.

<margin>
Comparison.

Whether the Dorian Mode sung in the Diatonic genus had the same power as when sung in the Chromatic and the Enharmonic.
</margin>

STR. Did the Dorian mode then have the same property when sung in the Diatonic Genus as in the Chromatic and the Enharmonic, or was it different? And in which genus of harmony did this or that Tone work its affects more vigorously?

BAR. In the Diatonic genus, when the same Tone was sung or played, those effects that were virile and strong operated more than in the Chromatic; and they operated less in the Enharmonic than in the Chromatic. In the Chromatic, on the contrary, the soft and effeminate effects had more efficacy than in any other. The use of this genus was so frequent by Timotheus the Lyric among the Spartans that they, as lovers of severe music, drove him from their borders. Nor is this surprising regarding Timotheus, considering that his homeland was an island of Greece called Melos <note>original: "Millo"</note>; the inhabitants of which were (so historians tell us) most lascivious and effeminate men, and such (from what I understand) they still are today.

<margin>The inhabitants of Melos being lascivious men.</margin>

STR. Was Timotheus himself not the author of the said Chromatic genus?

BAR. No, sir, if by that you mean the one who lived in the times of Alexander the Great.

<margin>In the second [book] of the Metaphysics at the second text.</margin>

STR. How can that be, since Aristotle says these specific words regarding him: "If it had not been for Timotheus, we would not have so many kinds of melodies." <note>original: "se non fusse stato Timoteo, noi non haueremmo tante forti di melodie."</note> Secondly, Suidas, speaking of the same man, says: "Timotheus, son of Thersander, changed ancient music into a softer and more delicate form," which is precisely the nature of the Chromatic compared to the ancient Ditonic <note>the standard Diatonic genus based on whole tones</note>. It is true that men of judgment blamed him for this, as is clearly seen by the testimony of Plutarch. Boethius also seems to imply the same when he says that Timotheus changed the ancient and severe music into the Chromatic genus, which is softer. And Zarlino <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), the most famous music theorist of the Renaissance and Galilei’s teacher, whom he often critiques in this dialogue.</note> finally, in chapter 32 of the second part of his *Institutions*, makes a very long discourse on it, as you know; in which he clearly says that Timotheus not only discovered the Chromatic genus, but recounts the manner in which he was able to find it.

<margin>
Timotheus was not the inventor of the Chromatic genus.

Error of Zarlino.
</margin>

BAR. Slowly, please. First, the words of the ancient writers you cited do not conclude that Timotheus was the author of the Chromatic, as it seems to you; but rather, as Boethius clearly says, that being in Sparta, he turned <note>original: "riuolgeua"</note> the grave and severe music he had received from the Spartans into the Chromatic, which is soft and effeminate. The use of this greatly harmed the tender years of children, making them become such; for which reason he was sent into exile, as has been said. And that this Timotheus could not in any way be the one who discovered the Chromatic genus, as Zarlino says, is clearly shown by the fact that Olympus the Phrygian, a scholar of Marsyas, lived before the Trojan War, and to him—as you will hear—is attributed the invention of the Enharmonic; but this was after the use of the Chromatic. Now you see how it can be that Timotheus, who lived so many decades after Olympus, could have first...

->Ancient & Modern<-

...the Chromatic genus <term>Chromatico</term> <note>One of the three ancient Greek musical scales, characterized by using semitones; it was considered more expressive and "colored" than the Diatonic.</note> was discovered. Furthermore, in the Decree that the Spartans issued against Timotheus <note>Timotheus of Miletus was a famous musician often accused of corrupting traditional music by adding more strings to the lyre.</note>, written in the language of that time, these words are read: "Timotheus abandoned the Enharmonic, retreating to the Chromatic as it was softer and easier." Therefore, if you wish for the account to match your calculations, it is necessary to find a new Olympus or a new Timotheus to whom the inventions of this or that genus of harmony—and not melody, as Aristotle says—may be attributed; for that word signifies something contrary to your opinion.

**STR.** It must necessarily be as you say; this matter, not being understood by modern musicians in its true form, has caused them to say a thousand vanities concerning it.

<margin>The Enharmonic found by Olympus, but in several stages.</margin>

**BAR.** Let that be their lot; let us attend to the task we have undertaken, and say that the Enharmonic <term>Enharmonio</term> <note>The most complex ancient Greek genus, using microtones (quarter-tones). It was considered highly sophisticated and difficult to perform.</note>, according to Aristoxenus and Plutarch, was found together with the law called "Curule" by the aforementioned Olympus. He also brought from Thrace to Greece the method of singing in consonance with the Pipe <term>Tibia</term> <note>The *aulos*, a double-reed wind instrument central to Greek music.</note>; although, in Plutarch’s account of how Olympus discovered it, he names only three strings of the Tetrachord <term>Tetracordo</term> <note>A four-note scale segment, the building block of Greek musical theory.</note>: namely the *Mese*, the *Parhypate*, and the *Hypate*, leaving aside the *Lichanos*. This makes me doubt that the two Enharmonic Quarter-tones <term>Dieſi</term> <note>In this context, the *diesis* is a microtonal interval smaller than a semitone.</note> were there to complete the number of the four strings of the Tetrachord established by someone else, or perhaps by himself some years later. For if it were otherwise, it seems a great matter to me that, as a most powerful reason for changing the use of the Diatonic and Chromatic genera into the Enharmonic, no mention was made of it by Plutarch in that regard; he mentions only the elegance of the compound Ditone <term>Ditono</term> <note>An interval of two whole tones, similar to a major third.</note> found between the *Mese* and the *Parhypate*. This genus of harmony was particularly used by Olympus himself in the Dorian Mode <term>Tuono Dorio</term>; <margin>In the Eighth [book] of the *Politics*.</margin> the art of which, according to Aristotle’s mind, had the power to fill souls with divine fury. And just as this man was the first to sing in the manner described with wind instruments, <margin>Olympus was the first to sing with wind instruments, and Archilochus with stringed instruments.</margin> Archilochus was likewise the first of all to sing to stringed instruments. The Enharmonic genus was used particularly by the Greeks, by virtue of its majesty, in celebrating the praises and honors of the gods in sacred temples; it is said to be aptly suited to singing. But despite all this, it always possessed less of the virile and natural than the Chromatic, and more of the artificial than any other. In such a way, the Tones necessarily had the same force and virtue in each of the Genera, though proportionally as much as the nature of each allows. <margin>The Enharmonic, used particularly in sacred temples in honor of the Gods; its nature.</margin> For the Diatonic, which by its nature is more common and, so to speak, natural, reasonably produced its effects more according to natural instinct than the other two; and of these, the Chromatic more vigorously than the Enharmonic, because it approaches the Diatonic more closely. <margin>Nature of the Diatonic. By "Greek Music," the Enharmonic was understood.</margin> By "Greek Music," the Enharmonic was understood; because it was more regulated than the other two and required greater diligence to express its affects well. Hence it was the last to come into use and the first to be lost, if not to say perished. The Distribution <note>The specific tuning or arrangement of intervals.</note> that Aristoxenus made of it many years after its origin was highly regarded. <margin>The Enharmonic of Aristoxenus, highly reputed.</margin> So much so that the singers who came some centuries later, thinking it too difficult to put into practice, said as an excuse for their own incompetence <note>original: "dappocaggine"</note> that such a genus of harmony was an invention of the learned, but that it was never truly put into practice. <margin>Ignorance of some ancient practitioners.</margin> They did not realize that in doing so they were confessing their own ignorance; it did not seem possible to them to carry the voice as distinctly as its tiny intervals required. <margin>The authority of Plutarch.</margin> What greater authority do they want for this fact than what Plutarch says of it, a man of truth and so reputed? He not only affirms it was in use among practitioners, but that this alone was greatly reputed and practiced by the Greeks; and the specific words he uses are these: "Because the ancients did not attend at all to the Diatonic nor the Chromatic, but applied their minds and every study to the Enharmonic alone." Furthermore, what a vanity it would have been for Aristoxenus, who was so devoted to the senses, and others after him so many years after its origin, to make so many new Distributions of it if none were ever put into practice? I have said that the Tones necessarily had the same force in all genera, because they were born in each from the nature of their System, either from low to high or high to low; this alteration, being a sign of intrinsic movement, necessarily always carried with it the affect from which it was born, representing it to others, as has been said, by this means.

<margin>In the sixth [book] of the *Stromata*. At the end of the 3rd [book] of the *Elements*. Zarlino in chapter 5 of the 4th part of his *Institutions*.</margin>

**BAR.** I do not know that such an opinion, so far from the truth, is read in Clement of Alexandria or Aristoxenus. Those from whom you learned such a thing must have no knowledge of the Genera of harmony to say such a simple thing; besides, in matters where the senses can very easily accept the truth, it is an impertinence to wish to contradict them with the authority of this or that person. I intend now to speak humanly of natural and ordinary things, and not of supernatural and divine ones. It is indeed true that the Alexandrian says that the Enharmonic genus is particularly suited to the Dorian harmony, and the Diatonic to the Phrygian, because it is truly high-pitched, as Aristoxenus affirms. Perhaps those people may have wanted to imply that the Phrygian Tone <term>Tuono Frygio</term> sung in the Diatonic genus is higher than the Dorian sung in the Chromatic and Enharmonic; or perhaps that the movable strings of the Tetrachords, and not of the whole System...

# ->Dialogue on Music<-

but (as they seem to understand it) they are more tense <note>In this context, "tense" refers to higher pitch or string tension.</note> than those of the Enharmonic and Chromatic in the same Tone <term>Tuono</term> <note>Referring to a musical Mode or key, such as the Dorian or Phrygian.</note>: but why such a vanity? Let me explain myself better. It seems impossible to those [moderns] that the Phrygian Mode <term>Frygio</term> <note>An ancient Greek musical mode associated with excitement or religious fervor.</note> sung in the Diatonic genus should be higher in pitch than the Dorian Mode <term>Dorio</term> <note>An ancient mode associated with stability and gravity.</note> sung in the Chromatic and Enharmonic genera; for no other reason than wanting to apply the ancient way of singing (not understood by them) to the singing of today. But who is so foolish that, once they have understood how the Tones were sung by ancient musicians, and in what manner the strings were distributed in the three famous and ancient species of harmony, would marvel at this?

<margin>The Genus used in its simple form, if it would produce a good effect.</margin>
**STR.** I have understood it all very well; but tell me another thing. Could each Genus be used today in its simple <note>Meaning "pure" or unmixed, without combining elements of different scales.</note> form in our modern way of composing and singing, so that it produced a good effect?

**BAR.** Aside from the Diatonic, and even then, not all of its nine species, I do not believe so.

**STR.** For what reason?

**BAR.** Principally with respect to the chords <term>accordi</term> <note>Galilei uses this to refer to the vertical harmonies or consonances between different vocal parts.</note> that modern practical contrapuntists use between the various parts of their songs. These chords are their principal foundation, and they are not found as frequently among the strings of the other two genera as in the Diatonic; and particularly in the Syntonic species of Aristoxenus <note>A famous Greek music theorist (4th century BCE) who emphasized the judgment of the ear over mathematical ratios.</note>, and in that of Didymus.

**STR.** Please do not be reluctant to reveal to me some of the difficulties that oppose the other two genera, should one wish to use them in their simple form according to this new practice.

<margin>Chromatic and Enharmonic have the Semiditone and the Ditone in place of the seconds.</margin>
**BAR.** In the ancient Chromatic and Enharmonic—leaving aside the distributions made by Aristoxenus—among the many species found in each genus, there are some suited to provide less imperfection than others (according to this way of composing and singing in consonance as it is practiced today). Nevertheless, the Fifth <term>Diapente</term> is not found in the first species of the Octave <term>Diapaſon</term> more than once; and this is between the *Hypatemeſon* and the *Parameſe* <note>original: "Hypatemeſon & la Parameſe" — specific string names in the ancient Greek Greater Perfect System.</note>; and in the Greater Perfect System <term>Syſtema maſſimo & perfetto</term>, it does not occur more than three times in total. Furthermore, the Thirds and Sixths, both major and minor, are dissonant. It is true that in the Diatonic Ditone species, the Fifth is found in each Pentachord <note>A five-note scale segment.</note>; excepting, however, that which is contained by the *Hypatehypaton* and the *Parypatemeſon*; which occurs in every other species of whatever Genus. Moreover, the Major Third <term>Ditono</term> is not found between three strings in the Chromatic, nor the Minor Third <term>Semiditono</term> in the Enharmonic, and vice versa, except in two places; because they have in their place the major and minor seconds, which remain dissonant just as the Major and Minor Thirds that are their origin are. And if these were consonant, then those seconds would be too, as can be seen and heard in both of the Syntonic Diatonics when inspected by the Chromatic and Enharmonic strings: and the same occurs to any other interval except the Octave <term>Diapaſon</term>, which is for this reason called the Queen of Consonances.

**STR.** The same, from what I have read and understood, must have happened among the ancients; and it is inevitable that they also did not use them purely, but went about mixing one genus with another as is the custom today, and for the same respect.

<margin>Zarlino in chapter 77 of the second part of his Institutions.</margin>
<margin>The ancients always used the species and genera of their harmonies in their pure form; Zarlino in chapters 31 and 38 of the second [part] of the Institutions.</margin>
**BAR.** On the contrary, the ancients used each of the three Genera in their purest and simplest forms, as well as whichever of their particular species (of which there were many). Because in that very simplicity truly consists the excellence of harmony and melody, and not in imperfection. Those of today who believe, or have believed or written otherwise, have been greatly mistaken; and to see that this is true, listen. First, any simple Genus or species did not bring to them the impediment of chords between the parts as it does to the moderns: because every one of their songs, whether it was sung by one alone or by many, was a "fixed song" <term>canto fermo</term> <note>Here referring to monophony or unison singing, like Gregorian chant.</note>, from which emerged a single melody <term>aria</term>, no differently than what we see in church when psalms are chanted during the Divine Office, and especially when celebrated solemnly. And this was born from knowing very well, as has been said, that the property of a low sound was one thing, that of a high sound another, and that of the middle yet another. They knew, furthermore, that contrary qualities, when mixed and confounded together, weakened and in a certain way blunted each other's power; so they not only sang the same words together and the same melody at the same time and pitch, but with the same quantity of time, and the same quality of number and rhythm. For a suppliant recommends himself with one kind of slowness of words, and utters them with a certain quantity of sound and voice, while he who has a quiet soul speaks differently; and the excited man, far from both of these, utters them differently in every respect, as I have told you another time.

**STR.** Did the ancient musicians not sing in consonance, then?

<margin>The ancients did not sing in consonance.</margin>
**BAR.** Certainly not, as I told you just a moment ago.

**STR.** Did you not say a little while ago that Olympus brought it from Thrace to Greece?

**BAR.** Yes, the method of singing in consonance with the Pipe <term>Tibia</term> <note>An ancient reed instrument, often played in pairs.</note>.

**STR.** Is it not the same thing?

**BAR.** No, sir.

**STR.** What is the difference between them?

<margin>Singing in consonance with the Pipe, how it is understood.</margin>
**BAR.** Singing in consonance with the Pipe in those times could be nothing other than the piper <term>Tibicine</term> playing his melody, while someone else sang the same melody, uttering the words at the same time,

# ->Ancient & Modern<-

but with a different sound regarding the high and low; as for example at the Octave, and perhaps at the Fifth: or that while one Flute player <note>original: *Tibicine*</note> played a tenor in the low range, another played an ornamented part <note>original: *parte diminuita*</note> in the high range, no differently than what the small pipe of the Bagpipe <note>original: *Piua*</note> does today over its drone <note>original: *bordone*</note>. For the ancients often used the word "singing" to mean "playing," and "playing" to mean "singing"; and they likewise used "strings" for "voices," "flutes" for "finger-holes," and vice versa. But that two or more singers sang different melodies in consonance and at the same time, in the manner used today, there is no one who has a good knowledge of their music who would believe it. And even if in some of their Choirs there were sometimes young men, old men, women, children, and others—who because of the difference of their ages, sex, and physical constitutions could not sing together in unison—this does not mean that by nature and by art they did not seek, with all their power and skill, to approach unison as much as they could. It is likely and reasonable that between their voices, octaves and double-octaves <note>original: *quintedecime*</note> were continuously produced; but this happened due to the natural disposition of the subjects, and not by law. The law in this matter paid more respect to what was possible than to what was fitting or decorous; as can be understood even today in the choirs of our Church chapels, where such a mixture of men occurs who have the same goal before their eyes, and this is a plainchant <term>canto fermo</term> <note>A traditional, unadorned church melody.</note>. It is true that at present they are more licentious than is appropriate, invited perhaps by "figured song" <note>original: *canto figurato*; complex polyphonic music</note>; which did not happen to the ancients for the reasons already given.
