### **BAR.**
I respond to this by saying that sciences have a different procedure and a different goal in their operation than arts do. Sciences seek the truth of all the accidents and properties of their subject, together with their causes, having for their goal the truth of knowledge and nothing more. Arts, however, have for their goal the *doing* <note>original: *l'operare*</note>, which is a different thing from understanding. Arithmetic seeks all the properties and accidents of numbers; as for example, if they are even, if they are odd, if they are evenly even, if they are
<margin>
Example.
</margin>
squares, if they are cubes, or perfect numbers, what proportion they have to one another, how such products are created, and a thousand other things pertaining to them. The Abacist <note>A practical mathematician or accountant using an abacus.</note>, then, does not make use of any of these things, but only attends to multiplying, dividing, subtracting, and adding numbers and the parts that originate from them, considering them as measurements or values of some subject and matter. This is because they sang a single melody as has been said, even if there were a hundred singing together; and they had no need for this [modern] way of doing things. For the power of their music

The Author’s reasons for persuading us that the ancients did not sing in consonance.

From this thing one clearly

The ancient Greeks called their melodies and Songs by that name, and what those were has already been demonstrated. Ancient Greek musicians, therefore, understood by *Harmony* the beautiful and gracious proceeding of the melody <note>original: *aria della Cantilena*</note>; the

<margin>

it mixes together without distinction melodies and Tones that are most dissimilar and of a nature contrary to one another, in addition to the diversity of words, tempo, and rhythm. And although each of these things has by its nature its own quality and force suited to awaken and move its own emotions through its similarity, nevertheless, it cannot commonly move any of them by itself. Rather, to anyone who considers it healthily, the contrary may manifestly appear (as has been said): that it has no way by its nature to even be reasonably thought capable of it. For it is necessary that the force and power of the melody and of the high Tones and fast movements should weaken and blunt the vigor and power of the low and slow ones; and conversely, the qualities of the latter are mutually weakened and enfeebled by the contrary natu...

# Dialogo della Musica

...of those: for which reason the soul of the listener can no longer—distracted at the same time toward different and almost opposite directions by the mixture of diverse notes that proportionately represent diverse and contrary emotions <note>original: *affetti*</note> to him—be pushed by the force of any one of them more toward this than toward 그것. For while one note pulls him violently in one way, the other pulls him back with equal force, no differently than what was said regarding the Column <note>Bardi previously used a metaphor of a column being pulled by equal forces in opposite directions, resulting in no movement at all</note>. But here it should be noted that those who wished to bring about the virtuous and miraculous effects narrated above, and similar ones, through their singing and playing, did not play or sing in consonance <note>meaning they did not play multiple different notes at once</note>. The Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans</note> primarily applied themselves to this simplicity of music, and they persevered in it more than anyone else, as did most of the nobles of all Greece. This good practice was abandoned and entirely lost over time through lewdness and luxury; afterward, a fake rather than a true music was transferred to the Latins <note>the Romans</note>. I return to the mixture of the Genera <term>Genera: the three types of ancient Greek scales—Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic</term> and species of the ancient musicians, and I say that no memory of them is found before Ptolemy; who, compared to those ancients, is in a certain way "modern." To this I add that before him, such a mixture of diverse Genera and species was truly never in use nor under any consideration; and this is gathered from what he himself says about it. Ptolemy recounts, then, that in his time it was customary to mix together certain Diatonic and Chromatic species; in which manner of mixtures, which were four (as you will understand), he made one of his distributions intervene in each. Furthermore, even if those mixtures made of diverse species that he teaches had been used in his time or before, they have nothing in the world to do with our modern way of composing; therefore, the comparison claiming that the ancients used them for the convenience of harmonies between the parts is not fitting.

STR. Please, do not be reluctant to explain these mixtures to me.

<margin>In chapter 15 of book 2.</margin>
BAR. According to Ptolemy, there were four manners of mixtures, because as it pleased him, they either mixed the Chromatic Syntonon <note>an "intense" or "stretched" version of the chromatic scale</note> with the Diatonic Tonic; or the Soft and delicate Diatonic with the Diatonic Tonic; or they truly mixed the latter with the Ditonic Diatonic <note>the traditional Pythagorean tuning</note>; or the Diatonic Tonic with the Diatonic Syntonon. Now consider that, except for the third manner of mixture where the Ditonic (which is the same as the very ancient Diatone) intervened in part, all the other species 
<margin>Ptolemy attributes the Tonic to himself.</margin>
are the inventions of Ptolemy. He attributed the Tonic to himself, which previously belonged to Archytas, no differently than was done with the Syntonon of Didymus. One would perhaps not believe something far from the truth if they believed that he himself was the author of such mixtures, and that he persuaded the craftsmen of his time to put such novelty into use. In that era, there did not flourish the quantity nor the quality of Illustrious Musicians that had flourished in the past; and regarding practice, little effort was given to anything other than that pertaining to the theater. These things gave Ptolemy even more occasion to tax <note>meaning to criticize or find fault with</note> some—indeed the majority—of his predecessors who were worthy of the highest praise. 
<margin>He refutes many ancient musicians worthy of praise.</margin>
He had already, with sword drawn, vilified without any respect and against all duty the Distributions of Aristoxenus (besides those of Didymus, Archytas, and Eratosthenes), which were perhaps more reputed than any others except for the most ancient Diatonic, and the two in the other Genera that took their being from it. He even began to rebuke and despise the ancient Diatonic, saying that except for the consonant intervals and the Whole Tone, the others were not in "superparticular" proportion <note>a mathematical ratio where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator, like 3:2 or 4:3</note> like those of the "Excited" Syntonon of Didymus—which he had unjustly made his own. It was this respect, and nothing else, that caused him to reorder it in such a manner. Nevertheless, this did not have the effect he desired; because, as I have said, no memory of such a mixture of one species with another is found in any writer other than Ptolemy himself. Perhaps it was not even put into practical use in his time or after; and even if it was, it did not satisfy, which is argued sufficiently by the fact that no memory of it remains.
<margin>His mixtures have nothing to do with the practice of today.</margin>
Now, the manner of the mixtures was as follows. In the Greater Perfect System <note>original: *Systema perfetto*</note>, the first and highest Tetrachord of the two high ones was Chromatic Syntonon, and the second and less high was Diatonic Tonic; and likewise the first and highest of the two lowest was Chromatic Syntonon, and the second and lowest was Diatonic Tonic; and the Tone of Disjunction <note>the interval separating the two tetrachord groups</note> remained fixed; and the same occurred in the other species.

STR. From what you have made me see clearly, so to speak, I realize that I was in a very great error in believing that the ancients used the species of their genera only in a mixed way. On the contrary, I have understood from your discourse that they used them only simple and pure. Furthermore, if one wanted to apply such a mixture to our modern way of composing, it would bring—with respect to "false encounters" <note>unpleasant dissonances or "false relations"</note> of fourths and fifths—greater difficulty, and not the facility I believed. It would be even more difficult because they lack the "imperfect" consonances <note>thirds and sixths, which were the basis of Renaissance harmony but not ancient theory</note>. If I could have a specific example of each of the Distributions made up until our times, they would be beyond measure pleasing to me; both for the understanding I would draw from them, and also to know how many there were, by whom they were made, and how they were distributed.

BAR. I have collected them all from various books with the greatest diligence I could, and I have placed them in the order required by the diversity of the times in which they were distributed and ordered by their authors. The first of these, leaving aside the very ancient Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic, were those made by Archytas, roughly at the same time as Timotheus.

<summary>Bardi argues that ancient Greek music was pure and simple, focusing on one emotion at a time, unlike the confusing mixtures introduced later by Ptolemy. He clarifies that Ptolemy's technical "mixtures" of different musical scales were a modern invention that has no relation to the complex polyphonic harmonies used in the Renaissance.</summary>

# Ancient and Modern.

<margin>
Diatonic criticized by Zarlino in chapter 31 of book 2. <note>Gioseffo Zarlino was a prominent 16th-century music theorist; Galilei often argued against his former teacher's views.</note>

Goal of the Pythagoreans.

Goal of the Aristoxenians.

Goal of the Ptolemaics.
</margin>
Aristoxenus followed shortly after; following him came Eratosthenes, and a long time later Didymus, after whom Ptolemy arrived not much later, and then Boethius. I present these Distributions <term>Distributions: the specific mathematical ratios or "tunings" assigned to the four notes of a tetrachord</term> to you; because without the knowledge and practice of them, their mixture cannot be properly understood. It should be noted that they were divided differently by their authors, according to their various designs and goals; and not because they were truly all approved and accepted by common use, or because one set of ideas drove the others from the field. For the great theorists <note>original: *speculatori*</note> judged what seemed right to them, and the public then followed whatever was most convenient for them, without any other regard for the theorists' speculations or judgments. Boethius can especially bear witness to this: in his work, you see only the most common ones recited, and despite all the reasons that Ptolemy and others had brought forward, only the most used were followed. Use has always remained firm—as long as men wished to use vocal singing for the purpose for which it was given to them by God—in choosing the *Diatono* <note>The "Diatonic Diatonos," a specific Pythagorean tuning based on perfect ratios</note> alone out of all the Diatonic scales, despite all the opposition raised against it by those great minds named above. Some of these thinkers primarily wanted to follow the logic of numbers, and these were the Pythagoreans, also called *Harmonici* <note>meaning "those who study harmony through mathematical ratios"</note>. Others prioritized the sense of hearing over the logic of those numbers; they were called *Canonici* or *Canonists* and were the Aristoxenians. Then, some wanted to reconcile the two groups in such a way that there would be no discrepancy between them; these were the Ptolemaics, for they said that judgment is refined and made correct when sense and reason concur in the same opinion. Thus, depending on what their logic dictated based on their proposed principles, one sect appeared different from another.

**STROZZI.** I thank you greatly for the favor and the courtesy shown to me in having given me such a beautiful collection of each of the Distributions <note>The various mathematical divisions of the musical scale or tetrachord.</note> that have been made up to the present day, and ordered with such diligence and distinction. However, before we leave the matters pertaining to them, tell me if others could be made, different from these, that might produce other effects; and if it is likely that, before these last two genera were found, composers proceeded in their Diatonic melodies by Ditones <note>Major thirds.</note> and Semiditones <note>Minor thirds.</note>.

<margin>Whether new distributions can be made.</margin>
**BARDI.** As for making new Distributions that would produce good effects, different from those of the ancients, I do not believe any could be made proportionately better than those you have seen; unless we wished to use the high intervals of the Tetrachords in place of the low ones, and the low ones where the high ones are. But I suspect that by starting the System of the Dorian Mode <note>One of the Greek musical modes, considered the most stable and serious.</note> in such a way from the Tritone <note>An interval of three whole tones, historically considered "the devil in music" for its dissonance.</note>, it would generate an effect entirely different from its original nature, and one that is not even good.

**STROZZI.** For what reason do we believe the ancients ordered the Tetrachords in that manner, rather than in this one, or another?

<margin>Whether in decreasing or increasing an interval, the change happens at the high or the low end.</margin>
**BARDI.** I told you in the beginning that when the ancient theorists found the ratio of the minor Semitone and the *Limma* <note>A small Pythagorean semitone.</note>, they subtracted two Whole Tones <note>The ratio 9:8, or Sesquioctave.</note> from the *Diatessaron* <note>The interval of a perfect fourth.</note>, and called the remainder the minor Semitone. Now, because in subtracting the Sesquioctave from the Sesquiterza <note>The ratio 4:3, a perfect fourth.</note>, it is more likely and reasonable that it be taken from the high side <note>Original: "acuta."</note> than from the low <note>Original: "graue."</note>; and conversely, in increasing it, it should grow from that side, and not from this; since we see that in decreasing it, it becomes lower <note>Original: "rimesso."</note>, and in increasing it, it becomes higher <note>Original: "teso."</note>; for the same reason, therefore, they were in the Diatessaron...

# Dialogue of Music

<margin>
Why the system of the Dorian mode starts on Are.
</margin>
Having established the Tetrachords <note>A group of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth; the building block of ancient Greek scales.</note> in two Tones in the high part, and not in the low, one might also take this opportunity to ask why the most famous and ancient arrangement, which is that of the Dorian mode, starts on Are and ends on Aa lamire <note>Are (A1) and Aa lamire (A2) are specific positions on the Guidonian Hand, the standard mnemonic system for naming notes in the Renaissance.</note>, rather than on two other notes. To which I briefly respond by saying that this occurred more by chance than by design, as will be sensibly seen in the progress of our discourse.

<margin>
If the progression by Ditone and Semiditone was permitted in the Diatonic genus.
</margin>
As for whether they progressed by the Ditone <term>Ditone: an interval of two whole tones, essentially a major third</term> and Semiditone <term>Semiditone: an interval of a tone and a half, essentially a minor third</term> in their Diatonic melodies, there is no doubt about it; and not only before, but even after the last two genera were rediscovered and in use. And that this is true is evidenced by the examples of ancient melodies that provide indubitable proof.

<margin>
Which intervals the Diatonic did not use.
</margin>
The singable intervals that the Diatonic genus never used were no more than three; which, before they were considered by men, could in no way be put into practice, and afterward it was not appropriate; for it is a reasonable thing that they remained particular and proper to the genera from which they took their origin, if for no other reason than to better distinguish these from those. Two of these were particular to the Chromatic, and the other to the Enharmonic. The hallmark of the Enharmonic was the Diesis, also called by the Greeks *Tetartemoria* <note>meaning "fourth-parts," referring to the quarter-tone intervals used in the Enharmonic genus.</note>, which is the smallest singable interval. Aristotle wishes this to be the common measure of every consonant interval of his time (called today perfect consonances), just as unity is the common measure of any number. By this Diesis, he undoubtedly means that of the Enharmonic 

<margin>
Tetartemoria, what it signifies.
</margin>
of Aristoxenus <note>Aristoxenus was a Greek philosopher and music theorist (c. 375 BCE) who argued that musical intervals should be judged by the ear rather than just mathematical ratios.</note> his student; because the Semitone is composed of two of them, and the Tone of four; which faculty no other Diesis has. But if it is true that the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> means by Diesis in that place what we have said, it will be the common measure not only of any perfect consonance, but of the imperfect ones and dissonances as well—both of the Syntonic Diatonic, the Tonic Chromatic, and the Enharmonic of the same Aristoxenus. This will further verify and expand what Aristotle intends in that place, where he makes no other mention of consonances, nor of perfect or imperfect dissonances as some modern interpreters would have it, which 

<margin>
Zarlino in chapter 48 of the second part.
</margin>
can be gathered from the very words of the text, which are these: "However, in Astrology this 'one' is the principle and measure; because they suppose the motion of the heaven to be equal and fastest, according to which they judge the others; and in Music the Diesis, because it is the smallest thing, and in the voice the element." And just as this Diesis is, as we have said, the smallest singable element, 

<margin>
Diesis as the smallest singable interval; and the Comma as the smallest perceptible.
</margin>
the Comma (leaving aside the consideration of the Schisma) is likewise the smallest perceptible interval. I return to say that the proper and particular Chromatic intervals were the Trihemitone <note>An interval of three semitones (a minor third).</note> and the Semitone often called "greater"; but do not understand by this the Apotome <note>A specific mathematical division of a tone in Pythagorean tuning.</note>, for you would be in error, but rather the second interval of each 

<margin>
Which intervals the Chromatic never used, and which the Enharmonic.
</margin>
of its tetrachords. The Enharmonic genus, then, never used the interval of the Tone, nor the major and minor Semitone, nor the Trihemitone; and the Chromatic always left aside in all its affairs the Tone and the Enharmonic Diesis; although I greatly doubt (though against common opinion) whether it was permissible for any genus of harmony to proceed through the Tone of disjunction <term>Tone of disjunction: the whole tone that separates two tetrachords in the Greek Greater Perfect System</term> in its system; as it is common to every species 

<margin>
The interval of the Tone was used by the ancients in every genus of harmony.
</margin>
of every genus, and not subject, along with the lowest [note], to alteration like all the others that are not contained by the stable strings of the Tetrachords. This opinion contradicts what Zarlino says in chapter 75 of the third part of his *Institutions*. For he wishes the Major Tone to be particular to the Diatonic, which, as has been shown, is not true at all; and even if the Diatonic that he understands to be sung today had its own 

<margin>
Zarlino in chapter 48 of the 2nd part of the Institutions.
</margin>
and particular Tone, it would sooner be the minor than the major: but this does not happen to him in any way. I do not want to keep silent about another thing that occurs to me, so that those who might consider it true and of some weight may know to give credit to its author: and this is, that even if the Diatonic sung today were truly what Zarlino maintains, he should not be thanked for it as a discovery of his; since that opinion (though not approved as impertinent) was diligently written by Lodovico Fogliano <note>An Italian theorist (1490–1538) who pioneered the mathematical justification for "Just Intonation."</note>, sixty or seventy years ago, in the second section of his *Theoretical Music*. There is no other difference between them than in the quantity and measure of the Semitones, in which regard both are mistaken; as anyone who has full knowledge of such things can sensibly see. That in every genus of harmony the two aforementioned Tones were ultimately sung is manifested plainly in the distribution of their strings, among which they are found, as everyone who has knowledge of the matter knows.

I also do not know what reason there was to prohibit, before the last two genera of harmony came into use, the progression by Ditone and Semiditone in the Ditonic Diatonic, and likewise afterward.

Apotome not sung by the ancients.
</margin>
**STROZZI.** It seems the same to me: but as far as I can see, the Apotome was never put into practice by the ancient practitioners.

Zarlino in chapter 15 of the 2nd of his Institutions.

### Ancient and Modern [Music]

It would not be inconvenient, when discussing this, to call it the "Chromatic major semitone," and not simply (for the reasons mentioned) the "major semitone"—unless we wished to say that this is the largest semitone actually found in the Chromatic genus, while the Apotome <note>original: *Apotome*. In Pythagorean tuning, this is the larger of the two semitones that make up a whole tone.</note> is that which exists potentially and by relationship when comparing (as was said) the *Trite synemmenon* <note>original: *Trite synemmenon*, the third string of the conjunct tetrachord.</note> to the *Paramese* <note>original: *Paramese*, the note 'B' in the ancient Greek system, positioned just above the middle note.</note>.

**STR.** This has been a welcome clarification for me; and now that you have removed every difficulty regarding the Tones, the Species, and the Genera of the musical distributions, I would be pleased, if it suits you, for you to explain in detail how it came to pass that the Lyre and the Cithara <note>The Lyre and Cithara were the primary stringed instruments of Ancient Greece, often associated with Apollo and Orpheus.</note> of the ancient musicians increased by such a large number of strings. At the beginning, they had no more than three or four; I hope with your help to clear up many things that make me greatly doubt them.

<margin>
At chapter 20 of the first [book] of his *Music*.

The order of numbering the strings according to the Greeks and according to the Latins.
</margin>

**BAR.** This whole matter is recounted to us by Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works transmitted Greek music theory to the Middle Ages.</note> in a very fine and distinct order, so that from his words you will draw whatever clarity you desire. There is no difference between him and the ancient Greek musicians other than the order of numbering them. For the first string, according to the Greek order, was the highest-pitched, the *Nete*; according to Boethius, it was the lowest-pitched, the *Proslambanomene* <note>original: *Proslambanomene*, literally "the added note," the lowest note of the Greek scale.</note>. Which of these is more reasonable to call "the first" can be understood from the natural order and arrangement of numbers, where one sees that two and three come before four and six or any other larger number.

**STR.** Please, do not find it a burden to tell me this story.

<margin>
Of the strings added to the Cithara of Mercury.

Arrangement of the strings of the Lyre of Mercury.

Opposition.

*Hypate*, what it implies.

*Parhypate*, what it signifies.

*Lycanos*, what it implies.
Consideration of the Author.
Consideration of Aristoxenus.
Opinion of Aristoxenus.
</margin>

**BAR.** Boethius recounts, on the authority of Nicomachus of Gerasa <note>A mathematician and music theorist from the 1st/2nd century AD.</note>, that the first stringed instrument of which we have memory was discovered by Mercury. Some ancient writers have doubted whether this was Mercury Trismegistus. According to the opinion of most ancient writers, this instrument was arranged by him with four strings and no more, in imitation of "world music" and the elements <note>The concept of *musica mundana*, the "music of the spheres," suggesting the harmony of the cosmos and the four elements.</note>. He stretched them, according to the mind of Boethius, in the arrangement you shall hear. From the first string (beginning from the low pitch according to the custom of this learned writer, as has been said) to the second string was a *Diatessaron* <term>Diatessaron: the interval of a perfect fourth</term>; from this to the third was a sesquioctave or Whole Tone; and from the third to the fourth and last, another *Diatessaron*. In this way, the first with the third, and the second with the fourth, sounded a *Diapente* <term>Diapente: the interval of a perfect fifth</term>, and the outer strings sounded a *Diapason* <term>Diapason: the interval of an octave</term>. 

This opinion, according to the judgment of certain judicious and learned men—whom I want us to follow as well—strays far from the manner of singing in those early times, and consequently from the truth. It has nothing reasonable about it, as we shall show in the proper place with authority, giving the reasons that move us to say this. Furthermore, Mercury desired (as others prefer) that the lowest string, being the first in the Lyre and more worthy than the others, be called *Hypate* <note>From the Greek *hypatos*, meaning "highest" or "principal," though it refers to the lowest pitch.</note>, because his father Jove [Jupiter] was called by that name, and also because the Consul is called by that name. This string was also attributed to Saturn, as the sluggishness of that planet matches the low gravity of the string. He named the second *Parhypate*, which means "next to" or "beside the *Hypate*." He named the third *Lycanos*, because the Greeks call that finger of the hand "next to the thumb" by that name—the one the Latins later called the "Index," from "pointing"—for no other reason than that this string was the first to be touched and struck by that finger in playing. This practice is seen even today among players of certain instruments whose strings are touched and struck by the fingers. 

To this consideration, we shall add this thought from Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and music theorist, pupil of Aristotle, who emphasized human hearing over mathematical ratios.</note>: that it was so named to demonstrate the intervals of the Tetrachord <note>A four-note scale segment.</note> in the middle of which it was placed, whether that distribution was Diatonic, Chromatic, or Enharmonic. Not without reason was such a faculty established in the *Meson* Tetrachord, as it was the first known and most famous, and the one in which the strings of the two latter genera of harmony were first distributed; indeed, they were discovered within it. One can also argue from what has been said that the strings of the Lyre were struck by fingers before they were struck by the Plectrum <note>A small tool used to pluck strings, like a modern guitar pick.</note>. He further willed that the fourth and last string be called *Mese*, the meaning of which is nothing other than "middle"—as if the immortal God foresaw that this string, in the Great and Perfect System, would hold the middle place. To this Cithara nothing was ever added, nor was the tuning of its strings changed, until the time of Orpheus; but the proportion we described was maintained between them, as seen noted here in the example. We have distributed its strings according to various opinions, but which of these is the most likely and reasonable will be stated in its place, as was said.

# Dialogue on Music

<margin>
Coroebus of Lydia adds the fifth string to the Lyre.
Hyagnis the Phrygian adds the sixth string to the Lyre.
Plutarch in the treatise *On the Customs of the Lacedaemonians*.
Terpander of Lesbos adds the seventh string to the Lyre.
</margin>

Next came Coroebus, son of King Atys of Lydia, who added the fifth string to the Cithara we have shown. He named it *Paramete* <note>original: *Paramete*, literally "beside the middle note."</note> and *Trite* <note>original: *Trite*, meaning "third."</note>. It was called *Paramete* because it was next to the *Mese* <note>original: *Mese*, the "middle" note and the central anchor of the Greek scale.</note>, and *Trite* because it was the third string in the *Synemmenon* <note>original: *Tetraccordo Synemmenon*, the "conjunct" or "connected" four-note scale segment.</note> tetrachord, where its position was later clarified, as you will hear. However, they began counting the strings from the high part of the tetrachord, as the ancient Greeks were accustomed to do, and not according to the method of Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century Roman scholar who transmitted Greek music theory to the Middle Ages.</note>. It seems that the license taken by this great Prince gave courage to Hyagnis the Phrygian (the first inventor of the pipes <note>original: *Tibie*, ancient reed instruments similar to an oboe.</note> and father of the reckless Marsyas) to add the sixth string to the Cithara, which he called the *Paranete*. Afterward, Terpander of Lesbos added the seventh string. By making this addition, he brought about the loss of his Cithara; for the most severe Spartan Ephors <note>Senior magistrates in ancient Sparta known for their cultural conservatism.</note> took it from him and hung it at the top of a very tall pillar, at the foot of which one could read the reason for this punishment. Terpander called the string he added to the Cithara the *Nete*, which in that language signifies what in ours means "inferior" or "below" <note>Though the *Nete* was the highest in pitch, it was the "lowest" or "bottom-most" string in terms of physical position on the instrument when held.</note>. But if Hyagnis the Phrygian was the first to play the pipes, as they say, one might argue from this that the Cithara was in use before the pipes—even though this seems difficult to believe given the complexity of the Cithara compared to the simplicity of the pipes. But let this consideration suffice for now. Once the Lyre was reduced to the number and limit of these seven strings, they were stretched in the manner described in this example.

<margin>
Meaning of *Synemmenon* and *Synaphe*.
Book 4, chapter 4. The *Tricord* and *Pandura* are the same. The *Pentachord*. The Author's considerations.

These strings were divided into two joined tetrachords, giving the lower one the name *Meson* <note>The tetrachord of the middle notes.</note> and the higher one *Synemmenon* or *Synaphe*, which simply means "joined" <note>original: *congiunto*. This refers to the overlapping note between two scale segments.</note>. It is likely, in my opinion, that these three strings were added to the Lyre and Cithara in a very short span of time, one after the other. This is because we find no mention among the Greeks of any other instrument named "Lyre" between the four-stringed version of Mercury and the seven-stringed one of Terpander. It is true that we have the testimony of Julius Pollux <note>A 2nd-century Greek grammarian and sophist.</note> that the Arabs discovered a different three-stringed instrument, later called the *Pandura* by the Assyrians, and that the Scythians were the first to use a five-stringed instrument. But in this passage, Boethius is speaking specifically of the Lyre of the ancient Greeks—even if their order of naming the strings varies from his, as I have said. To tell you more, I believe all three strings were added to the Cithara on the very same day. The reason that moves me to believe this is as follows: The son of the King of the Lydians could not reasonably have named the string he added *Paramete* or *Trite* if the strings mentioned after it did not already exist. For the name *Trite* not only signifies "the third" of something, but specifically the third of strings that (as you will soon understand) were not yet there. Furthermore, the name *Paranete* which Hyagnis the Phrygian gave to his string means "beside the *Nete*," and yet the *Nete* likewise did not exist yet. *Nete* then carries the meaning said above. Thus, if one considers the meaning of the words—which is the only light we can draw from Boethius's text on this matter—one might conclude that this whole business was pre-arranged by these authors to please that great Prince. Unless we wish to say that until they reached the number of seven, the strings had no proper names (which seems less likely). Indeed, it is most true according to the testimony of Plutarch, who says: "Terpander established the Citharistic laws with proper names for the melodies and the strings." Here I must note that Plutarch calls them "Citharistic" laws <note>Laws for the Cithara played alone as an instrument.</note> and not "Citharedic" <note>Songs performed while accompanying oneself on the Cithara.</note>, because of the difference mentioned earlier between these two types of performers.

Plutarch in the *Opuscula on Music*. Terpander gives the Citharistic laws. Why they were called "laws."
Names of the Citharistic laws.

</margin>

**STR.** For what reason were they called "laws"?

**BAR.** They were called so as if it had been prescribed by law that it was in no way permitted to change the tuning of the strings or the pitches in which they had first been arranged and set by Terpander. The names of their parts were these: *Beginning*, *The Begun*, *The Turning*, *After the Turning*, *The Navel*, *The Seal*, and *The Epilogue*. In imitation of these, Clonas, a singular player of the pipes, first gave laws to the pipes. The names of these (according to the same Plutarch) are: *Apotheto*, *Elego*, *Comarchio*, *Schenione*, *Capione*, *Dio*, and *Trimele*. # Ancient & Modern.

...that *Apotheto* <note>original: *Apotheto*, meaning "hidden" or "stored away."</note> signifies the same as "Recondite." *Elego*, from which "Elegy" derives, means the same as "Mourning" and "Lamentation." *Comarchio* is the name given to the Prince of the Village, or perhaps the Master of the Banquet. *Schenione* <note>original: *Schenione*, referring to the Greek "Schoenus," a measure of distance.</note> means the same as "measure." *Capione* is a proper name, and in this context, it means the same as *Terpandria* and *Hieracia* among the laws of the Lute-players <note>original: *Fidicinì*, players of stringed instruments.</note>. *Dio* signifies "Two," and *Trimale* means "three songs," or rather "Canzoni"; or perhaps he wishes to signify with that number three the song, the sound, and the dance together, as they many times used simultaneously; or to put it better, that law of Sacadas the Argive, which I named above, called "Tripartite." For a greater understanding of these laws, you must know that the ancient musicians had not only specific and particular laws for wind and string instruments, but they also had some that were common to both. Each of these took its name either from Rhythms, such as the *Orthia* <note>original: *Orthia*, meaning "high-pitched" or "upright."</note> and the *Trochea*; or from Modes or customs, such as the "acute" and the *Tetraida*. Others took their name from the inventors and the people, such as the *Aeolian* and the *Boeotian*, or the *Terpandria* and the *Hieracia* just now mentioned. At other times, the law took its name from the subject matter treated within, such as the "Pythian Battle" and the *Curule*. Let this suffice for now regarding the laws of musical instruments. You should also

<margin>
Virtue of Terpander.
Lasus, before anyone else, wrote books pertaining to the musical faculty. Suda.
</margin>

know that the Citharistic laws were composed in verse by the same Terpander and published. This singular Cithara-player sang to stringed instruments with marvelous art, more so than anyone else; he further added new modes to his verses and to those of Homer through particular rules. And just as these were the first who gave laws to stringed and wind instruments, Lasus <note>Lasus of Hermione, a 6th-century BC Greek lyric poet and musician.</note> was the one who, before any other, discovered the Dithyrambic contest and wrote (in the times of Darius, King of the Persians) volumes pertaining to the musical faculty. I do not wish to omit another consideration regarding the increasing of strings on the Lyre: it could very well be that Mercury’s Lyre, with its mere four strings, was used by men in that simplicity until the time of Coroebus. Having practiced on it and found it (as it truly was, regarding the expression of the diversity of concepts) quite poor in strings, Coroebus added one in that part which was not only conforming to the natural way of singing used by the province in which he was born and ruled, but truly where it was necessary; and this was the *acute* <note>The high-pitched string.</note>, as you will better understand in its proper place. To this Cithara, the sixth string was later added in the same part by Hyagnis the Phrygian, as has been said. And so they remained without any proper or particular name until Terpander came. Perhaps the men of those times distinguished them in the meantime by the names of First, Second, and Third, in the way the Spaniards today name the strings of the Lute. Terpander, adding the seventh, gave each a name and a suitable law, as the most learned man he was.

<margin>
Another consideration of the Author.
</margin>

What has been said also carries the appearance of truth regarding the consideration that Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle who wrote extensively on music theory.</note> makes concerning the name of the string *Lichanos* <note>original: *Lycanos*, the "forefinger" string.</note>; for if, when it acquired such a name, no other species of harmony had been in use than the Diatonic, the faculty that Aristoxenus attributed to it would have been entirely vain and useless, which is not believable. The span of time concerning this matter has been researched by me with every diligence to note it, knowing the knowledge that could be drawn from it; but I have found nothing certain and determined that is worthy of memory, but rather the greatest confusion. Thus, I judge it less harmful to stick to what writers tell us of such things without seeking further. They have sometimes incidentally mentioned this or that other musician while describing the life or recounting some deed of a Prince in whose service they were; as has also happened to many of the ancient Poets.

<margin>
Which string was first in use, the B-natural or the B-flat.
</margin>

From the first example of the Cithara with four strings, in the third of which (according to the mind of Plutarch, however) is found that which was later called *Paramese* <note>The note B-natural in the Greek system.</note>, and as such is received today; and from this one of seven, where the *Trite synemmenon* <note>The note B-flat in the Greek system.</note> was placed in the fifth position, one could draw the knowledge of which of the two was first in use: B-natural or B-flat. Speaking now as a pure practitioner, those who would not more subtly investigate this case—so many times disputed by chance in our times—would give the sentence in favor of those who hold that B-natural was in use before B-flat; nonetheless, from what I am about to say shortly below, the complete opposite will be gathered.

<margin>
Orpheus plays the Lyre in the arrangement established by Terpander.
The ancient musicians applied the seven strings to the wandering stars differently, and why.
Ptolemy in the last part of Book 3 of the *Harmonics*.
Cicero in Book 6 of the *Republic*.
</margin>

The Lyre was thus reduced to this state when Orpheus came; and in such a manner disposed, he used to play it, both with the fingers and with the Plectrum, as Virgil noted above. The musicians of those times applied each of these strings to one of the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note>. Some philosophers were of the opinion that the sound of the low strings—due to the slow motion they have regarding their slackness and thickness—corresponded with the highest planets; and the high-pitched, due to the thinness and speed of motion resulting from the intensity of the bodies from which they proceed, with the lower ones, as they also possess such qualities. Others, on the contrary, held that the low strings corresponded to the lower spheres, and the high ones to the highest. With these the Ptolemaics agreed, and following them Cicero, considering the position; and the Pythagoreans agreed with the former, considering the motion of the planets and the capacity of their heaven. According to these different opinions, one saw many times in stringed instruments—while being held in the arms to be played—now the basses and the drones <note>original: *bordoni*, the low strings.</note> in the place of the trebles and the *cati* <note>original: *cati*, likely referring to "catline" or thin gut strings.</note>, to apply these different designs of theirs to a modern instrument; and now, on the contrary, these in the place of those. But because the Cithara of those times did not have (so to speak) a body, or rather a

...bottom, and being able to be played from both one side and the other, not unlike the Harp; such variety of position did not bring him the difficulties that it would bring today to players of the Lute and the Viola, if they were practiced in only one manner. Afterward came Lycaon of Samos and added the eighth string to the Cithara <note>A professional version of the lyre with a wooden sounding box.</note>; although Pliny attributes this invention to Simonides. He placed it in the middle between the *Paranete* and the *Paramese*, which was also called the *Trite* <note>original: *Trite*, meaning "third."</note>; and because it became the third string from the *Nete* <note>The "highest" note in pitch, though physically the "lowest" on the instrument's frame.</note> (starting to count from the extreme high end coming toward the low, according to their custom, as I have said), they gave it the name of *Trite*. This was very appropriate for the reason mentioned above. He wished to assign this string to the heaven of the fixed stars; and they later called such an instrument the **Ottocordon of Lycaon of Samos**, to distinguish it from the Heptachord of Terpander of Lesbos, because of the number of its strings, which were arranged into two "disjoined" Tetrachords <note>A scale of four notes.</note>. Because of this disjunction, it was fitting that the high Tetrachord should leave behind the name *Synemmenon* <note>meaning "conjoined" or "linked."</note> and take instead the name *Diezeugmenon* or *Diezeusis*, which signifies "separated." Thus, the eight strings of the said instrument corresponded to each other in the proportions represented by the numbers in the example below; and the Cithara was in this state in the times of Aristoxenus, as he himself testifies.

In this, it should be considered that by Lycaon placing the string he added between the *Paramese* and the *Paranete*, it came to occupy the position of the string of Hyagnis the Phrygian, which was (naming it according to this new practice) C-sol-fa-ut <note>The pitch C.</note>, and to raise it so much in pitch that it became d-la-sol-re <note>The pitch D.</note>. The same happened to the string of the lawgiver Terpander; for while in the Heptachord it was d-la-sol-re, in the Octochord it became e-la-mi <note>The pitch E.</note>, which was later called the Dorian *Nete* of Terpander; and so it remained in the Greatest and Perfect System. And by raising the pitch of the string of Corebus of Lydia by an *Apotome* <note>A major semitone in Pythagorean tuning.</note>, where in the Heptachord it was B-flat <note>original: *b fa*</note>, in the Octochord it became B-natural <note>original: *h mi*</note>. In this manner, regarding the order, the eighth string came to the place of the sixth, the sixth to the place of the seventh, and this to the place of the eighth; it is likely that they remained with this number of strings for some time (due to the novelty of the distribution). Afterward came Profastus of Periota, or perhaps Perinthus, and added the ninth string; although according to Pliny, it was an invention of Timothy of Miletus, easily inferred from what was said above of the mind of the Philosopher <note>Referring to Aristotle.</note> regarding the same Timothy. He placed this string in the low register as far as sound is concerned, but "above" regarding its physical position; and he named it *Parhypate* after its placement. From this, one can argue that when the Lyre was held in the arms to be played, the lower strings faced the sky (in the manner of the Lute), and not the opposite. The strings of this instrument were afterward assigned to the choir of the nine Muses, and they called it the Enneachord. Nor did Profastus place the string he added to the Lyre in the low register for any other reason than to have the *Mese* <note>The central "middle" note of the Greek scale.</note> in the middle of them, as seen in the example below.

# Ancient & Modern Music

<margin>
Timotheus adds the eleventh string to the Cithara.
Suidas.
The Ephors <note>magistrates of Sparta</note> cut two strings from the Cithara of Timotheus.
Timotheus banished from Sparta.
Zarlino, Chapter 32 of Book 2 of the *Institutes*.
</margin>
...up to eleven, perhaps because of the aforementioned authority of Aristotle, or truly because of that Decree that the Spartans once made against him. Shortly before (as Plutarch tells us), one of their Ephors had publicly cut those strings added to the Cithara <note>original: *Cithara*, a professional wooden lyre</note> on the theater stage. But because he did not mend his ways—rather, having shortly after made a greater number of holes in the Tibia <note>original: *Tibia*, a double-reed pipe often called an aulos</note>, or having persuaded the Tibia-players of his time to do so (if indeed it was the same Timotheus, as most writers of this event seem to believe)—and by making music more varied and "soft" <note>meaning effeminate or overly complex compared to traditional styles</note> than it had been previously received, they ultimately banished him from their borders as a destroyer of ancient and severe music. He later went into the service of Alexander of Macedon. From this fact (contrary to the opinion of some), it appears clearly that one punishment was given to Timotheus when he added one or more strings to the Cithara, and another when (according to those writers) he invented the Chromatic genre <note>a style of music using smaller intervals, considered emotionally manipulative by ancients</note>. One can also understand from this that writers have mentioned Timotheus the Citharist and Timotheus the Flutist indiscriminately, as I hinted to you a little while ago.

**STR.** Please, do not be reluctant to bring back to my memory the contents of that Decree.

<margin>
Consideration of the Author.
Decree of the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> against Timotheus.
Thaletas of Gortyn called by the Spartans.
He frees them from the plague; and likewise the Argives.
Ptolemy in Ch. 5 of Book 2, and Aristoxenus in Book 2.
</margin>
**BAR.** The summary of the Decree, as Boethius recites it (though in the language in which it was made, it sounds otherwise as has been said), was this: The Spartans were angry with Timotheus of Miletus because, by making music more varied, he harmed the souls of children and hindered them from the modesty of virtue; and the harmony that he had received as modest, he turned into the Chromatic genre, which is softer; just as you said a moment ago regarding him. His exile was the occasion for the Lacedaemonians to summon, at great price, Thaletas of Gortyn the Cretan, author of the Paeans <note>solemn hymns</note>, to instruct their children in the discipline of grave and severe music. Through his work, the Lacedaemonians were furthermore liberated from the plague, as were the Argives likewise. It was a custom among the ancients, and lasted a long time especially among the Greeks, to greatly punish the transgressors of laws and, conversely, to greatly reward the good and those who loved them. From the acquisition of the two strings named above, the Musicians of those times created a new Tetrachord <note>a scale of four notes</note> for the Cithara in the low range; which, from the name of the strings that composed it, they called *Hypaton* <note>original: *Hypaton*, meaning "principal" or "lowest"</note>. But it should be noted that the *Hyperhypate* of the nine-string system was named *Lycanoshypaton* in the eleven-string system, and they joined it to the *Parhypate* by pushing it toward the high end by one Tone. They left to the fourth string, which was later called by the Latins "Almost the Highest" <note>original: *Pene Suprema*</note>, the same name it had before, accompanied however by this word *Meson* <note>meaning "of the middle"</note> like all the others of its Tetrachord. The fifth they called *Parhypate*, the sixth *Lycanos* (its first name), the seventh *Mese*, the eighth *Paramese*, the ninth *Trite*, the tenth *Paranete*, and the eleventh and last *Nete*. This number of strings they ordered and disposed in their eleven-string system into two joined Tetrachords on the low side, and into one separated from these on the high side. This constitution of strings had, as Ptolemy likes, the status of a Perfect System, because in those times (he says) no other Tones <note>modes</note> were in use except three: namely, Dorian, Phrygian, and Lydian; which were always more famous and reputed than the others. After there was full knowledge of the 15 strings—or rather, after they were generally received by everyone, divided and ordered into four Tetrachords, with such a constitution later called the "Greatest and Perfect Disjoined System"—they called the system of eleven (to distinguish it from this one of fifteen) the "Lesser and Imperfect System." Lesser regarding the quantity of strings, and imperfect regarding the number of Tones and consonances, for lacking the Octave-plus-Fifth <note>original: *Diapason Diapente*</note>, the Double Octave <note>original: *Bisdiapason*</note>, and the three species of the octave that later served the Plagal Tones <note>lower-range versions of musical modes</note>; as clearly appears in the following example.

Four very famous sects of Musicians.

BAR. <note>Bardi</note> You must first know that in the times of Epigonus, as in others, there were many "sects" or schools of musicians. Among these is counted that of Damon: according to the testimony Plato gives of him, he was the music teacher of Pericles, and lived in the same times as Socrates. At that time, the sect of Eratocles and that of Agenor also flourished; these held various opinions regarding practical music. Some wanted players to perform and sing in consonance <note>original: *consonanza*; here referring to harmony or polyphony</note>; others, on the contrary, forbade it as a pernicious thing; and still others wanted the instruments to play, but not the voices to sing. Therefore, the memory that writers kept of Timotheus's work arose from the novelty he brought to the place where he then found himself—which was among the very strict Spartans <note>original: *Lacedemoni*</note>, who were mortal enemies of any alteration to the statutes already approved in the Republic by the Senate. And although the sect of Epigonus had (so to speak) already infected many parts of Greece, this novelty was brought to the Spartans by Timotheus; for which reason they acted against him as you have heard.

And even if the number of strings on Epigonus's instrument, and the distance that Aristoxenus said existed between the *Hypertelie* and *Parthenie* pipes <note>original: *Tibie*; ancient reed instruments</note> of his time (which was an interval greater than three octaves <note>original: *Terdiapason*</note> from the lowest voice of the former to the highest of the latter), do not seem like effective arguments to persuade you that they played in consonance, let that truth at least be persuaded by what Socrates and Plato warn and command (principally to the nobles) in the Laws: namely, that they should play and sing *Proscorda* <note>playing a variation of the melody</note> and not *Sinfone* <note>sounding in harmony or unison</note>. This precept would have been warned and commanded in vain if some had not been playing and singing in consonance during that century. I believe that with what I have said, I have not only removed your doubt but also the objection recently made against Ptolemy.

In the demonstration of the Decachord <note>a ten-stringed instrument or system</note>, this other consideration must not be left behind: that since the *Mese* <note>the "middle note" of the Greek scale, serving as a functional center</note> joined the high tetrachord to the middle one, they accompanied it with its name, namely *Mesesynemmenon* <note>meaning "the conjunct middle note"</note>. Musicians of those times, still not fully content with any of the shown distributions and quantities of strings, decided to add an entire tetrachord to the high end, in addition to the eleven shown above. This took the name *Hyperboleon*—which means "exceeding"—primarily from its position and the strings that composed it. I find no memory of the author of this addition in the text of Boethius <note>an influential 6th-century Roman philosopher</note> nor elsewhere that I know of. Thus, they arrived at a total of fourteen strings and four tetrachords. Two of these were joined at the low end <note>the "Hypatōn" and "Mesōn" tetrachords</note>, and two others at the high end; between these two pairs, the Tone of Disjunction <note>original: *Tuono della disgiuntione*; a whole tone interval that separates two tetrachords rather than having them share a note</note> was placed, as seen described here.

Finally, it was considered that in this particular distribution of strings, the *Mese* did not actually fall in the middle of them, as its name implies; furthermore, among the five intervals accepted as consonants, the *Bisdiapason* <note>the double octave, or a range of fifteen notes</note> was missing. They therefore resolved once more to add a string at the low end, which would fall one Whole Tone below the *Hypate-hypaton*. They called this note *Proslambanomenos* <note>the "added note"</note> and others called it *Prosmelodos*. Its meaning was discussed above. The author of this addition has not come to my notice, and even if they had, it has slipped from my memory. With the acquisition of this note in the said position, the *Mese* reached its proper and desired place in the center; moreover, the extremes of the fifteen strings now corresponded to a Double Octave, as is clearly seen in the example.

### Dialogue on Music

<warning>A large rectangular paper flap is pasted over the middle of the page, obscuring the upper half of the musical diagram and parts of the background text on the underlying page.</warning>

<margin>
Zarlino in chapter 2 of the second part of the *Institutions* <note>Gioseffo Zarlino, a famous 16th-century theorist</note>.
</margin>
And they then called this quantity of strings, distributed in this way, the **Greater and Perfect Disjunct System** <note>original: *Systema massimo & perfetto disgiunto*; a fifteen-note scale consisting of four tetrachords and one added note</note>; in which (if understood according to the **Dorian Mode** in the **Diatonic genus** and in the most ancient **Ditonic Diatonic** species) <note>a tuning system based on whole tones of a 9:8 ratio and small semitones</note> having reached this number of strings, and having ordered them on the **Kithara** <note>original: *Cithara*; a professional ancient Greek lyre</note> according to the manner and arrangement shown by the numbers, their intellects were satisfied and at peace. They recognized very well that the human voice could not ascend higher or descend lower without great discomfort to the singer and very little satisfaction for the listeners, besides the other reasons cited for this. This was likewise the reason why **Pythagoras of Samos** commanded that one should not pass beyond the **Quadruple** <note>the ratio 4:1, representing a double octave</note>, and not because he ever believed or said that intervals larger than the **Double Octave** <note>original: *Bisdiapason*</note> were dissonant, as some moderns have written. For many centuries, the ancient musicians did not care to proceed or pass further into the bass or the treble for each of their own particular systems of whatever Tone and Mode they had. The Kithara was ultimately reduced to this number of strings, which they then used in every species and genus of harmony, solely by tightening some and widening other intervals and frets as required by the quality and nature of the piece. They did this to express it (aided by other circumstances) with the greatest **affect** <note>original: *affetto*; the emotional impact or mood of the music</note> that anyone could imagine. By these means, skilled musicians always achieved their desired goal. To be able to play conveniently in different Modes and Tones, according to their high or low pitch, they used wind and string instruments of various sizes, with holes and strings distributed differently to suit this purpose. For greater clarity, I wish to place the example of each of these distributions next to the other, so that by sight you may also minutely understand the difference found regarding the high and low pitch of the strings.

**STR.** I have understood everything very well; but from having heard you name the **Greater and Perfect System** several times above, with the addition of the word **Disjunct**, I am persuaded that there must also be, by relation, a **Greater and Perfect Conjunct System**.

**BAR.** Have no doubt about it, and if you wish for an example of that as well, here it is.

When this is considered, you will find it to be the same as the **Decachord** <note>a ten-string system</note>, with the addition, however, of the **Proslambanomene** <note>the "Added Note" at the bottom of the scale</note> and the **Hyperboleon Tetrachord** separated from the **Synemmenon** by a Tone called in that place the **Tone of Disjunction**.

<header>
->Ancient and Modern [Music]<-
</header>
**L**
<meta>catchword: mamente (extremely)</meta>

**STR.** I now clearly understand that the difference found between the **Disjunct System** and the **Conjunct System** is nothing more than what is called by today’s practical musicians **B-natural** or **B-flat** <note>original: *per h duro, ò per b molle*. In early music notation, a square 'b' (h) indicated a natural/hard note, while a rounded 'b' indicated a flat/soft note</note>.

<margin>In the sixth chapter of the second book of his *Harmonics*.</margin>
**BAR.** That is exactly right; and so that you may know more, **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century mathematician and music theorist</note> goes very subtly investigating this. He shows that just as in the **Greater and Perfect Disjunct System** (which existed before the Conjunct one), the three lowest **Tetrachords** <note>a scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth</note> were joined together, one could have just as conveniently joined the three highest ones. He proves demonstratively that this is so. Since you find it pleasing to understand this, I shall go on explaining it to you with great ease.

**STR.** This, and any other matter belonging to the knowledge of the musical faculty, will be more than pleasing to me.

<margin>The joining of Tetrachords can, according to Ptolemy, be done elsewhere.</margin>
**BAR.** Ptolemy says, then, to prove that one could join the three highest Tetrachords just as well as the three lowest in the Greater and Perfect Disjunct System, as follows. Let the fifteen strings of said System be contained between **B** (the extreme low string) and **A** (the extreme high string). Starting from that high **A** and moving toward the opposite [lower] side, let two Tetrachords be joined to it, labeled **AC** and **CD**. Immediately below these follows the **Tone of Disjunction** <note>original: *Tuono della disgiuntione*; a whole tone (9:8 ratio) that separates two tetrachords to complete an octave</note> at **DE**. Then, let two other Tetrachords be joined to the **E** (still moving toward the lower side), and let them be **EF** and **FG**. In this demonstration, there will be two Tetrachords joined in the high part and two in the low part; however, these are separated from those by the Tone of Disjunction at **ED**. This disjunction, if transported to the high or low part by a **Diatessaron** <note>term: *Diatessaron* — a perfect fourth interval</note>, will result in three Tetrachords joined one after another in the opposite part. And to show this is true: I leave the Tetrachord **AC** separated by the Tone of Disjunction at **CD**, from which **D** there follow three joined Tetrachords in the low part; these are **DE**, **EF**, and **FG**; but this requires using the string **Trite-synemmenon** <note>the 'third of the conjuncts,' equivalent to B-flat</note> in place of the **Paramese** <note>the 'neighbor to the middle,' equivalent to B-natural</note>. Now, Ptolemy similarly says that three can be joined in the high part in this other manner. Take the two joined Tetrachords from the high part of the ordinary Greater and Perfect Disjunct System, which are **AC** and **CD**. Raise the sixth string (counting from the low part) so much that it responds as a perfect **Diatessaron**—and not as a harsh fourth or **Tritone** <note>an unstable interval of three whole tones</note>—with the **Paramese** at the letter **D**. Then join, next to the two high Tetrachords of the Disjunct System (which are **AC** and **CD**), the third in the low part at **DE**. After these, the Tone of Disjunction follows immediately toward that side at **EF**, and let another Tetrachord follow below it, marked with the usual letters **FG**. Thus, there will be three Tetrachords joined in the high part just as there were in the low, in the manner clearly seen in the present **Demonstration** reduced to our modern practice.

<margin>Demonstration of the joining of Tetrachords according to Ptolemy, in Book 2, Chapter 6, applied to modern practice.</margin>

<image-desc>A musical diagram featuring several overlapping tetrachords (labeled AC, CD, DE, EF, FG) mapped onto a five-line musical staff. The notes are written as diamond-shaped semibreves. <margin>In the Greater and Perfect System there are no more than 15 strings and four Tetrachords. 
Zarlino in chapter 28 of the 2nd book, and 72 of the 3rd book of the *Institutions*. 
Zarlino in the same place.</margin>
**STR.** Among the many momentous things I have learned from this Demonstration are these: I see that the **Greater and Perfect System**, whether it be Conjunct or Disjunct, always contains no more than fifteen strings in four Tetrachords and two ordered Tones. Previously, along with others, I believed that the strings of different sounds were at least sixteen, and eighteen different by name, divided into five Tetrachords. Furthermore, I have learned that when the string **Trite-synemmenon** [B-flat] is found in modern compositions of the Disjunct System, it is not actually **Diatonic**, nor purely **Chromatic**, nor "accidental" as some say. Likewise, finding the **Paramese** [B-natural] in songs composed in the Conjunct System is not accidental, but rather a third, mixed thing. Or rather, we could more rightly say that the song then passes from one System to the other, and vice versa. But if the string **F-faut** <note>the note F</note> were altered, I do not know how that would work.

<margin>Considerations of Ptolemy.</margin>
**BAR.** If at the beginning of the song a cipher were marked at **F-faut** denoting that said string should be raised [sharpened] so that it would respond continuously, as has been said, as a perfect fourth with **B-natural** <note>original: *h mi*</note>, and if no other string were altered but that one, I would say that such a song was simply **Diatonic**. This matter, along with many others, Ptolemy goes about ingeniously investigating with his usual subtle diligence...

### Dialogue on Music
</header>

<margin>Zarlino in chapter 2 of the second part of the *Institutions* <note>Gioseffo Zarlino’s *Le istitutioni harmoniche* (1558), the most influential music theory text of the Renaissance</note>.</margin>

And they then called such a quantity of strings, distributed in this way, the **Greater and Perfect Disjunct System**; in which (when tuned according to the **Dorian Mode** <note>The Dorian mode was considered the most stable and "manly" of the ancient Greek musical scales</note> in the **Diatonic genus** and in the most ancient **Diatonic Ditonic** species), they arrived at this number of strings and arranged them on that **Kithara** <note>term: Kithara — a professional version of the lyre used by ancient Greek musicians</note> according to the manner and arrangement shown by the numbers. Their intellects were then satisfied and put to rest, knowing very well that the human voice could not ascend above or descend below this range without great discomfort to the singer and very little satisfaction for the listeners, in addition to the other reasons cited for this. This was also the reason why **Pythagoras of Samos** commanded that one should not go beyond the **Quadruple** <note>The "Quadruple" or *Quadrupla* refers to the interval of two octaves (a 4:1 ratio)</note>, and not because he ever believed or said that intervals larger than the **Double Octave** <note>original: *Bisdiapason*</note> were dissonant, as some modern writers have claimed. For many centuries, ancient musicians did not care to proceed or pass further into the low or high registers for any specific System of their various Tones and Modes; and the Kithara was ultimately reduced to this number of strings. They then used this in every species and genus of harmony, only by narrowing some intervals and widening others and adjusting the frets as required by the quality and nature of the piece, to express it (aided by other circumstances) with the greatest **affect** <note>original: *affetto* — the emotional state or "soul" of the music</note> that anyone could imagine. By these means, skilled musicians always achieved their desired end. To be able to play comfortably in different modes and Tones according to their high or low pitch, they possessed wind and string instruments of different sizes, with differently distributed holes and strings suited for this purpose. Of the diversity of these distributions, I wish—for greater clarity—to provide an example of each one next to the other, so that by sight you may also minutely understand the difference found between them regarding the high and low pitch of the strings.

# Ancient & Modern.

**STROZZI.** I now clearly understand that the difference found between the **Disjunct System** and the **Conjunct System** is nothing other than what practical musicians of today call "by **B-hard**" <note>original: *per h duro*; this refers to the use of B-natural</note> or "by **B-soft**" <note>original: *per b molle*; this refers to the use of B-flat</note>.

<margin>
In the sixth chapter of the second book of his *Harmonics*.
</margin>
**BARDI.** Exactly so. And so that you may know even more, Ptolemy investigates most subtly how, just as the three lowest **Tetrachords** <note>term: Tetrachord — a series of four notes spanning a perfect fourth, the building block of ancient Greek scales</note> were conjoined in the Greater and Perfect Disjunct System (which existed before the conjunct one), the three highest could also have been conveniently conjoined. He proves demonstratively that they can. Since you are interested in hearing this, I will go on to explain it to you with great ease.

**STROZZI.** This will be extremely pleasing to me, as would any other matter belonging to the knowledge of the musical faculty.

<margin>
The conjunction of Tetrachords can, according to Ptolemy, be done elsewhere.
</margin>
**BARDI.** Ptolemy says then, to prove that one could conjoin the three high tetrachords just as well as the three low ones in the Greater and Perfect Disjunct System, the following: Let the fifteen strings of the said System be contained between **B**, the extreme low string, and **A**, the extreme high string. Starting from this **A** and moving toward the opposite side, let two Tetrachords labeled **AC** and **CD** be joined to it. Immediately below these follows the **Tone of Disjunction** <note>term: Tone of Disjunction — the whole-step interval that separates two tetrachords to complete an octave</note> at **DE**. Then, let two other Tetrachords be joined at **E** (likewise moving toward that side), and let them be **EF** and **FG**. In this demonstration, there will be two tetrachords joined in the high part and two in the low; however, these are separated from those by the Tone of Disjunction at **ED**. If this disjunction is transposed to the high or low register by a **Diatessaron** <note>term: Diatessaron — the interval of a perfect fourth</note>, one will have three tetrachords joined one after the other in the opposite part. And if this is true, I leave Tetrachord **AC** separated in the low part...

<margin>
...if this is true, I leave what **D** follows in the **EF** and **FG**; but now he says similarly. Take the two ordinary and disjunct Tetrachords, counting from the part... by a fourth... then join next... and **CD**; the third in the Tone of Disjunction marked with the usual letters... which were held in the low register, reduced in this notation.
</margin>

In the Greater and Perfect System there are no more than 15 strings and four Tetrachords.

**STROZZI.** Among the many momentous things I have learned in this demonstration are these: I see that in the Greater and Perfect System, whether it be conjunct or disjunct, there are always contained no more than fifteen strings in four Tetrachords and two ordered Tones; whereas before, along with others, I believed that the strings differing in sound were at least sixteen, and eighteen different by name, divided into five Tetrachords. I had already noticed this to be the case in the mixing of the species and the genera taught by Ptolemy himself, where it is even clearer. Furthermore, I have learned that when the string **Trite synemmenon** <note>The note B-flat in the Greek system</note> is found in modern compositions of the Disjunct System, it is not simply Diatonic, nor pure Chromatic, nor "accidental" as some say. Likewise, finding the **Paramese** <note>The note B-natural in the Greek system</note> in those songs composed by the conjunct system is a third, mixed thing. Or rather, we could say with more reason that the song then passes from one System into the other, and vice versa. But if the string **F-faut** <note>The note F</note> were altered, I do not quite know how the matter would proceed.

<margin>
Considerations of Ptolemy.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation by Bardi regarding Ptolemy’s analysis of musical systems.
