# Dialogue on Music

<margin>
Zarlino, in chapter 16 of the fourth part of his *Institutions*, distances himself from this opinion.
</margin>
...[subtle]ly examining; in which place he gives the reason for where the origin might have been found for the **System of three conjoined Tetrachords** <note>term: System — a complete scale or set of notes; Tetrachord — a four-note scale segment spanning a perfect fourth</note> in the lower part—commonly called by modern practitioners **B-soft** <note>original: *b molle*; this refers to the use of B-flat</note>—which was sometimes held among ancient musicians to be a **Perfect System**. Because of this, he was required to show what purpose it served. It clearly appeared that one could doubt whether this system brought about alterations and mutations, primarily of four kinds to be considered in harmony: either by the nature of the **genus** <note>term: Genus — the three classifications of Greek scales: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic</note>, such as from Enharmonic to Chromatic; or by their **species**, such as from Syntonon Diatonic to Soft Diatonic; or by a change of **Tone** <note>note: "Tone" here refers to the Mode or key</note>, such as from Dorian to Phrygian; or by a change according to **ethos** <note>original: *costume*; the emotional character of the music</note>, from quiet to remiss, or from this to broad and almost splendid, or otherwise. 

Alternatively, it might change only regarding the order and "air" of the System and the constitution of the strings. Having set aside the matter of *ethos* for the moment, as it was a thing perhaps seen to be entirely distant from the matter he had at hand, he showed that this was not a mutation of Tone—because the whole System did not become more or less acute (high) or grave (low) because of it—nor was it a mutation of genus, because the distribution of the strings within the tetrachords was not altered at all. This is because their standing and moving strings all maintained the same intervals between them. Rather, it was in such a place a mutation, in a certain way, of the rising and falling of the song. 

Consequently, only the order of the tetrachords was changed. These are commonly placed together in such a way that, of the four present in the **Perfect System**, two are conjoined by a single common string at the high end, and two likewise at the low end. These [low ones] are separated from those [high ones] by the interval of a **Sesquioctave** <note>term: Sesquioctave — the mathematical ratio 9:8, which defines a whole tone</note>, otherwise called a **Tone**; thus the two lowest tetrachords are disjoined from the two highest, as has been shown. 

Where three are joined together, the form of the System is changed in that part where, after the first two, the **Tone of Disjunction** is usually placed—which is, as you know, between the **Mese** and the **Paramese** <note>term: Mese and Paramese — the central "middle" string and the "next-to-middle" string of the Greek scale; the gap between them traditionally created the whole tone that separated the scale into two halves</note>. Because, whereas one usually ascended from the string **A-la-mi-re** to the next by a sesquioctave interval, one [in this conjoined system] ascended by a much smaller one. This interval was—depending on the distribution, whether Diatonic, Chromatic, or Enharmonic—the lowest interval of the tetrachord, which in the Diatonic was a minor semitone. Likewise, it descended in such a way that the "size of the step" was changed in that part of the System, both in descending and ascending. This narrowing or lowering of the step, when used with method and at the proper time so that it fell proportionately and was suited to the song, succeeded in being graceful and accommodating through this mutation; but used too frequently, or out of occasion and place, it was both useless and even harmful. 

Now, this same alteration in the **Greater System** (where there were four tetrachords) could, for the same reason, be done by conjoining the three highest just as well as the three lowest. Nothing prevented the interval of disjunction from being moved comfortably beneath the three highest tetrachords instead of above the three lowest, without any disturbance to the distributions of the genera or the nature of the highness and lowness of the entire System. The same reason and cause serves for both this and that alteration. Since the interval of disjunction does not belong to the internal distribution of the strings of a tetrachord—rather, it is a common feature in all Perfect Systems of whatever genus or species they may be—and since the tetrachords are only related by a **Sesquitertia** <note>term: Sesquitertia — the ratio 4:3, defining the perfect fourth interval of a tetrachord</note> among themselves, it does not matter if they are moved from their ordinary place. The disjunction performs its office just as well in separating the three lowest from the fourth highest as it does in separating the three highest from the fourth lowest. 

Even though placing it [the whole tone] in the middle between the two high and two low tetrachords allows all seven species of the **Diapason** <note>term: Diapason — the octave</note> to appear in the System (which cannot appear if it is placed elsewhere), nonetheless, among the ancients at that time, moving it from that place caused no impediment. This is because, according to Ptolemy, as has been said, they had neither use for nor knowledge of more than three Tones—which are the **Dorian**, **Phrygian**, and **Lydian**—and thus other forms were not desired. 

In the case where the common disjunction and ascent are transposed—being joined before its ordinary place toward the high side—the highest of the two lower tetrachords is joined with the lowest of the two higher tetrachords. This results in three tetrachords being conjoined at the lower part. In this case, the lowest of the two conjoined high ones, separated from its companion and moved to the two lower ones, becomes the highest of all three. Similarly, if they are conjoined toward the low side after its usual disjunction, the lowest of the two high ones is joined with the highest of the low ones, and three tetrachords are again joined at the higher part, where the transposed one becomes the lowest of all three. These two distributions and positions of the tetrachords necessarily resulted in this way, which Ptolemy wanted to prove demonstratively in the manner that has been said and shown.

<margin>
Various doubts.
</margin>
**STROZZI.** This has been a subtle and useful consideration, truly worthy of Ptolemy; but please resolve these other difficulties for me. If conjoining the three high tetrachords is the same as conjoining the three low ones, for what reason did they conjoin these more than those? And why have those famous writers, who in their propositions have brought forward the **Greater and Perfect System** as an example, proposed the disjunct...

# Ancient & Modern Music

...to the conjoined [tetrachord]? And why did they not mark a string in the bass that responded by an **Octave** <note>original: *Ottaua*; the interval of an eighth</note> to the **Trite synemmenon**, placing it instead of the **Hypate hypaton**? <note>original: *Trite synemmenon* and *Hypate hypaton*; these refer to specific strings in the ancient Greek scale system. Strozzi is asking why the low-end tuning doesn't match the middle-scale's "B-flat" equivalent.</note> Furthermore, regarding these distributions of theirs, whether conjoined or disjoined, why did they always order them in every genus and species of harmony by **Tetrachords**, and never by **Pentachords**, or **Hexachords**, or other intervals? <note>term: Tetrachord — a four-note scale segment; Pentachord — five notes; Hexachord — six notes</note>

<margin>Resolutions of these questions. Why the strings of the System were divided by Tetrachords.</margin>
BARDI: Each of the first three difficulties you proposed to me can be cleared away by what I just told you regarding the mind of Ptolemy; <note>historical: Claudius Ptolemy was a 2nd-century mathematician and music theorist whose works were central to Renaissance musical thought.</note> that is, that the ancients ensured that in their **Great System** <note>term: Great System — the complete two-octave scale used in Greek theory</note>, each of the seven species of the **Diapason** <note>term: Diapason — the interval of an octave</note> could be found in order. As for the reasons why they ordered the strings of this System by Tetrachords rather than by other intervals, they are these. In my opinion, they were led to do this for no other reason than that their first and smallest consonance, which is the **Diatessaron** <note>term: Diatessaron — the interval of a Perfect Fourth</note>, is found in the **Sesquitertial** ratio <note>term: Sesquitertial — the mathematical ratio of 4:3</note> between four and three. With the larger number (four), they came to denote the quantity of the strings in any variation of genus, and with the smaller (three), they denoted the quantity of the spaces [intervals] between them; I do not know if this occurs with any other interval. Or perhaps they did this in memory of the number of strings on the **Lyre of Mercury**, which were distributed in that order. Furthermore, such a number of strings is capable of the modulation of any **Tone** <note>note: "Tone" here refers to the musical modes or keys</note>, as can be understood from the examples of Olympus and Terpander. <note>historical: Olympus and Terpander were legendary Greek musicians credited with early developments in melody and tuning.</note> And those who have said they were so ordered because the Tetrachord—without needing a larger number—has the faculty to show which genus such a distribution of strings belongs to, do not seem to carry much weight. This is because that arrangement was established by Mercury when the **Cithara** and **Lyre** <note>note: early stringed instruments similar to harps or lutes</note> had no more than four strings (as you will understand shortly below), and this was before the **Chromatic** and **Enharmonic** genera were in use. There are other opinions on this fact, recounted by Gaffurio in chapter 13 of the first treatise of his *Theorica*, <note>historical: Franchinus Gaffurius (1451–1522) was a leading Italian music theorist whose "Theoretical Music" influenced the Renaissance.</note> for which some moderns have taken credit. The same is true regarding the order held by **Guido of Arezzo** in distributing the twenty-two strings of his *Introduction* into seven Hexachords, along with many other things of even greater consequence; but enough has been said of that.

STROZZI: These two reasons of yours are very new and ingenious; and your mentioning the strings of the Lyre has awakened another not-insignificant difficulty in my mind.

BARDI: Tell me what it is.

<margin>Zarlino in chapters 28 and 30 of the 2nd part of the *Institutions*.</margin>
STROZZI: You have shown me with infinite reasons, examples, and authorities that the ancient Lyre and Cithara had been increased to the number of fifteen strings. Yet afterward, I see (besides other writers) that Virgil and Ovid—in whose times the number likely should have been greater rather than smaller (as is seen even in our own times)—make mention of only seven strings when speaking not only of Orpheus, but of Apollo, Linus, Amphion, and others. Why is this?

<margin>Law of the Assyrians and the Lacedaemonians, approved by Aristotle.</margin>
BARDI: For several respects. First, because in the time of Orpheus, the Lyre had not reached the number of fifteen strings, but only seven, as I told you above from the mind of **Boethius**. <note>historical: Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524), whose "Fundamentals of Music" transmitted Greek theory to the Middle Ages.</note> These were distinct in two conjoined Tetrachords, as you have seen; such that the extremes responded to each other by a **Lesser Heptachord**, <note>term: Heptachord — a seven-note scale or instrument</note> no differently than the Mixolydian Mode (the extreme high Tone) does with the Hypodorian (the extreme low Tone). The seven strings of the Lyre of Orpheus were arranged in this manner; some claim it was given to him by Mercury, and others that he himself was its discoverer. Furthermore, even after it was brought to the number of fifteen strings, it would perhaps not be far from the truth to believe that the reputable Citharists and Citharedes <note>note: performers who sang while playing the Cithara</note> did not usually have such a quantity of strings strung while they played and sang. This can be understood from the example of the **Ephor**, <note>note: a high-ranking official in Sparta (Lacedaemonia)</note> who publicly cut the two strings added by **Timotheus**; and also because they sought few strings in their songs, as has been said. Having used a number greater than seven—or up to eight for the perfection of the extremes—would have been a vanity. And to tell you this as well: among the Assyrians, as among the **Lacedaemonians** [Spartans], there was a particular law that no Citharede or Citharist should dare to use more than seven strings; an opinion in which Aristotle also concurred. Added to this is the fact that a Poet would not be faulted for simply mentioning the Lyre and Cithara as if they had used a larger number. And even though they had received it from Mercury with four and no more strings, it was not held in such high esteem until after it reached the number of seven. The author of this, as you have heard, was the great legislator **Terpander of Lesbos**. In his honor, writers have so many times mentioned this number of strings, or of **Reeds** <note>original: *Calami*; reed pipes or flutes</note>, or **Auloi** <note>original: *Auli*; ancient Greek wind instruments</note> if you prefer; and with such a quantity did Orpheus play the Cithara.

STROZZI: Since you have explained with such fine order and so many important warnings how the increasing of the strings on the Lyre occurred, please do not be reluctant to tell me by whom, and in what manner, this Lyre was discovered. For the history of its origin is told differently by various writers.

<margin>The matter of invention can be understood in several ways.</margin>
BARDI: The matter of invention is understood, as you know, in several ways. For we first call that person the inventor of a thing when, before they found it, it did not exist in practice; as for example...

# Dialogue on Music

<margin>In the ninth chapter of the 9th [book].</margin>
...the inventor of the sun dial; of which (according to Vitruvius) <note>historical: Vitruvius was a famous Roman architect and engineer whose works were rediscovered in the Renaissance.</note> Berossus the Chaldean was the author, and according to others Anaximander. <note>historical: Berossus (3rd century BCE) was a Babylonian writer; Anaximander (6th century BCE) was a Greek philosopher.</note> One is called an "inventor" when they take a thing that already exists and put it into consideration and into action, having not been known as such before; from which utility and convenience are then derived;

Giotto revives painting.
</margin>
as with the silkworms that make silk, or the **Cochineal** <note>term: Cochineal — a red dye made from crushed insects found in the Americas (the "Indies").</note> from which **Crimson** <note>original: *Chermisino*</note> is made, which is also a species of worm recently brought to us from the Indies; or if we wish to speak of the use of **Purple** <note>historical: Tyrian purple, a precious dye made from sea snails.</note>, of which Hercules was the inventor by means of one of his dogs. The invention of a thing is also attributed to the one who significantly improves it; as we might say of **Giotto** in painting; <note>historical: Giotto di Bondone (c. 1267–1337) is often credited with reviving the art of realistic painting in Italy.</note> at which time it is to be believed there were not only others who painted, but perhaps even those before him and in the same place; but because it was reduced to a less imperfect state by him, many attribute the palm of such invention to him (meaning, however, among modern-ancient painters). Sometimes the invention of a thing is also attributed to the one who, in putting it into practice, exceeds all others of his time and those who came before him in the memory of the men of that century; as with **Orpheus** in playing the Lyre. Finally, the invention of a thing is attributed to the one who teaches it, demonstrates it, or describes it with greater order, distinction, and ease than others; as **Aristotle** did with matters of Philosophy. These circumstances, considered in the various ways mentioned, often bring no small difficulty to those who seek to know the certainty of a thing's invention, and particularly who first found the Lyre, and in what manner—not only because of its antiquity, but with respect to the various opinions among those who have treated and written of it. Most of these are poets, and they have said many things in the form of fables; and according to the various subjects they had at hand, they took the opportunity to write in their propositions whatever was most convenient for them.

<margin>
In his hymn to Mercury.
In Greece.
In the Dialogue of Vulcan and Apollo.
</margin>
Homer, the most ancient and famous Poet, along with Hyginus (whose opinions we shall recount first), tells its origin in this manner. **Mercury**, <note>historical: The Roman god Mercury (Hermes in Greek), often credited with the invention of the lyre.</note> son of Jupiter and Maia (one of the twelve daughters of Atlas), was born on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia. In his tender infancy, walking outside the house after the third day of his birth, he encountered a **Tortoise** grazing on the grass—though Lucian claims it was dead. Seeing it and considering it well because of its novelty, he judged it fit to give color to the design that its shape brought to his mind. Taking it in his hand and conversing with himself as he returned to his home, he spoke to it thus: "I do not want you to wander alone through the woods grazing on grass any longer; but that in the future you should continuously dwell within royal palaces, around sumptuous banquet tables laden with precious foods, full of guests overflowing with joy, and particularly at new weddings." Having brought it home, he first took its life with a knife; and afterward, he diligently emptied every concave part of its shell of the skin, flesh, nerves, bones, and intestines. The method he then used to adapt the strings onto it is told by Homer himself in these few words:

<margin>The method Mercury used in making the Lyre.</margin>
> He fixed, by dividing with measurements, stalks of reed, passing through the back into the skin of the Tortoise; and around it he stretched ox hide by his ingenuity, and placed the arms, and fitted the yoke to both, and stretched seven consonant strings of sheep [gut].

But after he built it, carrying the lovely toy, he struck it part by part with the plectrum, and it resounded deeply under his hand, and the God sang sweetly, improvising as he played. These words are very obscure and need mature consideration to be well understood.

STROZZI: Let it not be a burden to tell me what you feel about them.

<margin>The Author's interpretation of Homer's words.</margin>
BARDI: I do not know how I shall satisfy you so suddenly and unexpectedly; nevertheless, to please you, I will say everything that comes to mind, as briefly as I can. "He fixed," says the Poet, "by dividing with measurements, stalks of reed, passing through the back into the skin of the Tortoise." That is to say: having first arranged seven stalks of reed equally divided. But here one must first note that **Calamo** <note>term: *Calamo* — a specific type of reed (calamus) used by the Greeks as a pen for writing.</note> among the Greeks is a particular species of reed which is quite thin, straight, and hard, and has nodes spaced far apart. It is ordinarily used by them for writing, as it has a particular faculty for drawing their characters excellently. Its segments are mostly about half a **braccio** <note>term: *braccio* — an old Italian unit of length, roughly 23 inches / 58 cm.</note> long, and are smooth, shiny, and equal. Thus, saying "stalks of reed" is an example, like one saying in our tongue that he took cypress wood—or even marsh reeds, though they are very different from these. So, every *Calamo* is a reed, but not every reed is a *Calamo*.

<margin>What "Back" [Dorso] signifies.</margin>
He therefore fixed the seven stalks of reed, first arranged to be equal in length to each other, through the "back"—that is, lengthwise—into the skin of the tortoise. By "skin," one can understand the bottom or top part of its shell, or perhaps (since the animal was no longer there) where the skin once was, or rather, the skin that he fitted around it, regarding which subject he adds: "and around it he stretched ox hide." He says he stretched ox hide around—that is, around the reeds, or perhaps around the circumference of the tortoise, through which skin those reeds passed. This was so that the "spirit of the air" struck by the strings (the cause of the sound) would not escape so easily from the parts that protruded from the shell in a proportionate and convenient length for his needs. "By his ingenuity" <note>original: *suo auuedimento*</note> means the same as if he said, "as the shrewd and astute being he was."

# Ancient & Modern.

<margin>What the arms are.</margin>
<margin>What the bridges are.</margin>
**He positioned the arms.** He calls those parts of the reeds that poked out—both above and below, beyond the edges of the shell—the "arms" <note>original: "cubiti"; literally cubits or elbows, referring here to the side-posts of the lyre</note>; the clever God had already envisioned in his mind the help and convenience he would derive from them. **And he fitted the bridge to both.** He calls the "bridges" <note>original: "gioghi"; literally yokes</note> (in my opinion) the small supports that coupled the strings and held them suspended at a suitable distance from the breastbone of the **Tortoise**; this is no different from what one sees today on the modern **Lute**. He did this so that when struck by the **Plectrum** or by the fingers, they would send forth a sound that was not muffled or confused, but sonorous and distinct. He fitted these bridges to both arms; that is, he placed the bridges upon the arms and not upon the bone of the animal, perhaps to have greater space to stretch the strings over them. To this, Homer adds: *and seven consonant strings of sheep.*

<margin>Why Mercury’s Lyre has seven strings.</margin>
Some maintain that Mercury stretched seven strings across the Lyre in memory of the **Pleiades**, the daughters of his grandfather, among whom is numbered **Maia**, his mother. They say furthermore that the aforementioned Mount Cyllene, after the Lyre was discovered there by Mercury, was called **Chelydrota**; from **Chelys** <note>original: "Chelyn"; Greek for tortoise or lyre</note>, which means the same thing as Lyre, as you know. The Lyre of **Amphion** is also described as having seven strings by **Lambin** in his commentary on Horace’s *Art of Poetry*; in memory of these strings, seven gates were made for the ancient City of **Thebes**. **Homer** adds: *Consonant strings*; that is, sonorous ones, because not all of them (in the arrangement Mercury used to stretch them) were in harmony with one another. He said, moreover, *of sheep* (plural), and not *of a sheep* (singular)—as might perhaps have been more appropriate, since one could pull a greater quantity of gut from a single animal than was needed for such a small instrument—to denote the inequality of their thickness. Each of these he attached to one of the ends of the reeds that formed one of the arms, in the most suitable way that occurred to his perceptive mind. This was likely at the end where the back legs emerged, which must have terminated in the knots or thicker parts of the reeds (whether they were split or whole); assuming, however, that a difference in thickness existed between them. At the other end, above the front legs or "arms" as we might call them, he easily fitted the **tuning pegs** <note>term: "bischeri"; the wooden pegs used to tighten or loosen strings to change their pitch</note>. The hollow bodies of the reeds provided a place where he could conveniently insert them, provided the reeds were not split down the middle from one end to the other—a design choice that, in this context, would have been neither unusual nor miraculous. It also seems more reasonable that he arranged it this way rather than any other, because it is more pleasing to the eye to look at a body that faces the heavens with its head, rather than facing the center of the earth. The Poet continues and says: *but after he built it, carrying the lovely toy.* That is, after having finished it, he carried it about from place to place for his own amusement, like the boy—or rather, the infant—that he was. **With the Plectrum he tested it part by part.** This is the same as saying that with the plectrum he carefully searched out string after string to fully understand the distances <note>meaning the musical intervals or pitches</note> found between one and the next. Having understood these, he began to play, and so the poet adds: *and it resounded deeply beneath his hand.* It resounded "beneath his hand"—not the hand that held the Lyre, but the one that gripped the **Plectrum** with which he struck the strings. *Deeply* <note>original: "grauemente"</note> means that when the strings were touched by the Plectrum in the hand of the God, each of them (by way of poetic hyperbole) seemed like a sonorous trumpet and a harmonious, most pleasant peal of thunder. *And the God sweetly sang, trying it out on the spot.* As if to say: and the God, though improvised and newly born, by "trying it out"—that is, by practicing—succeeded and sang sweet and sonorous heroic verses, most learned and elegant. I wish now to place this Lyre here at the bottom, drawn with its outlines, and it shall be thus:

And to remove the doubt from your mind that once arose in another man (while I was discussing this subject with him) concerning the size of the lyre, and how its strings could still resonate without a rose <note>The "rose" is the decorative, carved soundhole found in the center of instruments like the lute or guitar</note>—as is the custom in the **Lute**, the **Cittern**, and other modern instruments—I say that they respond and resonate just as well without the rose as when it is present. Indeed, it is placed there by craftsmen for no other reason than for the ornament and beauty of the instrument. I truly believe that in **Mercury's Lyre**, because of the thickness and hardness of the material from which it was made <note>the tortoise shell</note>, a rose might have produced some beneficial effect. Furthermore, regarding the size of the instrument, do not believe that they were all so small; for we read that Mercury himself fashioned the first one from the rib bones of one of the oxen he stole from **Apollo**. But let us leave the fable aside and come to history, where we shall see that not all the Lyres of the ancients—just like their **Tibiae** <note>The *tibia* was an ancient double-reed pipe, similar to an oboe</note>, which would not have allowed for it—were so small. Instead, they made them in large and medium sizes according to the need

and according to what purpose they were to serve. In this regard, one reads in **Suetonius Tranquillus** in his *Life of Nero* that the lyre the Emperor used to play on stage was supported at the time by the Prefects of the Praetorian Guard; in which passage the history mentions several men, and not just one alone. # Ancient & Modern

<margin>According to others, Mercury gave the Lyre to Orpheus.</margin>
...staying within its boundaries, it left various kinds of dead animals in the fields, among which was a **Tortoise**. Mercury, having found it after the flesh had already been consumed and only a few sinews remained, stretched and dried by the sun, happened to strike it with his foot, and it gave off a sound. In imitation of this, Mercury fashioned the *Lyre* and gave it to Orpheus. Others add that Mercury, having encountered Apollo—who was in a great rage with him 
<margin>Mercury gives the Lyre to Apollo.</margin>
for having secretly stolen some of his oxen—found himself in Apollo's hands and was about to be, as the proverb says, "sent down a bad path," had the charm and novelty of his *Lyre* not saved him from such fury. When Apollo saw it, he liked it beyond measure and desired it. Mercury, noticing this and making a virtue of necessity (to escape the danger hanging over him), offered it to him as a gift, though with an ill will. Apollo accepted it very willingly, and for this courtesy, he forgave the injury on the condition that Mercury entirely attribute the invention of such a thing to him, which Mercury generously promised. In exchange, Apollo furthermore gave him
<margin>Apollo gives the Caduceus to Mercury.</margin>
the *Caduceus*. The author of this account also claims that the instrument built by Mercury was first called *Chelyn* <note>From the Greek "chelys," meaning tortoise</note>; but because it served as a ransom, he called it *Lyra* in the future, almost like *litra* <note>original: "litra"; likely referring to the Greek "lytra," meaning the price by which a man is redeemed</note>. However, others have said that it took its name from the strings stretched upon it, because they resembled the furrows of a field, called *lyrin* by the Greeks. Censorinus, on the contrary, maintains that Apollo, and not Mercury, invented the *Lyre*, and that its origin came from the sound produced by the string of Diana's bow when struck. Nicomachus of Gerasa, a Greek author, tells this story in another way: he claims that Mercury himself built a *Lyre* of wood, upon which he stretched four strings—though others have said three—also made of sheep intestines. With the three strings, he alluded to the three seasons of the year: namely, heat, cold, and temperate <note>Summer, Winter, and Spring/Autumn</note>. He applied the high string to summer, the low string to winter, and the middle string (not to offend autumn, let us say spring) to the temperate season. For this reason, some have used the terms 
<margin>Boethius.</margin>
"heavy" sound and "light" sound instead of low and high. The four strings that Boethius also mentions were applied to the four elements. In the tuning of these, a difference arises between Bryennius and Boethius, his interpreters. Boethius maintains (as has been said and shown above) that from the first and lowest string to the second, there was a *Diatessaron* <note>The interval of a perfect fourth</note>; and from this to the penultimate, a *Tone*; which, with the highest string, resonated as another *Diatessaron*. From this arrangement of strings, it could easily be that Pythagoras of Samos, with his divine intellect, went about philosophizing on musical proportions and derived the ratios of numbers from them. It is said he drew 
<margin>Where Pythagoras derived musical proportions. Where Diocles derived them.</margin>
this invention from the weight and sound of hammers striking an anvil in a blacksmith's shop, rather by chance than by design. However, others, along with Suidas <note>The Suda, a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>, claim that not Pythagoras, but Diocles investigated this invention—not from blacksmiths, but that while passing by a potter's shop, he happened to strike some vessels with a rod. From the diversity of the size of their sounds regarding high and low, he then went investigating musical proportions. This story is more likely to be true than the one about the sound and weight of hammers; but in whatever way it was discovered, it had more of the divine than the human. I come now to the opinion of Bryennius regarding the arrangement of the strings of Mercury's *Lyre*. He, on the contrary, maintains that from the first and lowest string to the second, there was a minor *Semitone* or *Limma*; from this to the third, a *Tone*; and that the fourth and last, the highest of all, corresponded with the first and lowest of each by a *Diatessaron*. Regarding these opinions on the invention of the *Lyre*, although they are told to us as fables, the account of Benedetto Egio regarding Apollodorus fits better (due to its simplicity) than that of Homer—not only for having too much artifice and craftsmanship, but also regarding the smallness of the instrument. Furthermore, regarding the distribution of the strings, the majority of the learned and scientific experts in this profession of ancient music lean more toward the opinion of Bryennius than that of Boethius, as it is more simple and natural. We shall 
<margin>The Author's Consideration.</margin>
also lean toward this for several reasons: first, because the very names of the strings read in Boethius's own text reveal what those strings truly were and what distance was found between them; and secondly, seeing that the ancient musicians, in their playing and singing, acted as imitators of nature, proceeding by conjunct degrees <note>step-wise motion</note> rather than by separate leaps; and they sought out few notes, as you have heard. In this manner were the four strings of the *Lyre* of Amphion, son of Jupiter and Antiope, arranged when he, before all others, discovered the way to sing to it, 
<margin>Amphion, the first to sing to the Lyre. Linus of Negroponte, Poet & Musician. Philammon of Delphi, inventor of Choral singing.</margin>
even though the fabulous poets have told us otherwise. In his time, Linus of Negroponte <note>Linus of Euboea</note>, a most celebrated musician and poet, also flourished. These were succeeded by Philammon of Delphi, who found new ways of singing; he was also the one who established choral singing around the Temple of Delphi and who composed the birth of Latona, Diana, and Apollo in verse.

**STR.** It is clearly seen that the famous ancient musicians were also poets, and the poets must not have been ignorant of music. But returning to the distribution of the strings of the *Lyre* according to the mind of Boethius, I cannot imagine why, in those early times, they could not proceed by degrees of *Tone* and *Semitone* through the help of frets <note>original: "tasti"; the metal or gut strips on the neck of an instrument</note>, as is the custom today, particularly on the **Lute**.

# Dialogue on Music

<margin>Ancient string instruments never had frets.</margin>
BARDI: That was truly impossible; for the Lyre of those times was not only deprived of frets, but also of a neck, around which we see them arranged in modern instruments (which require them); nor was there ever any knowledge of these until the time of Guido of Arezzo <note>Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–1033) was a medieval music theorist whose work laid the foundation for modern notation and solfège.</note> and thereafter.

STROZZI: Did the ancient Lyres, then, have no frets?

BARDI: Certainly not.

<margin>In the 3rd Oration against Verres.</margin>
STROZZI: Oh, in what manner then shall we understand the words of Asconius Pedianus <note>A Roman grammarian and historian known for his commentaries on Cicero's orations.</note> regarding the third Oration of Cicero against Verres? They say this: "When the Citharists sing, they employ the service of both hands; the right hand uses the Plectrum, and this is called 'playing outside'; and the left hand touches the strings with the fingers, and this is 'singing inside'." To which he adds: "but what Aspendius <note>A famous ancient cithara player known for a unique technique.</note> did was a very difficult thing; for he did not use both hands to play, but embraced everything—that is, the whole song—with the left hand alone and 'sang it inside'." From these words, it seems to me one could argue that the ancient Cithara had frets, and consequently, a neck.

<margin>How "playing inside and outside" is to be understood.</margin>
BARDI: Regarding the passage from Asconius—setting aside for a moment the opposition raised against his interpretation of the facts and speaking only of the method of "playing inside and outside"—when playing with the right hand using the plectrum and the left hand with the fingers touching the strings, it is necessary that the Lyre be held upright. This can be seen easily by the small feet visible on both sides of the frame; it was held in the same manner as the Harp is today, though not quite so vertically. And because the side where the strings were struck with the plectrum was more visible than the other during performance, it was called the "outside"; consequently, the opposite side was called the "inside." Thus, the inside was more convenient for the left hand, just as the outside was for the right.

<margin>Aspendius and his skill.</margin>
Now, the skill of Aspendius must have arisen from having trained all five fingers of the left hand so industriously as to find the number of strings that best suited him, using only this hand to play. But in my opinion, it is difficult to believe that his industry reached the same perfection as that of other great artists who used both hands. Because this was such a new thing, and difficult to put into practice accurately—and since he succeeded, either through a naturally nimble left hand or long and industrious practice, where others did not—his work was held in high regard as something rare, more (I believe) for the novelty than for the excellence or perfection of the effect he produced. The proof of this is that we never read of others (as far as I know) who set out to imitate him.

<margin>Frets were not used by the ancients.</margin>
As for the claim that frets <note>original: "tastame"; refers to the system of frets on a fingerboard.</note> were in use in their string instruments as they are in our times, I know of no authority, whether writer or antiquity, that depicts it, and I do not believe it in any way. I tell you—and have continually told you freely—whatever is in my mind, more as a truth-seeker than as an orator, for I believe that is what you desire from me. Furthermore, it is believable that if such things had existed, they would reasonably have had a name; and in Julius Pollux <note>A Greek grammarian of the 2nd century whose "Onomasticon" provides a list of musical instrument parts.</note>, who names all their parts in every way they were ever called, there would likely be some indication of it, which has not come to my notice. Add to this that the arrangement by which the strings were stretched and disposed in their instruments was, for example, like that of the Harp, and not like that of the Lute or the bowed Viola. Just as frets are necessary on the latter, since one wishes to draw four or six different, just, and resonant notes from a single string according to need; in the Lyre, on the contrary, where each string makes its own particular sound without lacking what is necessary, frets would be vain and useless—no different than holes in the pipes of a well-ordered organ <note>original: "Stringhe"; here referring to the pipes of a keyboard instrument.</note>. This truth is further persuaded by the words Virgil used above when speaking of Orpheus. Moreover, frets would have caused the same effects in their instruments that they have caused in ours.

<margin>What frets would have caused.</margin>
That is, they would change the species from the Ditonic Diatonic <note>The Pythagorean tuning system based on pure fifths.</note>, or whatever other species it might be, into the Aristoxenian Intense <note>original: "Incitata d'Aristosseno"; refers to the "Syntonon" tuning of Aristoxenus, which moved toward equal temperament.</note>; for the instrument is naturally capable of no other. Nor should we leave behind this other consideration: that while Pythagoras, the supreme philosopher (or whoever it was), received great praise for having investigated musical proportions, if the instruments of those times had possessed frets, any ordinary man of mediocre talent could have investigated them without any difficulty. For the Lute with frets is nothing other than a harmonic rule <note>original: "Regola harmonica"; a reference to the monochord, a tool used to measure mathematical intervals.</note> with many strings. 

<margin>The Lute with frets is a harmonic rule with many strings. Modern singing originated from instruments without frets.</margin>
And to tell you another detail worthy of consideration on this subject, I say that an effective argument can be drawn from this: that our way of singing derived from those instruments that did not have frets, and consequently those which require frets were the last among the string instruments to be invented. Returning to the passage regarding Aspendius cited by you above, I say that it clearly manifests (to those who examine the fact with a healthy mind) that in the ancient Lyre, there were no frets in any way whatsoever.

STROZZI: What form did it have then, and in what manner were the strings arranged upon it?

BARDI: The form was similar to that which is sometimes seen in the hands of ancient statues, and modern ones made in imitation of them—of Apollo, and of Orpheus, and of others to whom such an instrument is appropriate. It can also be discerned on the reverses of some medals, particularly those of Nero, in addition to seeing them on many ancient sarcophagi <note>original: "Pili"</note> and marbles in low relief, which are no different...

<summary>Bardi argues that ancient instruments like the lyre and cithara lacked frets and necks, distinguishing them from modern lutes. He explains that "playing inside and outside" referred to the two sides of an upright, harp-like instrument rather than fingerboard positions.</summary>

<margin>Philostratus on the subject of Mercury’s Lyre. In Book 3.</margin>
To these various opinions regarding the invention of the Lyre, we shall add that of Philostratus; <note>Flavius Philostratus (c. 170–250 AD) was a Greek scholar; this reference likely comes from his *Imagines*, which describes ancient paintings and iconography.</note> who asserts that the first one was made from goat horns together with the bone from the middle of the forehead; and regarding the wood that was used around it for any necessary purpose, he maintains that boxwood <note>A very hard, heavy wood favored for its durability and fine grain.</note> was the best that could be employed; which Hyginus <note>Gaius Julius Hyginus (c. 64 BC – 17 AD) was a Latin author whose work *De Astronomica* described the constellations and their mythological origins.</note> then, in the book he wrote concerning celestial images, illustrates in this form.

# Dialogue on Music.

<margin>
In the *Dialogue of Doris and Galatea*. <note>A work by the Greek satirist Lucian of Samosata.</note>

And a similar one is described by Lucian in the hand of Polyphemus, made from the horns and the middle of the forehead of a stag. The form of this instrument (according to Plutarch) was later improved and reduced to its true proportions by Cepio, a pupil of Terpander. It was also called "Asian" because the players of Lesbos, who lived in the Lydian city of Asia, used it in that form; from there, it was brought to Lesbos by the aforementioned Cepio in a much better form than what is seen here. For this reason, perhaps, the divine Ariosto said, *In harmony with the sound of the horned lyre.* <note>original: "Concorde al suon della cornuta cetra." From *Orlando Furioso*, Canto 16, stanza 72.</note> Additionally, Julius Pollux <note>A 2nd-century Greek grammarian and sophist.</note> calls those two scrolls at the top of the Lyre "horns," which protrude outward like ears.

<margin>
In Canto 16, stanza 72.
</margin>

STR. <note>Strozzi, one of the two speakers in the dialogue.</note> You speak well, and I greatly like your reasoning; but this is hard for me to believe: because I cannot imagine in what manner a bow <note>term: <term>Arco</term> (bow). Strozzi is confusing the ancient plectrum with the modern violin/viola bow.</note> could perform its function on an instrument of that shape. This is both because the wood of the frame that composes and surrounds it appears to be more than two inches thick on every side—in the middle of which the strings are stretched and supported by bridges—and because the surface of these bridges is flat, and not curved in the manner of a hemisphere or a semi-oval. Furthermore, even if the strings were raised higher than the frame of the Lyre, the plectrum—or bow, as we might call it—could not touch one string at a time, especially those in the middle. This is first because the bridges upon which the strings are set do not have, as I said, a semi-oval or ear-like shape like those used today for greater convenience, but are entirely flat; and besides, the strings are very close to one another.

BAR. <note>Bardi, the other speaker, representing Galilei's own views.</note> In what manner and of what shape do you truly believe the plectrum of the ancient Citharists and Citharedes <note>Players of the cithara who either just played or sang while playing.</note> was made?

STR. I believe it was a bow similar to that used today by players of the *Viola da gamba* and *Viola da braccio*, which is called a Lyre in modern times.

BAR. Therein lies the whole error.

STR. How so, pray tell?

BAR. The plectrum of the ancients was an instrument about a palm long, or about a quarter of a *braccio* <note>A traditional Italian unit of measurement, roughly equivalent to an arm's length.</note> in length, of the form you see in the drawing here. According to Suidas, <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> Sappho was its inventor; though I do not know how that can be true, given that Homer—who attributes the invention to Mercury—lived before Sappho, who invented the Mixolydian mode.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of an ancient plectrum. It is a long, slightly curved tool, tapering to a sharp point on the left and ending in a wider, textured or ribbed section on the right, resembling a stylized animal horn or tusk.</image-desc>

---

This instrument was held with the right hand, while the left hand held that part of the Lyre where the tuning pegs <note>term: <term>Bischeri</term>. The wooden pins used to tension the strings.</note> were located. The other end, where the strings were attached—which, as you have seen, was somewhat wider—was rested against the chest, specifically in whichever spot provided the greatest convenience. In later times, when they began to play in consonance (as was said of Epigonius and Aspendius), the instrument was placed upright on a table or stool. With the two little tabs that extended above and below the fist (or at the sides, as we might say), the strings of the Lyre were struck and not "sawed" <note>Galilei uses the verb *secauano* (sawed) to disparagingly describe the action of a bow across strings.</note>; just as Virgil and Ovid told you a little while ago. These and other poets, to show greater force in touching the strings, used the word "strike" <note>original: *Ferire* (to wound or strike).</note> instead of "hit." In those early times, these tools were customarily made from the bones found in a goat's knees or the hooves of the front legs; they were worked and polished on a lathe or by other means, giving them that shape you have seen as the most suitable for its purpose. Some others maintain that the hoof itself served to strike the strings, gripping the little leg after it had been detached from the goat and dried.

And if you wish to see a very similar likeness of it—which I never look upon without wonder—direct your attention to the magnificent temple of Santa Maria Novella, in the chapel of one of your ancestors, painted by Filippo, son of Fra Filippo. <note>Filippino Lippi (c. 1457–1504). The chapel mentioned is the Strozzi Chapel.</note> On the left-hand wall, one sees two women, one of whom sings while the other holds in her hand an ancient Lyre made according to what I showed you above; in her right hand, she holds something similar to the drawing of the plectrum shown to you, at least in terms of its shape and its intended use. From this, one can argue for the great judgment of that excellent painter—unless, in that matter, he was assisted by some man of letters, such as one of the caliber of Poliziano, <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a renowned humanist scholar and poet.</note> who flourished in that same time and place. Being a man of letters, Poliziano could easily have had some knowledge of such an instrument and communicated it to Filippo, as he left behind several important writings on the subject of music. And so you know, it is not more than two years since such certainty came to the knowledge of a few individuals, thanks to a very ancient sarcophagus <note>original: *Pilo*.</note> recently found in Rome, which is today in the Palace of Cardinal Santacroce. There, the Muses are seen carved in low relief, and in the hand of one of them is the shape of the plectrum along with the instrument. This knowledge and certainty now allow us to recognize it on the reverses of many medals, where it was previously mistaken for anything other than a plectrum. # [Ancient and Modern Music]

<margin>In the discourse to an unlearned man.</margin>

That the strings of the ancient Lyre were struck in the end, and not sawn <note>The author uses "sawn" (*secassero*) as a disparaging metaphor for the back-and-forth motion of a bow.</note>, I confirm to you with the example of one Evangelus, a Noble of Tarentum, recounted to us by Lucian; the history of which will do you no harm to understand. On one occasion among others, either because he had a heavy hand, or because he wanted the strings to render a greater sound than their nature was capable of, he broke three of them: not through any particular defect in them, nor because of their tension, but because of the violence done to them by the <term>Plectrum</term> <note>A small flat tool used to pluck or strike the strings of a lyre or lute.</note>; and the story is this. Evangelus, a Noble of Tarentum, took a desire once in his youth,

<margin>What the Pythian Games were.</margin>
to win in the competitions and Pythian games, which were customary in Greece in honor of Apollo; in which, besides high strength and dexterity of body (called <term>saltatione</term> <note>From the Latin *saltatio*, referring to rhythmic movement, dance, or athletic agility.</note> by the ancients), they practiced playing and singing to the Lyre and the <term>Tibia</term> <note>An ancient reed instrument, often called an *aulos* in Greek.</note>. And knowing himself not to be very fit for labor, and consequently unable to win in that part where there was need of agility and strength of body, this Evangelus gave himself to learning to play and sing to the Lyre: judging the Tibia—as was indeed the case—to be an instrument unsuitable for nobles. And after a few months, he was persuaded by the flatterers who were constantly around him (thanks to his many riches, which he willingly spent on such friends) and by the burning desire he had to be reputed (rather than actually being) intelligent and wise, that he too easily believed himself to have become a very great <term>Citharoedus</term> <note>A professional performer who sings while playing the cithara or lyre.</note>. This is a vice into which fall the majority of those who have much to spend and know little.

<margin>Delphi, a place in Greece. <note>The original margin note calls Delphi an "Island" (*Isola*), likely confusing it with the sacred island of Delos.</note> Dress of the ancient Musicians.</margin>
It was (as said above) permitted to the noble Poets and Musicians of those times—which two different professions were most often found in the same subject, both because of the conformity they have together, and because it had not been declared which of them should hold the primacy and the role of "Architect" <note>Meaning the governing or master discipline.</note> in well-ordered Melodies—it was, I say, permitted to them to dress in the manner that Kings dressed: that is, with purple robes, with the laurel crown on the head, and with buskins <note>Boots reaching to the calf.</note> to the mid-leg. And in such dress one reads in histories of Orpheus and Arion, among others. Wherefore

<margin>Sumptuous dress of Evangelus. His proud crown. His most superb Lyre.</margin>
the aforementioned Evangelus, to appear richly dressed and sumptuously adorned, had made for himself a robe woven of gold and purple, and a crown of purest gold; which, to the sight of the onlookers, by means of enamels and other artistry, represented living laurel. In place of its berries and fruit, it had fine emeralds and other jewels of value set there; and the buskins corresponded to the rest of the dress. The Lyre then was a most superb thing to see and miraculous: for it was made of purest gold, adorned on every side with an infinite quantity of diverse jewels, all of great price. One could see on it, made in low relief by an industrious craftsman, the image of each of the nine Muses, that of Apollo, and that of Orpheus. He went therefore to Delphi, at the time when such games were to be practiced; and having arrived there, and the day having come to prove his worth, he appeared in the Theater and on the Stage ordained for it, in the dress you have heard. This Evangelus, besides the wonder that he brought with him, created in the minds of the spectators a very great desire to hear him play and sing; everyone hoping

<margin>Thespis of Thebes.</margin>
the name of one called Thespis of Thebes: who, both playing and singing, performed very well. When the one in charge of it drew the second scroll out of the urn, the name of Evangelus was read; in whose presence not only the men in the Theater fell silent, but the air and the waves together. And having begun to play, he made a harsh and disordered sound; and in

<margin>The foolishness of Evangelus.</margin>
striking the strings of the Lyre violently with the Plectrum, perhaps to overcome Thespis at least in noise, he broke three of them one after another. Which ruin a bow could hardly have caused; nor even, according to what Homer said above, could the strings have resonated under that hand that ruled it [the bow]; but they certainly did under the one that gripped the Plectrum. Evangelus, wishing to make up for this defect (perhaps caused on purpose to have an occasion to further show his skill, as some moderns have used and still use—unlike those who spend all day increasing it, so that those who are simpler than they (not to say ignorant) might greatly esteem their worth), he began therefore to sing over those [strings] that remained; but in such a foolish, ugly, and tiresome way that he moved all those present to both laughter and disdain at the same time, in the manner of Polyphemus <note>The Cyclops from the *Odyssey*, often depicted as a crude or unrefined musician.</note>.

It was exactly the opposite of what he would have achieved today in that dress and with those riches. Wherefore the ministers of the Theater, knowing his insolence and temerity, publicly drove him from the Stage with the sound of lashes; and such was the punishment that by law the place gave to the presumptuous and arrogant of those happy times, who loved virtue and not riches. It was truly a ridiculous thing to see such a rich and pompous Citharoedus, dragged against his will across the Stage by those who beat him without any discretion, so much so that the parts of his legs that were not defended by the gold and purple flowed with blood; and he, to further manifest the meanness of his spirit, went about gathering the scattered relics of his beautiful robe, Lyre, and crown, which the disrespectful lash-

After he was given his deserved punishment, the third and final <term>Citharode</term> <note>A professional performer who sang while playing the kithara (a type of lyre).</note> appeared on stage, named Eumelus of Aetolia. He possessed an old, worm-eaten Lyre with wooden tuning pegs; which, when valued alongside his robe, crown, and sandals, were not worth half a <term>scudo</term> <note>A gold or silver coin used in Italy during the 16th century.</note>. Yet he played and sang with such greater excellence than could be desired that he was heard and recognized as such by everyone. Whereupon, declared the victor by the judges and announced by the trumpeter, he carried away the rightful prize. This was a crown of olive, just as the prize for the Olympic contests held in honor of Jove was made of <term>celery</term> <note>original: "Appio." While the author attributes olive to the Olympics and celery to others, historically the Nemean and Isthmian games used wild celery.</note> and not of gold—having at that time only honor as the goal, and not profit, as is mostly the custom today. In that moment, everyone returned to laughing at the foolishness of Evangelus of Tarentum, whom his beautiful Lyre, his crown, and his many riches had not helped one bit. Furthermore, the author of the history says that the victor spoke thus to the loser: "You are adorned with a crown of gold, but what wonder is that since you are rich? I, who am poor, must be content with the crown of Apollo <note>The laurel crown, sacred to Apollo, was the traditional prize at the Pythian games.</note>. This sumptuous ornament of yours has brought you only this utility: that finding no one who has compassion for you, everyone holds you in hatred, for no other reason than your superfluous wealth." I do not wish to leave this subject without considering that from Lucian’s words, one draws the conclusion that the crown given as a prize to the victors of the Pythian games was of laurel rather than olive. This is not a matter for surprise, as such prizes were changed many times, as can be understood from the diversity of writers who lived in various times. Coming now to 

<margin>
In chapter 2 of the first [book].
</margin>
bring an end to the matter of the invention of the Lyre, I say that <term>Boethius</term> <note>An influential 6th-century Roman philosopher and music theorist.</note> maintains it was found by Mercury, but not that it derived from a land or aquatic tortoise; rather, he simply maintains that Mercury shared it with men without otherwise saying of what material or form it was made, only that it had four strings arranged in the proportions you have heard in the proper place.

<margin>
In the Opuscule on Music.
</margin>
In the distribution of these strings, there arises among writers another significant discrepancy. Some maintain, and among these is <term>Plutarch</term> <note>A Greek philosopher and biographer whose works often discussed music and ethics.</note>, that the lowest string rendered the sound of the <term>Hypate</term>; the one next to it, the <term>Mese</term>; above which a whole tone followed the string representing the <term>Paramese</term>; and that the highest extreme rendered the sound of the <term>Nete</term> <note>These are technical names for the notes in the ancient Greek musical system (the Greater Perfect System).</note>. He applied the number six to the first, eight to the second, nine to the third, and twelve to the fourth and last named, so that from these numbers one could clearly recognize the proportion in which one string stood to another.

<margin>
In chapter 1 of the 2nd [book] of his Institutions.
</margin>
Others, among whom is the Reverend Master <term>Gioseffo Zarlino</term> <note>A famous 16th-century music theorist and composer, a contemporary of the author.</note> (although in the sixth chapter of the first part of his *Institutions* he understands it differently), maintain that the first and lowest string—following the order observed in numbering them according to Plutarch’s mind—was the *Parhypatehypaton*, the second the *Parhypatemeson*, the third the *Lychanosmeson*, and the fourth and last the *Tritediezugmenon*. To the first of these they apply the number twelve, to the second nine, to the third eight, and to the fourth six, for the reason mentioned above; which is exactly the opposite of what occurred with the first group. We shall see if it is possible to reconcile this contradiction in the order of the numbers, or at least find which is better. Firstly, regarding the diversity of the strings, their entire difference lies in being more or less high-pitched. Nevertheless, those who healthily examine both opinions will find that Plutarch’s fits much better than the others. This is because it is more reasonable, when one must draw one of the seven species of the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The ancient Greek term for an octave.</note> from a quantity of fifteen strings where they are all found and bring it as an example, to take not only the one held in highest esteem, but the one that is most common. Thus Plutarch, with the greatest judgment as in all his other matters, takes the Fourth Species, which is the proper one of the <term>Dorian Mode</term>, reputed and esteemed more than any other. It is the one, as you know, that comes in the middle of the natural and ordinary system without spoiling or breaking the two <term>tetrachords</term> <note>A scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth.</note> that compose it, which are naturally separated by the Tone of Disjunction. Whereas the species encompassing the other part is the Diapason of the <term>Lydian Mode</term>, which is found only a semitone distant from the lowest extreme (which, according to the opinion of Ptolemy, is that of the <term>Mixolydian</term>, but transposed by an octave into the high register); furthermore, its tetrachords come out truncated and not whole, which did not happen to the one mentioned above. Since Plutarch accompanies his strings with numbers, he cannot in any way consider them as parts of a <term>Monochord</term> <note>A single-stringed instrument used for measuring musical intervals.</note>, but rather as weights attached to certain sounding subjects, and the others as measurements of similar things.

<margin>
Which of the Pythagorean hammers made the low sound and which the high.
</margin>
Plutarch can primarily consider them as weights, applying them to the <term>Pythagorean hammers</term> <note>A legendary account where Pythagoras discovered harmonic ratios by listening to hammers striking an anvil.</note>, as the same proportions are found among them. For the hammer that weighed twelve pounds, compared to the one that weighed six, responded to each other in an octave when struck; but the twelve-pound one made the high sound—as is the nature of solid, non-concave bodies—and the six-pound one made the low sound, no differently than the *Hypate* does with the *Nete*. The same proportion found among the other numbers occurs in the different weights and in the same order.

<margin>

</margin>
The same thing is seen to happen all day long even with concave and thin bodies, which make a low sound when struck; and if they were thick, even of the same capacity, they would make a higher or "less low" sound, as we might say. # Ancient and Modern

...the deep sound; this occurs for no other reason than the thinness of the vessel, due to the small quantity of material that the craftsmen of those times put into the form of their instrument bodies. One can also observe the same thing, and for the same reason, in the modern **Lute**; which, having its ribs (or "staves," as we might call them) thin, produces a sweet and deep sound; but when they are thick, it makes the sound harsh and shrill. The same can also happen due to the diversity of the material from which it is made: for **Ebony** and **Ivory** are apt by their nature to render a sound more shrill than **Fir** and **Beech**. However, excellent craftsmen have the skill, through their industry, to oppose and resist many of these natural qualities—I call them natural qualities because the immediate cause of sound is the tension of the air enclosed within the instruments. When struck, the air almost bursts out from the center by force; with its momentum, gathered together as it was in that narrow space, it strikes the surrounding air, pushing outward until the air closest to the ear, forced by that motion, strikes the cartilages of the ear. These, being struck, create the sensation of hearing; and this strike, once felt, is truly what sound is.

<margin>How sound is made.</margin>

Secondly, **Plutarch** <note>Plutarch (c. 46 – 120 AD) was a Greek philosopher whose works often discussed music theory and history.</note> could consider these same numbers applied to weights attached to four strings equal in length, thickness, and quality. When struck, one would hear the same musical intervals and in the same order as were heard in the four hammers; but they would be much more sonorous and distinct in the strings than in the hammers, as strings are more suited (after being stretched and struck) than four simple pieces of iron to render the sound intelligible and rational.

Those who arranged the numbers in the opposite way considered them, as has been said, in measurements that can be applied to vessels, pipes, strings, and other things. They could first consider them in vessels of copper, or other metal or material, which when struck are fit to render a sound that is measurable and distinct, rather than confused. If these vessels were of the same size, thickness, capacity, material, and proportion, and one were to put in them the same weight of water (in pounds) as the iron hammers weighed, they would produce (when struck with an iron rod or something else) the same sounds as the four strings to which those same numbers were applied in the same order. For the hollow body containing a greater quantity of water would make a deeper sound than the one containing less. This is no different from what children do every day: putting a little water in a glass of proper and suitable proportions—or even without water—and wetting the tip of the middle finger of the right hand, they move it gently in a circle around the rim of the mouth, while holding the foot of the glass with the left hand so it stays upright. From this rubbing, a most sweet and sonorous sound emerges, similar to that of a string of a **Viola** <note>Likely referring to the Viola da Gamba or a similar bowed instrument.</note> cut by the bow. And as the quantity of water is increased, along with the pressure of the finger circling the rim, the sound becomes deeper and louder.

<margin>Perpetual harmony to be heard near fountains.</margin>

By means of such instruments or similar ones, one could, with little difficulty and no expense, arrange for a perpetual harmony to be heard near fountains. One can also consider the aforementioned numbers in pipes of various sizes, made by nature or art. For example, if one takes an **Organ** pipe twelve <term>palms</term> <note>A traditional unit of measurement based on the width of a hand or the span of a finger.</note> or digits long, and another of the same thickness and internal bore that is six long, one will hear when sounding them together the consonance found between the **Parhypatehypaton** and the **Tritediezeugmenon** <note>original: "Parhypatehypaton & Tritediezeugmenon." In the ancient Greek system, these notes are an octave apart.</note>. The pipe containing twelve parts will produce the deep sound, and the one containing six will produce the shrill one. Now, the same will happen if one takes two strings of the same length, thickness, and quality; if these are stretched to unison over a flat surface, and one of them is deprived of half its length by means of a bridge, fret, or even the fingers of the hand, one will hear (as has been said before) the **Diapason** <note>The interval of an octave (ratio 2:1).</note> consonance every time they are struck together or one after the other. If one is deprived of a third part, one hears with the whole of the other the **Diapente** <note>The interval of a perfect fifth (ratio 3:2).</note>; if a fourth, the **Diatessaron** <note>The interval of a perfect fourth (ratio 4:3).</note>; and if a ninth, the **Tone** <note>The interval of a major second (ratio 9:8).</note>. The remaining parts always render the shrill sound, and the whole renders the deep one; and the larger the part removed from the string, the shriller the sound of what remains. From these observations, the use of the **Monochord** <note>A one-stringed scientific instrument used to demonstrate musical ratios.</note> easily took its origin.

<margin>Arabs as inventors of the Monochord; and Pythagoras of the Harmonic Rule.</margin>

But do not understand this to be that musical instrument used by the **Arabs**, to the sound of which (having only one string) they sang their songs; but rather the one discovered by **Pythagoras**, also called the **Harmonic Rule**. Because the intestine naturally tapers, the string is slightly thicker at one end, which affects its tuning and "trueness."</note>, even if they are of the same bundle, thickness, and length. This is one of the reasons why Lutenists many times—for example—when putting a treble string on a Lute that gives diminished intervals when fretted, find that by turning it upside down, it renders them perfect, or at other times superfluous. For as the intestine leaves the duodenum and moves toward the rectum, it gradually thickens and likewise hardens; so that throughout its length, there are trebles, seconds, and middles <note>original: "canti, delle sottane, & delle mezzane." These are specific names for the different registers of lute strings.</note>. Thus, when placed on the bridge of the Lute from the thicker side, it becomes harder when stretched, offering greater resistance than the opposite side, which by comparison is soft and thin. # Dialogue on Music

...stretching <note>original: "rizzatezza"; referring to the tension or stiffness of a material.</note> (so to speak) to make the sound more vigorous and sharp, no differently than what was said of the **Pythagorean hammers** <note>This refers to the legend of Pythagoras discovering musical ratios by listening to hammers of different weights striking an anvil.</note>.

**STR.** I am completely and entirely satisfied; but I desire next to know why it happens that when a string is **false** <note>A "false" string is one with physical defects, such as uneven thickness, which causes it to produce irregular vibrations and sound out of tune.</note>, its defect is more manifest to the sense when fretting it than when plucking it open. And if, regarding two **organ pipes** of equal length but different width of bore, it has been speculated by theorists by how much one must exceed the other, if one wishes that when played, the **Perfect Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente".</note> resonance is heard from them.

**BAR.** The reason the sound of a string, when it is false, is more manifest to the ear when it is pressed against the fingerboard and struck than when plucked open, arises because, in being further sharpened, it comes (as it is more tense) to strike the ear with greater force. Regarding then the proportion of pipes of the same length and different width, I have never found any record of it; but I hold for certain, indeed I am most sure of it, that if there are two pipes, each of which is two **braccia** <note>A "braccio" (plural "braccia") was a traditional Italian unit of length, roughly equivalent to 23 inches or the length of an arm.</note> long, and the bore of one (through which the air passes when playing) has a circumference of half a braccio consistently throughout, and the circumference of the other is three-quarters of a braccio, when played together one will hear between them the **Perfect Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente".</note> resonance. The latter will render the low sound, and the former the high. 

With the same considerations, one could obtain most of the musical intervals from pipes of equal length and unequal capacity; however, they will not all have that excellence and sonority found where the length also contributes in its proper proportion. But here it must be noted that the capacity of the pipe's bore, considered in this second manner, will not have the same relationship between them as in those first cases where the difference in length was considered for the same capacity. For those that correspond by an **Octave** <note>original: "Ottava" or "Diapason".</note>, the bore of the lower one, of whatever shape, will necessarily contain **four times** that of the higher one: although each of the sides, the diameter, and the circumference of them have a double (2:1) relationship to each other. Because of this, for those that contain the **Perfect Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente".</note> when played together, their bore will be in **double sesquiquarta** <note>A 9:4 ratio, which is the square of the 3:2 ratio normally used for a Fifth.</note> proportion; and those that sound the **Perfect Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron".</note> will be in the **one-and-seven-ninths** <note>original: "Supersettepartiente noue"; a 16:9 ratio, the square of 4:3.</note> proportion; from which one recognizes part of the imperfection of this interval. Those then that are to contain the **Major Third** must be in the **one-and-nine-sixteenths** <note>original: "Supernouepartiente sedici"; a 25:16 ratio, the square of 5:4.</note> proportion; and those of the **Minor Third**, in the **one-and-eleven-twenty-fifths** <note>original: "Superundicipartiente uenticinque"; a 36:25 ratio, the square of 6:5.</note> proportion; as can be clearly understood from the examples that follow.

**STR.** This is all well and good; but tell me, please: if we took two lead sheets—of the kind used to make **organ pipes**—after they have been hammered, planed, and cleaned all over; which were of a rectangular shape (not a perfect square), but where each of the longer sides was, for example, one **braccio** <note>A "braccio" (arm-length) was an Italian unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches.</note>, and the shorter sides were four-fifths of that: do we believe that in joining and soldering them together with due diligence—the longer sides of one and the shorter of the other—that when played together, they would respond in unison?

**BAR.** Undoubtedly; but as I have said another time, I want to make a particular **Discourse** concerning the matter of instruments, in which many important things will be treated in an orderly fashion—things perhaps never before said or heard, or only by a few—where the reason for everything will be given. However, let us say this last thing on the subject: if there are two organ pipes of equal length and their bore is of the same capacity, and if you close the top mouth of one of them (through which the air <note>original: "ſpirito"; refers here to the breath or moving air within the instrument.</note> secondary exits), you will hear, when playing them together, the same consonance found when singing the **Hypate** and the **Nete** <note>The lowest and highest notes of the ancient Greek musical system, forming an octave.</note>. The closed pipe will make the low sound, and the open one the high sound. It is true, however, that the closed one will need very little breath to sound, and the open one a great deal; and one could even breathe into the open one such that it would ascend above the other by a **Double Octave** <note>original: "Diſdiapaſon".</note>. In this way, from the same bore of the same pipe, one can obtain—by means of the quantity and quality of the air that breathes into it—the **Proslambanomene**, the **Mese**, and the extreme **Nete** <note>These are the names of specific pitches in the Greek scale: the lowest note, the middle note, and the highest note.</note>; but let this be said for now as far as is necessary.

**STR.** Having heard you several times name simply **Hypate** and **Nete** without going any further, I do not know which specific and particular strings I should understand by them. **BAR.** Speaking in such a way regarding these two strings has been done, not without reason, by the majority of those who have written on music; and particularly by Aristotle, Ptolemy, Plutarch, Suidas, and Boethius. By these names they have, by common opinion, understood the two extreme strings of the **Lyre of Terpander**; or better said, those of the **Octochord of Lycaon of Samos**, which are **Hypate-meson** and **Nete-diezeugmenon**. Regarding these, Aristotle says that the **Nete** is a **sesquialtera** <note>A 3:2 ratio, which defines the musical interval of a Perfect Fifth.</note> of the **Mese**. From this it easily follows that the Octave was called **Diapason** by the ancients, and not **Diocto** <note>A name based on the number eight (eight strings).</note> from the number of its strings, as with the **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente".</note>, the **Fourth** <note>original: "Diateſſaron".</note>, and the **Sixth** <note>original: "Eſſacordo".</note>. They called it **Diapason**, which means "through all" <note>original: "per l'vna & per l'altra"; referring to the Greek "dia pason chordon," meaning through all the strings.</note> for one and the other, or for each, as was said above. This opinion of mine agrees with what the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> says in the *Problems*, when he searches for the reason why the Octave was called **Diapason** rather than **Diocto**. He says it derived from nothing else than seeing, as I said, that it contained sometimes seven and sometimes eight strings and sounds; which were also called **Phtongi** <note>original: "Phtongi"; Greek for musical tones or pitches.</note> by some, to distinguish them from the intervals. But here, from Aristotle's words, someone might doubt whether the extreme strings of the **Cithara of Terpander** responded as an Octave, or rather as a minor Seventh, as Boethius affirms—given that the Octave took the name **Diapason** from the **Cithara** of Terpander and that of Lycaon. But if it were a Seventh, I do not know in what manner the *E* <note>original: "elami"; the note E in the hexachord system.</note> could be the Dorian **Nete** of Terpander. Therefore, I want us to save the dispute of such a curiosity for a better occasion; but let this be said as far as is necessary.

**STR.** Tell me, I pray you, what did the ancient musicians mean by the **Greatest Harmony**?

...division and separation of the **tetrachords** <note>The four-note building blocks of ancient Greek scales.</note>, of every other interval smaller and larger than them, and consequently of the diversity of the **genera** and the **species** <note>Classifications of scales in ancient music theory.</note>.
