<meta>The previous page introduced the various consonant intervals used by the ancients (Octave, Fifth, Fourth, etc.) and began discussing the mathematical "means" or divisors used to define these musical ratios. This page specifically examines the Harmonic Mean and critiques modern interpretations of the "Greatest Harmony" in relation to ancient systems like the Lyre of Mercury and the Pythagorean hammers.</meta>

established proportionality, and let us see if it contains all the conditions required of it. First, one sees that it contains the same interval toward the lower terms in the bass as toward the smaller terms in the treble; for both these and those are arranged in a **double proportion** <note>A ratio of 2:1, which creates an Octave.</note>; which is also found in its differences, which are 12 and 6, because the larger exceeds the smaller by its entire half. And if the divisor, which is 12, is multiplied by itself, it will give the same product as the extremes multiplied by one another, which are 24 and 6. In such a manner, all intervals composed of two equal parts can be divided, provided they are contained by known and rational numbers; such as the **Major Third** <note>original: "Ditono"</note>, the **Diminished Fifth** <note>original: "Semidiapente"</note>, and the minor **Seventh** <note>original: "Eptacordo"</note> of the ancient **Diatonic** scale and others, though all of these are dissonant from that point onwards, except for those consisting of multiple octaves. Considering finally the 8 in the middle of 12 and 6, one sees these two numbers are harmonically divided by it into two unequal parts, just as the arithmetic divisor did in the same interval contained by the same numbers, but with different considerations and effects. For where the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> divided arithmetically had the smaller part among its larger terms in the bass, the harmonic division, on the contrary, has the larger part there; and where the former had the larger part in the treble, this one has the smaller. Furthermore, where the differences of the arithmetic proportionality were equal, those of the harmonic are unequal, as clearly appears in its description, which is 12. 8. 6.
<margin>Harmonic proportionality. Method of finding its divisor. Boethius in the same place.</margin>
The divisor of which is found in this manner: first the extremes are joined together, from which one gets 18; then the difference of the extremes is multiplied by the smaller term, and one gets the product 36; this, divided by 18, results in 2, which, added together with the smaller term (which was 6), makes 8; this 8 is the sought-after divisor. In this proportionality, he who looks closely perceives that the same interval contained by its extremes is found between their differences. Thus 12 exceeds 8 by four, and 8 exceeds 6 by two; and the same proportion that exists between 12 and 6 is also found, as you know, between four and two. These come to be in the same order as the former, because the difference of four is found between 12 and 8, and that of two between 8 and 6, and not the other way around. Now, these are all the principal circumstances that the ancient Musicians considered to occur regarding the subject of the **Greatest Harmony** <note>original: "Massima armonia"</note>; which we have proved also exist in the previously shown progression and proportionality of the five proposed numbers. This would be very conveniently found in practice among the four strings of the **Lyre of Mercury**, following the opinion of **Boethius** and not the one (held to be more true) of **Manuel Bryennius** <note>A 14th-century Byzantine music theorist.</note>; if beneath the lowest of these a string had been added that responded in a **quadruple proportion** <note>A ratio of 4:1, or two octaves.</note> to the highest extreme. A similar harmony would likewise have been heard coming from the sound of the **Pythagorean hammers**, if that same hammer among the five which was rejected by Pythagoras himself had been in a **triple proportion** <note>A ratio of 3:1, an Octave plus a Fifth.</note> with the one weighing eight pounds; however, it would be as much less resonant than that of the Lyre of Mercury as was dictated by the different property and form of the materials which, when struck, rendered the sound.

Some have believed and still believe that among four strings stretched according to the proportion of the said Lyre, the Greatest Harmony is found with each of the narrated conditions; which opinion can be refuted with various reasons. Such people show they have not observed or noticed what **Boethius** particularly says regarding this in chapters 12, 13, and 14 of the second book of his *Music*; in addition to what he had said previously in the last chapter of the books he wrote on the **Arithmetic faculty**. 
<margin>Opinion of some moderns refuted by the Author.</margin>
The opinion of these people can first be refuted regarding the number of intervals, because the **Double Octave** <note>original: "Disdiapason"</note> is not actually found there, nor the **Octave-plus-Fifth** <note>original: "Diapason Diapente"</note>, nor even the **Geometric division** with the circumstances that suit its nature and quality. Among these, it lacks the requirement that the operation of its divisor must be made from one term and number, and not from two. What is more important is the desire to extract from a whole two parts of which it is not truly capable. Furthermore, the differences do not contain the same interval that one of the means (considered as a divisor) contains with the most remote extreme, into which the whole is divided as suits its dignity; which we shall demonstrate in this manner. These people consider the Geometric proportionality between these terms and numbers: 12. 9. 8. 6. These virtually contain the same intervals and in the same order as they are found in the **Cithara of Mercury**; and they say that between 12 and 8, and between 9 and 6, the **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note> is found in its **one-and-a-half ratio** <note>original: "Sesquialtera," or 3:2.</note>, which is very true; but it will not be true or possible to extract both of them from the interval contained by the extremes, which is a Fifth, unless we added a **Whole Tone** to it. Furthermore, the difference between 12 and 8 is four, and that found between 9 and 6 is three; these, compared together, have the relation of a **one-and-a-third ratio** <note>original: "Sesquiterza," or 4:3, which is a Fourth.</note> and not a one-and-a-half ratio, as reasonably suits the nature of such proportionality.
<margin>The Octave is the smallest multiple interval.</margin>
And that the **Octave-plus-Fifth** or the **Double Octave** are not and cannot be present among these strings in any way is shown by the extremes, which are tuned in a double proportion; and the largest interval found between them is the smallest multiple <note>The Octave (2:1) is the first "multiple" ratio in the Pythagorean system.</note>. This Greatest Harmony can indeed be considered in the **System of fifteen strings** <note>The Greater Perfect System of Greek music theory.</note>, by applying the number 24 to the **Proslambanomene** <note>The lowest note of the Greek system.</note>, 12 to the **Mese** <note>The central note, an octave above the Proslambanomene.</note>, 9 to the **Paranete diezeugmenon**, 8 to the **Nete diezeugmenon**, and 6 to the **Nete hyperboleon**. For no other reason did such a System acquire the name of "Greatest" and "Perfect" among ancient Musicians,

# Dialogue on Music

...if only because every one of their consonances was found within it; and the same occurred to that progression of numbers shown above for virtually containing it. Others, adorned with ignorance and presumption, said that the **Greatest Harmony** of the ancients was the **Octave** with the **Fifth** and the **Third** in the middle; and this is as much as I need to tell you for now on such matter.

**STR.** One other single doubt remains for me, Signor Giovanni, which will serve, if you please, as the seal of our conversation, and it is this. Whence does it happen that many who are reputed by the general public to be great players of both the **Lute** and **keyboard instruments**, do not succeed in the things composed by them for such instruments, as they were played by their own hand? And that others of value have left no other memory than their name? On the contrary, there are some not much reputed by the public who, writing in their profession, have succeeded excellently. There are also found very learned and scientific Musicians, and despite all this, their compositions have not satisfied anyone in the world, at least in that part pertaining to practice? Others, conversely, will barely know how to read, and will have very little knowledge and experience of the world's things, and particularly of Music; yet in **Counterpoint** <note>The art of combining different melodic lines according to specific rules.</note> they succeed admirably? In short, which of these and why should they be more or less reputed and valued?

<margin>Excellent players of the Lute and keyboards: Annibale Padovano, Fabritio Dentice.</margin>
**BAR.** To clarify your doubts well, it would be necessary that it be permitted (as you said at the beginning of our reasoning it is fitting for those who seek the truth of the matter) to speak freely: but because according to today's flatterers, it is bad manners to name anyone and rightly reprove him, so that having known his error he might amend himself, I will go on discussing them according to what I feel, in that order that will come to me spontaneously, and with the greatest modesty I can. Not because what could be said of some was not the mere truth, but to not be reputed a slanderer by the envious and malicious (though against all duty). I say then, that in our times there have been and are many excellent players of both the Lute and keyboards; among whom some have truly known how to both play well and write well—or shall we say compose—for their instrument; as, for the keyboard, an **Annibale Padovano** <note>A famous Venetian organist and composer (1527–1575).</note>, and for the Lute, a **Fabritio Dentice**, a noble Neapolitan. Others there have been and are who have written and write excellently, and who have also known how to play much, but not well.

**STR.** How can there be in the same person and at the same time, the knowing how to "play much," and yet not "playing well"?

**BAR.** In the same way as there is in the learned **Orator** much knowledge, but little grace granted to him by nature in demonstrating it when speaking with his living voice; which defect he often compensates for with the pen, demonstrating with it the excellence of his worth.

**STR.** I have understood very well, so you may continue and tell me minutely all that is needed for understanding this fact; and afterward some detail of the wind and stringed instruments of our times, regarding their excellence and antiquity.

<margin>Defect of some players and Counterpountists.</margin>
<margin>Another sort of players.</margin>

Others there are who have played well and play on one and the other instrument, and nonetheless will then have written poorly: part of whom, being more shrewd, have never cared to show the world that knowledge of theirs with the pen; and given that they may have composed and written something, they have not published it: for having known very well the little or no value of it, and consequently the blame it would have brought them in coming into the hand of this or that expert. There are others who have not known how to do this or that thing, nevertheless they have been and are reputed by many as men of worth; and the same that occurred among players, has also happened (as you will hear) to simple Counterpountists. Those like Annibale Padovano, who have known how to play well and write well, are very few in comparison to the number of keyboard players there are; and in all Italy, which is more abundant in them than any other part of the world, I do not believe in any way that they exceed the number of four. Among whom are numbered **Claudio da Coreggio** <note>Claudio Merulo (1533–1604), a celebrated organist from Correggio.</note>, **Giuseppe Guami**, and **Luzzasco Luzzaschi**; the other, whoever it is, we will declare another time. The reason why these satisfy both with the pen and with their playing is this: they have first been for many years under the discipline of the primary men of the world in that profession, and with many conveniences; they have seen and diligently examined all the good music of famous Counterpountists; by which means they have acquired...

# Ancient & Modern [Music]

<margin>
Excellent keyboard players and **Contrapuntists** <note>Those skilled in counterpoint—the art of layering different melodic lines.</note>. In what manner they have become such.
</margin>
...a most pure and exquisite Counterpoint; they have studied this instrument for all that time with the greatest diligence and assiduity that can be imagined, and they continue to study and learn; they have been to many parts of the world and practiced with diverse talented men of their profession; they have also been endowed by nature with a most beautiful intellect, great judgment, happy memory, and a fierce yet graceful dexterity of hands. Beyond this, they have (meritedly) had opportunities to serve not only great and wealthy Princes, but those who are most knowledgeable and judicious in the particularities of music, and moreover, liberal ones—you know how much this matters and what a stimulus it is to noble and virtuous souls.

<margin>Another sort of Musicians.</margin>
There are others (also of this first circle) who truly know and understand the matters of Theory and practice excellently, and are reputed as such by every intelligent person who has knowledge of them; but by a defect of nature, they are of such slow intellect and deprived of invention, that the things composed by them have so little grace that they not only fail to delight, but generate satiety and boredom in the listener within the first two lines. Nevertheless, they discourse on these matters and know how to demonstrate them admirably; these can be compared to that rotating **whetstone** <margin>Comparison.</margin>—or stone, if we wish to call it that—which sharpens and thins hard bodies so that they then cut in a manner that one could say they shave; yet, in the process, the stone itself becomes ever more blunt.

<margin>Another sort of players.</margin>
Others are desirous and believe themselves to deserve being numbered among these, solely for having in their playing such a fierceness and dexterity of hands that they make the majority of those who hear them marvel; yet, when they set themselves to write down their knowledge, they proceed so slowly in putting to paper what they previously played, that some who later see and examine their writings judge them to belong to anyone else but them. This arises from nothing other than the pen not having the same privilege in writing as the fingers have in playing or the tongue in speaking. Just as a brave Captain, wanting to be a good Knight, needs clearer signs of valor than merely placing the lance in its rest with grace. From this, one can also judge the importance of those things which sound so readily to the ears of the common people, when they do not dare to write them and reveal them to the refined judgment and hearing of the intelligent for the fear they have of them. I will not treat many particulars that I could concerning the Lute, as our **Galileo** <note>Refers to Vincenzo Galilei, the author of this treatise and father of the astronomer Galileo.</note> has treated them at length in his Dialogue entitled *Fronimo* <note>original: "Fronimo"; a famous work on lute intabulation by Vincenzo Galilei.</note>, which he published in years past; and from what he has told me, he wishes even now to reprint it anew with a greater abundance of secrets than the first impression, and other most useful things necessary to that faculty of which he treats.

**STR.** I wish for you to tell me, if you please, of a single particular common to keyboard instruments.

**BAR.** Tell me what it is.

**STR.** Are these two famous instruments equally suited to move the same affections in the listener?

**BAR.** No, sir.

**STR.** What is their difference?

<margin>Diverse nature of Stringed Instruments.</margin>
**BAR.** This: All stringed instruments such as **Harpsichords** <note>original: "Graui cimbali"</note>, **Harpsichords/Virginals** <note>original: "Arpicordi"</note>, **Spinets**, **Clavichords**, and other similar ones, are greatly suited to expressing the actions of both the body and the soul, like the **Phrygian** and **Lydian** harmonies <note>Refers to the ancient Greek modes; the Phrygian was associated with excitement and the Lydian with joy or lamentation.</note>, which have something of the excited and the Bacchic. Conversely, the **Lute** and the **Bowed Viol** are like the **Dorian** harmony <note>The Dorian mode was associated with gravity and solemnity.</note>: grave and severe. Experience, the mistress of things, can sufficiently teach us this, even if we set aside the diverse quality and size of the intervals found between them (which is of no small importance). Consider only the material that, when struck, renders the sound in each instrument, and what the intrinsic cause of that sound is.
<margin>Considerations of the Author.</margin>
The primary cause of sound in both of these, as you know, are the strings stretched above; but those of the Harpsichord and the other aforementioned keyboard instruments are of brass and steel, touched and then struck by the jacks (which in hardness resemble bone) made of crow or vulture quills. Those of the Lute and the Viol are made of the intestines of brute animals; if they were of rational ones [humans], I do not doubt at all, given the conformity and convenience they would have with our nature, that they would produce even better effects. Furthermore, the agent that draws across or strikes them is the bow, or the very fingers of a human. Consider now the difference between the strings and the intrinsic agent of these different instruments; regarding the material of which they are made, where and how they are generated, and the conformity or deformity they have with our nature. Without further discourse on this head, you will find for yourself, without much or any effort, all that you further desire.

**STR.** What shall we say next of the **Organ**?

**BAR.** The Organ, then, having many and varied pipes of different sizes and thicknesses made with diverse craftsmanship, and by the abundance of its registers, is suited to expressing not only all those sorts of affections that belong to the three famous and principal species of harmonies mentioned above, but even those more of the acute Lydian and the three more of the grave Dorian.

# Ancient & Modern [Music]

...following the rules of the aforementioned <term>Contrapuntists</term> <note>Composers skilled in counterpoint, the art of combining different melodic lines</note>; and whether, in that moment, each of the parts can be heard; if the cadences are diminished <note>Embellished with faster notes</note> where, when, and how it is appropriate; whether those notes which, for the perfection of the musical idea, require accidental signs <note>Sharps, flats, or naturals</note> to be played higher or lower than their positions show, are truly accommodated with due diligence at the proper time and place; whether irrelevant difficulties are judiciously removed by him; whether the bass part of the <term>Cantilena</term> <note>The vocal melody or musical line</note> that he plays has, according to the author's intention, the Third and the Fifth or any of their octaves; or if the harmony continues with due measure and proportion; he does not think of these things at all, nor can he think of them, being in no way capable,

<margin>Not understood by the common people and therefore not appreciated by them.</margin>
even though he presumptuously wishes to pass judgment on everything, and secretly bites and tears at this or that virtuous man. He despises and belittles all things known, said, and discovered by others that are outside of his own knowledge. Yet, the intelligent person primarily looks for this deep understanding and skill in a player; and when he finds it, he admires it, and it becomes even more joined to that "fast and simultaneously sonorous and graceful disposition of hands" mentioned many times before. But of this speed alone, without the other qualities, the expert not only makes no account, but laughs at it; and the reason that moves him is this:

<margin>Comparison.</margin>
If we were to find ourselves listening to a lecture on philosophy or another noble faculty, and the person reciting it performed with the greatest excellence one could desire—explaining very high and difficult concepts clothed in choice words, pronounced with the greatest grace imaginable, with a sonorous voice, with gestures conforming to them, and with admirable order—I believe that at the end, every listener would say that this was a rare and divine man, and he would be admired by all as one of the greatest scholars in the world in that faculty. But if afterward an intelligent and reputable man stepped forward and made it clear to us that this person had learned that lecture by heart, and was utterly ignorant of the things pertaining to philosophy or the matter he treated, everyone who gave undoubted faith to that word would (I believe) immediately change their opinion. They would praise in him only those parts that were truly his: such as the resonance of the voice, the clear pronunciation, the sweetness of the accents, the grace of the speech, the beauty of the gestures, the capacity of memory, and in short, everything except knowledge. For we see and hear these things happen all day long with infinite children of a very tender age, on stages, in teacher’s chairs, and in pulpits.

<margin>Another sort of Players.</margin>
That other sort of men, also reputed by the common people to be great players, who never write—or better said, never publish—anything of their own, act this way because they do not feel capable of satisfying an audience with the pen as they do with the instrument. By writing, they do not have to please the general public (who, as you know, usually have little knowledge of the goodness of things), but rather the specialists, who are often more knowledgeable than they are. And so, being more clever than the others of the same rank, they remain without caring at all to reveal to the world through writing the extent of their skill in playing.

<margin>Comparison.</margin>
They do no differently than the sagacious improvisers <note>original: "prouisanti," referring to poets or singers who performed extemporaneously</note> who, by singing unexpectedly, make (so to speak) everyone who listens to them marvel; without otherwise caring to bring to light or publish what they have said while singing. They know very well that the concepts and the quality of the words, rhymes, and verses would easily move to laughter the majority (if not all) of those who might read and hear them. This does not happen when they were reciting, because they gave the listeners no time to understand them, let alone consider them; and because, as has been said, those who read are different from those who listen. I could give you sensible examples of each of these types and point out exactly who they are, which I would do if it were appropriate.

STR. You have painted them so naturally in this discourse of yours that I recognize them distinctly, one by one, without you having to write their names underneath.

<margin>The author discusses the origin and excellence of the instruments of his time.</margin>
BAR. I did not wish to speak of any individual for this reason, and if by chance there were someone who presumed this was said to his discredit, I would want him to believe that I am discussing not the men, but the matter itself. It will be well, before I come to treat the fourth and last species of Musicians of our times—who are called by their proper name, the dance players, loved and favored by the masses—to say something more, according to your definition, about the invention and origin of artificial instruments, and some particulars about those who play the <term>Trombone</term>, the <term>Cornetto</term>, and the <term>Viola d'arco</term> <note>Bowed viola/violin family</note> and <term>Violone</term> <note>A large string instrument, ancestor of the double bass</note>. In the first place among these, we shall deservedly place the professors of the Viola; in the second, those of the Cornetto; and in the third and last, those who have applied themselves to the Trombone.

<margin>Warning.</margin>
Speaking of these professors in general, I say that each deserves to be esteemed for something, provided he performs with the excellence desired for his role. However, I must warn those who need it regarding this one detail: those who, to show the flexibility of their lip, the agility of their tongue, and the speed of their fingers (believing that knowledge consists in these), diminish the true essence, the air, the appearance, the form, and the natural beauty of whatever song comes into their hands. They wrap it from head to foot in the confused fog of those "winged passages" or runs, as they call them. By means of this disproportionate and unbecoming masking,

# Dialogue on Music

...for these [painters] to depict simple plants, birds, aquatic creatures, land animals, and finally rational beings, it was extremely difficult, if not impossible, to distinguish Borage from Nettle, a Sparrow from a Linnet, a Trout from a Weever fish, a Hare from a Rabbit, or Julius Caesar from Alexander the Great. But discerning and honorable men, to remove any doubt for those who looked upon their works with no small wonder, wrote their names beneath them. No less do the songs played by the hands of such musicians need this treatment—those who are accustomed to doing so—if they wish to distinguish one piece from another. Thus, one sometimes sees a "yard-long train" <note>An ornamental musical flourish or extension</note> added to one, and at another time, a "badly woven short-skirt" <note>Likely referring to poor or clipped musical phrasing</note> given to another. However, the aforementioned painters are not only worthy of excuse but (due to the simplicity of their age and their own nature, and the difficulty and novelty of the craft) worthy of infinite praise, having resurrected with their own hands the dead, beautiful, and noble art of Painting. In contrast, musicians of this sort are worthy of reprimand for their audacity—indeed, of no small punishment. There is no shortage of such people among players of the Lute and keyboard instruments, but let enough be said of them.

<margin>Cornetts and Trombones, why they were introduced.</margin>
The <term>Cornetts</term> <note>A curved woodwind instrument with a mouthpiece like a trumpet, popular in the Renaissance</note> and Trombones were rediscovered and introduced into musical ensembles more out of necessity for sopranos and basses—or we might say to provide body and noise, or perhaps for both reasons together—than for any good or necessary effect they produce. That this is true can be seen by observing that these instruments are not ordinarily heard elsewhere, except where there is a necessity for such voices. In those places where there is an abundance or sufficiency of voices, they are never heard—assuming we are speaking of places where musical ensembles are formed to truly taste the good qualities of the music of our times, provided any can be found there.

<margin>Practiced for the satisfaction of the common people.</margin>
<margin>The folly of the commoners.</margin>
<margin>Speech, why it was given to man.</margin>
They will certainly be heard often in masquerades, on stage, and upon the balconies of public squares for the satisfaction of the common people and the populace; and, against all propriety, in choirs and atop the organs of Holy Temples for solemn feasts. This is because of the folly of the commoners, who believe the Gods listen more willingly to the artificial noise made by pipes of bone, wood, and inspired metal <note>Blown into by breath</note> than to simple voices, words, and human concepts—which were given to man primarily for no other reason than to praise, honor, and give thanks to the Gods. These instruments are never heard in the private chambers of judicious Gentlemen, Lords, and Princes, where those who truly possess judgment, taste, and refined hearing gather. Indeed, they are totally banished from such places. This does not happen to the <term>Bowed Viol</term> <note>The Viola d'arco, a precursor to the violin family</note>, because of the suitability and proportion its sound has with the human voice and nature.

The Cornett is, in my opinion, an instrument more suited for use in armies—just as the Spartans once used the <term>Tibia</term> <note>Aulos or ancient pipe; original: "Tibia"</note>—than in private chambers. As for the Trombone, since its sound is very much like the bellowing of bulls, not to say buffalo, and is consequently formidable, it would be very appropriate in the woods for flushing wild beasts from their nests and dens, scaring them just as Astolfo scared Caligorante with his horn <note>A reference to Ludovico Ariosto's epic poem *Orlando Furioso*</note>, so they might more easily fall into the nets and snares set for them. These players cannot and should not, for various reasons, be compared to any of the esteemed players of the Lute and keyboards mentioned above: first, because of the great ease of the former and the difficulty of the latter; and also because they play only a single part, and usually from a book. Furthermore, a single one of these [wind players] is worth nothing in the world, as they always need (according to modern custom) four or six others for the perfection of the ensemble. Moreover, these practitioners are deprived while they play of both speech and, nearly, of the ability to reason.

<margin>Memory, the mother of music.</margin>
Furthermore, their playing can very well exist not only without any knowledge or practice of counterpoint or Theory, but even without the "mother of music" <note>Memory</note> or any other good and important thing.

<margin>Trombone and Cornett, why they are not used by nobles.</margin>
<margin>Alexander reputed to be the son of Jove. Plutarch in the 4th book of the Apophthegms.</margin>
The Trombone in particular (in addition to most other wind instruments) is an instrument less used by nobles than any other. As well-bred men, they do not wish to practice it, perhaps moved by the example of Minerva, or truly of Alcibiades <note>Ancient accounts say Minerva and Alcibiades rejected the pipes because they distorted the face when playing</note>, or perhaps so as not to be considered "children of Aeolus" <note>The god of the winds</note> by those who see them play, thereby insulting their mothers—not unlike what Alexander the Great did to his mother Olympia when he claimed to be the son of Jove <note>original: "Gioue" (Jupiter/Zeus)</note>.

These instruments are also worthy of contempt for the reason Aristotle gives in his refutation of the Pipe <note>original: "Tibia"</note>: because it produces, he says, an effect contrary to education by impeding the use of reason. Therefore, they forbade its practice to high-born youths. Furthermore, the goal aimed at by those who practice them (the Philosopher added) is not good; because the spectators, being base men, tend to want a variety of music, and thus those who labor for them become like them, and their very persons are shaped by their movements. This is not fitting for free men, but for servile and mechanical craftsmen, as he said elsewhere.

One cannot give a definite reason as to which of the modern instruments was found first or last by men, as there is no writer known to me who has left any memory of this. The same difficulty arises, as you have seen, regarding those of the ancients.

<margin>Apollo, inventor of playing and singing.</margin>
<margin>Statue of Apollo, in the Temple of Delphi.</margin>
Unless we wish to say, along with the fabulist Poets, that Apollo—full and adorned with every virtue and science—was not only the inventor of music, but of the Lyre, the Pipe, and the Panpipes: that is, of wind instruments, stringed instruments, and subsequently of singing. This is argued by the testimony of Plutarch, along with Alcaeus and others, that the men of those times, in memory of this benefit received from him, did not offer sacrifices without a choir and the aforementioned musical instruments. Furthermore, one could already see in the temple of Delphi a statue of the same God, in perpetual memory of these things, sculpted in this manner: the said statue of Apol- <note>Catchword: "d'Apol-" (of Apol-)</note>

### Ancient and Modern Music

...of Apollo holding the bow in his right hand; from his left side hung the arrows, and with his left hand he held the Graces. Each of these held a musical instrument: one the Lyre, the other the <term>Tibiae</term> <note>Ancient flutes or pipes, often played in pairs</note>, and the one in the middle was depicted putting the <term>Sampogna</term> <note>Panpipes or a rustic bagpipe-like instrument</note> to her mouth. The craftsmen of this [statue] are said to have lived in the time of Hercules, although others maintain that Apollo 

<margin>Apollo learns the art of music from Minerva, in the 8th [book] of the Republic <note>A reference to Plato's Republic, though the attribution of the invention of pipes to Minerva is more famously found in Aristotle and Ovid</note>.</margin>
learned this skill from Minerva. To her, Aristotle particularly attributes the invention of the Pipes; in his opinion, they were later despised and thrown away by her—not because holding them in her mouth and puffing out her cheeks made her look ugly, but because the discipline of such instruments, he says, contributes nothing to the mind, and to Minerva are attributed science and the arts. But leaving aside the ancient poems and fables regarding the invention of artificial instruments, and coming to the origin of those of our own times, I say: to anyone who will subtly go about conjecturing with sound judgment and examining the matter with diligence, it will not be difficult to find enough of their origin to be persuaded of at least the probability, if not the necessity,

<margin>Origin of keyboard instruments.</margin>
of whence they derived, by whom, why, and which were introduced first and which later. Among the stringed instruments in use today in Italy, I say that first is the Harp, which is nothing other than an ancient <term>Cithara</term> <note>A professional version of the lyre used in Antiquity</note> with many strings. Although it differs somewhat in shape—caused by the craftsmen of those times only by the quantity of the strings and their tension—it spans more than three octaves from the lowest to the highest notes. This very ancient instrument (commemorated by Dante) was brought to us from Ireland, where they are worked with excellence and in great 

<margin>The Harp came to us from Ireland.</margin>
abundance. The inhabitants of that island have practiced it for many, many centuries; moreover, it is the particular emblem of that kingdom, which they paint and sculpt on public buildings and on their coins, claiming as the reason for this that they are descended from the Royal Prophet David. The Harps used by said people are much larger than our ordinary ones and commonly have brass strings, with a few steel ones in the high register, similar to the <term>Grauicimbalo</term> <note>An early name for the harpsichord</note>. The players of these harps typically keep the fingernails of both hands quite long, trimming them artfully in the same manner as the quills in the <term>saltarelli</term> <note>The "jacks" of a harpsichord or spinet that pluck the strings</note> that strike the strings of the Spinets. The number of strings is fifty-four, fifty-six, or even sixty; although among the Hebrews, one does not read that the Prophet's Cithara or Psaltery exceeded the number ten. I obtained the distribution of the strings of this Harp some months ago (by means of a most refined Gentleman from Ireland), and after having diligently examined it, I find it to be the same as the one introduced into Italy a few years ago as the "double-strung" harp <note>The *arpa doppia*, which added a second row of strings to play chromatic notes</note>. Although some (against all reason) claim to have newly invented it, they seek to persuade the common people that no one but them knows how to play it or understands its tuning. They value this [tuning] so highly that they have ungratefully denied it to many; despite them, I wish to describe it in this place for the convenience of those who desire it. I remind them and all others of such a bad nature: if the rare men of the world in various noble professions had not, with such great labor, left so many volumes written about them (for the benefit of posterity), today's men would be most ignorant through their own fault, and the fame of those ancestors would be obscured. Whereas through the excellence of their writings, they live eternally in the memories of others, and everyone can become most knowledgeable and (if it can be said with truth) happy—if indeed happiness in this world consists in anything other than knowing and understanding the truth of things. Invited by their example, the noble and virtuous spirits of our times willingly toil to learn the sciences, for no other end than to then facilitate and illustrate them with their writings, without ever denying or hiding anything of importance they know from those who do not know it and desire to learn. These ungrateful people do not realize that the little they know, they learned from this person or that, and if others had been stingy or denied it to them, they would be most unhappy. But returning now to the tuning of the Harp, for the greater utility of those who seek to understand it, I wish to give some instructions. Therefore, I say that the extremes of the <insert>in</insert> 58 strings that are stretched upon it contain within their boundaries four Octaves and one additional Tone: neither larger nor smaller as some have dreamed, but of the measure I stated above for the keyboard instrument. The lowest string, then, for both <term>h duro</term> <note>B-natural (represented by the square 'b' or 'h')</note> and <term>b molle</term> <note>B-flat (represented by the rounded 'b')</note> is CC; and the highest string is Ddd. If you wish now to tune them for B-flat, the 16 low strings of the left side are distributed according to the nature of the common Diatonic; and the 14 opposite these, which come from the right side (leaving aside the unisons of D and A), must give, so to speak, the Chromatic genus, conforming in its nature to the said Diatonic. The 15 that follow these toward the high notes are tuned Diatonically according to the manner of the sixteen lower ones on the left side. The thirteen that follow above the first sixteen then perform the office of the lower ones on the right, as seen in the example. When you then wish to play in B-natural, the B-flats of each Diatonic are removed and placed in each Chromatic in the places of the B-naturals, and these are placed in the locations of the former in the Diatonic of the right and left sides. This manner of proceeding was thus ordered by its author for the convenience and ease that the fingers of both hands have in performing, particularly, diminutions and runs. There are found among said strings five times C, 5 d, 4 e, 4 f, 4 g, 4 a, 4 b, 4 h, 4 unisons of d.

# Ancient & Modern [Music]

<margin>The meaning of the word "Organ."</margin>
<margin>Brass and steel strings were unknown to the Greeks and Romans.</margin>
<margin>Where the wind instruments of our time are derived from.</margin>
As for King David, I do not know what he has to do with our <term>Organ</term><note>The word *organum* in Latin and *organon* in Greek originally meant any "tool" or "instrument," not just the keyboard pipe organ.</note> except for the name. Although the word "Organ" is read countless times in ancient writers concerning musical instruments and other things, this arises from the fact that it was generally understood to mean any instrument one might choose. Its meaning implies a "tool" or "instrument" that "ascends on high," which is the nature of every sound and voice. Eventually, this specific name remained for that instrument which has the power to most fully realize the effect of its meaning. I have said that among keyboard instruments, the Organ was found before the others because the making of strings from brass and steel for other instruments is a modern invention. No memory of such strings is found, as far as I know, among the ancient Greeks or Romans. And even if I have said that the people of Ireland use such strings in their harps, I do not mean that they used them until after they were invented by their author; previously, they used strings made of gut. I come now to treat those wind instruments to the sound of which they not only recited Tragedies, Comedies, and Satires (as I have said elsewhere), but to which the ancients also performed every kind of dance, of which there were many.

**STROZZI:** You have told me several times that the ancients sang their Tragedies and Comedies to the sound of the <term>Tibia</term><note>The *tibia* was the Roman version of the Greek *aulos*, a reed instrument often translated as "flute," though it functioned more like an oboe.</note> and the <term>Cithara</term><note>An ancient Greek stringed instrument related to the lyre.</note>, but you have not yet shown me the authority that moved you to say and believe this, nor told me for what reason they were led to do so. Therefore, before we discuss the wind instruments of our own or other times, I desire, if it pleases you, to better understand this truth.

<margin>The *Piva* (bagpipe), a very ancient instrument.</margin>
**BARDI:** You are quite right; now take note. That Tragedies and Comedies were truly sung by the Greeks (in the manner you have heard) is told to you—besides other trustworthy sources—by Aristotle in the section on Harmony, in <term>Problem 49</term><note>Referencing the *Problems* attributed to Aristotle, which contain significant detail on music theory.</note>. It is true that in the *Poetics*, when he comes to the definition of Tragedy, he seems to differ slightly from that first opinion. That such a custom was later embraced and followed by the Romans is fully attested (among other authoritative places) by the inscriptions of the comedies of Terence. As for the reasons for this, I believe they were these: when any kind of verse is sung by a single person, it seems more fitting and reasonable when accompanied by the sound of an instrument than when deprived of it. This same suitability is seen in the instrument as well; whenever a song air is played, it is enhanced when accompanied by the voice of someone singing along with it. And just as dancing seems inappropriate without sound, so too one does not have full satisfaction in hearing an air played without its singing, or hearing a song sung by one person without the sound of the instrument. This, in my opinion, was one of the reasons that induced the ancients to sing the verses of their Tragedies and Comedies to the instrument. Furthermore, when the <term>Actor</term><note>original: *Strione*, a term for a theatrical performer.</note> sang in unison (and not in consonance/harmony, as has been said and proven) with the instrument—be it the Tibia, Cithara, or another—he was more easily understood by everyone around him, and his voice became less fatigued. What was most important was that the Tibia-player or Cithara-player, as one skilled in the musical art, was able by means of the well-tuned instrument to keep the Actor in the proper voice and pitch regarding high and low notes. They also guided him in pronouncing the long and short syllables of the verses, sometimes with much and sometimes with little sound and voice, according to what was appropriate for the quality of the concept he sought to signify with the words. These nuances were not always understood by all Actors, nor would they have been entirely expressed with the proper details without the help of a practical Musician. And if you would like to know why the Actors used the Dorian and Phrygian harmonies, and the Chorus used the Lydian, and not others, reading the entire *Problem* of the Philosopher [Aristotle] whom we cited (once the many and significant errors in the text are removed) will make it known to you. 

Coming now to treat the origin of wind instruments as I promised: I say that among those of the Greeks, one finds first the <term>Aulos</term>; which is the same thing as the Latin Tibia and our <term>Piffero</term><note>A generic term for a pipe or shawm in the Renaissance.</note>. Only this difference can be found between those and ours: that while the Aulos and Tibia had their holes distributed according to the <term>Ditonic Diatonic</term><note>A tuning system based on pure fifths, often called Pythagorean.</note> species, those of the Piffero are ordered according to the <term>Syntonic</term> of Aristoxenus or others. Furthermore, for practical players of this instrument and other winds (excepting the Organ and the Trombone), it is not very difficult to make a semitone heard where there is normally a whole tone between finger holes, and vice versa. This practice, when well-exercised, brings great reputation to the professors of these instruments and convenience to those who use them in ensembles. The other difference that may arise between ours and theirs is in the number of holes; because it is likely that the Aulos and Tibia did not require as many notes as the Pifferos of our times do, given our use of playing in consonance [harmony] and therefore needing many notes. From this originated the <term>Piva</term> or <term>Cornamusa</term><note>The bagpipe.</note>, as they call it today—truly a very ancient instrument, as told to us by Dionysius Longinus with the testimony of Sophocles in these two verses, concerning a talkative and little-known orator of his time.

### Dialogue on Music

->Well swollen to play high bagpipes,<-
->But he lacks that sack filled with air.<-
<note>These lines appear to be a poetic fragment describing the mechanics of the bagpipe or perhaps a satirical jab at a musician.</note>

This instrument <note>original: *zampogne*, referring here to bagpipes</note> is greatly practiced by the people of Ireland. To its sound, those indomitable, wild, and bellicose people are accustomed to move their armies and encourage them to bravely lay hands upon their enemies. They also accompany their dead to the grave with it, making such mournful melodies that they invite, or rather force, the bystanders to weep. From the <term>Pipe</term><note>original: *Piffero*; a general term for a high-pitched woodwind or fife</note> then derived all other wind instruments, such as the straight flutes <note>recorders</note>, perhaps before the transverse flutes; for, compared to the former, the latter require much more artifice and difficulty to play. Furthermore, the sound of both is much more noble, delicate, and pleasing to our ears than that of the Pipe; although the Pipe is more stirred and shrill, and capable—by the volume and vehemence of its sound—of more effectively producing those emotions suited to its nature. It is not credible that the ancients had knowledge of these two types of flutes, as some commentators have believed, mistaking them for <term>Tibiae</term><note>The *Tibia* was a Roman reed instrument, often played in pairs</note>; no trace of them is found in any author of importance, nor in antiquity.

<margin>Zarlino in the *Institutes*, chapter 2 of the first part, and in chapter 4 of the fourth part.</margin>
**STROZZI:** It seems to me I have read that whenever Gaius Gracchus had to speak to the people, he kept a musician-servant behind him who, discreetly playing a flute or an ivory <term>Fife</term><note>original: *Zufolo*</note>, would bring him back to a pitch suitable for the expression of the concept he was handling.

<margin>Valerius Maximus, Book 8, chapter 10. Gellius in Book 1 of *Attic Nights*. By whom the Syrinx was discovered.</margin>
**BARDI:** Regarding this, writers mention the <term>Syrinx</term> and the <term>Fistula</term><note>Both terms refer to panpipes</note>, which amount to the same thing, and not the flute. This Syrinx is nothing other than those seven reeds (which in time increased to a greater number) of different lengths and thicknesses, joined together with wax and linen. They are usually depicted in the hand of the god Pan in memory of his beautiful and beloved Syrinx, who was turned into a reed by Jove. Its shape is similar to a bird's wing or a small organ; the invention of which is attributed to the Celts.

**STROZZI:** It has been very pleasing to hear these details; however, continue weaving the rest of your prepared tapestry.

<margin>Julius Pollux in chapter 2. Straight flutes found by the Gauls. Transverse flutes found by the Swiss.</margin>
<margin>The Trombone came to us.</margin>
<margin>In Canto 30 of the *Inferno*. Where the Lute was seen by us. Zarlino wants, in chapter 35 of the 4th part of his *Institutes*, for keyboard instruments to be more perfect in their tuning than the Lute: how far this is from the truth has been demonstrated in its proper place.</margin>
**BARDI:** Straight flutes were introduced into Italy by the Gauls, and transverse flutes by the Swiss. After the use of these—as they were more ingenious and required more effort to play—it is likely (though our rule regarding the invention of musical instruments often suffers exceptions) that the <term>Cornetti</term><note>Wooden pipes with trumpet-like mouthpieces</note> and <term>Trombones</term><note>Referring to the early trombone or sackbut</note> were found; but not before people began to sing (according to modern custom) several melodies together in consonance. Their inventors were moved by the necessity mentioned above; and also because men would grow beards before they knew how to sing well. In those early times, due to the coarseness of the age and the novelty of the thing—or shall we say the simplicity of those who have administered it until now—it was necessary to spend much time on it, so that boys' voices were lost before they could be enjoyed. The authors of the Trombone were the Saxons, although they were excellently crafted in Nuremberg, a famous city of Franconia. The Cornetto was brought to us from Styria, and today the best ones to be found are made in Venice. The Trombone has this particular excellence: it is capable (having no obligation to holes or keys in fixed places, but relying on the discretion and judgment of the skilled trombonist) of increasing or decreasing the space of its pipe to play every species of the three genera of harmony <note>Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic</note> with the greatest exactness one could desire. Good professors of the instrument can, without any effort or difficulty, sharpen or flatten the sound by any interval, however small or unusual. The <term>Viola da gamba</term> and <term>da braccio</term>, the Cittern, and the Lute—being more ingenious than the stringed instruments of the ancients because of the frets and the ability to draw four, six, or more different voices from a single instrument—were likely found one after another. That the Lute was in use before any of these others, even though it is more difficult, can be easily believed based on the authority of Dante. Concerning a certain Master Adam, a falsifier of coins, he mentions it saying:

> I saw one shaped in the fashion of a Lute.

He used this comparison to denote the thinness of the neck and the swelling of the body of a man with <term>Dropsy</term><note>original: *Hidropico*; a medical condition causing swelling, here compared to the rounded belly of the lute</note>. Nevertheless, it may well be that in that time it did not have as many strings, nor were those few arranged in the order they are today. For it would seem a great thing to me if an instrument—having been considered and practiced with the quantity and disposition of strings common today for only fifty years—had not just begun to be understood, but had already reached the excellence in which it is found. This most noble instrument was brought to us by the Pannonians <note>People from the region of modern Hungary</note> with the name *Laut*. This name was given by its author with no small judgment, though his glory is obscured to his own detriment. He wished to denote by it that the instrument is capable of the extreme musical sounds, and with the help of frets, those in the middle as well. This consideration should not be left behind: that

<margin>Guido d'Arezzo gives new ways to musical notes.</margin>
Guido d'Arezzo—who gave new names to the musical notes, drawing them from the first seven syllables of the first three verses of the Hymn of St. John the Baptist, which make the number six <note>Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La</note>—lived a few decades before Dante. From two of those syllables and names of the notes, as you have heard, the name of the Lute <note>original: *Liuto*, formed from *La* and *Ut*</note> was composed by its author.

# Ancient & Modern.

<margin>Why Guido of Arezzo named only six notes.</margin>
**STROZZI:** For what reason do we believe that *Guido of Arezzo* <note>Guido d'Arezzo (c. 991–1033) was a medieval music theorist whose system of naming notes—Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La—is the ancestor of modern Solfège.</note> did not at least give a new name to each of the seven lower strings found in the fourth species of the *Diapason* <term>Octave</term>, but only to the first six?

**BARDI:** If I may venture a guess, I believe this was the reason. Having, as you know, named a new string below the lowest *Proslambanomene* <note>original: *Proslambanomene*; the lowest note of the Greek "Greater Perfect System."</note> of the Greeks—which, along with the highest note of the *Hypaton Tetrachord*, contained a Major *Hexachord* <term>a six-note scale</term> (at least according to the numbers he uses in his *Introductory* when marking the strings)—he came to name his strings with the names you have heard. Thus, the lowest of them he said was the first, called *Gamma ut* <note>original: *Γ ut*; the Greek letter Gamma was used to represent the lowest note, giving us the word "gamut."</note>. Seeing then that on the second string of the same *Tetrachord* <term>a four-note scale segment</term>, as well as on every other second string of all the others in the Disjunct System, there was likewise the beginning of another *Hexachord* which also ended at the extreme of the one joined to it toward the high notes; and seeing that this quantity of names was sufficient to flesh out his design, he went no further. To this consideration, one might add that *Antiphons* <note>Short liturgical chants</note> were the first things sung in that century in the sacred temples using these notes, which (according to what I have seen in some very ancient books, and particularly in those still preserved today in our Abbey of Montepiano) required very few strings and voices at that time. Therefore, *Guido* had no need for a greater quantity of names. And returning to the Etymology <note>original: *Timologia*, an archaic form of *etimologia*</note> of the Lute, I say there have been others of the opinion that it was called *lauto*; that is, sumptuous, magnificent, noble, and splendid <note>original: *lauto* shares a root with "lavish" or "sumptuous" in Italian</note>; but let that be enough said on the matter.

<margin>Where the Cittern was brought to us from.</margin>
The Cittern <note>original: *Cetera*; a wire-strung instrument similar to a lute but with a flat back</note> was used first among the English rather than other nations, in which island they were once crafted to excellence; although today the most reputed ones among them are those crafted in Brescia. Despite this, it is used and appreciated by nobles, and was so named by its creators perhaps to resurrect the ancient *Cithara* <note>The lyre of classical antiquity</note>; but the difference between ours and that one can be clearly understood from what has been said above.

<margin>Who introduced the Viola da Gamba.</margin>
As for the Viola da Gamba <note>the leg-viol</note> and the Viola da Braccio <note>the arm-viol, ancestor of the violin</note>, I hold for certain that the Italians were their authors, and perhaps those of the Kingdom of Naples. The reason that moves me to believe this is as follows: in Spain they do not make them, and they are little used there; in France and England the same occurs, and likewise among the Flemish and in Germany—even though some have doubted they were the authors. On the contrary, among these peoples it is practiced less than in any of the named provinces, setting aside the courts of those Princes where they are practiced very well; but they are nonetheless brought from Italy, as are most of the players. Nor is it a marvel that in Germany they are little used by the general public, since the greater part of the country is, as you know, very cold. Because of this, the inhabitants stay most of the time in their "stoves" <note>original: *stufe*; heated rooms or saunas</note>, letting themselves be seen little in the open air for eight months of the year, and consequently they rarely gather together for this business. They usually attend to those things that a man can practice alone without the help of another, whereas in Italy, and particularly in the Kingdom of Naples, quite the opposite happens due to the kindness of the air. Furthermore, music for such instruments has been crafted and practiced there to excellence for many, many years. Men perhaps went investigating these things to have a stringed instrument that had the faculty of sustaining voices according to the value of the notes—and for as long as the discreet player pleased—without having to strike them again; not unlike what the Organ does among keyboard instruments and others do among the wind instruments. These instruments are played with the same bow (though not as precisely) as the Viola da Braccio, which was called the *Lira* <note>original: *lita*, likely a variant of *Lira* or *Lira da braccio*</note> not many years ago in imitation of the ancient name. This gives a manifest indication that the Viola was in use before the *Violone* <term>the double bass or large bass viol</term>; indeed, that the latter was the last to be invented

<margin>The Lyre first called the Viola.</margin>
(setting aside that instrument I told you above was given by the Duke of Saxony to the Duke of Bavaria). We can persuade ourselves of this by the number of players who concur for the perfection of a concert; however, it must not have been introduced before music was composed for at least four parts, and before a reasonable abundance of singers was found—unless we wish to say they were first practiced in dances no differently than the Pipes <note>original: *Pifferi*</note>; though I have no encounter with authority that would persuade me of this. Having finished what I wish to discuss for now regarding modern artificial instruments, their invention, origin, and antiquity—according to my opinion, which I submit to whoever understands better than I—I come to treat the fourth and last sort of Lute players, keyboardists, and musicians of our times as they are reputed by the common folk. These are the ones who truly know how to neither write nor play or sing anything of importance; but they will have only on the surface—like colored glass compared to jewels— a little appearance of I-know-not-what to tell me. They will play a *Galliard*, a *Saltarello*, and a *Passomezzo* <note>Standard Renaissance dance forms</note>, making a great racket <note>original: *fracasso*</note> on the outer strings of the instrument they have in hand, and particularly on the low ones. The common folk, entirely intent on that noise, become stupid and marvelling; and instead of sending for Hipponax the Pipe-player <note>original: *Hipponaco Tibicine*; a reference to a legendary musician mentioned by ancient authors</note> to teach them (as Aelian tells us), they admire and celebrate them as miracles.

<margin>Another sort of players and singers, reputed by the common folk.</margin>
<margin>In book 8, chapter 14 of the *Varia Historia*.</margin>
Others of this same order are unworthily numbered by the common folk among musicians because they sing a thousand filthy and dishonest follies on these instruments. By such means they move people to laughter, but never to tears; for to move the latter requires a different industry and knowledge than that affectation...

# Dialogue on Music

<margin>The Vice of Ignorance.</margin>

They are then celebrated by him as new Orpheuses and Amphions <note>Orpheus and Amphion are legendary figures of Greek mythology whose music could move stones and charm animals.</note>. Once these musicians realize this, and willingly consent to being so regarded by the unskilled masses, they become so insolent that they wish—without knowing the least reason why—to correct and give laws to the world. They consider themselves not merely equal, but superior to the first masters in industry and knowledge. Nothing happens in this or any other genre that they do not wish to comment upon with the greatest gravity and reputation in the world, telling you what they think of it; meanwhile, they despise and belittle all those things that
<margin>A comparison.</margin>
are outside their grasp. They can rightly be compared to that Miller’s Mouse recounted in the moral fables of Aesop <note>Aesop was a Greek storyteller credited with a collection of fables that use animals to teach moral lessons.</note>: who, having inadvertently floured his tail once, and appearing to himself thereby to have become the master of the mill, entered into such pride that he was bold enough not only to want to manage everything in his own way, but to tell the master to provide for himself elsewhere, as he no longer wanted him in the house.
<margin>Example.</margin>
One could also compare such musicians to that Shoemaker of Argos; who, having seen a statue from the hand of Praxiteles <note>Praxiteles (c. 395–330 BC) was one of the most famous Greek sculptors of the 4th century BC.</note>—the most beautiful and famous he ever made—greatly blamed it along with its creator.
<margin>Praxiteles of Cos, a most noble sculptor.</margin>
The statue represented a young Shepherd wrestling with his small Ram; yet he blamed it for nothing else but having the sandal straps backward. This the excellent and judicious Sculptor had done artfully, perhaps to denote the simplicity of the young shepherd. Even today, there is no lack of these Satraps <note>Originally high-ranking provincial governors in the Persian Empire; used here to mean arrogant or overbearing officials.</note> who, pregnant with envy upon seeing and examining the work of a virtuous man, note and preach only that thing which might be there—however small—that deserves correction, even if the rest were most ingenious, excellent, and worthy of highest praise. They appreciate only that and nothing else which they understand and know, and which therefore pleases them; conversely, they despise everything they do not know and do not understand, solely because they see it in another and see it greatly esteemed by the intelligent. They show outwardly that it displeases them, even though, withdrawn into themselves, they admire it and would consider themselves happy if they knew a thousandth part of what the author of that work knows. Furthermore, among these are some "Sir-Syllables," so to speak, who make a profession of being singers and claim to demonstrate such practice with excellence, without having any knowledge not only of numbers, proportions, or the **Monochord** <term>a single-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals mathematically</term>; but even of the measure of any musical interval, nor of the quantity of sound enclosed between this and that string. Beyond this, they are ignorant of which genre and species <note>Refers to the ancient Greek musical systems (Diatonic, Chromatic, Enharmonic).</note> is being sung today; without which understanding, God knows how the matter proceeds. And they will have at hand, instead of such knowledge, as an argument for their wisdom, more maxims of Burchiello and Bernia <note>Domenico di Giovanni (Burchiello) and Francesco Bernia were Italian poets famous for their satirical, humorous, and sometimes nonsensical verse.</note> than any other pedagogue of our mother tongue. See, I pray you, what the buffooneries of these two ridiculous poets have to do with knowing how to demonstrate the distances and proportions of musical intervals.
<margin>A comparison.</margin>
They remind me of certain of our matrons, who go about the house in the coldest season of the year wearing a *zimarra* or a *turcha* <note>Types of loose-fitting overgarments or gowns worn in the Renaissance.</note> of gauze or taffeta; which has only around the hem a display of fur no wider than a finger, while they are lightly armed underneath. They persuade themselves that the appearance of it and their presence is enough to resist not only the force and power of Boreas <note>The North Wind.</note>, but to frighten and mock him, in the same way that the sight of some simpletons is deceived from afar. They peddle this vain thought inside their houses, where the force of the North Wind does not entirely reach, nor the eyes of Lynceus <note>In mythology, Lynceus was an Argonaut with superhumanly keen eyesight.</note> penetrate. But going out in that habit through the public streets in the open, they are driven back into their houses by the wind with the greatest fury in the world; nor do they leave there until they have the strength and force to compete and resist its power, or until the courteous Apollo—moved to compassion for them—opposes (to avenge them) the Sagittarius.
<margin>Which musicians should be more esteemed than others and why.</margin>
Which, then, of all these sorts of men deserve most to be esteemed? It seems to me one can surely say that those who play, compose, and likewise write with excellence, deserve not only highest praise, but to be greatly valued and prized by any man of sound intellect. And no less than these do those deserve who do more than they, even if they were less favored by nature in the ready fieriness of the hand or in the invention of **Counterpoint** <term>the art of combining different melodic lines</term>; provided, however, that their knowledge not only supplies such a lack, but exceeds the former. For those who teach us virtues are much more to be esteemed—and the more so the rarer and more excellent they are—than those who simply (with their buffoonery) delight us. First, because it is a greater and higher thing to know what another does than to do that same thing he does; and second, because any simple pleasure of the sense (by its inconstancy) ultimately satiates us, but from the thirst for knowledge, one is never drawn away. And I say those deserve even more when their knowledge is joined to excellent morals, which should principally be desired in the perfect Musician and in every other virtuous person; so that by his example and his science, he makes those who practice and listen to him both learned and well-mannered. To which I add and say, that it is impossible to find a man who is truly a Musician and who is vicious; and
<margin>In Plutarch's booklet on music:</margin>
being thus, it will be difficult, rather impossible, for him to be virtuous and to make others virtuous. And to tell you further, he who in childhood used every due means and convenient care to learn the science of true music with all his work and labor,

Everything that is in accordance with decorum and honesty, he will praise and embrace; and the contrary, he will revile and flee. Such a man will be as far as possible from any ugly or dishonest action.
